<note>original: "सूर्यसिद्धान्त" (Sūryasiddhānta). This is one of the most important ancient Indian treatises on astronomy, traditionally attributed to a revelation from the Sun God.</note>

<meta>This is the opening page of the preface, establishing the author's motivation for translating and reviving ancient Indian astronomical texts.</meta>

# Introduction

---

Since ancient times, inhabitants of all nations have known that the residents of India have been highly proficient in scientific subjects. The scholars of Europe <note>original: "Vilayat" - often referring to Britain or the West in this period</note> honor India by describing it as the very birthplace of mathematics. When the philosophers of England prepare to examine Indian texts and behold the immense research within mathematical astronomy <term>Jyotish-shastra: the traditional Indian science of astronomy and astrology</term>, they begin to dive into an ocean of wonder, considering the context of that time and place. Among the eighteen most ancient and universally respected Siddhantas <note>authoritative treatises</note> of that mathematical science, very few Indians are acquainted with the text named "Shree Surya Siddhanta." Due to continuous neglect, the primary texts of this mathematical science are being buried under the all-consuming power of time. Indians have shown great indifference toward preserving the glory of their ancestors. I cannot hope that they will abandon this indifference at the request of a humble person like myself. Nevertheless, considering it my duty, I have labored intensely to publish this translated work for the current circle of astronomers and the general public, and I find great joy in doing so.

Nowadays, among those who are considered learned and who possess the influence to act, many do not even look at the scriptures. There are many who do not know the scriptures themselves, yet they continue to flaunt their supposed scholarship. This aforementioned aversion to texts and this arrogance are ruining everything, and they continue to exert their influence over astrologers. So much so, that the fruits of this short-sightedness have begun to appear. Today, astronomers remain preoccupied with the worries of earning a living <note>literally "stomach-anxiety"</note> and do not properly study or teach that science. For this reason, desiring to do less work, they use various simplified handbooks <term>Karana Granthas: practical astronomical manuals used for quick calculations</term> without even examining them properly. They invoke the name of the "Shree Surya Siddhanta"—the root of those manuals—and with the help of tables from other books, they obtain results from those manuals while claiming the authority of this extraordinary original text. However, while making a list of how many of them have actually observed the Shree Surya Siddhanta, one is struck with grief.

Apart from the sect following the Surya Siddhanta, a new kind of "Siddhanta-worshipper" has emerged in India. The creators of this school of thought wish to be called scholars and astronomers even before entering the study of astronomy, resembling the "Logic of the Half-Cooked Hen" <note>original: "Ardha-Kukkuti-Nyaya" - a logical fallacy where one tries to take only the useful part of a thing (like the egg-laying back of a hen) while discarding the "useless" part (the mouth that needs feeding), resulting in an impossible or contradictory situation</note>. Some are logicians <term>Naiyayika: a follower of the Nyaya school of logic</term>, some are highly intelligent in the work of masonry, some are merely proud of basic mathematics, some are skilled in promoting new opinions just to gain fame, some are students of some astrologer, or some are proficient in literature; that is all! Such people are the primary activists in this. Some [follow] the "Siddhanta Shiromani" composed by Bhaskaracharya <note>Bhaskara II, a famous 12th-century Indian mathematician</note>...

<summary>The author laments the decline of traditional Indian astronomical knowledge and the neglect of the Surya Siddhanta, criticizing contemporary scholars who rely on simplified manuals or lack deep expertise. He presents this translation as a duty to preserve ancestral scientific glory against modern indifference.</summary>

<keywords>Surya Siddhanta, Indian Astronomy, Jyotish-shastra, Mathematics, Bhaskaracharya, Siddhanta Shiromani, Karana Granthas, Scientific Heritage</keywords>

...is a follower of the chapter on mathematics <note>referring to the *Ganitadhyaya*, the section of astronomical calculations</note>. Some, having obtained a translation of one or two English "formulas" <note>original: "फॉर्म-डल" (formula)</note> received from their teacher, desire to attain the rank of an astrologer while boasting of their service to that teacher; others, without even knowing the principle of the precession of the equinoxes <term>Ayanamsha: the angular distance between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs</term>, simply imitate some Western astronomer who acts according to his own will. May all the aforementioned gentlemen read this original text, find honor at the feet of their respective teachers and the great sage who authored the *Surya Siddhanta*—the supreme teacher of Bhaskara and others—and thereby extinguish their internal vanity.

The humble translator dedicates his worthless attempt to the benefactor of the Sanskrit knowing population of India i. e. Khemaraj Shrikrishnadas Proprietor of the S. V. S. Press—Bombay.
->P. B. PRASADA.<-

## Dedication

### To the pillar of India's pride, the jewel of the Vaishya lineage, the most generous savior of the language of the gods <note>Sanskrit</note>, the honorable Seth Khemaraj Shrikrishnadas Gupta.

Honorable Sir!

By reviving the Sanskrit language, you have done a supreme favor for the people of India. There is no one else like you who protects the faith, practices such charity, and expands the reach of the ancient scriptures created by the Aryan sages.

Among the scriptural texts composed by the ancient sages and monks, the astronomical treatise named *Surya Siddhanta* is honored in all countries. There is no doubt that the science of astronomy <term>Jyotish: encompasses both astronomy and astrology in this context</term> is a preeminent science. Knowing that the protection and expansion of this science would bring welfare to the world, and encouraged by your enthusiasm, I have translated the *Surya Siddhanta* into the refined language <note>Standard Hindi</note> with great effort and much labor. You well know how difficult the science of mathematics is for the general public. By receiving this translation, there will be a special benefit to the learned astronomers. The specialty is that, by relying on the examples I have provided, it will not be very difficult to enter into the depths of this complex science.

By placing this translated work into the lotus-hands of you—the protector of all scriptures—I hope that by publishing it, you will circulate it throughout all of India. Without the help of wealthy people, no great work is accomplished in India. With this thought, and with the desire for this book to be publicized, I am joining it with your most illustrious name.

->Your grateful servant—<-
->**Baldevprasad Mishra;**<-
->Danidapura Neighborhood, Moradabad (North-Western Provinces)<-

# Introduction to the Surya Siddhanta

The name of the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>The "Sun Precept," the most important historical treatise on Indian astronomy</note> is extremely famous in the field of mathematical astronomy. Most of the almanacs <note>Panchangs</note> in India are prepared from this text, and all our daily rituals and dealings are conducted according to it. For this reason, it is not at all unlikely that every scholar would desire to examine such a work.

Many people are known to say that the *Surya Siddhanta* is so difficult that attempting to teach or study it is like stepping beyond one's rightful station. However, it is not a difficult matter to enter into this study gradually, provided one has a basic grasp of mathematics. Without a doubt, a great deal of numerical calculation <note>original: "ank-paat"</note> must be performed, but even that is not an insurmountable climb.

For new students, the knowledge of terminology <note>technical nomenclature</note> is what is truly difficult. Studying the text alongside practical examples is very beneficial. Once one or two subjects are mastered, understanding the other topics is no longer difficult. Afterward, one will be able to provide directions for the practical manuals <term>Karana-granthas: concise astronomical handbooks used for quick calculations</term> themselves, and will achieve full mastery over the original source. My only request now is this: if it seems difficult at first, do not abandon your studies; rather, continue looking through it. Wherever it feels difficult, cast your eyes over it two or four times, and you will certainly come to understand it with ease. It is convenient if the practical manuals are studied first.

During the time of calculation, there is generally no need for precise digits below the level of a *Vikala* <note>an arc-second</note>, and in many subjects, omitting them results in no significant loss or gain.

By the grace of the Government, the passion of our countrymen, and the financial assistance of wealthy and virtuous men, thousands of students become proficient in mathematics <note>original: "ank-shastra"</note> every year. It is hoped that many of these students will pay attention to the mathematics and astronomy of their own country. There are 14 chapters in this book. Among them—

**Chapter 1 contains:** The commencement of the text, divisions of time, the measure of the *Yugas* <note>cosmic ages</note>, the number of days, the *Ahargana* <term>the number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch</term>, the mean positions of the planets based on their revolutions, the *Mandoccha* <note>apogee/aphelion</note> and *Shighra* <note>perigee/perihelion</note>, the longitude of places, and the maximum latitude.

**Chapter 2 contains:** The cause of planetary motion, types of motion, the determination of Sines <note>original: "jya"</note>, declination, and the calculation of the "center"; the determination of results by calculating the circumference from the base and perpendicular; the true positions of planets, the correction for the equation of time <note>bhujantar</note>, true motion, true latitude, the measure of day and night, the ascensional difference, the lunar day <note>tithi</note>, the lunar mansion <note>nakshatra</note>, the *Yoga*, and the *Karana*.

**Chapter 3 contains:** The determination of the East-West line, the precession of the equinoxes <note>ayanansha</note>, the equinoctial shadow, the sine of latitude, the calculation of the zenith distance, the angle of the gnomon, the rising times of signs at the equator, the ascendant <note>lagna</note>, and the tenth house.

**Chapter 4 contains:** The true sizes of the Moon, the shadow, and the Sun; the magnitude of an eclipse, the half-duration of the eclipse, the "aspect" of the eclipse, and the deflection <note>valana</note>.

<summary>This page introduces the Surya Siddhanta as the foundational text for Indian almanacs and encourages students to persevere through its mathematical complexities. It begins a chapter-by-chapter summary of the astronomical topics covered, ranging from cosmic time cycles to eclipse calculations.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the Surya Siddhanta, concluding the chapter-by-chapter summary and providing the author's closing remarks and credits.</meta>

<page-num>6</page-num>
<header>Introduction to the Surya Siddhanta.</header>

In Chapter 5—Lunar parallax and solar eclipses <note>specifically 'avanati' or the depression of the sun</note>.
In Chapter 6—On the projection of eclipses <term>Parilekhadhikara: the graphical representation or drawing of an eclipse</term>.
In Chapter 7—On planetary conjunctions, including visibility corrections <note>Aksha-drikkarma and Ayana-drikkarma</note>, the size of planetary disks, and the observation of planetary wars <note>astronomical 'battles' when planets appear very close together</note>.
In Chapter 8—On the conjunction of stars and planets, and the positions of the lunar mansions <note>Nakshatras</note>.
In Chapter 9—On the rising and setting of celestial bodies, the determination of time, and degrees of time.
In Chapter 10—On the elevation of the Moon's horns <note>the phase and appearance of the crescent moon</note> and moonrise.
In Chapter 11—On the nodes <note>Pata</note>, particularly the malignant aspects <note>Vyatipata</note>, time determination, and transitional points <note>Gandaka and Bhasandhi</note>.

<header>( 6 ) Introduction to the Surya Siddhanta.</header>

In Chapter 12—Spiritual science, the arrangement of the celestial spheres, and the geography of the sacred mountains and cities: Meru, Bhadrashva, Yamakoti, Lanka, and Ketumala; also the distance of the stars from the Earth.
In Chapter 13—On the construction of the armillary sphere <note>Gola</note> and astronomical instruments.
In Chapter 14—On the determination of various systems of time.

Several trigonometric terms are used continuously, such as Radius <note>Trijya</note>, Arc <note>Dhanu</note>, Sine <note>Jya</note>, Cosine <note>Koti</note>, and Hypotenuse <note>Karna</note>; therefore, these should be understood beforehand. Parallax and the equinoctial shadow are determined by the latitude of one's own country. Latitude <note>Vikshepa</note>, Declination <note>Kranti</note>, and true positions <note>Sphuta</note> are based on the actual placement of the planets. The Mean position <note>Madhya</note>, Apogee <note>Mandochcha</note>, Perigee <note>Shighra</note>, and Circumference <note>Paridhi</note> are the sections used to calculate true positions.

The point of the zodiac which lies beyond the meridian is the tenth house and the rising sign <note>Lagna</note>. In the chapter on the three problems <note>Triprashnadhyaya</note>, it is shown how to determine direction and time, and later in the chapter on instruments, the method for making instruments and instructions for building an observatory <note>Manmandir</note> are given. Before concluding this introduction, many thanks are repeatedly given to the ornament of the assembly of virtuous men and the refuter of heretical views, the honorable Pandit Jwalaprasad Mishra and the honorable Vimalaprasad Siddhantasaraswati-ji, because great assistance was received from these gentlemen in the translation of this text. For the benefit of students, suitable and proper examples have also been provided in this book. Enough has been said.

Year 1952 of the Vikrami Era <note>approx. 1895 CE</note>.
Chaitra, Dark Fortnight, 2nd day, Sunday.

->Son of Sukhananda Mishra—<-
->**Baldev Prasad Mishra**,<-
->Deendarpura Neighborhood, Moradabad.<-
->North-Western Provinces.<-

# The Illustrious Surya Siddhanta.

## Accompanied by the Gudharthaprakashaka Commentary and the Hindi Exposition.

## Chapter One.

### Just as the crest is to the peacock, and the jewel to the serpent,
### So does Mathematics <note>original: "Ganita"; refers here to the combined science of astronomy and calculation</note> stand at the head of all the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas.

I bow to the curved-trunked Ganesha, born of Shiva, the giver of wisdom, by remembering whom a person attains the obstacle-free completion of their desired tasks. || 1 ||
Victory to my parents, Govinda and Ballala, who are like the goddess Parvati and Lord Shiva; from them were born five sons who are the causes of the world of light <note>meaning they are all experts in Jyotisha or astronomy/astrology</note>. || 2 ||
I bow to my brother, the wise Krishna, the teacher of the world, whose speech was a source of trust for the Universal Sovereign Jahangir <note>The Mughal Emperor, r. 1605–1627</note>. || 3 ||
Having examined various texts, I, Ranganatha, compose this commentary on the Surya Siddhanta to illuminate its hidden meanings. || 4 || <margin>(</margin> <margin>|</margin> <margin>||</margin> <margin>||</margin> <margin>||</margin>

Now, desiring to relate the dialogue between the man who was an incarnation of the Sun and the demon Maya—which contains the true essence of reality as known to him—to the sages who were curious about the movements of the planets and who had posed questions, the author first records the auspicious salutation to Brahma. This is done to ensure the obstacle-free completion of the work he has begun and to provide an example for his students:

> Salutations to Brahma, whose form is inconceivable and unmanifest, who is beyond the three qualities <note>the Gunas: Sattva (purity), Rajas (passion), and Tamas (inertia)</note>, yet is the soul of all qualities;
> The embodiment who is the support of the entire universe. || 1 ||

"To Brahma" means to the Supreme Lord who pervades the universe because of his greatness and lack of limitation; he is the one established by sacred scriptures in passages such as "From that very Self, space was born." "Salutations" means "I am bowed," in the sense of a specific mental state characterized by the movement of body and speech, acknowledging that "I am inferior compared to the supreme excellence of the Truth."

If one objects that pervasiveness alone would prove that this refers only to "Space," the author says: "The embodiment who is the support of the entire universe." This means he whose forms or natures are equal to Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva, acting as the foundation and refuge for the entire world—consisting of the moving and the unmoving—which undergoes creation, preservation, and destruction. The implication is that Space cannot be the subject here because it lacks that triune nature.

If one then asks if it is proper to meditate on the form of such a being, the author says: "Whose form is inconceivable and unmanifest." He is both inconceivable and of an unmanifest form. "Inconceivable" means he is not an object of ordinary meditation. The reason for this is his "unmanifest form." His nature or form is not manifest or perceptible; therefore, the author implies that a simple salutation is most appropriate since meditation on his true form is impossible.

If one asks how he can be of an unmanifest form, the author says: "Beyond the qualities." This means one from whom the qualities of Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas have departed; he transcends the qualities. And that...

# Surya Siddhanta: Chapter One

...and because He possesses the three qualities <note>The *Gunas*: Sattva (purity), Rajas (passion), and Tamas (inertia)</note> in a manifest form, while in His absence of these, He is of an unmanifest form. Now, one might argue that this implies He is entirely formless rather than "unmanifest." To this, the author says: *To the Soul of Qualities.* This means He whose nature consists of eternal knowledge and bliss—the qualities of the Self. This is supported by the scripture: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite." Thus, the idea that He lacks form is unproven. He is directly without qualities <note>Nirguna</note>, yet indirectly the soul of all qualities. How else could the creation of the universe be possible? As the Lord Himself said: "Governing My own nature, I send forth again and again this entire multitude of beings, who are powerless under the control of nature." Others interpret it this way. || 1 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Salutations to Brahman, who is inconceivable <note>beyond the reach of thought</note>, of unmanifest form, without qualities, the soul of all qualities, and the embodiment of the support of the entire universe. || 1 ||

Now, to prevent the suspicion that his words are merely his own invention, the author intends to describe the beginning of the dialogue. He explains in two verses how Mayasura first performed penance:

-> **When the Krita Age was nearly finished, a great demon named Maya,** <-
-> **desiring to know that supreme, holy, and hidden mystery,** <-
-> **the ultimate knowledge—the foremost limb of the Vedas,** <-
-> **the entire cause of the motion of the heavenly bodies—** <-
-> **performed most difficult penance to worship the Sun.** <-
-> **|| 2-3 ||** <-

"Maya" is the name of a certain great Daitya <note>a race of giants or demons in Vedic mythology</note>. He performed "penance" (*Tapas*), which consists of rules involving physical hardship, such as chanting, offerings, and meditation, to please a chosen deity. The penance of the Daityas is well-known at every step in the Puranas <note>ancient Hindu texts</note>. However, since their penance is usually famous for being directed toward a specific deity, one might ask: toward which god did he direct his penance? To this, the author says: *Worshipping the Sun.* He was serving Vivasvat <note>the Sun God</note>, who is Narayana <note>Vishnu</note> residing in the solar orb. 

But knowing this deity to be the enemy of the Daityas, how could he worship his own enemy to achieve his goals? Surely one's welfare is not achieved through an enemy, otherwise the very definition of enmity is contradicted. To address this, the author describes the penance as: *Most difficult to perform.* This means it could only be accomplished through extreme suffering and intense hardship. It is established hundreds of times in the Puranas that the Lord, out of affection for His devotees, is well-pleased by such penance and fulfills the desires even of the Daityas. This is the sense of "worshipping" here. 

One might ask: since this specific penance is not mentioned anywhere in the Puranas' accounts of Daitya penances, how can it be known as authoritative? To this, he says: *When the Krita Age was nearly finished.* In the age called Krita <note>the first and golden age of the world</note>, the word "but" implies it includes the transitional periods <note>Sandhya</note>. Thus, it refers to the end of the Krita Age proper. With a small amount of time remaining in that transition, Mayasura performed his penance. The idea is that this was performed by Mayasura so recently <note>in cosmic terms</note> that it is proven by the direct perception of all people and does not require the authority of other scriptures. Now, why did Mayasura perform penance? Not even a fool acts without a purpose. Therefore, the author describes Mayasura as: *Desirous of knowledge.* That by which something is known...

# Chapter 1 ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.

The seeker of knowledge desires to understand the scripture. The implication is that he performed penance for the purpose of obtaining scriptural knowledge. To clarify what that scripture is, the author provides an adjective for "knowledge": **of the luminaries**. This refers to the cause of the motion of the planets and stars situated in the region of the *Pravaha* wind <note>In ancient Indian cosmology, the *Pravaha* is the celestial wind that keeps the planets in constant motion</note>. Since roots meaning "to move" also mean "to know," the result is that he was desirous of knowing the Science of Astronomy (*Jyotisha Shastra*), which explains the knowledge of the positions, movements, and measurements of the heavenly bodies.

Now, one might argue that such great effort for the sake of astronomical knowledge is misplaced, as it is difficult to grasp even for the all-knowing. To this, he says: **entire**. This means the complete science of astronomy. Furthermore, thinking with a Daitya's <note>demon's</note> intellect that "because the Sages are human, my knowledge from them might not be complete or accurate," he served the Great Teacher—the Lord who knows the reality of the entire, difficult-to-grasp science of astronomy, who is non-deceiving and omniscient.

One might ask if it was proper for an Asura <note>demon</note> to engage with the science of astronomy, given a potential lack of spiritual fruit. To this, he says: **a limb of the Veda** <term>Vedanga: one of the six auxiliary disciplines used to support Vedic rituals</term>. The fruit that belongs to the whole belongs also to the limb; therefore, because the fruit of liberation exists here, his engagement is proper. For this very reason, it generates merit, as it is included among the fourteen sciences such as the Puranas.

Why is this a limb of the Veda? He says: **supreme**. It is said: "This Time is Lord Vishnu, infinite, the Supreme Lord. He who knows Time is truly honored; who else is considered more worthy of honor than him?" Because it explains Time, it is excellent and thus a limb of the Veda. The implication is that this distinguishes it from the Puranas and other texts.

But since there are six limbs of the Veda, such as Grammar, why engage specifically in this one? He says: **foremost**. It is the best among the six limbs of the Veda. Why? Because it is **excellent**, meaning it is the "eye," the primary limb. Just as a person without eyes is incapable of doing anything, this science of astronomy is the best among the limbs of the Veda.

Even so, one might say such effort is not justified. To this, he says: **a mystery**. As the Scripture <note>the Shruti</note> says: "Knowledge came to the Brahmana and said: 'Protect me, I am your treasure. Do not speak me to the envious, the crooked, or the undisciplined; thus may I remain powerful.'" This means it is to be kept secret. Since it was certain that this science should not be given away lightly, he undertook such great effort to obtain it. || 2 || 3 ||

---

**Hindi Commentary:** As the *Satya Yuga* <note>the first and golden age of the world</note> was coming to a close, the great Asura named Maya, being desirous of obtaining the supreme knowledge which is the cause of the motion of all the luminaries (planets and stars), the best among the limbs of the Veda and a supreme holy mystery, performed extremely rigorous penance to worship the Sun. || 2 || 3 ||

### Savita <note>the Sun</note> himself bestowed upon Maya the movement of the planets. || 4 ||

**Himself:** by his own accord. **Pleased:** of a happy nature. Or, this beautiful, perceptible Sun, though already satisfied, was **gratified**—rendered extremely content—by that very difficult-to-perform penance and worship. To that Asura named Maya, who was **seeking a boon**—that is, requesting and desiring to know his chosen boon, the Science of Astronomy—to him...

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter One]

To the seeker of the <term>Science of Light</term> <note>Sanskrit: Jyotish-shastra; refers to the combined study of astronomy and astrology</note>, he gave the knowledge of the movements of the planets and stars situated in the procreative winds. He gave it thoroughly, in its entirety, and according to its true essence. || 4 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Being satisfied by his penance, the <term>Sun God</term> himself was pleased and granted the knowledge of the movements of the planets to <term>Mayasura</term>, who desired this boon. || 4 ||

Now, one might ask: how could the Sun speak this to his own enemy <note>referring to the traditional enmity between Devas (gods) and Asuras (demons)</note> even if he had sought refuge for his own purpose? To translate the words spoken directly by the Sun to Maya, and to show the connection between them, he says:

->The Blessed Sun Spoke:<-

**"Your intention is known to me; I am indeed pleased by your penance.**
**I shall grant the knowledge based on Time, the great movement of the planets." || 5 ||**

"The Blessed Sun spoke": this means the Sun, shining with masses of brilliance, spoke to Mayasura. Otherwise, the connection between the fourth and fifth verses would be inconsistent. What did he say? He translates those words: O Mayasura, your "intention"—your desire in the form of curiosity for the <term>Science of Light</term>—is "known" by me, the Sun; even though unspoken by you, it was known by itself. Then what? My success is not achieved by this alone, so he says: "I." By the repetition of "to you," [it means] to you I shall give the "knowledge," the scripture which is "based on Time" (where Time is the primary element). The "great," immeasurable "movement" or majesty of the "planets" situated in the procreative winds. The resulting meaning is: the <term>Science of Light</term> which explains the positions and motions of the planets. I, residing in the solar orb, "shall give" it. Now, [Maya might think]: "Will these words to me, a demon, be deceptive?" To provide the reason for speaking without deception, he adds his own qualification: "pleased." "Indeed," because I am extremely satisfied by the "penance," the worship performed by you, therefore I shall give it. And so, by the power of your actions and my affection for my devotees, I have overlooked our natural enmity and shown compassion, just as [the Lord] showed compassion to Prahlada without deception. || 5 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The <term>Sun God</term> said: "I have known your intention, and I am also satisfied with your penance; I will give you the knowledge of the movements of the planets which are dependent on Time (Kal)." || 5 ||

Now, since the Sun is always blazing with heat, how could Maya be able to stand in his presence for the duration of the hearing? Or how could the Sun, who is in constant motion, cease his wandering to converse with Maya? Since giving [the knowledge personally] seems impossible, how could he say "I shall give"? He translates the Sun's next words:

**"No one can endure my brilliance, nor have I a moment to spare.**
**This person, who is a partial incarnation of myself, shall relate everything to you without remainder." || 6 ||**

O Maya, "this person" standing before you "shall relate" the "Science of Light" to you "without remainder," in its entirety. Now, [Maya might ask]: "Will he not speak the truth?" To this he says: "a partial incarnation of myself." He is a part of me, the Sun; meaning, he is produced from me. And so, he will speak only the truth to you, who are favored by me. By this, I...

# Chapter 1: With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries

The meaning of "I shall give," mentioned in the previous verse, is clarified here as "I shall give through my own partial manifestation <note>Sanskrit: *svāṃśa*; referring to a personified fragment of the Sun's energy</note>." If you ask why I [the Sun] should not speak it myself, the text says: No. No living being can withstand my splendor, for I reside in the solar orb with the brilliance of a thousand suns. The implication is that you, being unable to remain in my presence for a long duration, would not be able to hear the teaching from me. 

Now, if you argue, "By the power of my own penance, I am capable of staying near you for a long time to listen," the text responds: To tell. For me, residing in the solar orb and being constantly moved by the *Proavaha* wind <note>The celestial wind believed in ancient Indian cosmology to drive the planets</note>, I am never still by my own power; I do not have a single moment of leisure to speak. Because it is impossible to stop this rotation, it is impossible to stay in one place. Thus, since you are stationary and I am in constant motion, our long-term association is impossible, and hearing from me is unfeasible. Furthermore, you do not have the power to occupy my station to hear from me, as there is no divine command for such a thing. || 6 ||

*Hindi Commentary: No one can endure my splendor, and I also have no time. This person, who is my partial manifestation, will speak to you with full detail. || 6 ||*

Now, concluding the recitation of the Sun's words, the text describes the beginning of the dialogue between the Sun's partial manifestation and Mayasura:

### Having said this, the God vanished after commanding his partial manifestation. 
### That person then spoke this to Maya, who stood bowed with folded hands. || 7 ||

"The God," meaning the one residing in the solar orb, having spoken as previously described, and having commanded his "partial manifestation" <term>Suryanshapurusha: a personified being representing a portion of the Sun's power</term> who stood before him, saying: "Explain the entire greatness of the planets to Maya"—the word "and" should be understood here to imply that without such a command, he would not have spoken to Maya. "Vanished" means he became invisible to the eyes of the Sun's manifestation and Maya. 

Now to the subject at hand: "That person," commanded by the Sun, spoke the following words to Mayasura. If one asks why he spoke without being questioned, the text provides two adjectives for Maya: "bowed" and "standing with folded hands." "Bowed" means humble, performing a salutation with intense devotion and faith. "Folded hands" <note>Sanskrit: *Prāñjali*; the Anjali mudra</note> refers to the joining of the palms, which indicates a mental state of one-pointed concentration. This clearly describes a physical salutation involving a bowed head and joined palms. The implication is that by this salutation—which signals the request, "Lord, I bow to you, favor me and tell me this"—Maya did indeed ask, and thus the person spoke to him. || 7 ||

*Hindi Commentary: The Sun God, having said this and giving orders to his partial manifestation, vanished. And to Maya, who stood bowing with folded hands, the Sun's manifestation spoke. || 7 ||*

Now, wishing to impart the knowledge to Maya as promised in the dialogue, the Sun's manifestation says, "Listen to my words with care":

### Listen with a one-pointed mind to that supreme knowledge 
### which in age after age was told by the Sun himself to the Great Sages. || 8 ||

O Maya, "with a one-pointed mind" means one whose mind is fixed on a single object. Withdrawing your mind from other subjects and giving it to my words, listen to this science of light <term>Jyotisha: Vedic astronomy and astrology</term>. The meaning is: perceive it directly through the union of the soul and mind via the ears. If you ask...

<summary>The Sun God explains that his intense brilliance and constant motion make it impossible for him to teach Maya directly, delegating the task to a partial manifestation. Maya receives this surrogate teacher with deep humility and devotion, preparing to hear the eternal science of astronomy.</summary>

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter One]

Lest you think, "You will speak your own inventions," he explains the connection to that tradition by saying—**"In the past," etc.** That which was mentioned as the "eye-like knowledge," meaning the science of the stars <note>Jyotish-shastra: the traditional term for Indian astronomy and astrology</note>. At what time in the distant past? To this he says—**"In age after age."** The intended meaning is: to the great sages in every Great Age <note>Mahayuga: a vast cosmic cycle of 4,320,000 years</note>. By the Sun himself, "without an intermediary," meaning directly. The word "himself" is used to exclude the possibility of another being the intermediary, just as it is impossible for me to speak to you directly every day <note>The speaker is a partial manifestation or messenger of the Sun, not the full solar orb itself</note>. Because those sages had brought the Lord under their control through the power of their asceticism, and their desires were unimpeded due to His grace, it was possible for them to reside within the solar sphere; thus it was taught to them. The sense is: "What was spoken by the Sun is being told to you; it is not my own invention." || 8 ||

<insert>Hindi Commentary—In every Age, the Sun God himself speaks this supreme knowledge to the great sages; listen to this with a one-pointed mind. || 8 ||</insert>

Now, a doubt arises: since what the Sun says in each age might not be identical, which age’s scripture are you teaching? Otherwise, if it were always the same, the phrase "in age after age" would be redundant. To this he says—

### This is that same original scripture which the Sun spoke in the past.
### Only the difference of time is found here, through the revolution of the Ages <gloss>1</gloss>. || 9 ||

This science of the stars which is about to be told by me to you is that which was spoken by the Sun. By the use of the word "same," it means this is a repetition to you of what the Sun said, without any deviation into my own inventions. "Original" means spoken by the Sun in the earliest time. Now, since even what the Sun said in a recent age could be called "past," and thus confusion might arise, he provides a description of the word "original" as required by the context, saying—**"Which."** It refers to the scripture which the Sun spoke "in the past," meaning first, before which nothing else was spoken. "He spoke" means he explained it with great excellence and detail to the sages. And so, because there is no reason to go beyond the first, and because the first is the most detailed, and because what was said in subsequent ages is already contained in what was said before (and thus condensed and disregarded), the scripture of the first age is being taught. This is the intent.

But then, would this not imply that the scriptures spoken by the Sun in subsequent ages are useless? To this he says—**"Of the Ages."** Through the revolution—the repeated cycling—of the Great Ages, there is "only" a lack of difference in the scriptures spoken by the Sun; that is all it means. "Difference of time" refers to the interval created by time. The meaning is that the time of a later scripture is different from the time of the earlier scripture, but the difference in these scriptures is not a difference in the methods taught.

Furthermore, due to the power of time, some variation occurs in the motion of the planets <note>Grahachara: the calculated paths or movements of the heavenly bodies</note>. Therefore, in another age, having established those subsequent planetary motions, the Compassionate One [the Sun] spoke as if it were another scripture for the sake of the worldly dealings of the people living at that time; thus, the later scriptures are not useless. And so, the sense is: "I have accepted the planetary motions established in the scripture spoken by the Sun for the current age, and having disregarded the motions from the first age as they serve no current purpose, I am teaching you exactly what He said."

Even within an age, if a difference is observed in the planetary motions during intermediate times, the learned men of those times establish the corrections and compose books. They call this difference the "seed" <note>Bija: a correction factor applied to astronomical formulas to maintain accuracy over time</note> in the earlier texts. Because the ancient texts have been lost, the dialogue between the Sun and the Sages is no longer seen today. However, its lack of fame should not lead to doubt, as its authority comes from sacred tradition. || 9 ||

<header>Chapter 1) With Sanskrit Commentary and Hindi Translation.</header>

**Hindi Translation:** What the Sun God <note>original: "Bhāskara"</note> previously spoke is the original scripture; only due to the changing of the Ages <note>the Yugas</note> has there been a variation in time. That same knowledge I now declare. || 9 ||

Now, wishing to first define "Time" as it has arisen through the mention of "time-variations," the author divides Time:

### Time is the destroyer of worlds; another Time is that which is used for calculation.
### That is twofold due to being gross and subtle, called the Measurable and the Immeasurable. || 10 ||

Time is of two kinds. One is Time as an unbroken, continuous rod <note>eternal linear time</note>, established by the evidence of other scriptures. It is the "destroyer of worlds," meaning it brings an end to living beings and, by extension, even inanimate objects. Although Time is also the cause of their birth and maintenance, it is called the "destroyer" here to emphasize its power and because the state of destruction is infinite. By saying "destroyer," birth and maintenance are implied, for otherwise destruction would be impossible. Thus it is said in other texts: "Time creates all beings, and Time sweeps away all creatures."

The other, second type of Time is "divided time." It is "calculable," meaning it is an object of knowledge—it can be known and measured. This second, calculable Time is also twofold, divided by "grossness and subtlety," meaning by greatness and smallness. The "Measurable" <note>original: "Mūrtta," literally 'having form'</note> has a defined limit or magnitude. The "Immeasurable" <note>original: "Amūrtta," literally 'formless'</note> is defined differently by those who know the essence of Time. The word "and" <note>Sanskrit: 'ca'</note> indicates the sequence of cause and effect in the order of Measurable and Immeasurable. Thus, great time is Measurable, and infinitesimal time is Immeasurable. || 10 ||

**Hindi Translation:** One Time is the end-maker of the worlds, which is to say, beginningless; the second Time is calculable, meaning it is capable of being known. Divided time is Measurable and Immeasurable based on the distinction between gross and subtle. || 10 ||

Now, demonstrating the two aforementioned divisions in their own form and wishing to show the consistency of the text, the author describes the two divisions within their sub-categories:

### That which begins with a Breath is called Measurable; that which begins with a Truti is designated Immeasurable.
### Six Breaths make one Vināḍī; sixty of those are known as a Nāḍikā. || 11 ||

A "Breath" <note>original: "Prāṇa"</note> is the time taken for the inhalation and exhalation of a healthy person sitting at ease, equivalent to the time taken to pronounce ten long syllables. Time starting from this Breath is called Measurable. That which begins with a "Truti" <note>an infinitesimal unit, approx. 1/33,750th of a second</note>—including units like the *Tatpara* contained within a single Breath—is designated as Immeasurable. Now, because the Immeasurable is unfit for practical use, the author ignores the further subdivision of what was mentioned last and instead intends to explain the divisions of Measurable time, which was mentioned first and is primary for practical application. He first describes the *Pala* and the *Ghaṭī*: Six "Breaths" <note>original: "Asu"</note> make one *Pānīyapala* <note>a unit of weight/time</note>; sixty of these *Palas* are called a *Ghaṭikā* by those who know the essence of time. || 11 ||

**Hindi Translation:** Breath and the units above it are Measurable time; *Truti* and the units below it are named Immeasurable. 6 Breaths make one *Vināḍī* (Pala) and 60 Palas make one *Nāḍī* (Daṇḍa). || 11 ||

Now he describes the Day and the Month:

### Sixty Nāḍīs make one Sidereal Day and Night.
### Thirty of those make a Month; likewise, a Civil Month is measured by sunrises. || 12 ||

<page-num>18</page-num>
-> Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter One] <-

A period of sixty <term>ghatis</term><note>A ghata or ghati is 24 minutes</note> is called a sidereal day and night. By stating that the day and night are sidereal, it is implied that the aforementioned <term>ghatis</term> are also sidereal in nature. Since the circle of asterisms <note>the fixed stars</note> completes one revolution in these sixty <term>ghatis</term>, a sidereal month consists of thirty such sidereal days. Because there are many types of months, the author next defines the <term>Savana</term> month: "In the same way..." meaning thirty days and nights measured by successive sunrises. This means the measurement of a day and night is the duration from one sunrise to the next. This is a <term>Savana</term> month. || 12 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** 60 <term>nadis</term> <note>synonym for ghati</note> make one sidereal day and night, and 30 such days make one month. The time from one sunrise until the next sunrise is a <term>Savana</term> day. || 12 ||

Next, after defining the Lunar and Solar months, the author describes the year and the "Divine Day":

## A lunar month is formed by lunar days; likewise, a solar month is defined by the sun's transit.
## Twelve months make a year; that is called a Day of the Gods. || 13 ||

In the same way, a lunar month consists of thirty <term>tithis</term> <note>lunar days</note>. In the scriptures, this is primarily explained as ending either with the New Moon or the Full Moon. However, in this specific treatise, the month ending with the New Moon is considered primary. A month measured from any other desired <term>tithi</term> is considered secondary. A solar month is described by experts as the time taken for a <term>Sankranti</term> <note>the transit of the sun</note>. A <term>Sankranti</term> is the moment the center of the solar disc moves into a new sign of the zodiac. Twelve months make a year. The year should be understood to match the measurement of the months used. This year is called "Solar" because of its proximity to the solar months. A "Day" here means a full day and night. "Divine" means "belonging to heaven." The meaning is that experts in the principles of measurement state that one solar year is equal to one day and night of the Gods. || 13 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** A lunar month is determined by <term>tithis</term>, and a solar month is determined by the sun entering a zodiac sign. Twelve months make one year, and this is one day for the Gods. || 13 ||

Now, one might ask: "If the day and night of the Gods has been described, why has the day and night of the <term>Asuras</term> <note>demons/titans</note> not been mentioned?" Answering this, the author describes the year of both the Gods and the Demons:

## For the Gods and the Demons, day and night are mutually reversed.
## Six times sixty of those make a Divine year, and likewise for the Demons. || 14 ||

The plural is used because there are many Gods and Demons. "Mutually" means "to each other." "Reversed" means "inverted." The meaning is this: what is day for the Gods is night for the Demons. What is night for the Gods is day for the Demons. What is day for the Demons is night for the Gods, and what is night for the Demons is day for the Gods. Thus, the difference between the Gods and Demons lies only in the inversion of day and night, not in the measurement itself. Since their day-and-night units are identical in length, the measurement for the Demons is implied by the description of the Gods. To explain the <term>Yugas</term> <note>Great Ages</note>, the author defines the "Divine Year" in another way to highlight its special nature, even though it is easy to understand: "Six times sixty." Sixty divine days and nights make a "Divine Season," and when multiplied by the six seasons of the year, it becomes a Divine Year, pertaining to the Gods and the Demons. And...

In combination. This means "of the two." A year. The word "only" is used to dispel the slow-witted doubt that there might be a difference in the year based on the distinction between their day and night. || 14 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** The day and night of the Gods and Demons are opposites; that is, when it is day for one, it is night for the other. 360 such divine days and nights constitute one year of the Gods and Demons. || 14 ||

Now, wishing to explain the measure of a *Kalpa* <note>A vast cosmic period consisting of 1,000 Great Ages</note>, the author first describes the measure of the Yugas and other cycles in two verses:

->Twelve thousand of those are called a Four-Age cycle (Chaturyuga).<-
->In the count of solar years, this is four hundred and thirty-two multiplied by ten thousand.<- || 15 ||
->That Four-Age cycle is to be understood as including the dawns and twilights.<-
->The arrangement of the Golden Age and others is determined by the quarters of Virtue (Dharma).<- || 16 ||

Twelve thousand of those divine years constitute a *Chaturyuga* <term>Chaturyuga: A cycle of four ages</term>. This means a "Great Age" (*Mahayuga*), which is the sum or combination of the four ages known as *Krita*, *Treta*, *Dvapara*, and *Kali*. The word "four" is used specifically to indicate this; otherwise, simply saying "Age" (*Yuga*) would be redundant. This is stated by those expert in measurement. Now, he describes the specific number according to solar measurement: "In the count of solar years." That *Chaturyuga* mentioned by the measurement of the Gods and Demons—the Great Age consisting of 12,000 years—includes the "dawns" (*Sandhya*) and "twilights" (*Sandhyansha*). Each part of the Age is joined at its beginning and end by a dawn and a twilight respectively; these are included within the divine measure and are not separate. In terms of solar years, it is "two-three-oceans" <note>original: "dvitri-sagara"</note>. Following the rule "numbers move from right to left" <note>original: "ankanam vamato gatih" - a traditional Indian mathematical convention where digits are read from units place upwards</note>, this results in 432 multiplied by a "myriad" (*Ayuta*), which is ten thousand. This means it should be known as 4,320,000 years. 

Now, since the specific measurements of the individual quarters of the *Chaturyuga* are not explicitly heard, one might apply the logic that "in the absence of specific instruction, parts should be equal," implying each age is one-fourth of a Great Age. He refutes this result by saying: "The arrangement of the Golden Age (*Krita*) and others." This arrangement is based on the "quarters of Virtue" (*Dharma-pada*). This upcoming arrangement must be understood as based on the status of the legs of Virtue, not as a status of equal time duration. The meaning is this: In the *Krita* Age, Virtue has four legs, so its measure is greatest. Then, in *Treta*, because Virtue has three legs, the measure of *Treta* is less in proportion. Similarly, because Virtue has two legs and one leg in *Dvapara* and *Kali* respectively, their measures are less in accordance with the aforementioned sequence following the *Krita* and *Treta* measures. The measures are not equal. || 15 || 16 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** 12,000 years of the divine measure make one "cycle-age" (Chaukadi-Yuga). The number in solar years is 4,320,000 years. || 15 || In the Four-Age cycle, which includes the dawn and twilight periods, the arrangement of the measures of the *Krita* and other ages is according to the quarters of Virtue. || 16 ||

Now, if the Great Age consists of ten parts by the total combination of all quarters of Virtue, then what is the specific knowledge of the measures of the *Krita* and other ages by proportion of their own quarters of Virtue? He explains this with specific detail:

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter One]

> -> A tenth part of the Age multiplied by four, three, two, and one, <-
> -> respectively, gives the duration of the Golden Age and the others; a sixth part of each belongs to their respective dawns and twilights. || 17 || <-

The tenth part of the Age <note>the Mahayuga or "Great Age" of 12,000 divine years mentioned previously</note> is multiplied sequentially by four, three, two, and one. This calculation results in the measurements for the *Krita* <note>Golden Age</note>, *Treta* <note>Silver Age</note>, *Dvapara* <note>Bronze Age</note>, and *Kali* <note>Iron Age</note> eras. 

Now, a contradiction might be noted: in the *Manu Smriti* <note>The Laws of Manu</note>, the durations of the *Krita* and other ages are given as 4,000, 3,000, 2,000, and 1,000 divine years. However, here the measurements are 4,800, 3,600, 2,400, and 1,200. To resolve this, the text says: **"a sixth part."** This refers to the combined time of the two *Sandhyas* <note>the "junctions" or the dawn and twilight periods</note> at the beginning and end of each age. 

Thus, for the measurements I have stated (4,800, 3,600, 2,400, and 1,200), their sixth parts are 800, 600, 400, and 200 respectively. These represent the total transition time for each age. Half of each is the specific dawn or twilight period. For example, the dawn and twilight of the *Krita* age are 400 years each. If you subtract these transition periods from my totals, you arrive at the numbers mentioned in other texts. 

The breakdown is as follows:
*   **Golden Age (Krita):** 400 (dawn) + 4,000 (core age) + 400 (twilight) = 4,800
*   **Silver Age (Treta):** 300 (dawn) + 3,000 (core age) + 300 (twilight) = 3,600
*   **Bronze Age (Dvapara):** 200 (dawn) + 2,000 (core age) + 200 (twilight) = 2,400
*   **Iron Age (Kali):** 100 (dawn) + 1,000 (core age) + 100 (twilight) = 1,200

Therefore, there is no contradiction, as my figures include the transition periods inherent to each age. || 17 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** By multiplying the tenth part of the four-age cycle by 4, 3, 2, and 1, the durations of the *Krita* and other ages are found. One-sixth of each is its transition period (*Sandhya*). || 17 ||

---

Now, to determine the measurement of a *Kalpa* <note>an Aeon or "Day of Brahma"</note>, the author describes the measurement of a *Manvantara* <note>the reign of a Manu</note> and its transition period:

> -> Seventy-one cycles of the Ages are here called a Manvantara. <-
> -> At its end, a transition period is declared equal to the number of years in a Golden Age, which is a time of deluge. || 18 || <-

Seventy-one cycles of the four ages <note>Mahayugas</note> constitute one *Manvantara* in this system of measurable time. When a Manu's reign ends, a transition period (*Sandhi*) occurs. Time-reckoners state that this period is equal to the length of a *Krita Yuga* (Golden Age). This period serves as the junction between the end of one Manu's reign and the start of the next. Its nature is described as **"a time of deluge"** (*Jalapluva*): during this time of world-dissolution, the entire Earth becomes submerged in water. || 18 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Seventy-one Yugas make one *Manvantara*; at its conclusion, there is a transition period equal to the length of a *Krita Yuga*. At that time, a deluge (flood) occurs. || 18 ||

<summary>This page explains the mathematical ratios of the four world ages (4:3:2:1) and clarifies that the Surya Siddhanta's figures include transition periods (Sandhyas). It also defines a Manvantara as 71 Mahayugas, followed by a transitional deluge equal to a Golden Age.</summary>

### Now, he describes the measurement of a Kalpa in detail—

->**Fourteen Manus, along with their respective twilights, are known to constitute a Kalpa.**<-
->**A fifteenth twilight, equal to the length of a Golden Age, is said to occur at the beginning of the Kalpa. || 19 ||**<-

Those fourteen <term>Manus</term><note>Progenitors of humanity who rule over specific spans of time</note>, starting with Svayambhuva, each consisting of seventy-one <term>Yugas</term><note>A Great Age or Maha Yuga</note>, should be understood to exist within the period of a Kalpa along with their respective <term>Sandhis</term><note>Twilights or transitional periods between eras</note>. The meaning is that a Kalpa is formed by fourteen Manus, each joined with their twilight. 

Now, a doubt arises: other texts state the measure of a Kalpa is one thousand Yugas. However, by your calculation, the measure of a Manu is 71 Yugas (306,720,000 years), and when the twilight of a <term>Krita Yuga</term><note>The Golden Age, lasting 1,728,000 years</note> is added, the total for one Manu-interval is 308,448,000 years. If this is multiplied by fourteen, the total Kalpa duration would fall short of a thousand Yugas. To address this, he says: "A fifteenth twilight." At the very beginning of the Kalpa, before the first Manu begins, there is an initial twilight equal to the years of a Golden Age. Thus, by adding this extra period at the start, there is no contradiction with the total of one thousand Yugas. || 19 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In a Kalpa, there are 14 Manus along with their twilights. At the beginning of the Kalpa, there is one twilight the size of a Golden Age; thus, in a Kalpa, there are 14 Manus and fifteen twilights. || 19 ||

---

### Now, he states the measurement of Brahma’s day and night—

->**Thus, by a thousand Yugas, the Kalpa is formed, which brings about the destruction of all beings.**<-
->**This is called a Day of Brahma; his Night is of the same duration. || 20 ||**<-

In this manner, through the thousand Yugas established by the previous method, the time of a Kalpa—which causes the dissolution of all beings—is called a Day of <term>Brahma</term><note>The Creator deity in the Hindu trinity</note> by those who know time. His Night is of the same duration as the Day. The result is that two Kalpas together make one full day and night of Brahma. || 20 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In this way, a Kalpa of a thousand Yugas causes the destruction of beings; this is one day of Brahma, and his night is exactly the same. || 20 ||

---

### Now, he states the total lifespan of Brahma and the age already passed—

->**His supreme age is one hundred years, according to that sequence of days and nights.**<-
->**One half of his life has passed; this current Kalpa is the first in the second half, known as the White Boar Kalpa. || 21 ||**<-

Listen to another point <note>original: "paramaparam"</note>—you have heard what was said before, now hear what is to be said next. Or, "Parama" may be an address to the Great Demon <note>The student/interlocutor Maya</note>. You should know that the lifespan of Brahma—the duration he holds his body—is one hundred years, calculated by the aforementioned day and night (the two Kalpas). The meaning is this: from the measurement of the day and night, a month is calculated by the previous definitions, and from that, a year of Brahma is calculated. One hundred such years constitute the life of Brahma. 

One might object that if we take the literal meaning, his life would only be two hundred Kalpas <note>100 days and 100 nights</note>. But just as with humans, where the lifespan is not stated merely in days, it is impossible for Brahma's life to consist of only a hundred literal days...

As stated in the *Vishnu Purana*: “By his own measure of time, his lifespan is recorded as one hundred years.” <note>original: "निजेनैव तु मानेन आयुर्वर्षशतं स्मृतम्"</note> By this, the idea of an "ultimate lifespan" is settled, as it is impossible for Brahma to have an indefinite life. Of this lifespan of Brahma, consisting of one hundred years, one half—measuring fifty years—has passed. This current period is the first <term>Kalpa</term> <note>A "Day of Brahma," lasting 4.32 billion years</note> of the remaining half of his life; it is the first day of the second half of Brahma's life. This is the resulting meaning. || 21 ||

**Commentary:** According to the calculation of Brahma's day and night, the total lifespan of Brahma is one hundred years. Half of his life passed in the previous <term>Kalpa</term>. This current Kalpa is the first day of the second half (the *Dvitiya-parardha*). || 21 ||

Now, he describes how much of this current day has also elapsed:

### From the beginning of this Kalpa, six Manvantaras have passed, along with their transitional twilights.
### And of the current Manu, Vaivasvata, twenty-seven Great Ages have passed. || 22 ||

From the start of this current Kalpa (Brahma's day), six <term>Manus</term> <note>Progenitors of humanity; each rules for a Manvantara cycle</note>—each consisting of seventy-one Great Ages—have passed, along with their seven <term>Sandhis</term> <note>Transitional periods or "twilights" between ages, each equal to the length of a Golden Age (Krita Yuga)</note>. The word "and" (*ca*) is used to aggregate this with the previously mentioned half-lifespan. Of the current seventh <term>Manu named Vaivasvata</term>, a <term>Tri-ghana</term> <note>Literally "three cubed" (3 x 3 x 3), equaling 27</note> of Great Ages—meaning twenty-seven cycles—has passed. This means twenty-seven <term>Mahayugas</term> have gone by. || 22 ||

**Commentary:** From the beginning of the Kalpa, 6 Manus have passed including their transitional periods prior to <term>Vaivasvata Manu</term>. And of this Vaivasvata Manu, 27 Great Ages (*Yugas*) have also passed. || 22 ||

Now, stating that a portion of the current Great Age has also passed, he explains that the sum of years should be calculated forward to the desired time:

### From this twenty-eighth Great Age, the Golden Age (Krita Yuga) has passed.
### From this point, having calculated the time, one should assemble the sum in one place. || 23 ||

From the current twenty-eighth <term>Mahayuga</term> <note>A Great Age cycle consisting of the Krita, Treta, Dvapara, and Kali Yugas</note>, the <term>Krita Yuga</term> <note>The first and longest "Golden Age" of the four-age cycle</note> has just recently passed. Therefore, after the end of the Golden Age, having calculated the time in years up to the desired moment, one should <term>Pindayet</term> <note>To "heap" or "collect" into a single sum</note> the figures—which may be held in different decimal places—into one place. This means one should perform the addition of all elapsed time. || 23 ||

**Commentary:** The Golden Age (*Krita Yuga*) of this twenty-eighth Great Age has passed. For this reason, calculate the number of years and establish the total elapsed years in one place. || 23 ||

Now he describes the time taken for the creation of the planets and the stars at the beginning of the Kalpa, which marks the start of planetary motion:

### While he was creating the planets, stars, gods, demons, and all things moving and unmoving,
### One hundred times four hundred and seventy-four divine years of Brahma passed. || 24 ||

# Chapter 1 ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. ( 13 )

For this current Brahma <note>The creator deity in Hindu cosmology</note>, while creating the world consisting of moving and stationary beings—including planets, stars, gods, demons, humans, monsters, kings, mountains, and trees—four hundred and seventy-four multiplied by one hundred <note>47,400</note> divine years have elapsed. The implied meaning is that during these divine years, Brahma completed the work of arranging the planets and stars within the system of the *Pravaha* wind <note>The celestial wind believed to drive the motion of the heavens</note>. || 24 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** From the beginning of the *Kalpa* <note>an eon or "Day of Brahma"</note>, 47,400 years by divine measurement have passed, during which the creation of the moving and stationary world—planets, stars, gods, demons, etc.—took place. || 24 ||

---

->Now he explains the cause of the apparent eastward motion of the planets:<-

## Moving westward with great speed along with the stars, the planets, ##
## being constantly outpaced, lag behind as if moving in their own paths. ## 25 ##

"Afterward," meaning subsequently, or by turning back toward the West along with the stars and constellations, the planets (the Sun and others) move continuously due to the swift force of the *Pravaha* wind. While situated in their own orbits, they are "outpaced" or defeated by the stars, because the stars move faster ahead of them. The intended meaning is that they become "heavy" as if out of shame. "Equally" means exactly so; the word "only" excludes any more or less. They "lag behind," appearing to be suspended toward the East from their original positions. Just as one who is ashamed falls behind and does not stay in front. The word "but" <note>original: *tu*</note> implies that according to the order of the orbits from lowest to highest, the "heaviness" decreases from Saturn down to the Moon. Saturn is the heaviest (slowest); Jupiter is slightly less so, then Mars, and so on. He whose orbit is large has greater heaviness; he whose lag is great has a corresponding degree of heaviness.

The point is this: Brahma established the physical sphere of the stars within the *Pravaha* wind. Inside that, the planets like Saturn were placed in their respective celestial spheres. They were aligned with the starting point of the zodiac (Aries), specifically near the junction star *Revati* <note>Zeta Piscium</note> on the Ecliptic <term>Kranti-vritta: the sun's apparent path</term> situated within the stellar sphere. The Ecliptic intersects the Celestial Equator <term>Vishuvad-vritta</term> at the points of Aries and Libra. The parts of the Ecliptic three signs away from these points (Capricorn and Cancer) are at a distance of twenty-four degrees North and South from the Equator. This twelve-sign circle is the path of the planets. The Equator is centered between the poles and passes directly over the Earth's equator <term>Niraksha-desha: the place with no latitude</term>. 

There, the physical sphere of stars revolves according to sidereal time due to the impact of the *Pravaha* wind. Although the planets also rotate due to the winds within or their impacts, they do not move at the same rate as the Aries-point on the stellar Ecliptic because the winds are weaker, the impact is less, and the planetary bodies are heavy. Therefore, a "lagging" of the planets is seen from those positions. This is why they do not rise at the same time as the stars on the second day; rather, the planet, being in a lagged position, comes up later. This lagging of Saturn and others is due to their heaviness relative to their orbits and the varying strength of the wind impacts. Although this lagging should technically occur along the Equator, it is calculated along the Ecliptic to account for the signs and revolutions <term>Bhagana: a full orbit</term> to be described later. Nevertheless, being lagged by the wind...

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter One]

Even if a planet moves along the equatorial path, it is pulled by its own line of sight within the celestial sphere of the planets toward the region of the ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path</note> adjacent to that equatorial region; thus, there is no inconsistency. Therefore, the phrase "their own paths" refers to the orbits situated within their respective celestial spheres following the ecliptic—this is the summary. || 25 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The planets, trailing behind the stars which always move very rapidly, are defeated <note>left behind</note> and thus appear to linger equally within their own circles. || 25 ||

Now, because of this, the eastward motion of the planets is established in the world; he says:

->**Therefore, their motion is eastward; through revolutions, their daily motion**<-
->**is distinct due to the circumference [of their orbits]; by that, they traverse the signs.**<- || 26 ||

Therefore, due to this "lagging behind" <note>the Sanskrit term *avalambana* here refers to the planet falling behind the faster fixed stars</note>, the "eastward-moving-ness" of those planets—meaning the state of those whose motion is in the eastern direction—is established. The eastward motion of the planets is actually generated by the nature of this lagging; it is perceived directly by observers who are ignorant of the true causes and is imagined to be produced by a specific power. 

As to how much that motion is, he says: "through revolutions." Through the revolutions to be mentioned hereafter, the daily motion—taking the form of eastward movement—is determined. Since revolutions are produced from motion, the revolutions of a planet are obtained by the solar days <note>civil days from sunrise to sunrise</note> related to those revolutions; then, by proportion, the motion for one day should be known. 

Now, one might object: "Since the revolutions of the planets are not equal, the daily motion of the planets is different; therefore, the previously mentioned motion as 'lagging' is incorrectly stated, because the lagging of the planets should be uniform." To this, he says: "due to the circumference." *Parinaha* means the circumference of the orbit <term>Kaksha-paridhi: the perimeter of a planet's orbital circle</term>. Due to that, and in accordance with it, this planetary motion is distinct yet proportional. 

This is the intended meaning: The lagging of the planets is not in a uniform space, but rather in their own respective orbits. In that space, the minutes of arc <note>kalas</note> which are equal are the motion-minutes; however, these are few in a large orbital circle and many in a small orbital circle. This is because all orbital circumferences are marked with the same number of minutes <note>21,600 minutes in a circle</note>. Regarding the revolutions: by virtue of motion, one whose orbital circle is large has fewer revolutions, and one whose orbital circle is small has many; the motion produced from that is likewise—thus there is no contradiction. 

If one asks, "Why is a varying motion accepted instead of a uniform motion?" he says: "by that." By virtue of the differing speeds, the planets "traverse the signs"—meaning they move through the constellations. And so, for the purpose of knowing the enjoyment <note>passage</note> of signs and other divisions, this specific motion is useful, not a uniform one. || 26 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Due to the revolutions produced by different orbits, there is a distinction in the daily motion; for that reason, there is variation in the time taken to traverse the signs and other divisions. || 26 ||

Now, while explaining the specific details of traversing the constellations, he states the nature of the revolutions to be mentioned:

->**The fast-moving planet traverses them in a short time; the slow-mover in a long time.**<-
->**Through their revolution, a "bhagana" [total revolution] is completed at the end of Revati.**<- || 27 ||

The word "now" indicates the specific detail previously mentioned. A fast-moving planet does not traverse those constellations in a short time <insert>correction: traverses in a short time</insert>, while a slow-moving planet traverses them in <unclear>much</unclear> time. The specific meaning is that the passage through equal signs does not occur in equal time for slow and fast-moving planets. "By the revolution"—meaning the circling—of those signs. The word "but" <note>original: 'tu'</note> indicates the result of the motion and passage of the planets...

It clarifies that while all orbits are divided into the same number of units, the physical distance traveled varies by the size of the planet's orbital circumference.</summary>

# Chapter 1 ]      With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.

<page-num>( 15 )</page-num>

Therefore, the <term>Bhagana</term><note>A complete revolution through the zodiac</note> is described by the wise. Since there are twelve signs in the <term>Ecliptic</term><note>The sun's apparent path, original: "Krāntivṛtta"</note>, a "cycle completion" occurs when a planet, having moved from a starting point, returns to that same spot. This is also called a <term>Parivarta</term><note>A turn or revolution</note>; the meaning is that a revolution consists of traversing the twelve signs. Now, one might ask: since a revolution could begin from any point on the ecliptic, which specific place is considered the starting point? To this, the author says: **At the end of Revati.** At the beginning of creation, Brahma placed all the planets in the ecliptic near the junction star of the constellation <term>Revati</term><note>Zeta Piscium, marking the zero point of the ancient Indian zodiac</note>, and their motion is measured from that limit. "At the end of Revati" means the region near that junction star; thus, the location immediately adjacent to the star Revati is the boundary for both the beginning and the end of a cycle. || 27 ||

**Hindi Commentary—** Fast-moving planets complete the circuit in a short time, while slow-moving ones take a longer time. A revolution (<term>Bhagana</term>) is completed by returning to the end of Revati. || 27 ||

One might object that the term "Bhagana" for a revolution is inappropriate because terms like "minutes" and "signs" are also part of the revolution. Therefore, under the guise of defining technical terms, the author explains the nature of a revolution:

->**Sixty seconds make a minute; sixty of those make a degree.**<-
->**Thirty of those make a sign, and twelve of those are a revolution.**<- || 28 ||

Just as the "breath" (<term>Prāna</term>) is the primary unit of measurable time, so in the definitions of space, "seconds" (<term>Vikalā</term>) are the subtle primary units. Sixty of those make one "minute" (<term>Kalā</term>). Sixty minutes are called a "degree" (<term>Bhāga</term> or <term>Ansha</term>) by those expert in spatial definitions. Thirty degrees make a "sign" (<term>Rāshi</term>). There are exactly twelve such signs. The word "exactly" is used to exclude systems using three or four signs. Thus, because the word "Gana" (group/count) implies totality, and the movement of this entire group is called a <term>Bhagana</term>, the previous statement is justified. || 28 ||

**Hindi Commentary—** 60 seconds make one minute, and 60 minutes make one degree. 30 degrees make one sign, and 12 signs make one revolution. || 28 ||

Now, wishing to state the number of revolutions, the author first gives the revolutions for the Sun, Mercury, and Venus, and the "conjunction points" (<term>Shighrochcha</term>) of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn:

->**In an Age, the revolutions of the Sun, Mercury, and Venus are 4,320,000.**<-
->**The same number applies to the Conjunctions of Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter, which move eastward.**<- || 29 ||

In a <term>Mahayuga</term><note>A Great Age of 4,320,000 solar years</note>, the revolutions of the Sun, Mercury, and Venus are represented by four zeros (in the units, tens, hundreds, and thousands places), followed by the numbers for "teeth" (32) and "oceans" (4). Thus, the solar years of an Age—4,320,000—are the number of revolutions (completions of the twelve signs). The "conjunctions" (<term>Shighrochcha</term>) of Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter also have this same number of revolutions. The word "and" is used here to imply a collective grouping. Here, Jupiter is not listed in the middle according to the order of the celestial spheres or the order of movement; this is either because the author is independent in his arrangement or because it didn't fit the meter. Now, one might ask: since these planets have no physical bodies visible in the sky <insert>at these specific mathematical points</insert>, and thus no downward weight or movement, how can "revolutions" be attributed to them? To this, he says: **Moving eastward.** Eastward—

# Chapter 1 ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.

The revolutions of the Moon’s apsis <note>the point where the moon is closest or furthest from Earth</note> in a Great Age are 488,203. Here, the mention of the "Age" is used to distinguish these from the revolutions of the planets' apsides and nodes which pertain to a Kalpa <note>a much longer cosmic cycle</note>. The revolutions of the planets' apsides and nodes do not occur in every single Age; this will be clarified in the chapter on the "True Places of the Planets" <note>Spashta-adhikara</note> regarding the determination of the nature of the slow-moving apsides and nodes. || 33 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The revolutions for the Moon’s high point (apsis) are 488,203, and for the Moon’s node (Rahu), reading from right to left, the revolutions are 232,238. || 33 ||

Now, to understand the nature of sidereal days in an Age, the author explains the nature of the planets' civil (solar) days and the method for knowing their number:

-> ### The sidereal revolutions are 1,582,237,828. ### <-
-> ### The terrestrial days of each planet in an Age are its own sidereal days minus its own revolutions. ### || 34 ||

Even though the stars <note>bhanam</note> have no motion of their own, they appear to revolve due to the *Pravaha* wind <note>the celestial wind believed to drive the stars westward</note>; thus, their revolutions are equal to their own days. Therefore, the rule of "reading from right to left" mentioned previously applies here: the number is eight, two, eight, seven, nine, three, eight, five, one <note>1,582,237,828</note>. One might ask: since planets also appear to rise due to the *Pravaha* wind, how are their days to be known? He says: "The terrestrial days" <note>bhodaya</note>. The word "rising" <note>udaya</note> etymologically refers to a day—the period from one rising to the next. Thus, these stated sidereal days, when diminished by the planet's own previously mentioned revolutions, become the civil (solar) days of that specific planet in an Age. In any desired time within an Age, the sidereal days minus the revolutions (and signs, degrees, etc.) of the planet's motion result in the desired civil days of that planet. However, it is suggested that signs should be multiplied by five and degrees by ten to properly subtract them from the minutes of time, otherwise, the difference cannot be calculated due to dissimilar units.

**The Logic:** If the planets did not have an eastward motion, then because the rising of a planet and the rising of a star would have the same cause, there would be no difference between a sidereal day and a civil day. But because planets lag behind <note>lambana</note> the stars, the civil days are fewer than the sidereal days. The difference is exactly the number of revolutions the planet makes in an Age. This is logical because the *Pravaha* wind does not make the planet complete a full westward circuit relative to the stars. From this, it is also established that the sum of revolutions and civil days equals the sidereal days. || 34 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The revolutions of the stars are 1,582,237,828. By subtracting the revolutions of a planet from the sidereal revolutions, the number of its own risings (civil days) in an Age is found. || 34 ||

Now, he explains the nature and method for knowing the number of lunar days and intercalary months <note>Adhimasa</note>:

-> ### The lunar months are the difference between the revolutions of the Moon and the Sun. ### <-
-> ### Those months, minus the solar months, are the intercalary months. ### || 35 ||

The difference between the revolutions of the Sun and the Moon constitutes the lunar months. These lunar months, when diminished by the solar months—which are the Sun's revolutions multiplied by twelve—result in the remainder...
