# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter One]

The remaining lunar months are indeed intercalary months <note>original: *adhimāsa*</note> and none other. By this, the lunar nature of intercalary months is clarified. The proof here is as follows: A lunar month, which consists of thirty lunar days <note>original: *tithis*</note> and ends at the moment of conjunction between the Sun and Moon, is established by the distance between the Sun and Moon measuring twelve signs. How else could the conjunction of the slow-moving Sun and fast-moving Moon, occurring at the end of one lunar month, happen again at the end of the next? Since a difference of twelve signs constitutes one revolution, a lunar month is established by one revolution of difference. The excess of lunar months relative to solar months is defined as the "intercalary month" <note>original: *adhimāsa*</note>, a definition provided here for its utility in upcoming calculations.

**Commentary:** The difference in revolutions between the Moon and the Sun constitutes a lunar month. Subtracting solar months from lunar months results in the intercalary months. || 35 ||

-> Now he describes the nature of omitted days and terrestrial civil days, which will be discussed later: <-

> -> Subtracting the civil days from the lunar days gives the omitted days. <-
> -> From one sunrise of the Sun to the next are the terrestrial civil days. || 36 || <-

From the lunar days <note>the lunar days to be mentioned hereafter</note>, subtracting or setting aside the civil days <note>original: *sāvana* days</note>, the remainder is the "omitted days" <note>original: *tithiksaya*, literally "loss of lunar days"</note>. This represents the "loss" or deficiency of civil days relative to lunar days. Alternatively, the term "omitted day" is defined here as the civil day's deficiency from the lunar day for the sake of future calculations. Now, since civil days for all planets were previously mentioned in the section beginning with "The revolutions of the stars..." <note>referring to verse 15-16</note>, one might ask whose days are to be taken here. He answers this under the guise of defining the Sun's civil day: "From sunrise..." The period starting from the moment of the Sun's sunrise until its next immediate sunrise is one day. Such days are "terrestrial civil days" <note>original: *bhūmisāvanavāsarāḥ*</note>. They are called "terrestrial" because sunrise is perceived in relation to the Earth. The implication is that when the terms "civil" <note>*sāvana*</note> or "terrestrial" <note>*bhūmi*</note> are used without qualification, they refer only to the Sun's days and not those of other planets, as the latter would require specific qualifiers. || 36 ||

**Commentary:** By removing civil days from lunar days, the "omitted day" <note>*tithiksaya*</note> is found. From one sunrise of the Sun to the next sunrise is one terrestrial or solar-civil day. || 36 ||

-> To answer how many of these there are, he gives their quantity and the quantity of lunar days: <-

> -> In a cycle, there are 1,577,917,828 terrestrial civil days. <-
> -> The lunar days are 1,603,000,080. || 37 || <-

In a cycle <note>a *Yuga*</note>, there are 1,577,917,828 terrestrial civil days. The lunar days in a cycle are more. These lunar days, when divided by thirty, result in the lunar months already mentioned. By this, the logic of lunar days is clarified: they are the lunar months (the difference between the revolutions of the Sun and Moon) multiplied by thirty. || 37 ||

**Commentary:** In a *Yuga*, there are 1,577,917,828 solar-civil days and 1,603,000,080 lunar days <note>*tithis*</note>. || 37 ||

<term>Sāvana</term>: A civil day measured from sunrise to sunrise.
<term>Yuga</term>: A vast astronomical cycle of time used in Hindu cosmology to calculate planetary positions.

The intent is that they were stated in Yuga format for the sake of brevity. || 40 ||

# Chapter 1: With Sanskrit and Language Commentaries

->**Summing the time of the six Manus with their respective transitions,**<-
->**along with the transition at the beginning of the Kalpa, and likewise for the current Vaivasvata Manu,**<-
->**twenty-seven Great Ages have passed, as well as this present Golden Age;**<-
->**subtracting from this the time of creation previously mentioned in divine years,**<-
->**the elapsed years at the end of the Golden Age are known by the number of solar years:**<-
->**1,953,720,000.**<- <note>The text uses a mnemonic system: "Ciphers (0) four times, twins (2), mountains (7), fires (3), arrows (5), nine (9), and the moon (1)" read right-to-left.</note>

---

Summing together the time of the six Manus in solar years along with their transitions—the six transitions being equal to the duration of a Golden Age <term>Krita Yuga: The first and longest of the four ages, lasting 1,728,000 solar years</term>—and including the transition at the very beginning of the Kalpa <note>The Kalpa-adi-sandhi is the dawn period before the first Manu</note> which is also the measure of a Golden Age. By the word "but" (tu), the idea that the transition is only half the lifespan is refuted.

For the current seventh Manu, named Vaivasvata, twenty-seven Great Ages <term>Mahayuga: A cycle of four ages totaling 4,320,000 years</term> have passed; these are likewise added. Then, this present Golden Age within the twenty-eighth Great Age is also added as having passed. From this total, one must subtract the time spent by the Creator in the act of creation. This duration was previously stated in "divine years" <note>original: "divya-sankhyaya"</note>—specifically, it was mentioned that the creation period lasts for a certain number of divine years <insert>one hundred times four hundred</insert>. The essential meaning is that this must be converted into the count of solar years by multiplying by 360.

By this, it is clarified that the previous summation was in solar years, while the creation time was in divine years. After "subtracting" <note>original: "projhya" meaning to reduce or deduct</note> this, the remaining figures—represented by the mnemonic "void, sky, void, sky, two, seven, three, five, nine, and eighteen"—are to be known as the years elapsed at the end of the Golden Age.

One might ask: "Since the total time was already mentioned in the previous section starting with 'From this Kalpa, the Manus...', does this verse starting with 'Of the six Manus...' not seem repetitive?"

It is not repetitive. The previous mention was for the purpose of knowing the total age of Brahma <note>The creator deity</note>, whereas this is for the purpose of calculating the positions of the planets. Otherwise, one might mistakenly try to calculate planetary positions from the total elapsed age of Brahma. It must be understood that planetary motion is relevant only within the "Day of Brahma" (the Kalpa). If one did not know the elapsed years since the start of the Brahma-day, planetary calculation would be impossible, as the planetary system is destroyed at the end of his day and recreated at the start. Therefore, the years used for planetary motion are those elapsed in the current Brahma-day, not his total lifespan. Furthermore, the time spent in the "delay of creation" <note>The period before planets were set in motion</note> is subtracted, because if planets were not yet moving during that time, calculating them would lead to errors. This is the direction of the explanation.

For example:
A Divine Year = 360 Solar Years.
A Great Age (12,000 divine years) = 4,320,000 years.
This multiplied by 71 (one Manu) = 306,720,000 years.
This multiplied by 6 (six Manus) = 1,840,320,000 years.

"From that point" means after the end of the Golden Age. These are "converted into months," meaning multiplied by twelve. Here, an intercalary month <term>Adhimasa: an extra month added to the lunar calendar to keep it in sync with the solar year</term> is included if it has occurred, as it becomes the start of the following month and consists of sixty days. This sum is "set aside," multiplied by the intercalary months of a Great Age, and divided by the solar months of a Great Age. The resulting whole number of intercalary months is added to the total. # Chapter 1: With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries (Page 23)

The student should keep in mind that if the desired time for calculating the <term>Ahargana</term><note>The total number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch, usually the start of creation or the Kali Yuga.</note> is separated by thirty days, an error occurs. These completed months are multiplied by thirty to convert them into days. **"Added to the days"** means adding the elapsed lunar days (<term>tithis</term>) starting from the bright fortnight of the current month. 

These values are placed in two positions. In one position, they are multiplied by the **intercalary days** of the age and divided by the **lunar days** of the age. The resulting "omitted days" (<term>kshaya tithis</term>) are subtracted from the other position. The result is the **Civil Day Count** (<term>Savana Ahargana</term>) calculated for midnight at the location of **Lanka**<note>The prime meridian in ancient Indian astronomy, located on the equator.</note>.

From this calculated day-count, the lords of the day, month, and year are determined, starting from the Sun. Regarding the knowledge of the **Lord of the Day** (<term>Vareshvara</term>), the text says: **"By seven."** This day-count is divided by seven, and the remainder determines the result. The remainder indicates the lord of the day, counting from Sunday. The next day is the current lord of the day.

### The Mathematical Proof (Upapatti)
In converting solar years into months, the fractional solar months related to the time since the beginning of creation up to the last intercalary month are considered. These are combined with the fractional lunar months from that point up to the desired start of the month of Chaitra. If one asks why solar years are multiplied by twelve, listen: it is undisputed that twelve times the solar years equals the solar months at the start of a solar year. When the calculated fractional **intercalary months** (<term>Adhimasa</term>) are added to these, they become fractional lunar months at the start of the solar year. 

When the fractional parts are removed, these become the whole lunar months at the start of the month of Chaitra. The fractional part represents the "intercalary residue" (<term>Adhishesa</term>), which is the difference between the start of the solar year and the start of the lunar month of Chaitra. These months, when reduced by the whole intercalary months, result in the twelve-fold solar years at the start of Chaitra. Otherwise, how could they equal the lunar month measurement at the start of Chaitra by simply adding whole intercalary months? 

These are then added to the elapsed months of the current year (starting from the bright half of Chaitra) to reach the desired time. This refutes the criticism that one cannot add lunar months of Chaitra to solar months (multiplied by twelve) because they are of different "species" or units. According to the stated method, since lunar months are already inherent in that calculation, they are of the same species and can be added. We did not perform an "unnatural" addition; the identity of the twelve-fold solar years is self-evident.

Now, the whole intercalary months must be added. From the fractional solar months elapsed since the beginning of creation to the last intercalary month, the whole intercalary months are derived by the proportion: *If the solar months of an Age yield the intercalary months of an Age, then what do these solar months yield?* 

To find the fractional part of the intercalary month at the desired time, the proportion is: *If the lunar months of an Age yield the intercalary months of an Age, then what do the fractional lunar months between the last intercalary month and the desired month yield?* This yields the solar fractional part because it was calculated from lunar months. However, the fraction and the whole must be of the same species. To achieve this, a further proportion is used involving the solar and lunar months of the Age. <insert>Age...</insert> Through the cancellation of equal multipliers and divisors, the result is that the desired lunar months multiplied by the intercalary months of the Age and divided by the solar months of the Age gives the **intercalary fraction in lunar terms**. 

Since it is difficult to know the solar and lunar months separately, if there is a single divisor but different multipliers, the sum of the solar and lunar months is used...

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter One]

<page-num>24</page-num>

This value, multiplied by the intercalary months of an Age <note>Yuga-adhimasa</note> and divided by the solar months of an Age <note>Yuga-surya-masa</note>, results in the number of intercalary months. The remainder is not used for the calculation of the **Ahargana** <note>the total count of civil days elapsed from a fixed epoch</note>. In this context, since only whole intercalary months are lacking, it is necessary to add only those. This establishes the count of lunar months from the beginning of creation <note>Srishti-adi</note> up to the desired month. 

However, many scholars argue that since the solar months (solar years multiplied by twelve) from the start of the solar year to the desired time are unknown, one should simply add the known lunar months elapsed since the month of *Chaitra*. But in the desired solar months, there is an excess remainder of intercalary months; by discarding that remainder and adding only the whole intercalary months, continuity is maintained. They say the calculation of intercalary months is based on the lunar months being treated as the desired solar months. This should be considered carefully. Continuity is achieved only by adding the whole intercalary months, derived from the solar months, to those solar months which include the intercalary remainder. Otherwise, if the intercalary remainder multiplied by the Age-intercalary months is divided by the Age-solar months, the result would show an excess. If the solar months are taken with the remainder, the proportion would yield one extra intercalary month, making the lunar month count higher by one.

Now, to convert these lunar months into lunar days, they are multiplied by thirty. To this, the lunar days <note>Tithis</note> elapsed since the bright fortnight <note>Shukla-paksha</note> are added to find the lunar days at the desired time. This is the **Lunar Ahargana**. By applying the proportion—"If these many Age-lunar days yield these many omitted lunar days <note>Avama-ratra</note>, then what for the current lunar days?"—one gets the omitted days with fractions. When the Lunar Ahargana is reduced by these, it becomes the **Civil Ahargana** <note>Savana Ahargana</note> at the end of the lunar day. 

Because the movement of the planets is calculated from sunrise at the location of **Yamakoti** <note>a legendary city 90 degrees east of Lanka</note>, one must add the fraction of the omitted day (the difference between the end of the lunar day and sunrise) to obtain a whole-number Ahargana from that point. Therefore, the fraction previously discarded is not used here; the Lunar Ahargana reduced by the whole omitted days becomes the Civil Ahargana. This whole-number Ahargana is for sunrise at Yamakoti. Since that location is not well-known, the difference in longitude is described relative to the famous city of **Lanka** <note>the prime meridian in ancient Indian astronomy</note>. Since the sequence of weekdays has existed since the beginning of creation, the lords of the day, month, and year are calculated from that start. Because there are seven planets, the Ahargana is divided by seven; the remainder indicates the elapsed weekday. || 48 || 49 || 50 || 51 ||

---

**Commentary:** Add the aforementioned number to the years elapsed in the **Krita Yuga** <note>the first Golden Age</note>, convert them to months, and then add the number of months elapsed since the bright fortnight. || 48 || In another step, multiply that month count by the intercalary months, divide by the solar months, add the result to the month count, convert to days, and add the elapsed days. || 49 || Elsewhere, multiply the day count by the "loss of lunar days" <note>Tithi-kshaya</note>, divide by the lunar days of an Age, and subtract this from the total days to find the **Ahargana** at midnight in Lanka. || 50 || From the Ahargana, the lords of the day, month, and year are derived. Divide the Ahargana by 7; counting the remainder starting from Sunday <note>Ravi</note> gives the Lord of the Day. || 51 ||

-> Multiply the Ahargana by two and three, add one, and divide by the appropriate numbers; <-

# Chapter 1: Including Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries

From the *Ahargana* <note>The total count of days elapsed from a fixed epoch</note>, in one place, divide by the number of days in a month, which is thirty. In another place, divide by the number of days in a year, which is three hundred and sixty. The remainders are discarded as they are not useful here. The two resulting quotients should be multiplied by two and three respectively, and one should be added to each total. After dividing by seven and discarding the quotient, the remainders are to be known as the Lord of the Month and the Lord of the Year respectively. Just as the Lord of the Day is counted in a specific order, so too are these, but this calculation is for the current period.

The logic here is as follows: From the beginning of creation, a period of thirty solar-civil days constitutes one month, and the Sun is its lord because the Sun is the lord of the first day of the month. Similarly, at the start of the second month, Mars is the lord of the day, so Mars is the Lord of the second month. Thus, the difference between successive Lords of the Month is two, because thirty days divided by seven leaves a remainder of two. 

Similarly, three hundred and sixty solar-civil days constitute one year, and the Sun is its lord. At the start of the second year, Mercury is the lord of the day, so Mercury is the Lord of the second year. Thus, the difference between successive Lords of the Year is three, because three hundred and sixty days divided by seven leaves a remainder of three. 

To find how many months and years have passed in the current time, the *Ahargana* is divided by thirty to get elapsed months, and by three hundred and sixty to get elapsed years. Since one month shifts the day-lord by two, the elapsed months are multiplied by two, and one is added to find the current lord. Since one year shifts the day-lord by three, the elapsed years are multiplied by three, and one is added to find the current lord. Since there are seven days of the week, the remainders after dividing by seven (starting from the Sun) indicate the Lord of the Month and the Lord of the Year. || 52 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Divide the *Ahargana* by the number of days in a month (30) and a year (360). Multiply the results by 2 and 3 respectively, and add 1 to each. Then, divide by 7; the remainder, counted from Sunday, will be the Lord of the Month and the Lord of the Year. || 52 ||

### Now, the calculation of the planets is described:

-> The total days (*Ahargana*) multiplied by the planet's own revolutions and divided by the total civil days of the cycle results in the mean position of the planet, beginning with the number of completed revolutions. || 53 || <-

The "total days" refers to the *Ahargana*. This is multiplied by the planet's own stated revolutions (*Bhagana*)—meaning the revolutions in a *Yuga* <note>an immense cycle of time</note> or a *Kalpa* <note>an even larger cosmic age</note>. This is then divided by the "civil days" (*Kuvasara*) of that same period (either *Yuga* or *Kalpa*). The result is the planet whose revolutions were used, expressed in revolutions, signs, degrees, minutes, and seconds. 

This is the "mean motion" (*Madhyagati*), not the "true motion" which varies daily; the method for finding the true position based on that will be explained later. This means the result is the Mean Planet. 

The logic is: If in the total civil days of a *Yuga*, a planet completes its total *Yuga*-revolutions, then how many does it complete in one day? This gives the mean daily motion. Then, if this is the motion for one day, what is the motion for the desired *Ahargana*? Although this involves two steps of proportion, it is shown here as one for the sake of brevity to demonstrate the mean position. || 53 ||

<note>original: "अहर्गण" (Ahargana) - total days; "मासेश्वर" (Maseshvara) - Lord of the Month; "वर्षेश्वर" (Varsheshvara) - Lord of the Year; "भगण" (Bhagana) - Revolutions; "कुवासर" (Kuvasara) - Civil days; "मध्यगति" (Madhyagati) - Mean motion.</note>

# Surya Siddhanta
## [Chapter One]
### (Page 26)

**Commentary:** By multiplying the total number of elapsed days (the *Ahargana* <note>literally "heap of days"</note>) by the specific revolutions of a planet and dividing by the total terrestrial days in an eon, the mean position of the planet—expressed in revolutions, signs, and degrees—is obtained. || 53 ||

Now, the author applies this same method to the calculation of the "apogees" and "nodes":

->**In the same manner, the "Fast" and "Slow" apogees, which move eastward, are calculated.**<-
->**The Nodes, which move in reverse, are likewise calculated but must be subtracted from a full circle.**<- || 54 ||

Those which move eastward (in the direction of the zodiacal signs) are the "Fast Apogees" (*Shighrochcha*) and "Slow Apogees" (*Mandochcha*) <note>These terms refer to the points in a planet's orbit that account for its varying speed and distance</note>. These are calculated using the same planetary math mentioned previously. But if the eastward movers are calculated this way, how do we find the Nodes (*Pata*) <note>The points where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> which move westward? The text says: "move in reverse." The Nodes are also calculated using the same ratio of revolutions to total days, but with this distinction: the resulting position must be subtracted from twelve signs (a full circle). 

**The reasoning:** Eastward planets move through Aries, Taurus, Gemini, etc. Westward movers go backwards through Aries, Pisces, Aquarius. Because people are not accustomed to counting backwards, we subtract the result from 12 signs to convert the position into the standard zodiacal order. || 54 ||

**Commentary:** Thus, the mean positions of the eastward-moving apogees are determined. However, because all Nodes move in reverse (retrograde), their mean position is found by subtracting the calculated result from the 12 signs of the zodiac. || 54 ||

Next, the calculation of the [Jovian] Year (*Samvatsara*):

->**Multiply the elapsed revolutions of Jupiter by twelve; add the signs of the current revolution.**<-
->**Divide by sixty; the remainder indicates the year, starting from Vijaya.**<- || 55 ||

Take the revolutions of Jupiter as calculated from the total elapsed days. Multiply these completed revolutions by twelve and add the number of signs Jupiter has traversed in its current incomplete revolution. Divide this total by sixty. The remainder tells you which year of the sixty-year cycle is currently active, beginning the count with the year "Vijaya." 

**The reasoning:** According to the *Laghu Vashistha Siddhanta*, one "Year of Jupiter" is the time it takes for Jupiter to pass through one zodiacal sign by its mean motion. To find the total signs traversed since the beginning of creation, we multiply its revolutions by twelve and add the current signs. Since there are sixty years in a full cycle, we divide by sixty. The remainder identifies the current year. In this system, the cycle at the start of creation began with the year named Vijaya. || 55 ||

# [Chapter 1] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries (27)

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiply the revolutions of Jupiter by 12, add the current sign, and divide by 60; the quotient will be the year in the <term>Vijayadi Samvatsara</term><note>A 60-year cycle of Jupiter used in Indian chronology</note> cycle. || 55 ||

Now, concluding what has been said, the author describes the calculation of planets by a simplified method:

->**This has been described in detail; now, for practical use,**<-
->**the mean calculation of planets should be done from the desired Age.**<- || 56 ||

This calculation of planets, which was previously described in detail starting with the phrase "having summed the six," involves extensive mathematical operations. For <term>practical use</term><note>original: "vyavaharikam"; referring to everyday civil or astrological application</note> in the world, it should be understood through a concise method requiring less mathematical effort. He says: "the mean calculation." The mean positions of the planets should be calculated from the "desired" current Age, such as the <term>Treta Yuga</term><note>The second of the four world ages</note>. By using the elapsed years from the beginning of the Treta Age (a quarter of a Great Age), which are fewer in number, one should calculate the <term>Ahargana</term><note>The total count of elapsed civil days</note> and then determine the mean planets according to the previously stated rules. || 56 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** All this has been told in detail; for the sake of brevity in work, it is proper to bring the planets to their mean positions starting from the beginning of the Treta Age. || 56 ||

Now, since the movement of planets began at the start of Creation, one might ask: how can planets calculated from a later point be considered equal to the actual ones? To answer this, he says:

->**At the end of this Golden Age, all planets in their mean motion,**<-
->**excepting the nodes and apsides, reached equality at the beginning of Aries.**<- || 57 ||

At the conclusion of this current <term>Krita Yuga</term><note>The Golden Age or first age of the world</note>, all seven planets (Sun, etc.) in their mean motion reached a state of equality—meaning they were at the same point in signs and degrees—at the beginning of <term>Aries</term><note>original: "meshadi"; the first point of the zodiac</note>. This excludes the <term>nodes</term><note>original: "pata"; the points where an orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> and the <term>apsides</term><note>original: "mandocca"; the point of a planet's orbit farthest from Earth</note>. Because the planets and their "swift points" (<term>shighrocca</term>) completed full revolutions at that moment, the signs and degrees calculated from the time elapsed since the start of the Treta Age will be identical to those calculated from the beginning of Creation. The total number of completed revolutions is irrelevant to the current position. || 57 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** At the end of this Krita Yuga, except for the nodes and the slow and fast apsides, all planets were at the first point of mean Aries. || 57 ||

Now he describes the specific positions of the apsides and nodes:

->**The Moon’s apsis was at the beginning of Capricorn, and its node at the beginning of Libra.**<-
->**The others, being slow-moving, are not stated to have reached zero degrees.**<- || 58 ||

At that time, the Moon's <term>apsis</term><note>original: "mandocca"</note> was at the beginning of Capricorn, and the Moon's <term>node</term><note>original: "pata"</note> was at the beginning of Libra. Therefore, their calculation from the start of the Treta Age is easy by adding or subtracting nine or six signs respectively. One might ask: why not state the positions of the others to make their calculation easy as well? He answers: "The others... are slow-moving." The remaining apsides and nodes move very slowly, as previously described in the section on revolutions (<term>bhagana</term>). <insert>They had not reached the zero point of Aries.</insert> || 58 ||

# Surya Siddhanta - [Chapter One]

Because of the word "and" <note>referring to a grammatical conjunction in the previous verse</note>, at the end of this Golden Age, these [planets] had not reached a state of zero degrees (dimensionless). Furthermore, explaining their signs and degrees is cumbersome; because of their slow motion, the values calculated once remain useful for up to a thousand years. Therefore, there is no constant necessity to calculate them, and the intent is that their derivation from the years elapsed since the Silver Age (Treta Yuga) has been omitted. If they are to be calculated from that point, they must be added to their respective "epoch constants" <term>Kshepa: a constant value added to a calculation to adjust for a specific starting epoch</term>.

The epoch constants for the signs, degrees, etc., of the Sun’s slow apogee <term>Mandoccha: the point in a planet's orbit furthest from the Earth, used to calculate equations of center</term> are 0s 7° 28' 12".
For Mars: 3s 3° 14' 24".
For Mercury: 5s 4° 4' 48".
For Jupiter: 0s 9° 0' 0".
For Venus: 11s 13° 21' 0".
For Saturn: 4s 20° 13' 12".
For the Node <term>Pata: the ascending node where the planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</term> of Mars: 9s 11° 20' 12".
For Mercury: 8s 11° 16' 48".
For Jupiter: 8s 56' 24".
For Venus: 4s 17° 25' 48".
For the Node of Saturn: 4s 20° 13' 12".
In this way, the planets are to be calculated for any desired time after first adding their respective epoch constants. // 58 //

**Vernacular Commentary:** The Moon's apogee was at the beginning of Capricorn and the Moon's node was at the beginning of Libra. The degrees of the slow-moving apogees were not stated for this reason [their slow motion]. // 58 //

Now, in order to calculate the "longitude correction" <term>Deshantara-phala: the correction applied to planetary positions to account for the distance between the prime meridian and the observer's location</term> of the planets, he [the author] speaks, first stating the Earth's diameter which is the basis for the calculation:

-> The diameter of the Earth is twice eight hundred Yojanas. <-
-> The square root of ten times the square of that is the Earth's circumference. // 59 // <-

"Twice eight hundred" means sixteen hundred *Yojanas* is the Earth's diameter <term>Bhukarna: literally 'Earth-ear' or hypotenuse, used here for diameter</term>. The diameter of the terrestrial globe is the line passing through the center of the circumference. By saying "twice," it is indicated that eight hundred is the measure of the straight line from the center to the circumference [the radius]. Just as the term "Karna" is used for the radius of the planetary orbit, it is used here for the Earth. Although this [measurement] contradicts the *Puranas* <note>Ancient Hindu religious texts which often give much larger, mythological dimensions for the Earth</note>, it is established by the authority of tradition supported by direct observation.

From this, he explains the knowledge of the circumference: "From the square of that." The square root of ten times the product of the Earth's diameter squared. The method of finding the square root is well-known in other mathematical treatises. This is the Earth's circumference.

The derivation is as follows: Since the radius <term>Trijya</term> is 3438 <note>original: "Gaja-Agni-Veda-Rama" - a mnemonic code where Elephant=8, Fire=3, Veda=4, Rama=3, read backwards</note>, for a diameter that is twice the radius, the circumference is equal to the minutes in a circle, which is 21,600. If that is the case, what is the circumference for the desired diameter? The multiplier is 21,600 and the divisor is 6876. When simplified, the divisor becomes 1 and the multiplier becomes 3 plus a fraction of approximately 1/8. Thus, the diameter multiplied by this gives the circumference. To make the multiplier a single value, the Lord [the author] squared it: 9.52.52. Due to a very small difference, it is taken as 10. Since it is said "multiply the square by the square," the square of the diameter is multiplied by ten, and its square root becomes the diameter multiplied by the root-multiplier. Although using ten in place of the true square is a rough calculation, the most merciful Lord accepted it for the sake of simplifying the mathematics for the benefit of the people. In reality, the Lord calculated the circumference for a diameter of 11,384...

He explains the calculation of the corrected circumference, the longitudinal correction, and its application in two verses:

-> The local corrected circumference of the Earth is the [standard] circumference multiplied by the cosine of latitude and divided by the radius. <-
-> The daily motion of the planet, multiplied by the distance in longitude and divided by that [corrected circumference], <-
-> results in minutes of arc. This result should be subtracted from the planets if the location is east of the prime meridian. <-
-> If the location is to the west of the meridian, it should be added; thus, the planets are corrected for one's own location. <- || 60–61 ||

The hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow <note>Akshakarna</note> is the square root of the sum of the squares of twelve and the equinoctial shadow. By this, the radius multiplied by twelve is divided; the result is the <term>Lambajya</term> <note>the R-sine of colatitude or cosine of latitude</note>. The Earth's circumference multiplied by this and divided by the radius—measured here as 3,438 <note>represented by: elephants (8), fires (3), Vedas (4), Rama (3)</note>—results in the "own" or "corrected" Earth's circumference <note>Sphuta-bhuparidhi</note> pertaining to one's own country.

The daily motion of a planet is multiplied by the <term>Deshantara</term> <note>the distance in Yojanas between the prime meridian and one's local position</note>. This is then divided by the corrected circumference. The result, in minutes of arc and so on, should be subtracted from the planet's position if one's country is situated to the east of the prime meridian <note>the line passing through Ujjain and Lanka</note>. If the country is situated to the west of the meridian, the calculator should add that value to the planet's position. These corrected planets then become "local" <note>Svadeshaja</note>. This is because the previous planetary calculations were for the location of Lanka, and the resulting positions were specific to Lanka.

**The Rationale:** Although the Earth is spherical like a ball and its circumference might seem uniform everywhere, the stated circumference applies specifically to the equator <note>Niraksha-desha</note>, which is imagined as the center. Elsewhere, because the circles [of latitude] become smaller, the circumference decreases as one moves north or south; this is called the "corrected circumference" <note>Sphuta</note> for one's location. Thus, at the 90-degree latitude of Mount Meru <note>the North Pole</note> or the Vadava fire <note>the South Pole</note>, the circumference is zero. Where the latitude is zero (the equator), the colatitude is at its maximum of 90 degrees. The nature of latitude and colatitude will be explained later. 

Just as the colatitude decreases, the circumference also decreases. Therefore, the proportion is: if the standard circumference exists at the maximum colatitude of 90 degrees, what will it be at the local colatitude? Although direct proportions on circular parts are often avoided, the use of Sines <note>Jya</note> is accepted by all authorities. Here, the "standard" value is the maximum Sine (Radius), and the "desired" value is the Sine of colatitude <note>Lambajya</note>. This proves the calculation for the corrected circumference.

Regarding the rationale for longitude <note>Deshantara</note>: a planet calculated for Lanka must be adjusted for one's own location, specifically for the point on the equator directly south or north of one's position. For this, knowing the distance in Yojanas between Lanka and one's local meridian is necessary. Since measuring this directly on the ground is difficult, it is calculated based on the distance between one's local meridian and the prime meridian on the local circumference.

<header>Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter One]</header>

From this, the distance in <term>yojanas</term> <note>a traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note> is known by using one's own local circumference. Then, by a proportion—"if this is the distance on the stated circumference, what is it on the Earth's circumference?"—the distance between Lanka and one's own meridian is determined. Since the Sun traverses the Earth's circumference in the time between two sunrises, the planets also traverse their own daily motion in minutes of arc during that time. Therefore, by the proportion: "if the daily motion of a planet occurs over the full circumference, what motion occurs over the distance in yojanas between Lanka and one's own meridian?" 

Because the multipliers and divisors (the circumferences) cancel each other out due to their equality, the resulting formula is: the distance in yojanas between the Prime Meridian and one's local place, multiplied by the planet's daily motion and divided by the local circumference of the Earth, equals the "correction in minutes" (<term>deshantara-phala</term>) for that planet. 

Even though this correction could be derived by a single proportion (if the local circumference gives the daily motion, what does the distance from the meridian give?), the text provides a double proportion. This is done for the benefit of very slow-witted students who might not understand how a result relates to the equator without seeing the connection to equatorial places. 

The logic of the correction is as follows: If one's meridian is east of Lanka, midnight occurs there earlier than at Lanka. Because of the force of the <term>pravaha</term> wind <note>the celestial wind believed to drive the stars westward</note>, the sun rises earlier in the east. Therefore, to find the planet's position for the later time (Lanka midnight), the correction must be subtracted. Conversely, if one's meridian is west of Lanka, midnight occurs later than at Lanka; therefore, the correction must be added to the planet's position. Note that for the ascending node (<term>pata</term>), which moves in reverse, this calculation is applied oppositely. Since a place and its corresponding point on the equator share the same north-south line, their midnights are identical; thus, the planetary positions calculated for the equatorial midnight apply unchanged to the local midnight. This explains the entire process. || 60 || 61 ||

Commentary: Multiply the Earth's circumference by the cosine of the local latitude and divide by the radius to find the **True Local Circumference** (<term>bhuparidhi</term>). (Sines and related functions should be studied in the second chapter). Multiply the planet's daily motion by the **Longitudinal Distance** (<term>deshantara</term>) and divide by the True Local Circumference. If the place is east of the Prime Meridian, subtract the resulting minutes from the planet's position; if west, add them. || 60 || 61 ||

->Now the nature of the Prime Meridian and the cities situated upon it are described:<-

### It passes through the middle of the Abode of the Rakshasas and the Mountain of the Gods;
### It also passes through Rohitaka, Avanti, and the nearby lake. || 62 ||

The **Abode of the Rakshasas** is <term>Lanka</term> <note>the traditional zero-point on the equator</note>, and the **Mountain of the Gods** is <term>Meru</term> <note>the North Pole</note>. The straight line between these two is called the **Prime Meridian** (<term>rekha</term>). Places south of Lanka are not mentioned as they are beyond human reach. To illustrate, he names specific locations: **Rohitaka** <note>modern Rohtak</note>, the city of **Avanti** <note>Ujjain</note>, and the nearby lake **Kurukshetra**. The word "and" implies other nearby places should also be understood as being on this line. || 62 ||

Now, a question arises: if someone does not know whether their own location is to the east or west of the prime meridian <note>The "Rekha" or line of Ujjain, the historical Indian prime meridian</note>, or by how many *yojanas* <note>A traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note> it is separated, how can they calculate the "difference of place" <term>Deshantara: the longitudinal correction required to adjust mean planetary positions from the prime meridian to one's local meridian</term> and other related factors? To answer this, the author provides three verses:

->If the actual emergence of the Moon occurs after the time calculated by mathematics,<-
->then one's own location is to the East of the central line.<-
->If it occurs before reaching that calculated time, it is to the West. The same applies to the immersion.<-
->Multiply the difference in time (in nadis) by the corrected circumference of the Earth.<-
->Divide by sixty; the resulting yojanas, whether East or West,<-
->reveal the distance of one's own place. Use these for the beneficial calculation of longitude.<-

The emergence <note>original: "unmilana"</note> refers to the moment the Moon begins to exit the Earth's shadow during a total eclipse. The "calculated time" refers to the moment determined through the mathematical methods taught in the chapter on lunar eclipses. If the observed emergence happens *after* the calculated time—the word "after" is used here for easy understanding, as "exceeding" and "after" would otherwise be redundant—then the observer's location is situated to the East of the prime meridian. 

<margin>Alternative reading: "If the observed emergence of the Moon exceeds the calculated..."</margin>

If the emergence occurs *before* reaching the calculated time—indicated by the word "before"—then the location is to the West of the prime meridian. 

One might ask: why is the moment of "emergence" specifically chosen among the various stages of an eclipse (contact, immersion, emergence, and separation)? The text says "The same applies" <note>original: "evam"</note> to indicate that this also works with the moment of immersion <note>original: "sammilana," when the Moon is first fully covered by the shadow</note>. If the immersion occurs after the calculated time, the place is East; if before, it is West. The word "also" <note>original: "api"</note> is used for emphasis, ensuring there is no confusion between the methods for emergence and immersion. The mention of emergence is illustrative; while the beginning and end of an eclipse are harder to pinpoint exactly, the moments of total immersion and the start of emergence are more precise for observation.

Now, the author explains how to derive the actual distance in *yojanas*: Take the difference in *ghatis* <note>original: "nadis," a unit of 24 minutes</note> between the observed time and the calculated time. Multiply this by the "corrected circumference of the Earth" <note>The circumference of the Earth at the observer's specific latitude</note>. Divide that product by sixty <note>Since there are 60 ghatis in a day</note>. The resulting *yojanas* represent the distance to the East or West from the prime meridian. This distance defines the "local circumference" or the specific position of one's own place relative to the central line. This must be known by the calculators—

# ( 32 ) Surya-Siddhanta — [ Chapter One

...is the remainder. The resulting meaning is that the distance in <term>yojanas</term> <note>a traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note> between one's own location and the prime meridian is the result. With those distance-yojanas, the calculator should determine the "longitudinal correction" (<term>deshantara-phala</term>) of the planets in terms of arc-minutes, following the method previously described. Because of the word "hi" <note>a Sanskrit particle used for emphasis or logical connection</note>, the corrective process is the same because the nature of the calculation is identical.

The reasoning here is as follows: Without the longitudinal correction, planetary calculations are valid only for the prime meridian. Therefore, the times for the beginning and end of an eclipse calculated through mathematics are accurate for the prime meridian. If one's own location is to the East, one's own sunrise occurs first, and the meridian's sunrise occurs later. Since a lunar eclipse occurs simultaneously for all locations, the observed time of contact will occur after the mathematically calculated time for the meridian. Similarly, if one's location is to the West, the meridian's sunrise occurs first and one's own later; thus, the time of contact will occur earlier than the calculated time (in <term>ghatis</term> <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>) for the meridian.

Thus, what was stated in the previous verse and a half is well-proven. The difference between the time of sunrise at the meridian and at one's own location, measured in <term>ghatis</term>, is established as the "longitude-ghatis." Since the Sun traverses the earth's circumference in the time between two sunrises, the proportion is: if the earth's circumference at one's latitude corresponds to 60 <term>savana-ghatis</term> <note>terrestrial time units</note>, then what distance corresponds to the "longitude-ghatis" (the time difference)? This calculation yields the distance in <term>yojanas</term> between the meridian and one's location. From these known values, the longitude is determined in the eastern direction. It should be noted that because a solar eclipse does not appear the same at all places simultaneously, this specific knowledge cannot be gained from the timing of its phases in the same way. || 63 || 64 || 65 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** If a lunar eclipse is observed to occur after the time calculated in the texts, that place should be known as being to the East of the prime meridian; if it occurs earlier, it is to the West. By multiplying the difference between the observed and calculated time (in <term>dandas</term> <note>synonymous with ghati, 24 minutes</note>) by the local circumference of the earth and dividing by 60, the distance in <term>yojanas</term> to one's location is obtained. From this, one should determine the local earth circumference and longitude. || 63 || 64 || 65 ||

### Now he describes the knowledge of the time when the weekday begins—

->**In a country to the East, the start of the weekday occurs at midnight plus the longitude-ghatis.**<-
->**In a country to the West, it should be indicated as midnight minus those longitude-ghatis. || 66 ||**<-

In a desired location situated to the East of the prime meridian, the start of the weekday occurs at midnight plus the "longitude-ghatis" (calculated as previously described)—meaning the time of the longitude-ghatis after midnight. In a location to the West of the meridian, the calculator should state that the weekday begins at midnight minus the longitude-ghatis—meaning the time of the longitude-ghatis before midnight.

The reasoning here is: The time of sunrise at <term>Yamakoti</term> <note>a legendary city on the equator to the East</note> is the same as the time of midnight at <term>Lanka</term> <note>the reference point on the prime meridian</note>, which marks the start of planetary motion. When does this occur at one's own location? For places East or West of the meridian, that midnight occurs sequentially according to the longitude-ghatis. This is because midnight occurs simultaneously only for places on the same terrestrial meridian. Thus, it is proven.

# Chapter 1 ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.

Regarding the "commencement of the weekday" <note>Sanskrit: *vārapravṛtti*</note> and so forth: One might ask, what is the purpose of explaining this knowledge of time if there is no practical application? This is not so. Since a planet calculated from the "heap of days" <note>Sanskrit: *ahargaṇa*; the total number of days elapsed from a fixed epoch</note> corresponds to a specific moment, by knowing that time—specifically the interval between one's own local midnight and that moment—one can adjust the planet's position. By moving the planet by that interval, the planet is established as it was previously calculated for local midnight. This serves to satisfy the student's understanding and simplifies the process of applying the "longitude correction" <note>Sanskrit: *deśāntara-saṃskāra*; a correction for the difference in longitude between the observer and the prime meridian</note> by knowing the exact time. Therefore, the instruction for "moving" <note>Sanskrit: *cālana*; adjusting the planetary position based on time elapsed</note> the planet follows immediately to achieve the planet's position at the desired time.

The result of this is that, in reality, "half-night" <note>Sanskrit: *kṣapārdha*</note> refers to fifteen *ghatikas* <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 15 ghatikas equal 6 hours</note> after sunset on the equator. In the northern hemisphere, it is the time measured by the remaining *ghatikas* until sunrise; in the southern hemisphere, it is the time measured by the *ghatikas* elapsed since sunrise. The interpretation that the weekday begins at the time of sunrise in Lanka <note>The Hindu prime meridian, located on the equator</note>, adjusted by the *ghatikas* of longitude for eastern or western regions, is refuted. This is because the word "that" refers to the previous mention of midnight, and a fifteen-*ghatika* period cannot be established by the word "half-night" otherwise. Furthermore, since the Blessed One <note>Referring to the author or the divine source of the text, likely Surya</note> stated that the "heap of days" is calculated for midnight at Lanka, the explanation of knowing the commencement of the weekday at one's own location would be inconsistent. There would also be a lack of harmony with the practical usage of the weekday beginning at sunrise in Lanka. || 66 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** By adding the longitude *ghatikas* to the local midnight for eastern countries and subtracting them for western countries, the weekday etc., will be determined. || 66 ||

### Now he describes the method for calculating the planet's position for a specific moment:

<margin>1. The "desired pulse" <note>Sanskrit: *iṣṭa-nāḍī*</note> is the name for the distance of the desired time from midnight. When the desired time is reached, the *iṣṭa-daṇḍa* (desired time unit) is obtained.</margin>

> ->The daily motion multiplied by the desired pulses, divided by sixty, gives the minutes of arc and so on.<-
> ->By adding this to the planet if the time is in the future, or subtracting if in the past, the planet becomes "instantaneous" <note>Sanskrit: *tātkālika*; the position at the exact desired moment</note>.<- || 67 ||

The mean motion of the planet is multiplied by the "desired *ghatikas*" (the time elapsed or remaining between the time the planet was calculated for and the desired moment) and divided by sixty. The result is in minutes of arc <note>Sanskrit: *kalā*</note> and so on. If the desired time is in the past <note>Sanskrit: *gate*</note>, it should be subtracted from the planet's position. If the desired time is in the future <note>Sanskrit: *gamye*</note>, the calculator should add it to the planet's position. Thus, the planet becomes "instantaneous"—that is, the planet at the calculator's desired moment.

The mathematical proof is as follows: If in 60 solar *ghatikas* the motion is equal to the daily rate, then what is it in the desired elapsed or remaining *ghatikas*? By this proportion, the adjustment in minutes is found. By adding or subtracting this, the planet becomes instantaneous. It should be noted that for the "Node" <note>Sanskrit: *pāta*</note>, which is subtracted from the cycle, the rule is reversed. The instruction for moving the planet is given here to indicate that if the mean planet is adjusted and then the "true" <note>Sanskrit: *spaṣṭa*</note> position is calculated, it is more accurate than adjusting a previously calculated true position. || 67 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** By multiplying the daily motion <note>Sanskrit: *bhukti*</note> by the desired pulses and dividing by 60, one finds the result. By adding for future time and subtracting for past time, the planet for that moment will be found. || 67 ||

### Now he states the value of the maximum latitude of the Moon:

> ->One-eightieth of the minutes in the zodiac circle is the maximum north-south deviation.<-
> ->The Moon is deflected by its Node from the end of its own declination.<- || 68 ||

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Two]

The Moon, whose rays are not hot <note>original: "anushnagu" — a poetic epithet for the Moon</note>, is suspended according to the equator from the edge of its own luster. It is attracted by the region of the ecliptic <term>ecliptic: the sun's apparent path in the sky</term> nearest to it. Thus, from its own position—which is the desired spot on the ecliptic bounded by the nearest junction star of the Revati constellation—it is cast or thrown <note>original: "vikshipyate" — the root of the term for celestial latitude</note> to the north or south by its node <term>node: the point where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</term>. The lunar disk is not permitted by the node to remain exactly on the ecliptic at its calculated position; rather, the lunar disk is moved to another spot at a slight distance along a north-south line. By the phrase "whose rays are not hot," it is also implied that because the Sun lacks a node, its disk remains exactly at its calculated position on the ecliptic and is never deflected.

Now, the author describes the specifics of this maximum north-south deflection: "of the circle of signs." The circle of signs consists of 21,600 minutes <note>360 degrees × 60 minutes</note>. One-eightieth part of this is 270. This is the maximum north-south deflection. The result is that the maximum latitude of the Moon is 270 minutes <note>4° 30'</note>. Some explain the logic here: since the Sun has no latitude, and the circle of signs is the fifth orbit from it, and the Moon's orbit is even lower, the maximum lunar latitude in the two directions (north and south) is one-eightieth of the minutes of the zodiac.

**Vernacular Commentary:** By the node of the Moon, the maximum latitude occurs at the 80th part of the total minutes of the zodiac, either north or south of the ecliptic. || 68 ||

Next, he states the maximum latitudes for Mars and the other planets, as they are also deflected by their respective nodes:

-> ### **Two times its ninth part for Jupiter; three times for Mars;** <-
-> ### **Mercury, Venus, and Saturn are deflected by their nodes four times that amount. || 69 ||** <-

"Its ninth part" refers to a ninth of the Moon's maximum latitude (270), which is 30. Twice that is 60 minutes; this is the maximum distance by which Jupiter is deflected north or south by its node. Mars is deflected by three times that amount, which is 90 minutes. Mercury, Venus, and Saturn are each deflected by their own nodes by four times that amount, which is 120 minutes, away from their positions on the ecliptic. Some offer this logic: for Jupiter, whose disk is 33 minutes, a deflection of 60 minutes is appropriate; since Mars is below Jupiter, a triple deflection (90) is right; and since Mercury and Venus have smaller/larger disks and are lower still, a quadruple deflection (120) is fitting. Even though Saturn is in a high orbit, because of its slow motion, a maximum deflection equal to that of Mercury and Venus is considered appropriate. || 69 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** Twice its ninth part for Jupiter, three times for Mars, and four times for Mercury, Venus, and Saturn—these are the deflections caused by their nodes. || 69 ||

Now, to show the relevance of stating these here, he concludes what was said previously:

-> ### **Thus, by three, nine, and twelve, multiplied by ten,** <-
-> ### **the mean latitudes in minutes are stated for the Moon and the others in order. || 70 ||** <-

Since the maximum latitude minutes are later described as variable, the intent here is to state them specifically as mean values in this context. || 70 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Likewise, by multiplying 27, 9, 12, 6, 12, and 12 by 10, the minutes of latitude for the Moon and other planets are obtained in sequence. || 70 ||

# Chapter Two

Now, the Chapter on True Motions <note>original: "Spashtadhikara"; the section dealing with calculating the actual observed positions of planets</note> is explained. Here, the cause for the "true" calculation of planets, beyond their mean motion, is stated:

> The unseen forms of Time, residing in the zodiac,
> known as the Swift Conjunctions, Slow Conjunctions, and Nodes,
> are the causes of the motions of the planets. || 1 ||

Specific entities <note>original: "jiva-visheshah"</note> named the Swift Conjunction <note>term: "shighrochcha" - the point related to the planet's orbital speed</note>, the Slow Conjunction <note>term: "mandochcha" - the apogee or point furthest from Earth</note>, and the Node <note>term: "pata" - the point where the planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> are the causes of the motion of the Sun and other planets. One might argue that motion occurs by Time alone, and thus these are not the causes; to this, the text says: "of Time." These are the forms of the previously established Time; thus, as "Forms of Time," there is no contradiction in them being the causes of planetary motion. If one asks how they can be Forms of Time when they do not look like units of time such as hours <note>original: "ghati"</note>, the text says: "residing in the zodiac." This means they are located in the regions of the planetary spheres following the ecliptic in the celestial sphere, and are measured in signs <note>zodiac signs</note>. Since the experience of planetary signs and degrees is produced only by the power of Time, these entities, being composed of that, are indeed Forms of Time. If one asks why they are not seen, the text says: "unseen forms." They possess aerial bodies <note>original: "vayaviya-sharira"</note> and are imperceptible due to their unmanifest nature. The significance is that because of the existence of these apogees and nodes, the process of "true" <note>accurate/observed</note> calculation arises. || 1 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The Swift Conjunction, Slow Conjunction, and Nodes, etc., are unseen, reside in the zodiac, are forms of Time, and are the causes of the planets' motions. || 1 ||

Now, he explains the cause of the motion of the planets' Apogees <note>original: "ucca" - the highest point in an orbit where the planet moves slowest</note> and Nodes <note>original: "pāta" - the points where an orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> relative to their mean positions:

## Bound by those cords of wind, by those right and left hands,
## they are pulled forward and backward toward their own directions, according to their proximity. || 2 ||

The planetary bodies, which are bound by cords or rays made of wind belonging to those divine beings known as the Apogees, are pulled by the right and left hands of those beings. Because there are many Apogees, the plural "hands" is used to mean "by a pair of hands." As the planetary disc <note>original: "graha-bimba"</note> becomes near to them, it is pulled "toward its own direction"—meaning toward the being itself—via the eastern and western paths.

The intended meaning is this: The Apogees and Nodes of the planets stay in their respective places on the ecliptic <note>original: "krānti-vṛtta"</note> within the celestial sphere. There exists a cord-like mechanism made of wind (distinct from the *Pravaha* or Great Wind) which does not shake by its own motion. This cord is threaded through the east and west sides of the planetary disc and is held between the two hands of the Apogee-deity. 

Now, even as the planetary disc moves eastward from the position of the Apogee by its own power, it is continuously pulled backward toward the deity by the cord in the left hand—which, being a large cord-segment, stretches from the Apogee in the east to the planet's position in the west—until there is a distance of six signs <note>180 degrees</note> between them. After that, as pulling from that direction becomes impossible, the planetary disc moving eastward is then pulled forward toward the deity by the cord in the right hand—which stretches from the Apogee in the west to the planet's position in the east—until the distance between them disappears. || 2 ||

> Translation of the Commentary: Those invisible rays of wind, pulling with left and right hands, lead the planets from their positions toward the front, either east or west. || 2 ||

Because of this, the planets abandon the uniform motion understood in the previous chapter and attain a different motion every day; therefore, he says:

## The wind named *Pravaha* impels them toward their own Apogees;
## thus pulled to the east and west, they move with varying speeds. || 3 ||

The wind named *Pravaha* <note>The "Provector" wind responsible for the daily rotation of the heavens</note>, which rotates toward the west, impels those planets—and the word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> implies the Apogees as well—toward their own "highness." This refers to the direction in which the planet's elevation lies, specifically the eastern direction, as the planets are seen moving toward the east relative to the *Pravaha* rotation. This is the essential meaning: it moves them by supporting the planets as previously described. 

For this reason, those planets are "pulled east and west" by the Apogee-deities; being drawn toward the eastern and western directions, they "attain varying speeds"—meaning they reach a state of motion that differs every moment from the single, uniform type of motion first understood. The idea is that through this support and pulling, the daily motion of the planets becomes different, and thus the "true" or "corrected" <note>term: "spaṣṭa" - the mathematically corrected position of a planet as seen from Earth</note> motion of the planets is produced. Or rather: one might ask, how can wind-cords...

# Chapter 2 | With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries | ( 37 )

It might be asked how the attraction of planets is possible, given that the "ropes" <note>referring to the invisible forces or 'strings' of air mentioned in earlier verses</note> are sparse and not solid enough to pull anything. To this, the author says: **By the Pravaha.** The cords, which are shaped like the planetary orbits and held in the two hands of the high deities, are moved by the wind. Because of its connection to the *Pravaha* wind, this force is called *Pravaha*—though this is not the same as the wind that causes the westward diurnal revolution. It impels or moves those planets toward their own *Ucca* <term>Ucca: The 'apex' or point of highest influence, often translated as apogee</term>, toward the station of the deity of the *Ucca*. The word "but" (tu) implies that if the planet is east of the *Ucca*, the wind moves it with a westward motion; if it is west, the wind moves it with an eastward motion. The idea is that the orbit-shaped cord rotates in various ways at various times, and it is said figuratively to be "pulled by the deities." Therefore, the true motion of the planets is produced. He says: **Pulled eastward and westward.** The planets, pulled toward the east and west by the deities of the *Ucca*, attain a distinct kind of motion—a movement different from their mean (average) motion. Thus, the calculation cannot be managed by mean motion alone. ॥ 3 ॥

**Hindi Commentary:** The wind named *Pravaha* carries the planet toward its high directions. In this way, by pulling it in the east and west directions, the planet attains a distinct motion. ॥ 3 ॥

Now, he clarifies what was said about being pulled forward and backward:

->**An Ucca located in the first six signs (half-circle) ahead of a planet pulls the planet eastward.**<-
->**Similarly, one located in the rear half-circle pulls the planet westward.**<- ॥ 4 ॥

The *Ucca* spirit <note>Jiva/Deity</note> situated in the six signs (half-circle) ahead of the planet's position pulls the planetary orb toward the east, toward itself. The *Ucca* spirit situated in the six signs behind the planet's position pulls the planetary orb toward the west, toward itself, in the same manner. ॥ 4 ॥

**Hindi Commentary:** An *Ucca* situated in the first half of the revolution pulls the planet to the east, and one situated in the second half pulls it to the west. ॥ 4 ॥

Now he states the result established by the previous points:

->**When planets, pulled by their Uccas, move eastward in the revolution,**<-
->**that amount is called "plus" (addition); but in the westward movements, it is "minus" (subtraction).**<- ॥ 5 ॥

Planets attracted by their *Ucca* spirits move eastward by certain degrees or signs within the zodiac of the celestial sphere. Whatever that measured amount is—the result in degrees and so on—should be added (as a "plus" correction) to the previously calculated mean positions of the planets. In the case of westward movements—meaning the amount in degrees the planet moves toward the west when pulled westward—the word "but" (tu) indicates that this amount should be "minus" or subtracted. This is what was stated by the ancients. ॥ 5 ॥

**Hindi Commentary:** When planets move in the eastern direction being pulled by their *Ucca*, it is "plus" (positive). Conversely, if they go in the western direction, it is "minus" (negative). ॥ 5 ॥

Now he explains how the Nodes cause the planetary motion known as "deviation" (latitude):

->**In the same way, the Node (Rahu) pulls the planet toward the north and south by its own speed.**<-
->**This creates the "Vikshepa" (latitude) of the Moon and others away from the ecliptic.**<- ॥ 6 ॥

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Two]

The deviation of the Moon and other planets—excluding the Sun—occurs to the south or the north from the ecliptic <note>the apparent path of the Sun</note>, starting from the calculated true position of the planet. The word "also" <note>original: "api"</note> is used here to include the eastward and westward motions. This "Node" <term>Pāta: the point where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</term> is a calculated position in signs, degrees, etc. Here too, the word "also" connects this with the "Apogee" <term>Ucca: the highest or furthest point in an orbit</term>. Just as the Apogee causes a difference in the eastward and westward results, so too does this. It "throws" or creates a "latitude" <term>Vikṣepa: celestial latitude or deviation from the ecliptic</term> by its own inherent velocity. In technical terms, when words describing specific actions are used alongside general terms, the object of the action is understood; thus, the meaning is that it "deflects the Moon and other planets."

Now, one might ask: if the Apogee attracts a planet through the living deity presiding over it, how can the Node—which is inanimate and lacks velocity—deflect a planet? To this, the text says: **Rahu**. The presiding deity of the Node is Rahu, who is a specific living entity. In the case of the Moon's node, it is the specific demon Rahu. The etymology of "Rahu" comes from the root meaning "to leave or abandon," because he causes the planet to leave its path. || 6 ||

<margin>Hindi Commentary: The Node, Rahu, by its own power, deflects the planets into the southern and northern directions. The distance of the Moon and others from the ecliptic is called "Vikṣepa" (latitude). || 6 ||</margin>

### Now, he clarifies this:

> ## The Node, when situated in the western half-orbit, deflects the planet toward the North.
> ## When situated in the eastern half-orbit, it pulls the planet toward the South. || 7 ||

A Node situated in the "western half-orbit"—meaning the six signs constituting the western section relative to the planet's position—deflects the planetary orb toward the northern direction from its calculated position in the signs. When it is in the "eastern half-orbit"—the six signs in the eastern section relative to the planet—it pulls or deflects it toward the southern direction. || 7 ||

<margin>Hindi Commentary: A Node that has moved into the western half-orbit pulls the planets toward the North, and a Node in the eastern half-orbit pulls the planets toward the South. || 7 ||</margin>

### Now, he states the specific rule for Mercury and Venus:

> ## In the case of Mercury and Venus, when the Node is similarly situated relative to their "Fast-Apogee,"
> ## Then, due to the attraction of that Fast-Apogee, those two are deflected as previously described. || 8 ||

The singular form is used for the "Fast-Apogee" <term>Śīghrocca: the point used to calculate the inner planets' orbits, often associated with the Sun's position</term> of Mercury and Venus to refer to the category. Similarly, "Node" is used in the singular. "Similarly" means when the Node is within the western or eastern half-orbits. The word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> implies "at the time when [the planet is moved] by the two nodes." <warning>A series of dots followed by a question mark indicates a gap or lacuna in the source text.</warning> ................................................................( ? )
Those two, Mercury and Venus, are deflected toward the South or North in the order of the eastern and western halves as stated before. But how can the Nodes, being positioned relative to the Apogee, deflect Mercury and Venus when there is no direct connection? Otherwise, there would be an error of "disjointedness." To explain this, he says: "due to the attraction of that Fast-Apogee." This refers to the attraction exerted by the Fast-Apogees of Mercury and Venus. Thus, the presiding deities of those Apogees deflect the planets to the South or North when the Nodes are so situated; this is established by the logic previously mentioned...

# Chapter 2. Including Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries (39)

The sense is that because Mercury and Venus are bound as if by a cord, their <term>latitudinal deviation<note>Sanskrit: *vikshepana*; the angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic.</note></term> is established through this logic. Now, one might ask: why was this not stated for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn? Or why was it stated only for these two, when it is proper to describe all planets using a uniform method? Furthermore, the argument that the "deities of the apogees" for Jupiter, Mars, and Saturn reside in their respective halves holds true; however, for Mercury and Venus, the deities of their apogees are situated to the north and south of the orbit. Thus, the previous reasoning fails because the specific "provector wind" <note>The *Pravaha* wind, believed in ancient Indian cosmology to drive the planets.</note> cords connected to the deities possess the shape of the Earth's circumference and do not follow the shape of the orbit. Without an orbital shape, even Brahma himself could not produce the resulting motion. 

One should not argue that even if the wind-cord connected to the deity lacks an orbital shape in the celestial sphere, it is "equivalent" to an orbit in another location, and thus the result is produced by imagining the north-south distance. Because if the location of the apogee-deity is south of the orbit, then the opposite point must necessarily be north; therefore, the rule that the deviation of the apogee, Mercury, and Venus must be in the same direction would fail. 

If one asks: "How then is this statement by the Lord <note>Referring to the Sun God in the *Surya Siddhanta*.</note> consistent?" It is said here: If someone, following their own whim, accepts an inconsistent meaning and then exposes flaws to insult the Lord, their tongue should be cut out by revealing the true philosophical meaning! Specifically: the distance in signs between Mercury or Venus and their own <term>conjunction/fast apogee<note>Sanskrit: *shighrochcha*; the point of mean conjunction used to calculate planetary equations.</note></term> is added to the previously mentioned <term>node<note>Sanskrit: *pata*; the point where the planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note></term>. This is what is meant. Just as Mercury and Venus are situated in the order of the latter and former halves, so it is from the apogee. Due to that "fast-attraction," there is an attraction from those two nodes with great velocity, because of the arrangement of the wind-cords connected to the planets held in the hands of the deities residing at those nodal points. Those two, Mercury and Venus, are deflected north and south as described. 

Here, by the word "node," one should understand the node as adjusted by the circle. Otherwise, the calculation of the center—which is the distance to the fast apogee—would be established, but the calculation of the center touching the planet minus the fast apogee would be impossible. Thus, while the description of deviation is common to all planets, it is stated separately for Mercury and Venus to show the difference in their nodes. One should not doubt that the previous system is being subverted. The reason for stating the difference in nodes is as Bhaskaracharya said: *"Because the revolutions of the nodes of Mercury and Venus stated here are greater than the revolutions of their fast centers; they are stated as small for the sake of easy calculation, and those two nodes should be made by subtracting the read cycles from the fast center."* This is the direction of the argument. || 8 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The nodes of Mercury and Venus, being situated according to the previously described method of the "fast" motion, are deflected as before due to the "fast-attraction" (*shighrakarshana*). || 8 ||

It might be asked: since there is no difference between the two "apogee-deities" of the Sun and the Moon, why is their result not equal? To this, he says:

->**Because of the greatness of its orb, the Sun is pulled only slightly.**<-
->**Because of the smallness of its orb, the Moon is pulled much more than that. || 9 ||**<-

Because of the "greatness" or heaviness of its orb (disk), the Sun's maximum result is "slight" compared to other planets; the word "only" is used for emphasis. It is pulled by the "apogee-force" (*uchcha-jiva*). The Moon, due to the "smallness" or lightness of its orb, is pulled "much more"—meaning its maximum result is greater than the Sun's—by the apogee-force. || 9 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Because the solar orb is heavier, it is pulled less; because the Moon is small, it is pulled more. || 9 ||

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Two]

Now, for this very reason, because Mars and the others have smaller bodies, it is possible for them to have greater results <note>The "results" or *phala* refer to the trigonometric corrections needed to find the true position of a planet from its mean position</note> from these two [apogees]. He says:

> **Because Mars and the others have small bodies, they are pulled very far and with great velocity by the deities known as the Fast and Slow Apogees.** || 10 ||

The five planets, Mars and the others, because of their small bodies—that is, having smaller diameters—are pulled very far, to a great extent, by the deities named the Fast Apogee <term>Shighrochcha: the point representing the planet's orbital motion around the Sun, used to calculate the synodic equation</term> and the Slow Apogee <term>Mandrochcha: the apsis or apogee, used to calculate the equation of center</term>. Therefore, they possess "great velocity," meaning those who have acquired extreme speed. The meaning is that due to the lightness of their disks and the attraction of the two apogees, they have large maximum corrections.

Now, one might object: "It is proper to produce the correction for the Sun and Moon by the movement of the *Pravaha* wind <note>In ancient Indian cosmology, the *Pravaha* is the celestial wind that drives the stars and planets westward</note> which differs from the shape of the orbit. But for Mars and the others, since each has two apogees, and attraction by wind is impossible, how can the production of the correction by a wind movement differing from the orbit be accepted? Since the two apogees are not in the same place, a single atmosphere cannot simultaneously be the support for two contradictory motions."

To this we reply: No, because for Mars and the others, the attraction of the planetary disks is arranged by the power of the two deities of the Fast and Slow Apogees along the path of their cords <note>The "cords" or *sutras* are invisible lines of force connecting the planet to its points of correction</note>. There is no need to imagine the movement of an atmosphere. Furthermore, there is no obstacle to accepting this same principle for the Sun and Moon. The imagination of an atmosphere is not very useful. As for the statement "by the rays of those [planets]," it is supported by the description of the planets' positions as being situated in their respective celestial spheres in a straight-line connection with the *Pravaha* wind, which consists of westward rotation. This is not a reason to suspect an inconsistency here. By the concept of the Apogee-Deities, the production of a single result in the form of the combination of two corrections is consistent, as they pull the planets in the sky this way and that by their own power. Therefore, the idea that the "cord" is the same as the planetary orbit is also rejected. If they were pulled from two apogees in opposite directions, the circularity of the cord-orbit would be broken. || 10 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** Because Mars and others have small forms, they are pulled far by the *Shighra* and *Manda* apogee deities and move very quickly. || 10 ||

Now, he summarizes this:

> **Therefore, their gain and loss is very great due to their motion. Thus being pulled by them, they move in the sky, struck by the wind.** || 11 ||

Therefore, from the previously mentioned explanation of being pulled very far, a very great "gain and loss" <term>Dhanarna: additive (positive) and subtractive (negative) corrections</term> arises for Mars and the others due to the movement produced by that attraction. Now, one might ask: "Why is the movement produced by attraction not visible?" He says: "Being pulled." Being pulled in this manner by those deities of the apogees and nodes, these planets—Mars and the others—move in the sky, in their respective celestial spheres, "struck by the wind," meaning they are hit by the continuous *Pravaha* wind facing westward. Just as the eastward motion produced by the support [of the spheres] is not directly perceived, so too this movement of attraction, which is a modification of the eastward motion, is not perceived because of the dominance of the rotation of the *Pravaha* wind. This is the intent. || 11 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** Due to this motion, their "plus" and "minus" [corrections] are extremely large. In this way, being pulled in the path of the sky, they move with the help of the wind. || 11 ||

<summary>This page explains that the five planets (Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn) require larger orbital corrections than the Sun or Moon because their smaller physical size makes them more susceptible to the "pull" of the deities residing at their orbital apogees. It clarifies that these corrections are invisible to the naked eye because they are masked by the powerful westward-driving celestial wind (Pravaha).</summary>
