# Chapter 2 ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries ( 41 )

Now, he describes the eightfold nature of the motion of the planets, such as Mars and others, whose causes and collections have been grasped:

->**Retrograde, sub-retrograde, crooked, slow, very slow, and even;**<-

The motion of the planets—Mars and the others, excluding the Sun and Moon <note>The Sun and Moon are never retrograde in Indian astronomy</note>—is of eight types for the purpose of predicting results. Among these, the six types from "retrograde" to "even" are mentioned, along with the two motions "very fast" and "fast." The word "likewise" serves as a conjunction. The specific definitions of these motions will be clarified further on. || 12 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** Retrograde, sub-retrograde, crooked, slow, very slow, even, fast, and very fast—these are the eight types of motion. || 12 ||

Now, he categorizes this eightfold motion into two primary divisions:

->**Among these, very fast, fast, slow, very slow, and even—**<-
->**these five are known as "direct"; that which is retrograde includes sub-retrograde. || 13 ||**<-

Among those eight types of motion, the five starting from "very fast" up to "even" are to be known as "direct" <term>Rijvi (direct/straight): the normal forward motion of a planet through the zodiac</term> motion. That motion which exists alongside sub-retrograde and crooked motion—referred to in the previous verse by the names sub-retrograde and crooked—is known as "retrograde" motion. Thus, for the planets starting with Mars, there are two general categories of motion <note>Direct and Retrograde</note>. || 13 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** Among them, very fast, fast, slow, very slow, and even are the five "straight" motions; crooked, retrograde, and sub-retrograde are the three "retrograde" motions. || 13 ||

Now, he promises to explain the process for calculating the "true" (corrected) positions of the planets:

->**the "correction" so that the planets daily attain correspondence with observation. || 14 ||**<-

"Daily" means every day. "According to those respective motions" means that because the motions change—fast one day, very fast the next—the calculation must follow that relationship. I shall explain the "correction" <term>Sphutikarana: the mathematical process of converting a mean planetary position into a true, observable position</term>, which is the mathematical method by which the planets like the Sun and others reach "correspondence with observation" <term>Driktulyata: the state where the calculated position matches the observed position in the sky</term>. I say "carefully" to indicate the removal of any inconsistencies. I will speak of this by explaining the subtle principles. || 14 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** Governed by these motions, the planets always attain correspondence with observation. I will now describe that same "correction" with due respect. || 14 ||

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Two]

### By dividing the preceding sums by the first, and adding the result to the difference,
### there are twenty-four segments; these are the sine-sums in order. || 16 ||

The eighth part of the minutes in a single sign (1800') is 225 <note>original: "tattvashvi" (225)</note>. This first value is called the first whole sine-segment <term>Jyārdhapiṇḍa: the half-chord or sine value</term>. From this first sine, the others are derived. By dividing the first sine by itself, the quotient is subtracted from the first sine; the result is then added to the first sine to produce the second sine-segment. The first value is doubled and decreased by one. To bring forth the third and subsequent values, the following method is applied: "By the first." This means by the first sine-segment (225). 

In this manner, by dividing the established sums by the first segment, the first segment is diminished by the resulting quotients; these adjusted segments, when added to the preceding established sine-sums, become the new sine-sums. 

For example:
*   The first segment is 225. Divided by the first (225), the result is 1.
*   The second segment is 449. Divided by the first, the result is 2 <note>The text notes that fractions greater than half are rounded up to the next whole number according to tradition</note>.
*   The first segment (225) minus the sum of previous results (1) equals 224. Adding this to the second segment (449) gives the third: 671.
*   This (671) divided by the first segment gives a result of 3. The sum of previous results (3) is added to the next, making 6. The first segment (225) minus this sum (6) is 219. Adding 219 to the third (671) gives the fourth: 890.
*   This (890) divided by the first segment gives 4. The first segment minus the previous sum (219) is the difference; subtracting 4 gives 215. Adding 215 to the fourth gives the fifth: 1105.

And so on, following this rule. Regarding the rule for the number of segments, it says: "there are." Thus, twenty-four sine-segments are to be calculated, and no more. 

Here, one should note the position in the *Brahma-Siddhanta* <note>The astronomical treatise by Brahmagupta, c. 628 CE</note> which states: "From the twenty-first, the twentieth, and after the fifteenth; from the seventh, twelfth, and seventeenth, a half-unit increase is not accepted." This is because the calculation must remain unaltered. 

Why are the established sums not stated directly? He says: "In order." These established sums are stated in a regular sequence. 

**The Proof:** On level ground, a circle is marked with the minutes of the zodiac. It is divided into four parts by horizontal and vertical diameter lines. Counting equal divisions on both sides from where the vertical line meets the circumference, a cord tied between those two points is the "full chord" of the full arc. In this calculation, since only the "half-chord" <term>Jyārdha: Sine</term> from the vertical line is needed, the half-chord of that half-arc is used. Thus, in a quadrant of the circle, the desired half-chords of the desired arcs are calculated from the vertical line. 

There, the Lord <note>referring to the Sun God, the revealed author of the text</note> by his own will, envisioned twenty-four sines in a quadrant of three signs (90°). The knowledge of this comes from the marking of the circle's minutes; the radius of that circumference is the final sine of the three signs. If for a circumference of 3927 <note>original: "Bhanamdagni"</note> the diameter is 1250 <note>original: "Kabanhasurya"</note>, then what is the diameter for a circumference of 21600 minutes? By this proportion, the diameter is calculated: 21600 multiplied by 1250 equals 27,000,000. Divided by 3927, the diameter is 6876. Half of this is the final sine: 3438. 

Now, regarding the distinction between the arc and the sine in the circle: although they are unequal, the Lord considers a certain portion of the circle to be equal [to the sine], otherwise the calculation...

# Chapter 2 | With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries ( 43 )

Thinking that in the beginning of the arc, there would be no deviation like a mustard seed <note>meaning the curve is so slight it appears straight</note>, the sine of that portion is considered equal to the arc itself. As stated by Shakalya: "The ninety-sixth part of a circle appears like a straight staff." The eighth part of the minutes in one sign <note>30 degrees or 1800 minutes</note>, which is the first sine-arc division, is 225 <term>Tattvashvi: a numerical code where Tattva=25 and Ashvi=2; read right-to-left as 225</term>. With this measure as the first arc, and using this interval, there are twenty-four desired sines. 

Now, since the twenty-four sines increase successively, their differences (sine-segments) must decrease successively, as is visible when marking sines on a circle. The difference between these sine-segments increases successively. The difference between the differences of the 22nd, 23rd, and 24th sines is the maximum segment-difference, determined by the method of calculating precise sines as 15 | 16 | 48. Now, by proportion: if this is the segment-difference for the Radius, what will it be for the first sine? By dividing the first sine by 225, the result is the difference between the first and second segments. Subtracting this from the first segment gives the second segment. Here, the first segment is equal to the first sine. Adding the second segment to the first sine gives the second sine. Similarly, the second segment divided by 225 gives the difference between the second and third segments; subtracting this from the second segment gives the third segment, which added to the second sine gives the third sine. This continues for the fourth and so on. In some places, where a fraction exceeds a half, it is rounded up to one to account for potential cumulative errors in the latter half. Thus, the two verses are explained. || 15 || 16 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The eighth part of the minutes of a sign (1800) is the first sine-half (225). Dividing that by itself, subtracting the quotient from the original, and adding it to the previous value gives the second sine-half. || 15 || By successively dividing the previous accumulated sums by 225, collecting the quotients, subtracting them from 225, and adding the result to the previous segment, the segments are formed. In this manner, the following 24 sine-half totals are fixed. || 16 ||

In the same collection: Take the previously mentioned Sine portions (Kramajya). By subtracting each of them in reverse order—starting from the penultimate portion back to the first—from the Radius <term>Trijya; the radius of a circle, literally "the sine of three signs"</term> (which represents the maximum portion), the Versed Sine portions are produced in sequence. 

For example, the 23rd Sine portion mentioned as "3431" <note>original: "rupagnisaraguna"</note> and "3438" <note>original: "vasvagnikrtavahnayah"</note>—when the former is subtracted from the final portion (the radius), the first Versed Sine portion is obtained. Similarly, the 22nd portion subtracted from the final gives the second Versed Sine portion. Proceeding in this manner, there are twenty-four Versed Sine portions. 

**The Logic:**
The Versed Sine is the difference in the form of an arrow <term>Bana; the segment of the radius between the sine and the arc</term> between the arc and the sine. Although, unlike the Sine of the first half-quadrant, a "half-arrow" does not technically exist, it is appropriate to call these "Versed Sine portions" <note>original: Utkramajya-pinda</note> rather than "half-portions." However, the Lord <note>referring to the divine origin of the Surya Siddhanta</note> used the term "half-versed sine" to follow established terminology, as the Versed Sine represents the full segment of the arrow when the outer arc-segment is absent. 

Furthermore, in a quadrant of a circle, when all sines are marked, the amount by which a sine is less than the radius is clearly seen to be the Versed Sine of its complementary degrees. Therefore, to find the Versed Sine using the stated Sine portions, the radius is reduced by those portions in reverse order. This explains the instruction "by subtracting" etc. || 17-22 ||

Now, in five verses, the author records the previously established Versed Sine portions:

> Seven, nine, and two (297); six and six (66); seven and seven (77);
> Eight, one, and zero (108); six, three, and two (236); four, five, and three (354); || 23 ||
> Zero, six, and four (460); nine, four, and five (549); zero, seven, and eight (870);
> Seven, zero, zero, and one (1007); one, seven, and eleven (1171); || 24 ||
> Five, four, and three (345); eight, two, five, and one (1528);
> Nine, one, seven, and one (1719); eight, one, nine, and one (1918); || 25 ||
> Three, two, one, and two (2123); three, three, three, and two (2333);
> Eight, four, five, and two (2548); seven, six, seven, and two (2767); || 26 ||
> Nine, eight, nine, and two (2989); three, one, two, and three (3213);
> Eight, three, four, and three (3438) are the Versed Sine portions. || 27 ||

These Versed Sine portions are recorded as previously established. "Mountain" <note>symbolic number for 7</note> and so on are used. It should be noted that when the Sine is zero, the Versed Sine of the complement is at its maximum; thus, the radius minus zero sine equals the radius, which is the final Versed Sine portion. Since the radius is the maximum in both cases, the final portion is established by the logic of the calculation. || 23-27 ||

Now, by way of context, while stating the sine of the maximum declination, he describes the method for calculating declination:

## The sine of the maximum declination is 1397.
## The sine [of the longitude] multiplied by that and divided by the radius; the arc of that result is called the declination. || 28 ||

The sine of the maximum declination <term>Paramāpakramajyā | the sine of the greatest distance from the celestial equator</term> is 1397 <note>original: "saptarandhraguṇendavaḥ" - a mnemonic code where sapta=7, randhra=9, guṇa=3, indu=1, read backwards as 1397</note>. The sine of the desired longitude multiplied by the maximum declination sine and divided by the radius <term>Trijyā | the total sine of 90 degrees, 3438</term> gives a result; the arc of this result, in minutes, is called the declination <term>Krānti | the angular distance of a planet north or south of the celestial equator</term> by those who know the truth. 

The logic here: Declination is the north-south distance of a point on the ecliptic from the celestial equator. At the beginning of Aries or Libra, there is no distance. At the beginning of Cancer or Capricorn, the distance is at its maximum. Therefore, the declination is proportional to the sine of the longitude. The proportion is: if for a radius-sized sine the declination is the maximum sine, then for the desired sine, what is it? The resulting arc is the declination in minutes. || 28 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The sine of maximum declination is 1397. Multiplying this by the sine [of the planet's longitude] and dividing by the radius (3438) gives the sine of the declination. Converting this sine back into an arc gives the declination. || 28 ||

Now, to calculate the equation, he explains how to find the base and perpendicular sines from the anomaly:

## Subtract the planet from its slow anomaly, and likewise from its fast anomaly.
## The remainder is the anomaly; from that, find the base sine and perpendicular sine. || 29 ||

Subtract the planet's position (in signs, degrees, etc.) from the previously calculated position of its <term>Mandocca | slow apogee/aphelion</term> and from its <term>Śīghrocca | fast apogee/conjunction</term>. The remainder is the <term>Kendra | anomaly</term>. A planet subtracted from its slow apogee is the "slow anomaly" (Manda-kendra). A planet subtracted from its fast apogee is the "fast anomaly" (Śīghra-kendra). From that anomaly, one should determine the quadrant—odd or even—consisting of three signs each.

# Surya Siddhanta — Chapter Two

If the anomaly <note>kendra: the angular distance of a planet from its apsis</note> is within three signs <note>90 degrees</note>, it is in the first **odd** quadrant. If it is within six signs, the anomaly minus three signs is the second **even** quadrant. If within nine signs, the anomaly minus six signs is the third **odd** quadrant. If within twelve signs, the anomaly minus nine signs is the fourth **even** quadrant. From these quadrants, both the **sine of the base** <term>bhujajya: the sine of the arc</term> and the **sine of the complement** <term>kotijya: the cosine</term> are determined together. This means both are derived from a single calculation.

The reasoning here is as follows: Since the planets are said to be pulled by divine forces toward their high points <note>ucca: apogee or aphelion</note>, the "anomaly" is calculated by subtracting the high point from the planet's position to know the distance. The Lord <note>referring to the divine source of the text</note> established this anomaly as the interval between the planet and its high point according to His will. In either case, the base and complement remain consistent. In a circle marked with twelve signs, each of the four sections from the high point consists of three signs and is called a "quadrant" <term>pada</term>. To find which quadrant a planet occupies, the anomaly is reduced by zero, three, six, or nine signs, as the sines are contained within these quadrants. Thus, the sine and cosine are known from the quadrant occupied by the planet. // 29 //

**Hindi Commentary:** The anomaly is found by subtracting the mean planet from the slow high point <note>mandocca: apogee</note> or by subtracting the mean planet from the fast high point <note>shighrocca: apex of quick motion</note>. From the quadrant in which the anomaly falls, the sine and cosine are established. // 29 //

Now, one might ask: since the signs in a quadrant are uniform, how are the sine and cosine calculated? He says:

-> **In an odd quadrant, the sine is from the elapsed part and the cosine from the remaining part.** <-
-> **In an even quadrant, the sine is from the remaining part and the cosine from the elapsed part.** // 30 // <-

In an **odd** quadrant, the sine is derived from the "elapsed" <note>gata: the portion of the quadrant already traversed</note> signs and degrees. The cosine is derived from the "remaining" <note>gamya: the portion yet to be traversed</note>, which is the quadrant (three signs) minus the elapsed part. In an **even** quadrant, the sine is from the remaining part and the cosine is from the elapsed part. The word "but" <note>original: tu</note> indicates a distinction. Thus, both values are calculated from one position as described.

The reasoning is: In an odd quadrant, the result is produced according to the distance from the vertical line of the planet's high point. The half-chord within the circle representing that distance is the "base" <note>bhuja</note>, and its arc is the "elapsed" degrees on the circle. The distance from the horizontal line to the vertical center is the "complement" <note>koti</note>, which is equal to the radius minus the versed sine; its arc is the quadrant minus the base, hence the "remaining" part. In an even quadrant, the distance from the vertical line is the horizontal half-chord (base), and its arc is the "remaining" part; the distance from the horizontal line is the "complement," and its arc is the "elapsed" part of the quadrant. // 30 //

**Hindi Commentary:** In an odd quadrant, the sine comes from the elapsed and the cosine from the remaining. In an even quadrant, the sine comes from the remaining and the cosine from the elapsed. // 30 //

Now, he describes the method for calculating the sines for a desired time in two verses:

-> **Divide the minutes by 225; the quotient is the number of elapsed sine-segments.** <-
-> **Multiply the remainder by the difference between the elapsed and next sine-segments and divide by 225.** // 31 // <-

--- Page 61 ---
<page-num>47</page-num>
<header>Chapter 2 ] Including Sanskrit Commentary and Hindi Translation.</header>

->Add the result of that multiplication to the sine-segment known as the "passed" segment.<-
->This is the rule for the Sine; it is also prescribed for the Versine. || 32 ||<-

When one desires to calculate the sine of an arc-value within a quadrant, the arc should be converted into minutes. Divide these by 225 <note>original: "tattvashvibhih" (the number 225, representing the 225 minutes in each sine segment)</note>. The quotient indicates the number of "passed" sine-segments among the twenty-four previously mentioned segments. The next segment is the "to-be-passed" <note>the upcoming segment</note>. Previously, for the sake of defining their nature, they were called "half-chords" <term>jyardha: the geometric half-chord used in Indian trigonometry</term>, but now they are referred to simply as "sine-segments" <term>jyapinda</term> by dropping the "half" part. This is done because including the term "half" in mathematical operations causes confusion. It is not that they should be taken as double the previous segments; the "half" is omitted simply to avoid wordiness in calculation. 

Multiply the remainder of the division by the difference between the "passed" and "to-be-passed" segments, and divide by 225. The resulting minutes and seconds should be added to the "passed" sine-segment. For the Versine <term>utkramajya: the versed sine or 1 - cos</term>, the Sine of the desired arc-minutes is calculated in the same way. This method is stated for the Versine-segments. This means the Versine is found using the Versine-segments according to the same rule. 

**The Logic:** If 225 minutes correspond to one sine-segment, then how much for the desired minutes? By this proportion, the passed sine is found. Then, if 225 minutes yield the difference between the passed and the next segment, how much does the remaining arc-minutes yield? Adding this result to the passed sine gives the desired sine. || 31 || 32 ||

> **Hindi Translation:** Dividing the arc-minutes of the center by 225, the quotient shows how many sine-segments have passed. Multiply the remainder by the difference between the passed and the upcoming sine-segment and divide by 225. || 31 || Add the quotient to the passed sine-segment. In this way, the rule for the Sine and Versine is established. In the case of the Versine, the Versine-segment differences should be used. || 32 ||

Now, the author describes how to derive the arc from the sine:

->Subtract the [nearest] sine, multiply the remainder by 225, and divide by the difference.<-
->Add this to the product of the segment-count and 225; this is called the arc. || 33 ||<-

For whatever sine one wishes to find the arc, subtract the nearest smaller sine-segment from it. Multiply the remainder by 225 <note>original: "panchakriti" (the square of five, 25, multiplied by nine, or simply 225)</note> and divide by the difference between the subtracted segment and the next one. Take the number of the segment that was subtracted, multiply it by 225, and add the previous result to it. This is declared to be the arc. 

**The Logic:** The arc-minutes corresponding to the number of segments subtracted are found by multiplying that number by 225. Then, by the proportion: "If the difference between sines corresponds to 225 arc-minutes, then what does the remaining sine-value correspond to?", the additional minutes are found. Adding these makes the process easy to understand as the reverse of the previous rule. || 33 ||

> **Hindi Translation:** Subtract the nearest smaller sine-segment from the given sine. Multiply the remainder by 225 and divide by the difference between that smaller sine and the next sine. Adding this quotient to the product of the segment-count and 225 will yield the arc-minutes. || 33 ||

<margin>1</margin> If the center-sign etc. is less than 3 signs, it is the first quadrant; up to 6 signs is the second quadrant; up to 9 signs is the third quadrant; and the rest is within the fourth quadrant. The first and third quadrants are "odd," while the second and fourth are "even." "Passed" refers to how much of that quadrant has been traversed; "To-be-passed" refers to how much remains to complete that quadrant. That is, how much remains after separating it from the 3-sign markers. The center determined in this way is called the "Center-point." Here, there is no functional difference between the Sine <term>jya</term> and the Half-Sine <term>jyardha</term>.

It clarifies that while technically "half-chords," these values are treated as sines for ease of calculation using the base unit of 225 minutes.</summary>

# Surya Siddhanta: [Chapter Two]

Now, wishing to describe the degrees of the <term>Manda</term> epicycles <note>The 'Manda' epicycle relates to the equation of center, accounting for the elliptical-like eccentricity of an orbit</note> of the planets, the author first speaks of the Sun and the Moon:

> **The degrees of the Manda epicycle for the Sun are fourteen; for the Moon, thirty-two.**
> **At the end of even quadrants and odd quadrants, these are diminished by twenty minutes for both. || 34 ||**

The degrees of the <term>Manda</term> epicycle represent the arc on a circle—generated with a radius equal to the maximum equation—that corresponds to the degrees on the orbit. At the end of the even quadrants of the anomaly <note>0° and 180°</note>, when the Sun is at its perigee or apogee, these degrees are fourteen; for the Moon, they are thirty-two. At the end of the odd quadrants <note>90° and 270°</note>, which are three signs away from the perigee or apogee, the aforementioned degrees for the Sun and Moon are diminished by twenty minutes <note>1 degree = 60 minutes</note>. || 34 ||

**Commentary:** At the end of the even quadrants, the Sun's Manda circumference is 14°, and the Moon's is 32°. At the end of the odd quadrants, they are 20 minutes less (i.e., Sun 13° 40', Moon 31° 40'). || 34 ||

Now, he speaks of Mars and the other planets:

> **At the end of the even quadrants, [the degrees are] seventy-five, thirty, thirty-three, twelve, and forty-nine.**
> **In the odd [quadrants], they are seventy-two, twenty-eight, thirty-one, eleven, and forty-eight. || 35 ||**

For Mars, seventy-five; for Mercury, thirty; for Jupiter, thirty-three <note>The Sanskrit text 'surāḥ' (gods/33) is interpreted here</note>; for Venus, twelve; for Saturn, forty-nine. These are the previously mentioned Manda epicycle degrees for Mars and the others at the end of the even quadrants. In the odd quadrants, they are: for Mars, seventy-two; for Mercury, twenty-eight; for Jupiter, thirty-one; for Venus, eleven; and for Saturn, forty-eight. || 35 ||

**Commentary:** At the end of the even quadrants, the Manda circumference in degrees is: Mars 75, Mercury 30, Jupiter 33, Venus 12, Saturn 49. At the end of the odd quadrants: Mars 72, Mercury 28, Jupiter 31, Venus 11, Saturn 48. || 35 ||

Now, he states the degrees of the <term>Shighra</term> epicycles <note>The 'Shighra' epicycle accounts for the relative motion of the Earth and the planet, effectively converting heliocentric motion to geocentric observation</note> for Mars and the others at the end of the even quadrants:

> **For Mars and the others, the Shighra [degrees] at the end of the even quadrants are: two hundred thirty-five,**
> **one hundred thirty-three, seventy, two hundred sixty-two, and thirty-nine. || 36 ||**

Following the description of the Manda epicycles, the Shighra epicycle degrees at the end of the even quadrants are: for Mars, two hundred thirty-five; for Mercury, one hundred thirty-three; for Jupiter, seventy; for Venus, two hundred sixty-two; and for Saturn, thirty-nine. || 36 ||

**Commentary:** At the end of the even quadrants, the Shighra circumference degrees are: Mars 235, Mercury 133, Jupiter 70, Venus 262, Saturn 39. || 36 ||

Now, he states the Shighra epicycle degrees for these at the end of the odd quadrants:

> **At the end of the odd quadrants, they are [respectively] two hundred thirty-two, one hundred thirty-two, seventy-two,**
> **two hundred sixty, and forty; these are declared for the Shighra calculations. || 37 ||**

# Chapter 2 | With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries | ( 49 )

The circumferences <note>original: *paridhayah*; refers to the dimensions of the epicycles used to calculate planetary positions</note> for the "Fast" operations <note>original: *shighra-karmani*; the calculations for the second inequality of planetary motion, similar to the modern concept of relative motion from Earth</note> are stated at the end of the odd quadrants <note>original: *vishama-pada*; the 1st and 3rd quadrants of a circle (90° and 270°)</note> to achieve quick results. These Fast circumferences for Mars and the others follow the previous rules. For **Mars**, they are 232. For **Mercury**, 132. For **Jupiter**, 72. For **Venus**, 260. For **Saturn**, 40. It is mentioned here that since there is no "result" <note>correction</note> at the end of even quadrants, how can circumferences exist there? Therefore, because the maximum result occurs at the end of the odd quadrants, the circumferences are properly assigned there. Any doubt regarding the sequence of Saturn’s Slow and Fast circumferences being inconsistent with their definitions should be dismissed based on the authority of tradition <note>original: *agama-pramanya*</note>. As stated in the *Brahma-Siddhanta*: "Where sacred tradition is the authority, what use is mere logic, O Narada?" || 37 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** At the end of the odd quadrants, the Fast circumferences in degrees are: Mars 232, Mercury 132, Jupiter 72, Venus 260, Saturn 40. || 37 ||

### Now, he describes the method for calculating the circumference based on the desired anomaly:

> The sine of the anomaly <note>original: *bhujajya*</note> multiplied by the difference between the odd and even [circumferences] and divided by the radius <note>original: *trijya*</note> [gives the result]. This is added to or subtracted from the even circle circumference to find the true [circumference] depending on whether the odd is less or greater. || 38 ||

The sine of the anomaly <term>Bhujajya: the sine of the angular distance from the planet's apogee</term> for which the circumference is to be corrected, is multiplied by the difference between the circumferences at the odd and even quadrant ends. This is divided by the radius (3438'). The result is applied to the circumference at the even quadrant end. If the odd-quadrant circumference is less than the even, subtract; if greater, add. This gives the **True Circumference** <note>original: *sphuta-paridhi*</note>. The logic is: the difference between the even and odd quadrant circumferences accumulates according to the sine of the anomaly. If the radius gives the full difference, what does the desired sine give? This proportion is applied to the even circumference. || 38 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiply the sine of the anomaly by the difference between the odd and even circumferences and divide by the radius. By adding or subtracting this result from the even circumference, the True Circumference is obtained. If the odd end is greater than the even end, add the result; otherwise, subtract. || 38 ||

### Now, he describes the calculation of the Sine-results and the "Slow" correction:

> The sine and cosine of the anomaly multiplied by that [True Circumference] and divided by the degrees in a circle [360] give the results. The arc of that sine-result is the "Slow" correction <note>original: *manda-phala*</note> in minutes and so on. || 39 ||

The sine and cosine of the anomaly <note>the distance between the planet and its Slow or Fast apex</note> are multiplied by their respective True Circumferences and divided by 360. This produces the Sine-result <note>original: *bhujajya-phala*</note> and Cosine-result <note>original: *kotijya-phala*</note>. The arc of the result produced from the Slow anomaly is the "Slow" correction. **The Logic:** The deity at the high point <note>apogee</note> on the orbit pulls the planet-disk, which is threaded on a cord held in the deity's hand. By this attraction, the planet is pulled from its mean position on the orbit toward a position determined by the maximum correction, moving along a diagonal path <note>hypotenuse</note>. Thus, on a circle created with the maximum correction as the radius...

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Two]

The planet is located on the circumference of the epicycle at a distance from the "high point" <note>the apogee</note> equal to the mean anomaly, moving in a direction opposite to the order of the zodiac signs. On that epicycle, the horizontal distance from the vertical line is the **Sine of the Base-result** <term>Bhujaphala: the lateral displacement of the planet due to its elliptical-like path</term>, and the vertical distance from the horizontal diameter is the **Sine of the Perpendicular-result** <term>Kotiphala: the longitudinal displacement</term>. These are proportional to the maximum possible correction. Since these results are on the epicycle, they are calculated by the proportion: if the full circle of 360 degrees gives the given circumference of the epicycle, then what do the Sine of the base and perpendicular of the anomaly give?

The true position of the planet is where the line connecting the center of the Earth to the planet on its epicycle intersects the celestial circle. The arc distance on the celestial circle between the mean planet and this intersection is the "result" <note>the correction</note>. The Lord <note>the author/divine source</note> has accepted the **Base-result** as the **Sine of the Manda-correction** without further division by the hypotenuse, because the **Manda-hypotenuse** <term>Manda-karna</term> is very close to the value of the **Radius** <term>Trijya</term>, and the difference is negligible. The arc of that Sine is the Manda-correction. All this is explained for understanding, and the diagrammatic representation follows. || 39 ||

*Commentary: By multiplying the circumference by the Sine of the base and perpendicular and dividing by 360, the Base-result and Perpendicular-result are obtained. From the arc of the Base-result, the Manda-correction is determined.* || 39 ||

### Now, the Shighra-correction is described in three verses:

> The Shighra Perpendicular-result is added to the radius when the anomaly is in the six signs beginning with Capricorn. It is subtracted from the radius when the anomaly is in the six signs beginning with Cancer. || 40 ||
> The square root of the sum of the squares of that <insert>adjusted radius</insert> and the Base-result is the hypotenuse, called the **Variable Hypotenuse** <term>Chala-karna</term>. The Base-result multiplied by the radius and divided by the Variable Hypotenuse... || 41 ||
> ...the arc of the result obtained is the Shighra-correction in minutes and so on. This is applied in the first and fourth operations for Mars and the other planets. || 42 ||

The **Shighra Perpendicular-result** is added to the radius when the Shighra-anomaly is in the six signs starting with Capricorn <note>Signs 10, 11, 12, 1, 2, 3</note>. In the six signs starting with Cancer <note>Signs 4 through 9</note>, <unclear>the result</unclear> produced from the perpendicular is subtracted from the radius. This specific process distinguishes it from the Manda-hypotenuse calculation. The square root of the sum of the squares of the adjusted radius and the Base-result is the **Shighra-hypotenuse**. The Base-result is multiplied by the radius and divided by this Shighra-hypotenuse; the arc of that value is the Shighra-correction. This correction for Mars and the others is used in the first and fourth steps of the calculation. The word "and" implies it is not used in the second and third steps, where the Manda-correction is instead applied.

The logic <term>Upapatti</term> is as follows: From the position of the "Manda-corrected" planet on the celestial circle, the physical body of the planet is pulled toward the **Shighra-high-point** <note>the point of conjunction, often related to the Sun's position</note> by the deity of that point using a "cord" consisting of the maximum Shighra-sine. Because of this pull from the Manda-corrected position...

# Chapter 2. With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries ( 51 )

In the process known as **Shighra** <note>The "fast" correction, relating to the planet's conjunction with the Sun</note>, following the previous method, the planetary disc is positioned from the point of the **Shighra-uchcha** <note>apex of fast motion/apogee</note> by the distance of the **Shighra-kendra** <note>anomaly of conjunction</note> in a direction opposite to the orbital path. There, as before, the **Kotiphala** <note>cosine result</note> and **Bhujaphala** <note>sine result</note> serve as the vertical and horizontal sides. From the transverse line of the orbit, at a distance of the **Trijya** <note>radius</note> of the **Shighra-nichochcha-vritta** <note>epicycle of fast motion</note> transverse diameter, the **Kotiphala** is added to the **Trijya** when in the signs beginning with Capricorn. In the signs beginning with Cancer, the **Kotiphala** is subtracted from the **Trijya**. The **Koti** <note>adjacent side</note> is the string-like distance between the planet on the epicycle and the horizontal line of the Earth. The distance between the base of the **Koti** and the center is equal to the **Bhujaphala**, which is the **Bhuja** <note>opposite side</note>. The line from the Earth's center to the planet is the **Karna** <note>hypotenuse</note>.

The square root of the sum of the squares of the **Koti** and **Bhujaphala** gives the **Karna** <note>hypotenuse</note> in the orbit. Where this hypotenuse meets the orbit is the **Spashta** <note>true/corrected</note> position of the planet. The arc-shaped line from the orbital center-line to the true position is the **Shighraphala-jya** <note>sine of the fast correction</note>. By proportion: if the **Bhujaphala** is at the end of the **Shighra-karna**, what will it be at the end of the **Trijya**? The arc of this result is the **Shighraphala**, which is the difference between the **Manda-spashta** <note>corrected for slow motion</note> and the final **Spashta** <note>true</note> planetary positions. Now, to find the center of the epicycle, the **Manda-spashta** position is necessary. Then, by applying the **Shighraphala** correction, the true position is known. Here, the mean planet corrected by the **Mandaphala** <note>slow/equation of center correction</note> is called **Manda-spashta** (refined). To achieve near-true accuracy for the mean planet, these corrections are necessary. First, the **Mandaphala** calculated from a mean planet already corrected by the **Shighraphala** is more accurate; thus, the **Mandaphala** derived from the **Shighra**-corrected mean planet should be applied to the mean planet to bring it closer to the true position. ॥ 40 ॥ 41 ॥ 42 ॥

**Hindi Commentary—** In the **Shighra** calculation, the **Kotiphala** <term>result of the cosine</term> must be added to the **Trijya** <term>radius</term> in the 6 signs starting from Capricorn and subtracted in those starting from Cancer. By adding the square of this sum to the square of the **Shighra** **Bhujaphala** <term>result of the sine</term> and taking the square root, the **Shighra-karna** <term>fast hypotenuse</term> is found. Multiplying the **Shighra Bhujaphala** by the **Trijya** and dividing by the **Shighra-karna** gives a value; determining the **Dhanu** <term>arc/bow</term> according to that value yields the **Shighraphala**. This **Shighraphala** is required for the first and fourth corrections of Mars and the other planets. ॥ 40 ॥ 41 ॥ 42 ॥

Now, a question arises: since the Sun and Moon lack a **Shighraphala**, how is their true position determined? Answering this, the author clarifies the process for Mars and the others:

> For the Sun and Moon, there is only one **Manda** operation. For Mars and the others, it is said:
> **Shighra**, **Manda**, then **Manda** again, and **Shighra**—four in sequence. ॥ 43 ॥

For the Sun and Moon, there is only one **Manda** <note>slow/equation of center</note> operation; because they lack a **Shighraphala**, their true position is found by the **Mandaphala** alone. By saying "one," it means the **Mandaphala** is calculated only once. Since the center of the **Manda-nichochcha-mandala** <term>slow epicycle</term> is known from the mean planet, the logic is clear that no other operation is needed. Next, the process for Mars and the others is described. What was mentioned before is now stated clearly: First, the **Shighraphala** calculated from the mean planet is applied to the mean planet. From this, the **Mandaphala** is calculated and applied. From that result, a second **Mandaphala** is calculated and applied to the mean planet to get the **Manda-spashta**. Finally, the **Shighraphala** is calculated from that and applied. Thus, there are four operations in sequence; this is the meaning of the previous statement. ॥ 43 ॥

**Hindi Commentary—** For the Sun and Moon, the **Mandya-karma** <term>slow correction</term> is a single correction. For Mars and the others, there are four corrections in order: **Shaighrya** <term>fast</term>, **Mandya** <term>slow</term>, **Mandya** again, and finally **Shaighrya**. ॥ 43 ॥

<page-num>52</page-num>
<header>( 52 ) Surya Siddhanta — [ Chapter Two ]</header>

Now, he describes a specific rule in this context:

> ->Apply half of the *shighra-phala* <note>equation of conjunction</note> to the mean planet, then half of the *manda-phala* <note>equation of center</note>.<-
> ->Then apply the full *manda-phala* to the mean planet, followed by the full *shighra-phala*. || 44 ||<-

One should apply half of the calculated *shighra-phala* to the mean planet. From that result, one calculates half of the *manda-phala* and applies it to the same. The resulting value is the "half-corrected" planet. From this, the full *manda-phala* is calculated and applied to the mean planet to obtain the *manda-spashta* <note>the planet corrected for its elliptical orbit</note>. Finally, the full *shighra-phala* is calculated from that and applied. The word "and" implies the sequence. The word "only" emphasizes that the true planet is obtained only through this method and no other. 

**The Logic:** The *manda-phala* should ideally be calculated from the true position, but the true position itself depends on the *manda-phala*. To resolve this circular dependency <note>original: "anyonya-ashraya"</note>, the Lord <note>Surya</note> provided a method of successive approximations. By using half-corrections, we arrive at a position closer to the truth than using the mean planet alone.

**Vernacular Commentary:** Apply half of the *shighra* correction to the mean planet (addition or subtraction per verse 45). Using that result, find half of the *manda* correction and apply it. Then, using that doubly-corrected position, find the full *manda* correction and apply it to the original mean planet. Finally, find the full *shighra* correction based on that result and apply it to get the *sphuta* <note>true/clear</note> longitude. || 44 ||

Now, if one asks how these corrections should be applied (added or subtracted), he says:

> ->In the *ajadi* <note>Aries etc.</note> half of the anomaly, for all planets in both *shighra* and *manda* operations,<-
> ->The minutes of arc are additive; in the *tuladi* <note>Libra etc.</note> half, they are subtractive. || 45 ||<-

For all planets, in both the *shighra* and *manda* processes, the correction in minutes should be added if the *kendra* <note>anomaly/angular distance</note> falls within the six signs starting from Aries. It should be subtracted if the *kendra* falls within the six signs starting from Libra. The word "and" establishes the rule, and "only" confirms that despite different calculation methods for the two types of equations, the rule for addition and subtraction remains the same. 

**The Logic:** As stated previously, when the pull is forward, the correction is positive (additive); when the pull is backward, it is negative (subtractive). When the anomaly is measured from the planet to its *uchcha* <note>apex/apsis</note>, the forward pull corresponds to the Aries-half of the circle, and the backward pull to the Libra-half. || 45 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** In the Aries-centered anomaly, the *shighra* and *manda* corrections of the planets should be added, and in the Libra-centered anomaly, the results (in degrees/minutes) should be subtracted. || 45 ||

<header>Chapter 2. ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. ( 53 )</header>

## Now he describes the correction for the difference in the Sun's arc (Bhujantara-phala) for the planets—

### **The motion of the planet, multiplied by the Sun’s arc-correction and divided by the minutes of the zodiac, results in minutes that should be applied to the planet just as they are to the Sun. || 46 ||**

The true motion of the planets, such as the Sun and others, is multiplied by the Sun’s arc-correction <note>original: *mandaphala*, the correction for the equation of center</note> in minutes, and divided by the total minutes in the twelve signs of the zodiac, which is twenty-one thousand and six hundred (21,600). The resulting minutes should be applied to the planets, such as the Sun and others, in the same way as the Sun’s correction—meaning they should be added or subtracted according to whether the Sun’s correction is positive or negative. This is the meaning of the word "should be done" <note>original: *kāryāḥ*</note>; the word "but" <note>original: *tu*</note> implies the operation of addition or subtraction.

The reasoning <note>original: *upapatti*</note> is as follows: Since the calculation of the total elapsed days <note>term: *ahargaṇa* - the count of days since the beginning of the epoch</note> is based on a uniform mean measure, the planets derived from it are accurate for mean midnight. At mean midnight, the mean Sun is at the lower meridian on the ecliptic. From this time, true midnight—defined by the true Sun crossing the lower meridian—occurs either before or after, depending on the positive or negative value of the Sun's correction. Therefore, because of the time associated with the movement of the minutes of the correction, the planet at the time of true midnight will be slightly different from its position at mean midnight. By this operation, the planets are adjusted to the time of true midnight. It was previously argued that this correction is not for the Sun itself, as the Sun is already at true midnight; however, this is refuted here. If the other planets are at mean midnight while the Sun is at true midnight, there would be a lack of temporal consistency in the day-count. 

Furthermore, the time for the minutes of the correction is found by the proportion: if the rising periods <note>original: *udayasavaḥ*</note> of the signs are obtained for the minutes of a sign, then what is obtained for the minutes of the correction? Then, using the daily rotation of the earth, if the daily motion is obtained for the total breaths of a day, what is obtained for the breaths of the correction? Thus, it is established that the correction should be added or subtracted based on the Sun's correction. Here, the Lord <note>referring to the author or the Sun God</note>, out of compassion for the world, has simplified this: assuming the planet's motion over a sidereal day, if the motion occurs in the minutes of a full circle (21,600), what motion occurs during the displacement caused by the Sun's correction? This single proportion is used for ease of calculation. || 46 ||

<term>Hindi Commentary</term>—Multiply the planet's daily motion by the Sun's arc-correction <note>original: *bhuja-māndya-phala*</note> and divide by 21,600. The resulting minutes should be applied as a correction to the planets. That is, if the Sun's correction is added to reach the true time, add it; if it is subtracted, subtract it. || 46 ||

## Now, wishing to describe the true motion, he first states the specific rule for the Moon—

### **The mean motion of the Moon, diminished by the motion of its own slow-point (apogee), is the basis. Having calculated the difference of the sine of the arc, the correction to the motion becomes negative or positive. || 47 ||**

In the method for calculating planetary motion to be described, the "result of motion" <note>original: *gatiphala*</note> is calculated from the planet's motion. However, for the Moon's motion, the result is not calculated directly. Instead, the mean motion of the Moon should be diminished by the daily motion of its own "slow-point" <note>term: *mandocca* - apogee</note>. From that resultant motion, the "difference of the sine of the arc" <note>original: *dorjyāntara*</note> and so on are used. Since the result of the motion arises from this difference of sines—as will be explained in the rule "motion is the multiplier of the difference of sines"—the correction is then added to or subtracted from the Moon's mean motion according to the upcoming rules. The reasoning for this is...

<page-num>54</page-num>
<header>The Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter 2]</header>

By the phrase "established by the motion of the center," it is meant that for the Sun and other planets (excluding the Moon), the motion of their *Mandocca* <note>The apogee, or the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note> is extremely slow; therefore, the correction for their velocity is stated based on their own mean motion. In the case of the Moon, because its *Mandocca* moves significantly, the correction is calculated using the "motion of the center" (the mean motion of the Moon minus the motion of its apogee). To avoid the confusion that the correction should be applied to the motion from which it was derived, the text specifies "in the Moon's motion." Otherwise, one might mistakenly calculate the clarity of the center's motion rather than the Moon's actual velocity. || 47 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In the Moon's daily motion, after subtracting its *Mandocca* motion (as described below) and calculating the difference in the sines (*dorjyantara*), the "true velocity" (*spashta-gati*) is obtained by adding to or subtracting from the mean motion. || 47 ||

Now, with two verses, the author explains the method for bringing forth the velocity correction, preceded by an indication of the theory behind the corrected velocity of the planets:

### The correction for the planet's motion should be performed like the *Manda* process for the planet itself.
### The daily motion is multiplied by the difference of the sines and divided by 225. || 48 ||
### Then, multiplied by the planet's own *Manda* circumference and divided by the degrees in a circle (360), the result is in minutes.
### This is added in the signs beginning with Cancer, and subtracted in those beginning with Capricorn. || 49 ||

"For the *Manda* operations" means for the purpose of calculating the correction for the slow motion. Following the method for finding a planet's *Manda* correction—multiplying by the circumference and dividing by the degrees of the circle—one should calculate the minutes of the planet's *Manda* velocity correction from the planet's motion. Just as the *Manda* correction was calculated from the sine of the anomaly, this velocity correction is calculated from the planet's motion. Specifically, since the difference between two *Manda* corrections for successive days constitutes the velocity correction, the result is the difference between the sines of the anomalies. This difference in sines is determined by the "sine-segments" <note>standard trigonometric tables used in ancient Indian astronomy</note> measured by 225. He explains this: "multiplied by the difference of the sines." The mean motion of the planet is treated as the motion of the center, as the motion of the apogee is negligible. It is multiplied by the difference between the current and next sine-segments used during the calculation of the *Bhujajya* <note>the sine of the arc</note> and divided by 225. Then, it is multiplied by the corrected *Manda* circumference and divided by 360. The result is the minutes of the velocity correction. Although it is technically proper to find the arc of the sine of the velocity, since the planet's motion is less than 225, the sine and the arc are essentially equal, so there is no harm in omitting that step. For the Moon, the slight difference is ignored. To achieve the "true-clear" velocity, he describes the adjustment to the mean motion: "In Cancer, etc." In the mean motion of the planet, the previously calculated result is added if the center is within the six signs starting with Cancer, and subtracted if within the six signs starting with Capricorn. The word "but" (*tu*) implies that the true velocity is thus established. The rationale is: when a negative correction is increasing, the next value is less than the previous, so the difference is subtracted from the motion. When a negative correction is decreasing, the difference is added. When a positive correction is increasing, the difference is added. The decrease of negative correction occurs in the three signs before Capricorn; the increase of positive correction occurs in the three signs before Libra. Thus, in the center starting with Cancer, the velocity correction is positive.

# Chapter 2 | With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries

If the subsequent result is less than the previous result, the difference is subtractive. The decrease of the additive result occurs in the three signs starting from Cancer; the increase of the subtractive result occurs in the three signs starting from Aries. Thus, in the center starting from Capricorn, the velocity correction is proven to be subtractive. **[48–49]**

**Hindi Commentary:** In the place of the remaining "slow" <term>Manda: the correction for the planet's elliptical orbit</term> process, multiply the difference of the sine of the anomaly by the daily motion and divide by 225. Multiply that quotient by the corrected circumference and divide by 360 to get the result in minutes of arc. In the center starting from Cancer, add this to the motion; in the center starting from Capricorn, subtract it to find the "slow-corrected" velocity. **[48–49]**

Now, he explains the calculation of the true velocity in two verses:

-> Subtract the "slow-corrected" velocity from the velocity of the "fast apex" <term>Shighrochcha: the highest point of the fast anomaly, often corresponding to the mean Sun</term>. Multiply that remainder by the difference between the radius and the variable hypotenuse. **[50]** <-

-> Divide by the variable hypotenuse. Add this to the velocity if the hypotenuse is greater than the radius; subtract if it is less. If the result to be subtracted is greater than the velocity itself, the remainder becomes the retrograde motion. **[51]** <-

Having subtracted the previously established "slow-corrected" velocity from the velocity of the fast apex, multiply the remainder by the difference between the radius and the final "fast" hypotenuse. <note>The author notes that for consistency across texts, "radius" here refers to the cosine of the second fast result.</note> Divide the product by the second fast hypotenuse. If this hypotenuse is greater than the radius (the cosine of the result), add the quotient to the slow-corrected velocity; if it is less, subtract it. This yields the **true velocity**. 

Now, what if the velocity correction is greater than the slow-corrected velocity itself? In that case, subtraction seems impossible. This is not an impossible scenario; when a planet is near its perigee, the hypotenuse is smaller than the difference of the cosine, making the correction necessarily larger than the slow-corrected velocity. Therefore, he says: *If it is greater*. Subtract the slow-corrected velocity from the larger correction; the remainder is the **retrograde motion** (backward motion or westward motion). Thus, there is no error in the logic.

**The Derivation:** "The daily motion of the fast anomaly, multiplied by the difference of the result and divided by the hypotenuse, should be subtracted from its own fast velocity to find the true planet's motion; if the subtraction is reversed, the remainder is retrograde." This is the precise method stated in the *Crown of Treatises* <note>original: "Siddhanta Shiromani"</note> and the *Treatise of Elder Vasistha*. The explanation is clear in those commentaries. For the sake of the fast anomaly's motion, the first half was stated. This motion is multiplied by the cosine and divided by the hypotenuse, and the result is subtracted from the velocity of the fast apex. To simplify the calculation using a common denominator, the fast apex velocity is first multiplied by the hypotenuse... <note>The text continues to explain the algebraic simplification of multiplying the center's motion by the difference between the hypotenuse and cosine to save steps.</note>

# Surya Siddhanta: [Chapter Two]

Because the velocity is greater, when subtracted from the velocity of the swift apex <note>shighrocha</note>, the result of the velocity correction <note>gati-phala</note>—which is greater due to the loss of the swift anomaly's velocity—is ultimately subtracted from the slow-corrected velocity <note>manda-spashta-gati</note>. When the hypotenuse <note>karna</note> is greater, the result of the previous method is less than the velocity of the swift anomaly; when that lesser value is subtracted from the swift apex velocity, the resulting value is greater than the slow-corrected velocity, which is then established as the true velocity <note>spashta-gati</note>. Here, by taking the velocity of the swift anomaly in place of the swift apex velocity, the resulting correction is indeed the velocity correction. This is added to or subtracted from the slow-corrected velocity depending on whether the hypotenuse is greater or less than the cosine of the correction; this is established in the section ending with "eight." If the negative correction is greater than the slow-corrected velocity, the remainder after reverse subtraction is the true velocity in a westward direction <note>retrograde</note>; thus, the entire logic is faultless. || 50-51 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Subtract the slow-corrected velocity from the swift motion and multiply by the difference between the radius <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: trijya</note> and the second swift hypotenuse. Divide the product by the second swift hypotenuse. The result should be added to the slow-corrected motion if the second swift hypotenuse is greater than the radius; otherwise, it should be subtracted to find the true velocity. If the result of subtraction is negative, the motion becomes retrograde <note>vakra-gati</note>. || 50-51 ||

### Now he explains the reasoning for retrograde motion—

->**When planets are far from their swift apex, with their rays slackened,**<-
->**their bodies are pulled to the left or right, and their motion becomes retrograde. || 52 ||**<-

When a planet (Mars and the others) is situated far from its swift apex—separated by more than three signs <note>90 degrees</note>—it is pulled by "slackened rays," which are the ropes of the planetary disks held in the hands of the deities of the swift apex. Its body (the physical disk) is pulled to the left or right of the deity; at that time, the motion becomes retrograde. The idea is this: a planet separated by less than three signs can be pulled by the deities with taut circular ropes, but a planet separated by more than three signs cannot be pulled by the deities with slackened circular ropes. Therefore, in place of a small positive or negative correction, the planet becomes retrograde. Due to the lack of strong attraction, it is possible for an object on a circular path to move downward <note>backward</note>. || 52 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Remaining far from their swift apex, the planets are pulled to the right and left with slackened rays—that is, with diminished force—and from this, retrograde motion occurs. || 52 ||

### Now, he describes the degrees of anomaly at which the velocity correction is negative and equal to the slow-corrected velocity—marking the start and end of retrogradation—in two verses, to provide a method for knowing the beginning and end of a planet's retrograde state without constant velocity calculations:

->**At the anomaly degrees of 164, 144, 130, 163,**<-
->**and 115 for the fourth, Mars and the others**<-
->**become retrograde. When these degrees are subtracted from a full circle <note>360 degrees</note>,**<-
->**at those remaining degrees of their own anomalies, they abandon their retrogradation. || 53-54 ||**<-

# Chapter 2: With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries (Page 57)

Mars and the other planets, in their fourth operations <note>referring to the calculation of true planetary position</note>, become retrograde in order when their degrees of Fast Anomaly reach the values previously stated, such as those represented by the mnemonic "Kritartuchandra" <note>a numerical code representing 164</note>. By subtracting these specific degrees from a full circle of 360 degrees, the remaining values represent the degrees of the fourth anomaly at which the planets Mars and the others abandon their retrograde motion. The word "Tu" in the verse implies the sequence. This occurs because, in the revolution, the velocity of the planet near its perigee <note>the point closest to Earth</note> matches the velocity of its mean motion at two specific points, creating the appearance of stationary or retrograde motion. || 53 || 54 ||

**Hindi Commentary—** Retrograde motion begins when the remaining Fast Anomaly is: Mars 164°, Mercury 144°, Jupiter 130°, Venus 163°, and Saturn 115°. || 53 || Retrograde motion is abandoned (by subtracting the above figures from the 360° circle) when the Fast Anomaly reaches: Mars 196°, Mercury 216°, Jupiter 230°, Venus 197°, and Saturn 245°. || 54 ||

### Now, another reason is given for the inequality of the degrees at the end of retrogradation—

-> **Because of the greatness of the Fast Circumference, Venus and Mars [end retrogradation] in the 7th sign;** <-
-> **Jupiter and Mercury in the 8th; and Saturn in the 9th. || 55 ||** <-

Venus and Mars abandon their retrograde state in the 7th sign of the Fast Anomaly <note>between 180° and 210°</note>. Jupiter and Mercury are fit to abandon retrogradation in the 8th sign <note>210° to 240°</note>. Here, the mention of Venus and Jupiter first indicates their higher status relative to the others. Saturn abandons retrogradation in the 9th sign <note>240° to 270°</note>. The word "Tu" here acts as an exclusive: only Saturn abandons it there, no others. The reason given is "due to greatness"—meaning the Fast Circumference <term>Shighra-paridhi: the epicycle used to calculate the planet's distance and speed</term> of the others is larger than that of Saturn. Because the circumference is larger, the abandonment of retrogradation occurs earlier. This is why Mars and Venus are mentioned before Mercury and Jupiter. In the case of Saturn, since its circumference is the smallest, it stays retrograde longer. 

If one asks for the logic of why a larger circumference leads to abandoning retrogradation in an earlier sign, listen: through the inverse method of calculating the "Fast Sine" <term>Shighra-karna</term> related to zero velocity, the sine of the arc is determined. Because the divisors (the circumferences) vary, the resulting arcs where the planet's velocity appears to stop will differ. These arcs, when added to the six signs (180°) for the end of retrogradation, result in the values mentioned. For the start of retrogradation in the second quadrant, these arcs are subtracted from six signs. Thus, it should be understood that Mars and Venus start in the 6th sign, Mercury and Jupiter in the 5th, and Saturn in the 4th. This was stated by the Lord <note>the author or the divine source of the text</note> as a simplified rule for the benefit of the world, allowing one to know the end of retrogradation simply by knowing the sign of the Fast Anomaly without complex calculations. || 55 ||

<header>Surya-Siddhanta — [Chapter Two]</header>

**Hindi Commentary:** According to the rules of the *Shighra-paridhi* <note>the epicycle of conjunction</note>, Venus and Mars cease their retrograde motion when they are in the seventh sign from their conjunction, Jupiter and Mercury in the eighth sign, and Saturn in the ninth sign. || 55 ||

### Now, he describes the calculation of the celestial latitude (Vikshepa) of the Moon and other planets in two verses—

**The correction resulting from the *Shighra* <note>conjunction</note> for Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter is applied to their Nodes just as it is to the planets themselves. For Mercury and Venus, the *Manda* <note>equation of center</note> correction from the third operation is applied to their Nodes in reverse.** || 56 ||

**The Sine is calculated from the planet minus its own Node; however, for Mars and Mercury <note>meaning the inner planets Mercury and Venus</note>, it is calculated from the *Shighra* <note>conjunction</note>. Multiply this by the maximum latitude and divide by the final hypotenuse; for the Moon, divide by the Radius.** || 57 ||

The Nodes of Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter, as determined in the chapter on mean motions, should have the *Shighra-phala* <note>equation of conjunction</note> applied to them. This correction, derived from the fourth operation of the respective planet, is applied to the Node exactly as it was applied to the planet. This means if the *Shighra-phala* was added to the planet, it must be added to its Node; if subtracted, it must be subtracted. For Mercury and Venus, the *Manda-phala* <note>equation of center</note> from the third operation is applied to their Nodes in reverse <term>Vamam</term>: if the correction was positive for the planet, it is negative for the Node, and vice versa. Since no specific rule is mentioned for the Moon, its Node is taken as it is. The Sine <term>Bhujajya</term> is then derived from the rectified planet minus its corrected Node. 

He mentions a specific rule for Mercury and Venus: "From the *Shighra*." For Venus and Mercury, the Sine is calculated from the *Shighra* <note>the anomaly of conjunction</note> minus the Node, not from the planet's position itself. This specific rule supersedes the general rule. Thus, the previous rule applies to the Moon, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. The result is multiplied by the mean latitude minutes stated in the chapter on mean motions and divided by the *Shighra-karna* <note>hypotenuse of conjunction</note> found in the fourth operation; the result is the true celestial latitude <term>Vikshepa</term> in minutes. 

Now, since the Moon has no *Shighra-karna*, one might ask what the Sine of its Node-distance should be divided by. He answers: "By the Radius" <term>Trijyaya</term>. In calculating the Moon's latitude, that Sine is divided by the Radius <note>3438'</note>. 

**The logic <term>Upapatti</term> is as follows:** Just as Declination <term>Kranti</term> is the north-south distance from the Celestial Equator to the Ecliptic, Celestial Latitude <term>Vikshepa</term> is the north-south distance from the Ecliptic to the planet's orbit, directed toward the celestial pole of the Ecliptic <term>Kadamba</term>. The orbits of the six planets (excluding the Sun) are distinct within their respective spheres. The Sun always remains on the Ecliptic. These orbits intersect the Ecliptic at the Nodes. When a planet is at its Node or 180 degrees <note>six signs</note> away from it, the orbits coincide, and there is no latitude. As the planet moves away from the Node, the north or south distance between the planet and the Ecliptic increases; this is called *Vikshepa*. This latitude is at its maximum when the planet is three signs <note>90 degrees</note> from the Node. The distance between the Node and the planet's position on the Ecliptic is the argument; the proportion is: if the Radius gives the maximum latitude, what does the Sine of the current distance give? For the Moon, this is calculated within the sphere of the Radius because its maximum latitude and calculated Node are fixed to that scale.

# Chapter 2. ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. ( 59 )

For others <note>referring to other astronomers or schools of thought</note>, the maximum latitudes are observed at the radius of the "fast-corrector" <term>Shighra-karna: the hypotenuse or distance from the earth to the planet in its epicycle</term> in the imaginary circle occupied by the planetary disk, which is drawn by the deity of the "fast-apex" <term>Shighrocha: the point of conjunction or the sun's mean position used for inner planets</term>. Otherwise, how could the clarity of the planet be justified by the "fast-fruit" <term>Shighra-phala: the equation of the center or anomaly</term> correction? If the planetary disk is situated there, it is proper that its node <term>Pata: the point where the orbit crosses the ecliptic</term> is also situated there. In the circle occupied by the planetary disk, since the planetary longitude is the "slow-clear" position <term>Manda-spashta: the planet's position corrected for its elliptical orbit but not yet for its relative position to Earth</term>, the calculation of latitude from the calculated node and the "slow-clear" position is appropriate.

As stated in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>A famous 12th-century astronomical treatise by Bhaskara II</note>: "The planet wanders in the 'fast-proportional-circle' as the 'slow-clear' planet, and its node is also there. From this 'slow-clear' position, joined with the calculated node, the latitude of the moving body is derived."

Therefore, to calculate the latitude from the "clear" <term>Spashta: the final corrected position</term> planet, the "fast-fruit" is applied to the node. Because the "clear" planet, when corrected inversely by the "fast-fruit," results in the "slow-clear" position, the node is subtracted from the "clear" planet to establish the node of the "slow-clear" planet. Now, the actual revolutions of the nodes of Mercury and Venus are not explicitly stated. They exceed the revolutions of the "fast-center" <term>Shighra-kendra: the anomaly from the fast-apex</term>. Therefore, the node is found by taking the calculated node, adding the "fast-center" (which is the "fast-apex" minus the mean planet), and subtracting from twelve signs <note>360 degrees</note>. Because the previous node was subtracted from twelve signs, the "fast-center" must be added to the remainder of the circle.

For simplicity, the "center" (the "fast-apex" minus the mean planet) is added to the calculated node. Since this node is subtracted from the "slow-clear" position (which is the mean position corrected by the "slow-fruit"), the mean positions cancel out, proving that the "fast-apex" corrected by the "slow-fruit" is the node. Even there, the "slow-fruit" is applied inversely to the node, and that is subtracted from the "fast-apex," because the corrected nodes are joined in the sequence. Now, this calculated latitude is on a circle with the radius of the "hypotenuse" <term>Karna</term> at the position of the "clear" planet on the radius of the "sines" <term>Trijya: the standard radius of 3438 minutes</term>. Thus, by proportion: if this is the latitude at the end of the hypotenuse, what is it at the end of the radius? The radius is the multiplier and the hypotenuse is the divisor. Since the radius was the divisor previously, the radii cancel out. Thus, the sine of the longitude multiplied by the maximum latitude and divided by the "fast-hypotenuse" <term>Shighra-karna</term> is proven correct. || 56 || 57 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The "fast-fruit" <term>Shighra-phala</term> derived from the fourth correction for Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter should be applied to their nodes in the same way they were applied to the planets. In the case of Mercury and Venus, the third "slow-fruit" <term>Mandya-phala</term> should be applied to their nodes in the *opposite* manner to how it was applied to the planet. That is, if the "slow-fruit" was added to the planet, subtract it from the node; if it was subtracted, add it. For the Moon, Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter, subtract the "clear-node" from the "clear-planet." For Venus and Mercury, subtract the "clear-node" from the "fast-apex" <term>Shighra</term> to determine the "arm-sine" <term>Bhuja-jya</term>. Multiply the "arm-sine" by the maximum latitude (from Chapter 1, Verse 70) and divide by the "fast-hypotenuse" <term>Shighra-karna</term> to find the "clear-latitude." In the case of the Moon, simply dividing by the radius <term>Trijya</term> will result in the "clear-latitude." || 56 || 57 ||

Now, wishing to explain the "shadow-calculation" <term>Chara-anayana: the correction for the length of the day</term> to know the measure of day and night, he first describes the "clear-declination" <term>Spashta-kranti</term>:

-> When the latitude and declination are in the same direction, the clear declination is their sum. <-
-> When the directions differ, it is their difference, just as the declination of the Sun was calculated. || 58 || <-

For whichever planet the "clear-declination" is desired, one must first find the declination from the "arm-sine" of the planet (corrected for the precession of the equinoxes) using the rule "from the maximum declination sine," etc. This declination follows the direction (North or South) of the planet's hemisphere. Its latitude is also calculated as previously described...

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter 2]

<margin>1. The six signs starting with Aries are in the northern direction, and the six signs starting with Libra are in the southern direction.</margin>

The direction of the node <note>the point where the planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> determines the direction of the celestial latitude. The "sphere" (Gol) is defined as northern for the six signs beginning with Aries and southern for the six signs beginning with Libra. Now, if the celestial latitude and the declination <note>distance from the celestial equator</note> are in the same direction, the true declination is found by adding the latitude (in minutes) to the declination. If they are in opposite directions, the true declination is the difference between the two. 

One might ask: since the Sun has no celestial latitude <note>because the Sun's path defines the ecliptic</note>, how is its true declination determined? To this, the text says: **Regarding the Sun**, the previously calculated declination is itself the true declination. 

**The Logic (Upapatti):** The true declination is the north or south distance from the celestial equator to the center of the planetary disk. If both are in the same direction, the distance is their sum; if in different directions, it is their difference. Here, the compassionate Lord <note>the divine author of the text</note> has ignored certain complex corrections for the latitude out of concern for the confusion of the common people and because the difference is very slight. Otherwise, the Lord's statement regarding the planet's orientation toward the pole and the calculations for visibility (Ayana-drik-karma) would be contradicted. Enough on this. || 58 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** If a planet's latitude and declination are in the same direction, add the latitude to the mean declination; if they are in different directions, subtract them to find the true declination. For the Sun, the mean declination is the true declination. || 58 ||

->Now, to determine the length of day and night, the respiration-counts (Asus) of the day-and-night cycle are calculated:<-

### The planet's daily motion, multiplied by the rising-time (Prana) of the sign it occupies and divided by 1800, 
### added to the respiration-counts of a full circle (Chakra), is known as the planet's own day-and-night respiration-counts (Ahoratrasu). || 59 ||

The planet's true daily motion (in minutes) is multiplied by the rising-time (in respiration-counts at the equator) of the zodiac sign the planet occupies (adjusted for precession). This product is divided by 1800 <note>the number of minutes in one sign, or 30 degrees</note>. The resulting value is added to the respiration-counts of a full circle—which is 21,600 (the number of respirations in 60 Ghatikas or 24 hours). This sum is declared by the experts of time-theory to be the specific day-and-night duration (Ahoratrasu) for that planet.

**The Logic (Upapatti):** A planet lags behind due to its eastward motion. After one full rotation of the starry sphere (the sidereal day), the planet rises only after it has covered its daily motion. Therefore, the duration of a planet's day-and-night cycle is the time of one full rotation (60 Ghatikas) plus the time it takes to cover its daily motion. By proportion: if 1800 minutes (one sign) corresponds to the rising-time of that sign, then how many respiration-counts correspond to the planet's daily motion? This calculation yields the "motion-respirations." 

In this verse, the Lord has also implied the "Equation of the Rising" (Udyantara-karma). Specifically, because the mean planets calculated by proportion are fixed to a certain day-and-night length, they are not perfectly accurate at midnight. Since the Sun's motion-respirations vary in each sign, the length of a solar day is not constant. The Lord ignored the specific correction for the "Equation of the Rising" because the difference is minimal. Otherwise, why would the Lord describe the respiration-counts of the daily motion instead of treating them as uniform? This variation arises from the difference in the respiration-counts of the daily motion. || 59 ||
