**Hindi Commentary:** Multiply the number of breaths <note>Prana: a unit of time equal to 4 seconds</note> of the sign in which the tropical planet <note>original: "Sayana-graha"</note> is situated by its true motion. Divide this by 1800; the result will be the daily number of breaths, which is the true duration of the day and night <note>original: "Ahoratramana"</note> for that planet. || 59 ||

Now, he describes the **Sine of Declination** <term>Kranti-jya: the angular distance of a planet north or south of the celestial equator</term> and the **Radius of the Diurnal Circle** <term>Dyu-jya: the radius of the planet's daily path</term> used for calculating the ascensional difference:

-> **Having determined both the Sine and the Versine of the declination, the Radius minus the Versine is the semi-diameter of the day-circle, whether in the north or south. || 60 ||** <-

**Sanskrit Commentary:** Having calculated both the Sine <note>Kramajya</note> and the Versine <note>Utkramajya</note> of the true declination, among them, the Radius <term>Trijya: the standard radius of 3438 minutes</term> diminished by the Versine of the declination is the semi-diameter of the day-circle—<term>this means the Dyu-jya</term>. That semi-diameter of the day-circle exists in both the southern and northern hemispheres, as declination exists in both hemispheres. The other is simply the Sine of declination. 

The mathematical proof is as follows: The Sine of the degrees of declination is the base <note>Bhuja</note> following the celestial equator. In both hemispheres, the Radius is the hypotenuse <note>Karna</note> and the Radius of the day-circle is the upright <note>Koti</note>. This is visible in the armillary sphere. It is also visible in the Radius-circle, the horizon <note>Unmandala</note>, or the meridian. There, the square root of the difference between the squares of the hypotenuse and the base is the upright; thus, the square root of the Radius squared minus the Sine of declination squared is the Dyu-jya. Furthermore, as seen in the circle, the Radius minus the Versine of the base becomes the Sine of the upright. Therefore, for the sake of brevity and to avoid calculating square roots, the Lord <note>the divine author of the text</note> stated "from the declination," etc. || 60 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Determine the **Sine** <term>Kramajya</term> and **Versine** <term>Utkramajya</term> from the **Declination** <term>Kranti</term>. By subtracting the Versine from the **Radius** <term>Trijya</term>, the diameter for that day is fixed according to the north or south direction. || 60 ||

Now, in three verses, he explains the calculation of the duration of day and night by first finding the ascensional difference <note>Chara</note>:

-> **The Sine of declination multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by twelve is the Earth-sine. || 61 ||** <-
-> **Multiplied by the Radius and divided by the semi-diameter of the day-circle, the result is the Sine of the ascensional difference. The arcs of these are the breaths of the ascensional difference. || 62 ||** <-
-> **In northern declination, these are added to and subtracted from the two separate positions of the quarter of the planet's own day-and-night circle to find the half-day and half-night. || 62 ||** <-
-> **In southern declination, the process is reversed. For the stars, the same applies using their own declination as increased or decreased by their latitude. || 63 ||** <-

**Sanskrit Commentary:** The **Sine of declination** <term>Kranti-jya</term> is to be multiplied by the **equinoctial shadow** <term>Vishuvadbha: the shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</term> and divided by twelve; the result is the **Earth-sine** <term>Kujya</term>. That, multiplied by the Radius and divided by the semi-diameter of the day-circle <note>Dyu-jya</note>, gives the **Sine of the ascensional difference** <term>Charajya</term>. The arcs of this Sine are the breaths of the ascensional difference <note>Charasava</note>. 

Take the previously mentioned breaths of the day-and-night circle of the planet related to the **ascensional difference** <term>Chara</term>, and place a fourth part of them in two separate positions. If there is northern declination, the breaths of the ascensional difference are to be added and subtracted <insert>to find the half-day and half-night respectively</insert>...

# Surya Siddhanta
## [Chapter Two]

Those [two values] are respectively called the midday and midnight by those who know time. When there is southern declination, the process is reversed: where it was subtracted, that is midday, and where it was added, that is midnight. By the word "but," it is implied that doubling these midday and midnight values gives the total measure of the day and the total measure of the night for a planet. The author states that the measure of day and night for the stars (Nakshatras) should also be calculated in the same manner—starting with "By latitude," etc. By using the calculated declination of the stars' fixed positions, adjusted by the star's celestial latitude <note>original: "vikshepa"</note>—adding if they are in the same direction or subtracting if different—one should determine the measure of day and night for each star according to the previously mentioned method.

The geometric proof here is as follows: The <term>twelve-inch gnomon</term> <note>a vertical pillar used to measure shadows</note> is the <term>vertical side</term>, the <term>equinoctial shadow</term> is the <term>horizontal side</term>, and the <term>hypotenuse of the latitude</term> is the <term>hypotenuse</term>. Furthermore, the <term>sine of declination</term> is the <term>vertical side</term>, the <term>earth-sine</term> <note>original: "kujya"</note> is the <term>horizontal side</term>, and the <term>amplitude-hypotenuse</term> is the [other] hypotenuse. These two "latitude-triangles" are well known. In this context, if the horizontal side is the equinoctial shadow when the vertical side is twelve, then what is the horizontal side when the vertical side is the sine of declination? By this proportion, we find the <term>earth-sine</term>. Its nature is the sine of the arc of the diurnal circle situated between the horizon of the equator and the local horizon. When measured by the <term>radius of the diurnal circle</term>, it is that sine; when measured by the <term>total radius</term> (3438'), it is the <term>sine of ascensional difference</term> <note>original: "charajya"</note>. The proportion is: if the earth-sine is given by the radius of the diurnal circle, what is it for the total radius? The result is the <term>sine of ascensional difference</term>. The arc of that sine represents the "ascensional breaths" <note>units of time where 1 breath = 4 seconds</note>. In the northern hemisphere, because the local horizon lies below the equatorial horizon, these breaths are added to the fourth part of the day-circle (90 degrees) and subtracted from the fourth part of the night-circle. In the southern hemisphere, because the local horizon lies above the equatorial horizon, they are subtracted from the midday and added to the midnight. Thus, all is proven regarding the sine of declination, etc. || 61 || 62 || 63 ||

**Vernacular Commentary**—By multiplying the sine of declination by the equinoctial shadow and dividing by 12, the result is the earth-sine. By multiplying the earth-sine by the total radius and dividing by the radius of the diurnal circle, and then determining the arc, one obtains the number of breaths for the ascensional difference || 61 ||. Placing the fourth part of the day-and-night (15 ghatis or 90 degrees) in two places, add the calculated breaths of ascensional difference to one and subtract from the other. If there is northern declination, the sum is the measure of half the day (midday) and the difference is the measure of half the night || 62 ||. However, in southern declination, it is the opposite: the difference is half the day and the sum is half the night. By doubling these, the total measure of the day and night is found. In this way, by determining the declination through the celestial latitude of the stars, the measure of their day and night is also decided || 63 ||.

### Now he describes the calculation of the stars for a planet:

> The portion of a star is eight hundred minutes; likewise, that of a lunar day (tithi) is seven hundred and twenty.
> The minutes of a planet, divided by the portion of a star, gives the stars passed; from the remainder, the days etc. [passed in the current star] are found by the planet's daily motion. || 64 ||

The portion <note>the longitudinal space occupied</note> of a star is 800 minutes (13° 20'). In this context, he also mentions the portion of a lunar day: "seven hundred and twenty." This means the portion of a lunar day is 720 minutes (12°). For whichever planet the knowledge of the star is desired, the signs of that planet should be multiplied by thirty to get degrees, then multiplied by sixty to get minutes, according to the standard definition. These minutes are divided by the portion of a star (800). The quotient represents the stars already passed by the planet. The remainder represents the minutes passed in the current star. From that, he explains how to calculate the days etc. passed: "by the daily motion." By dividing the remainder by the planet's daily motion in minutes, the elapsed time in days etc. is found...

The remaining time and other factors are to be calculated. Here is the rationale: A planet traverses the twenty-seven lunar mansions, starting with Ashvini, by completing one full circle of the zodiac. Therefore, if the total minutes of the zodiac—21,600 minutes <note>original: 21,600 is the total arc of 360 degrees converted to minutes</note>—correspond to twenty-seven mansions, then by proportion, one mansion equals 800 minutes. Similarly, since a lunar day (Tithi) is one-thirtieth of a lunar month, and a lunar month is completed by one full revolution of the distance between the Sun and the Moon, the total minutes of the zodiac correspond to thirty lunar days. By proportion, one lunar day equals 720 minutes. Now, if 800 minutes make one mansion, how many are in the planet's current position? By this proportion, the result gives the number of mansions passed (Ashvini, etc.). The remaining minutes represent the portion of the current mansion already traversed. By subtracting this from the total mansion duration (800), the remaining portion is found. Using the planet's daily motion, one can then calculate the days and other units passed or remaining. The daily mansion of the Moon is to be known in this same way. || 64 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The duration of a lunar mansion is 800 minutes, and a lunar day is 720 minutes. By dividing the planet's position (in minutes) by 800, the quotient gives the mansions passed. By dividing the remainder by the planet's clear motion, the elapsed time is determined. || 64 ||

### Now, in this context, the calculation of the "Yogas" is described:

->**From the sum of the minutes of the Sun and Moon, the Yogas are found by dividing by the mansion-duration.**<-
->**The passed and remaining portions, multiplied by sixty and divided by the sum of their motions, give the time in Ghatikas.**<- <note>A Ghatika or Nadika is a unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note> **|| 65 ||**

The sum of the Sun and Moon's positions, converted into minutes, provides the basis for the Yogas (such as Vishkambha, etc.) when divided by the mansion-duration (800 minutes) mentioned previously. Each Yoga has a duration equal to one mansion-duration. By subtracting this from the total sum, the number of completed Yogas is found. The one that cannot be fully subtracted is the current Yoga. The remainder represents the "passed" portion; subtracting this from 800 gives the "remaining" portion. To find the time in Ghatikas (units of 24 minutes), he says: "The passed and remaining..." The minutes should be multiplied by sixty and divided by the sum of the daily motions of the Sun and Moon. The result is the elapsed or remaining time in Ghatikas. The rationale is: because these Yogas (named Vishkambha, etc.) are produced by the combined positions of the Sun and Moon, their calculation follows the previous method. Since the combined motion of the Sun and Moon covers a certain distance in sixty solar Ghatikas, the proportion used to find the time for the passed or remaining minutes is mathematically sound. || 65 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Add the clear positions of the Sun and Moon together and convert to minutes. Divide by 800; the quotient is the number of Yogas passed. The remainder is the passed portion, and subtracting it from 800 gives the remaining portion. Multiply these by 60 and divide by the sum of their daily motions to find the passed and remaining time in Dandas <note>Danda is a synonym for Ghatika</note>. || 65 ||

### Now, in this context, the calculation of the lunar days (Tithis) is described:

->**From the minutes of the Moon minus the Sun, the lunar days are found by dividing by the duration.**<-
->**The passed and remaining portions, multiplied by sixty and divided by the difference in their motions, give the Ghatikas.**<- **|| 66 ||**

The explanation of the first half of the verse should be understood in the same manner as the first half of the previous verse; the second half is clear. Here is the mathematical rationale: If one lunar day <term>tithi; 1/30th of a lunar month</term> is constituted by the arc of the lunar day, then what is the result of the arc of the Moon minus the Sun? By this proportion, the result is the elapsed lunar days. The remaining arc and the arc subtracted from the total <note>720 minutes of arc</note> represent the elapsed and remaining portions of the current lunar day. From these, using the difference in daily motion <note>the relative speed between the Moon and Sun</note>, the elapsed and remaining ghatikas <term>ghatika; a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term> are found as before. || 66 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In a lunar month, by subtracting the Sun's position from the Moon's and dividing by the arc of a lunar day (720'), the elapsed lunar days are obtained. By subtracting the remainder from 720, the elapsed and remaining portions are found. Multiplying these by 60 and dividing by the difference between the Moon's and Sun's daily motion gives the elapsed and remaining time in danda <note>equivalent to a ghatika</note>. || 66 ||

### Now, wishing to explain the remaining parts of the Five-Fold Calendar (Panchanga), he first describes the Fixed Karanas:

**The fixed ones are Shakuni, Naga, the third is Chatushpada,**
**And Kimstughna; these occur from the second half of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.** || 67 ||

This means starting from the second half of the fourteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight <term>Krishna Paksha; the waning moon</term>. The word "and" is used for emphasis. Thus, the "Fixed Karanas" <term>Karana; half of a lunar day</term> exclude other lunar days and the first half of this specific day. He names them: Shakuni, etc. By mentioning the third as Chatushpada, the first and second are indicated as Shakuni and Naga respectively. The word "tu" <note>but/and</note> implies they occur in sequence during the halves of the lunar days. Kimstughna is the fourth. The word "tu" also acts as a limit, indicating there are no fixed Karanas beyond these four. || 67 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Shakuni, Naga, Chatushpada, and Kimstughna are these four fixed Karanas. they are experienced in sequence starting from the latter half of the dark fourteenth lunar day. || 67 ||

### Now he describes the Movable Karanas:

**Then the seven Movable Karanas, beginning with Bava,**
**Each of these Karanas occurs eight times within a month.** || 68 ||

"Then," meaning after the completion of the Fixed Karanas, the seven Movable Karanas beginning with Bava and ending with Bhadra occur from the second half of the first day of the bright fortnight <term>Shukla Paksha; the waxing moon</term> until the [first half of the] fourteenth. If one asks which Karanas occur from the fifth day onwards, he says: "In a month." Among the seven Movable Karanas (Bava, etc.), each one occurs eight times in a month—here "month" refers to the thirty lunar days minus the time occupied by the Fixed Karanas. They "prevail," meaning they repeat in a cycle. Thus, from the first half of the first day, these Karanas rotate again and again until the first half of the dark fourteenth day. || 68 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The seven Movable Karanas starting with Bava rotate eight times in sequence during one lunar month. || 68 ||

Now, regarding the statement on Fixed Karanas, by saying "from the second half," it is appropriate that those four stay in sequence through the halves of the lunar days until the [first half] of the first day of the bright fortnight. As for the Movable Karanas, by the simple statement, thereafter until the first half of the dark fourteenth...

# Chapter 2. ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. ( 69 )

To address the question of why there should be a single rotation [of the astrological "Karana" divisions] up to a certain point, the author states the following:

> One should assign half the duration of a lunar day <note>tithi</note> as the period of influence for all the *Karanas*.
> This is declared to be the computed true motion of the sun and the other wandering heavenly bodies. || 69 ||

For each of the seven mobile *Karanas* <note>astrological divisions of a day</note>, one should calculate their duration as lasting for half of a lunar day. Based on the principle that a rule established in one part of the scripture applies elsewhere, their position as *Karanas* should be made equal to that duration. Therefore, it is said that "half a lunar day is remembered as a *Karana*." Since a lunar month consists of thirty lunar days containing sixty *Karanas*, the mobile *Karanas* rotate such that they do not align with the same lunar days every month. To ensure the correct calculation of these shifting lunar day associations, it is taught that after the mobile *Karanas* have rotated eight times, the fixed *Karanas* are placed in the remaining four halves of the lunar days. Specifically, this arrangement begins from the second half of the 14th day of the dark fortnight <note>the waning moon</note>, according to the divine will, which is independent and beyond external command.

Now, to conclude this section and avoid inconsistency with the following text, the author summarizes: "This..." Oh Maya <note>the recipient of this revelation</note>, this discourse starting from the visual observations and ending with the calculations is the "True Motion" <term>Sphuta-gati: the actual observed position of a planet as opposed to its mean or average position</term> of the seven planets including the Sun. I have declared this to you as the means to achieve knowledge of the true planetary operations. By this, it is indicated that the Chapter on True Motion is now complete. || 69 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The *Karanas* enjoy half of a lunar day. In this manner, the true motion of the Sun and other planets has been described. || 69 ||

Now the Chapter on the Three Problems <note>Triprasna-adhikara</note> is explained. > Where the tip of its shadow touches the circle in the forenoon and afternoon... || 2 ||

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for astronomical orientation and the construction of a sundial (gnomon) layout, following the traditional methods of the Surya Siddhanta.</meta>

<header>
Surya Siddhanta: [Chapter Three]
</header>

### There, having marked two points on the circle named East and West, ||
### Between them, a North-South line should be made by means of a "fish." || 3 ||
### Between the North and South directions, an East-West [line is made] by a "fish."
### The intermediate directions are to be established exactly like that, by means of "fishes" between the directions. || 4 ||

Regarding the commencement of determining the directions: First, on a stone surface leveled with water like the surface of a pond; or otherwise, in the absence of that, on a courtyard or similar place made level with "diamond-paste" <note>Vajralepe: a traditional hard-setting lime or plaster</note> by grinding and smoothing. One should draw a circle with a radius of a desired number of digits <note>Angulas: a traditional unit of measurement, roughly a finger-breadth</note> taken from the markings on a gnomon <term>Shanku: a vertical pillar or peg used in ancient astronomy to cast a shadow</term>. This means that from the center to the circumference, the line should be equal in all directions.

Then, in the center—which is the middle point—one should place a gnomon made of a straight wooden rod with a level top and circumference, marked with twelve equal divisions. Then, in the first and second parts of the day (forenoon and afternoon), one marks where the tip of the shadow of the established gnomon touches the circumference of the circle. In the first part of the day, as the shadow decreases every moment, it "enters" the circle; in the latter part of the day, as the shadow increases every moment, it "exits" the circle.

At those two points of entry and exit, one should mark two points on the circumference line, named East and West respectively. Between those East and West points, a line should be made by means of a "fish" <term>Timi/Matsya: a fish-shaped figure formed by the intersection of two circles, used in geometry to ensure a perpendicular bisector</term>; that becomes the North-South line.

The "fish" is formed by taking the distance between the two points as the radius, treating the two points as centers, and drawing two circles. The area contained within the intersection of the two circumferences is the fish-shaped space. There, one intersection is the "mouth" (by clearing away the outer parts of the circles) and the other intersection is the "tail." The straight line passing through the middle of the mouth and tail is the North-South line. There, the end of the line to the left of the [East] point is the South direction, and the end of the line to the left of the West point is the North direction. Afterward, the first circle and the "fish" should be erased. The gnomon should also be removed from its place, leaving only the North-South line standing.

In the middle of the North and South directions, using the North-South line as the radius and the North and South positions as centers, one should draw circles as before. By means of the "fish" established as before, the East-West line should be made. There, the end of the line near the East point is East, and the end near the West point is West. By erasing the "fish," the East-West line alone is established.

Now, from the intersection of the lines, where the lines touch the circumference of the circle drawn at the start of the direction-finding process, that is the direction. Thus, the four cardinal directions are established in the circle. "Exactly like that" means in the same manner that the East-West line was derived from the North-South. The word "exactly" <note>original: 'eva'</note> is used to exclude other methods. "Indeed" <note>original: 'hi'</note> emphasizes certainty. The intermediate directions (North-East, etc.) are to be perfectly established by "middle fishes" produced between the two immediate cardinal directions using small circles <note>likely 'laghu-vrittaih'</note>. These are to be known by the points where the lines and circles intersect.

The rationale here: The intersections of the horizon and the East-West circle are located in the East and West sectors... <meta>Catchword: sectors-</meta>

# Chapter 3. | With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.

Knowledge of the East and West points is gained through the rising and setting of the sun. In that context, the knowledge of where the East-West circle meets the horizon is achieved by knowing the rising and setting points of the sun when it is at the intersection of the celestial equator <note>the equinoctial circle</note> and the ecliptic. This is because the celestial equator is connected to the intersection points of the East-West and horizon circles. Now, on other days, the rising and setting points of the sun are shifted toward the North or South by the amount of the sun's amplitude <note>the angular distance from the true East/West</note>. Because the horizon is vast and distant, it is impossible to determine the East-West direction accurately just by looking at the sun's rising and setting points. Therefore, to know this in one's desired location, a circle is drawn on a desired level surface to mimic the horizon.

Even there, because it is difficult to know the exact line of the sun's rising and setting, a gnomon <term>Shanku: a vertical pillar used to cast a shadow for astronomical measurements</term> should be established for the sake of the shadow. However, at sunrise, the shadow is too long to touch the circumference of the outer circle. But as the sun rises higher, the shadow shortens. At the moment the shadow enters the circumference of the circle, the "arm" <note>the sine of the amplitude</note> for that time (which will be explained later) should be applied in reverse as a half-chord. Where this versed sine <note>the distance from the arc to the chord</note> touches the circumference, that point is West of the gnomon's position. This is because the shadow falls North or South of the East-West line and the shadow itself falls in the East-West direction.

Similarly, in the afternoon, as the sun moves lower, the shadow increases. When the gnomon's shadow exits the circumference of the circle, the "arm" for that time should be applied in reverse as a half-chord from that point. Where that versed sine touches the circumference, that point is East of the gnomon's position. This line is the East-West line. This is understood through the gnomon as an indicator, and thus the East-West line of a place is known by the indicator of the shadow.

To explain: where the shadow-tip enters is the West, and where the shadow-tip exits is the East. However, since the entry and exit cannot happen at the same time, the entry is real at its own time (when the shadow is in the West), but the exit cannot be "East" at that same moment. Likewise, at the time of exit, the exit point is truly East, but the entry point cannot be "West" at that same moment. To achieve a simultaneous result, one of the two marks must be moved. The Eastern mark should be moved by the number of digits <note>Angulas</note> representing the difference between the "arms" <note>amplitudes</note> of the two times, in the direction of the sun's course <note>the Solstice direction</note>. Or, the Western mark should be moved in the opposite direction. That resulting line is the East-West line for the center of the circle. This is identical to the East-West line proven by applying the "arm" to the entry and exit points of the shadow of a gnomon placed in the center.

> As stated in the **Siddhanta Shiromani** <note>A major 12th-century astronomical treatise by Bhaskara II</note>: "The Eastern point is shifted in the direction of the sun's course by digits equal to the difference between the two sines of amplitude multiplied by the radius and divided by the cosine of latitude."

Out of compassion for the world, the Lord <note>the author of the original text</note> did not mention this shifting of one point in the alternative explanation; for the sake of simplicity, the entry and exit points were roughly called East and West. Thus, the East-West direction should be established in the desired place by setting up the gnomon at the center of the circle so that the desired spot is in the middle of the entry-exit line. The North-South line is then found by the "fish" <note>a vesica piscis geometric construction</note> produced between those two points. It is correctly stated that the North-South direction is found by the fish in the middle of the East-West line, and the East-West direction by the fish in the middle of the North-South line. Now, one might ask: if the North-South line is made by a fish from the East-West points, and a line made by a fish from those North-South ends touches the East-West points, isn't the second step redundant? If not, the North-South line itself would be inconsistent...

# Surya Siddhanta: [Chapter Three]

If this is true: some say that the re-calculation of the clear East-West line from the two points is solely for the purpose of purifying <note>correcting/aligning</note> the North-South line. However, in reality, because the circle drawn from the center—which is the intersection of the North-South and East-West lines—is necessary for future applications, and because the diameter of that circle is greater than the line connecting the two points, the line between those points must be extended at both ends. That extended line becomes the East-West line in that circle. Because there might occasionally be a curvature above or below those points, it is more accurate to establish the East-West line again using the "fish" <note>the vesica piscis shape formed by intersecting arcs</note> generated from the points. Since the line passing through the tail of the <insert>fish established between the points</insert> is longer than the distance between the points, the resulting straight line is much longer and more accurate. This is the truth of the matter. In this same way, by using four small "fish" generated between the immediate directions, the intermediate directions (corners) are established in the circle. Thus, the ten directions <note>the eight compass points plus up and down</note> are established in the circle centered at the desired location. || 1 || 2 || 3 || 4 ||

**Commentary:** On a stone surface as level as water, or on a leveled piece of ground, draw a "Even Circle" (a perfect circle) of a desired number of digits <term>Angulas: a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to a finger's breadth</term>. In the center, place a Gnomon <term>Shanku: a vertical peg used to cast a shadow</term> of 12 digits in height. Mark the two points where the tip of the shadow touches the circumference of the circle in the forenoon and the afternoon; these are designated as the East and West points. From these, one should draw the North and South lines. By taking the North and South points as centers and drawing arcs with a radius, a "fish" <note>original: "Timi," a large fish or whale, referring to the shape of the intersection</note> will be formed. From that, the East-West line is constructed. From the "fish" in the middle of the directions, one should determine the Northeast and other intermediate directions. || 1 || 2 || 3 || 4 ||

Now, he describes the position of the shadow's tip at a given time from the desired location (the intersection of the directional lines):

->**One should construct a square outside by means of lines exiting from the center.**<-
->**The shadow at a desired time is known by applying the digits of the "base" line there.**<- || 5 ||

"From the center" means from the intersection of the directional lines at the desired location. "Exiting" means extending outward in the form of directional lines. "Outside" means outside the central circle where the directions intersect. This implies the previous construction of a circle, which was not explicitly mentioned before; otherwise, the word "outside" would be illogical. If one only took the previous circle, the intersection of the directional lines would not function as the "center" in this context. One should create a square—a four-sided figure where the two diagonals are equal to the extended lines of the corner directions. This is the visualization. In that square, by applying the digits of the "base" <term>Bhuja: the polar sine or the side of a right triangle</term> (which will be explained later), corresponding to the time of the shadow's entry or exit, and by following the chords of the East-West lines, the point on the circle where the end of the "base" falls is said to be the tip of the shadow at the time of entry or exit. This realization is to be understood by means of the gnomon placed at the intersection of the directional lines. The logic here is: since the "base" is defined as the distance between the shadow's tip and the East-West line, the knowledge of the directions from the shadow's tip is accurate. The purpose of making the square is to ensure the straightness of the lines—whether inside or outside the circle—that mimic the East-West lines used to calculate the "Agras" <note>amplitude/displacement</note> to be discussed later. || 5 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Having drawn a circle based on the measure of the shadow, one should imagine a perfect square outside the circle aligned with the East-West line. Within the circle, the "arms" <note>Sanskrit: *bhuja*, referring to the sides of a right-angled triangle formed by the shadow</note> are drawn according to the shadow. By drawing these toward the East, West, North, or South and connecting the tip to the center, the direction of the desired shadow will be determined. || 5 ||

### Now, he states the alternative names for the East-West line—

> **The line resting upon the East and West is called the Prime Vertical (Samamandala).**
> **It is also celebrated as the Unmandala (Equinoctial Circle) and the Vishuvanmandala (Celestial Equator). || 6 ||**

The established line connected to the East and West is called the Prime Vertical. That same line is the *Unmandala* and the *Vishuvanmandala*. The word "and" implies a collection of terms; it is called by both names. Here is the rationale: The intersections of the horizon and the East-West circle are the East and West points; the line passing through them is the East-West cord. Since the East-West circle is not seen on the ground as a vertical or downward-curving circle, but appears only as a line, that cord represents the East-West circle itself. Because the East-West circle is designated as the Prime Vertical (*Samamandala*), this line is given that name. Furthermore, because it is attached to the intersections of the circle called *Unmandala* located on the horizon of the equatorial region <note>original: *niraksha-desha*, a place with no latitude</note>, the East-West cord, being the central cord, is also named *Unmandala*. By this, the definition of the horizon of one's own location is established through the definition of the horizon of another location; thus, the East-West cord is shown to be the horizon circle. This is because the horizon circle is attached to the East and West points and the inscribed circle follows the horizon. Similarly, the East-West circle of the equatorial region is called the *Vishuvanmandala* (Equator); since it is attached to the East and West points, the East-West cord is established as its central cord and thus named *Vishuvanmandala*. One should note that because the Ecliptic <note>original: *krantivritta*</note> and the Vertical Circle <note>original: *drigvritta*</note> are moving and only occasionally attached to the East-West points, they are not given these names. || 6 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The line resting on the East and West is the *Samamandala*, *Unmandala*, or *Vishuvanmandala*. || 6 ||

### Now, he explains the knowledge of the Agra (Amplitude)—

> **An East-West line should be established from the tip of the equinoctial staff.**
> **The interval between the desired shadow and the equinoctial line is called the Agra. || 7 ||**

In that square, to the north of the East-West line, at a distance of the digits of the latitude <note>original: *akshama-angula*, the measure of the observer's latitude expressed in the length of the equinoctial shadow</note>... <insert>this means at the tip of the latitude</insert>. An East-West line should be made parallel to the primary East-West line, just as the desired shadow line is made according to the "arm" (*bhuja*), so this is made according to the latitude. Thereafter, the "middle"—meaning the space in digits within the square between the desired shadow and the equinoctial line—is constant everywhere. This is called the *Agra* <note>Amplitude: the angular distance of a celestial body from the East or West point</note> at the edge of the hypotenuse circle. The rationale is: the *Agra* of the hypotenuse circle is said to be the "arm" (*bhuja*) when corrected by the equinoctial shadow (*palabha*); in the southern hemisphere...

<header>The Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Three]</header>

Because the northern side <term>Bhuja</term><note>The "arm" or base of a triangle, here representing the distance of the shadow from the east-west line</note> is greater than the <term>Palabha</term><note>The equinoctial midday shadow at a specific location</note>, the <term>Agra</term><note>Celestial amplitude; the distance of the sun's rising/setting point from the true east/west points</note> is found by subtracting the Palabha from the Bhuja. Since the latitude line is north of the east-west line in the middle of the Bhuja, the distance between these two lines is the Agra, expressed as the Bhuja minus the Palabha. Similarly, in the northern hemisphere, because the northern Bhuja is smaller than the Palabha, the Agra is the Palabha minus the Bhuja. The Palabha line is north of the east-west line, even further north than the Bhuja line; thus, the distance between these two lines is the Palabha minus the Bhuja, which represents the Agra on the hypotenuse circle. Furthermore, for the southern Bhuja, since the Agra is the Palabha minus the Bhuja, the Bhuja plus the Agra equals the Palabha. Because the Bhuja and the Palabha lines are respectively south and north of the east-west line, the sum of their distances is the Palabha. This is consistent with the shadow's relationship, as the Agra-Palabha relationship serves as a substitute for the <term>Shankutala</term><note>The distance from the base of the gnomon to the rising-setting line</note>. In the celestial sphere, this is justified because the Shankutala is southern and the shadow exists in the direction of the planet. Therefore, the calculation of the latitude line south of the east-west line based on the southern Bhuja—which would otherwise be illogical—is correctly explained as being north of the east-west line, as stated in the section on the equinoctial Agra. || 7 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** At the measure of the equinoctial shadow (<term>Vishuvacchaya</term>), establish a straight line distant from the east-west line. The distance from this equinoctial line to the desired shadow line is called the <term>Agra</term>. || 7 ||

->Now, following this, he explains the method for finding the hypotenuse from a known shadow, and its verification:<-

### The square root of the sum of the squares of the gnomon and the shadow is the hypotenuse. 
### By subtracting the square of the gnomon from the square of the hypotenuse, the square root is the shadow; the gnomon is found by the reverse. || 8 ||

The square root of the sum of the squares of the twelve-digit gnomon and its shadow is the shadow-hypotenuse (<term>Chayakarna</term>). Now, he describes the verification or the method for finding the shadow: "From its..." meaning from the square of the shadow-hypotenuse, subtract the square of the gnomon (which is 144, the square of twelve) and the square root is the shadow. He then gives the reverse method for finding the gnomon: "The gnomon..." meaning by reversing the shadow calculation, subtract the square of the shadow from the square of the hypotenuse to find the root. The gnomon is measured as twelve digits (<term>Angulas</term>). 

**The Proof:** The twelve-digit gnomon is the vertical side (<term>Koti</term>), the shadow is the horizontal side (<term>Bhuja</term>), and the square root of the sum of their squares is the hypotenuse; this is the equinoctial triangle. This is proven by the methods mentioned for the equinoctial field. 

**Objection:** Why did the All-Knowing Lord <note>referring to the divine source of the Surya Siddhanta</note> describe the calculation of the hypotenuse of the desired shadow after the determination of the directions, since the Agra and other elements are described independently later? One should not say this was stated to understand the Agra without mathematical labor. Because the knowledge of the Bhuja (to be described later) depends on the Agra, and the Agra depends on the Bhuja, there is a circularity (<term>Anyonyashraya</term>). Furthermore, recalculating an Agra already found through mathematics is useless. 

One might argue there is no circularity because the shadow circle is known by the digits of the Bhuja-formula, and by knowing the shadow circle on the circumference from the gnomon at the intersection of the direction lines, the Bhuja is mathematically known from the distance to the east-west line. However, it is improper to suggest the All-Knowing Lord speaks without purpose. Even a dull person does not speak without a motive. It is not that Agra and Bhuja are strictly necessary for determining directions in a way that requires this specific statement. Moreover, this calculation of the hypotenuse is identical to the mathematical calculation to be described later, making its placement here seem redundant. In the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>A major astronomical work by Bhaskara II</note>, for the purpose of determining directions, it is said "from the product of the shadow and hypotenuse..."

# Chapter 3: With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries

<page-num>( 71 )</page-num>

Since the shadow-hypotenuse <note>original: *chāyākarṇa*</note> is used here, its logic is sound. If someone argues that the four verses starting with "the square..." were inserted by some dull-witted person and not spoken by the Lord <note>referring to the divine origin of the Surya Siddhanta</note>, that is not so. The calculation of the amplitude <note>original: *agra*</note> is stated here for the sake of purifying the determination of the directions; once the amplitude is established according to this method—which relies on the calculation of the "arm" <note>the sine of the distance from the east-west line</note>—the directions are correctly established. Furthermore, the calculation of the hypotenuse is mentioned so that one may verify the accuracy by comparing it with the hypotenuse derived from the ratio: "if the amplitude on the radius-circle <note>original: *trijyā-vṛtta*</note> yields this, then what does the calculated amplitude yield?" Some say the hypotenuse calculation is for the purpose of bringing the result equal to the radius.

In reality, in the circle <note>the sundial or mandala</note>, there are two lines representing the east and west points where the shadow enters and exits. These two lines must be made equidistant everywhere. One of the points should be moved by that distance; those two corrected east-west points then form the true east-west line for the center of that space. Because the measurement in digits <note>original: *angula*</note> between the two point-lines is too small to calculate, one should treat each line as an east-west line and draw two circles from the center. In these, the respective east-west lines should touch their circles. The "arms" <note>sine values</note> for the respective times should be placed in the circles. At their ends, the shadow-lines should be drawn. In the respective circles, lines should be drawn at a distance of the equinoctial shadow digits <note>original: *akṣabhā*</note> to the north of the east-west lines. Then, the difference between those lines in the circles can be calculated more easily at the ends of the hypotenuse-circles for both times because it is larger. That difference is the north-south distance between the two eastern points, brought about by the explanation of the hypotenuse-circle amplitude; this results from the difference of the "arms" being the difference between the points, which in turn results in the difference of the amplitudes. On the day of the equinox, or when the celestial hemispheres change, the difference of the "arms" is used. Therefore, the point should be moved in the stated manner; that line is the clear east-west line. With this intention, the Lord described the amplitude here, and the hypotenuse was also calculated to ensure its purity. This is the truth. || 8 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The square root of the sum of the square of the gnomon's shadow and the square of the gnomon is the shadow-hypotenuse <term>Shadow-hypotenuse: the distance from the tip of the gnomon to the tip of its shadow</term>. Subtracting the square of the gnomon from the square of the hypotenuse and taking the root gives the shadow; conversely, subtracting the square of the shadow from the square of the hypotenuse gives the square of the gnomon. || 8 ||

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Three]

<page-num>72</page-num>

...meaning "that." **It hangs down** <note>original: "parilambate"</note>; it hangs from the door of the position of the celestial sphere which is supported by the Pole Star. Here, by saying "it hangs down," the absence of a complete revolution of the zodiac is stated; otherwise, it would have been mentioned in the first chapter on Mean Motions in the context of planetary revolutions. And so, by saying it hangs from that door, it is understood that it returns to its original position. It is further indicated that it hangs down in the same way to the west from its own place. 

Thus, the zodiac first moves a certain number of degrees to the west by the **Will of God**; then, having turned back, it returns to its original position. From there, it moves gradually to the east by the same number of degrees, and turning back from there, it returns to its original position—this constitutes one unique **revolution** <term>Bhagana: a complete cycle or orbital revolution</term>. Therefore, the term "dependent" is an illustration. Because of the westward hanging, but because of its absence at the time of observation, the reading "thirty times" here is an error. This is because it contradicts the *Soma Siddhanta*, which states: "In an Age, the zodiac hangs eastward six hundred times." It also contradicts the statement in the *Brahma Siddhanta* that "the circle moved backward."

From the **total number of elapsed days** <term>Ahargana: the count of civil days since the epoch</term>, multiplied by that [number of revolutions] and divided by the number of terrestrial days (the solar civil days in an Age), the result is obtained in revolutions and so on. Ignoring the full revolutions, the **sine** <note>original: "bhuja"</note> of the remaining signs and degrees should be calculated. From that, the degrees are divided by ten and the resulting parts are multiplied by three; these should be known as the **Ayanamsha** <term>Ayanamsha: the arc between the moving vernal equinox and the fixed starting point of the zodiac</term>. The essential meaning is: the degrees of the sine multiplied by three and divided by ten are the resulting degrees of precession.

From the planet corrected by those degrees—which is increased or decreased due to the eastward and westward movement of the zodiac—one understands the movement of the zodiac. From the "precession-corrected planet," one should calculate the **declination** <note>original: "kranti"</note>, the **shadow**, and the **half-variation of daylight** <note>original: "charadala"</note> according to whether it falls within or outside the six signs. This is not done from the uncorrected planet alone, as indicated by the word "and so on." The "shadow" will be described later; the "half-variation of daylight" or *Chara* was mentioned in the previous chapter. By the word "and so on," the **precessional shifting** <note>original: "ayanavalana"</note> and the **visibility correction** <note>original: "ayanadrikkarma"</note> are included. 

Although one could simply say that declination is derived from the corrected planet, and mentioning other things is redundant since they depend on it, the mention of "shadow and half-variation" is to indicate that for the sake of knowing the declination alone, the declination must be calculated from the corrected planet. To prevent the calculation of declination for the Sun alone, the mention of shadow and half-variation indicates that the declination which serves other purposes must be calculated from the corrected planet.

**The logic here is as follows:** By the Will of God, the **ecliptic** <note>original: "kranti-vritta"</note> moves along its own path to the west by twenty-seven degrees, increasing gradually; then, turning back, it comes to its own place. From that place, it moves twenty-seven degrees to the east. Thus, the point of the ecliptic situated at the intersection of the ecliptic and the **equator** <note>original: "vishuvad-vritta"</note> at the beginning of creation—which is near the star **Revati** <note>the fixed starting point of the Hindu zodiac</note> and serves as the limit for the planetary positions calculated previously—has moved east or west from its original place along the path of the ecliptic. On the equator, however, the western or eastern part of that section has moved; at the intersection, there is no declination because there is no north-south distance between those two circles. But at the previous intersection point, declination is produced because of the north-south distance between them. 

Therefore, declination calculated from the "as-is" planetary position is inconsistent; it is proper to calculate declination from the planetary position measured from the [current] intersection. To know the planetary position relative to the [current] intersection, the planetary position relative to the previous intersection (as stated in the previous chapter) is increased or decreased by the degrees of the interval between the current intersection and the point on the ecliptic where the previous intersection was; these degrees are called *Ayanamsha*, depending on whether the previous intersection point is to the east or west. Since the factors dependent on declination also arise from the current intersection, their calculation is also from the corrected planet. 

Now, for the knowledge of the *Ayanamsha* degrees: from the six hundred revolutions, following the previous rule of proportion from the total elapsed days, the planetary position is obtained in revolutions etc. There, the number of completed revolutions represents the completed "hangings" of the zodiac to the east and west. The current one, however, because it begins with a westward hanging, [is calculated from] the signs...

# Chapter 3. ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. ( 73 )

When the zodiacal sign and degrees are within the visual range, there is a westward leaning; when outside, an eastward leaning. Furthermore, the movement and reversal occur according to whether the position is within or outside the three signs <note>90 degrees</note>; thus the "arm" (sine) is calculated. Then, by the proportion: "If 90 degrees gives 27 degrees, then what do the degrees of the 'arm' give?", the multiplier and divisor are reduced by nine. Thus, the degrees of the "arm" multiplied by three and divided by ten provide the result. All this is logically proven. || 9 || 10 ||

**Hindi Commentary—** In a Great Age (*Mahayuga*), the circle of asterisms <note>the zodiac</note> leans toward the east 600 times. Multiplying that number by the total elapsed days and dividing by the number of terrestrial days in a Yuga, the quotient will be the revolutions and signs. (Discarding the full revolutions) calculate the "arm" (*bhuja*) as previously described. Multiplying the "arm" by three and dividing by ten gives the Precession (*Ayana*). By applying this Precession correction to a planet, one should determine the declination, ascensional difference (*chara*), etc. This is easily observable at both equinoxes. || 9 || 10 ||

-> Now, he states in one and a half verses that the aforementioned difference is proven by direct observation: <-

> The movement becomes clearly visible to the eye at the two solstices and the two equinoxes. ||
> If the calculated Sun is less than the Sun determined by the shadow, the celestial circle has moved East. ||
> If it is greater, the circle has turned back toward the West by the remaining degrees of difference. || 11 ||

At the solstices (the junctions of the southern and northern paths) and the two equinoxes (the junctions of the celestial spheres), the shifted circle reaches visibility—meaning it is perceived clearly and without effort. The meaning is that the difference measured there is seen through direct observation. Furthermore, at the beginning of creation, the equinoxes and solstices occurred at the beginning of Aries/Libra and Cancer/Capricorn near the junction star of Revati <note>Zeta Piscium</note>; however, they are now observed elsewhere. Therefore, the ecliptic has shifted; otherwise, this discrepancy would be impossible. 

Now, how is it to be known whether it has moved East or West? He says: "From the East..." etc. If, on the day of the Sun's solstice reversal or when it stands on the East-West line at sunrise, the Sun is calculated from the midday shadow in the manner to be described—that is the "Shadow Sun." The "Calculated Sun" is the clear Sun brought forth by the previously mentioned mathematical methods. If the calculated Sun is less, then the circle (the ecliptic) is known to have moved East by the degrees of difference between the two Suns. If it is greater, then by the remaining degrees of difference, the circle is known to have turned back and moved Westward. 

The logic here: The Sun derived from the shadow is measured from the current intersection point <note>the vernal equinox</note>, whereas the calculated Sun is measured from the fixed point near the star Revati. Therefore, the difference between them is the degrees of Precession (*Ayanamsha*). If the ecliptic moves East, the Shadow Sun will be greater than the Calculated Sun. If it moves West, it will be less. This is perfectly proven. || 11 ||

**Hindi Commentary—** If the calculated Sun is less than the Sun derived from the shadow, the circle is moving Eastward. If it is greater, it is moving Westward (going backwards). The ecliptic moves by the magnitude of the degrees of difference. || 11 ||

# ( 74 ) Surya Siddhanta - [Chapter Three]

In one's desired location, the <term>Equinoctial</term> <note>original: Vishuvati; refers to the celestial equator</note> is associated with the day the sun crosses the equator. Because the sun is near the star Revati <note>the historical zero-point of the Hindu zodiac</note>, it is figuratively called the Equinox. The <term>Midday Shadow</term> <note>original: Dinardhaja</note> is the shadow of a twelve-digit gnomon cast on the north-south line at noon. Depending on whether the location is north or south of the terrestrial equator, the shadow falls to the north or south. Without the shadow falling exactly on the north-south line, it cannot be true noon; therefore, that specific measurement at the desired location is called the <term>Equinoctial Shadow</term> <note>original: Vishuvat-prabha; the shadow cast at noon on the day of the equinox</note>. By this method, the <term>Twelve-digit Gnomon</term> <note>original: Dvadashangula-shanku</note> is the vertical side, the <term>Equinoctial Shadow</term> <note>original: Palabha</note> is the horizontal side, and the square root of the sum of their squares is the <term>Hypotenuse</term> <note>original: Karna</note>, specifically the Latitude-Hypotenuse. This "Latitude Triangle" is shown to be useful for calculations described later. Because the sun is then situated on the <term>Equinoctial Circle</term> <note>the celestial equator</note>, the name "Equinoctial Shadow" is used. || 12 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In this manner, the <term>Shadow</term> of the <term>Noon</term> on the <term>Equinox Day</term> is seen on the <term>North-South Line</term>; that indeed is the <term>Equinoctial Shadow</term> of that place. || 12 ||

### Now, the calculation of the Co-latitude and Latitude is stated—

> **The Sine of the Radius multiplied by the Gnomon and the Shadow, divided by the Equinoctial Hypotenuse, yields the Sines of the Co-latitude and Latitude. The arcs of those two are the Co-latitude and Latitude, which are always south.** <note>This refers to the direction of the zenith relative to the equator in the northern hemisphere</note> **|| 13 ||**

The <term>Radius</term> <note>original: Trijya; the sinus totus used in trigonometry</note> is placed in two positions. One is multiplied by the <term>Gnomon</term> (twelve) and the other by the aforementioned <term>Shadow</term>. Both are then divided by the <term>Equinoctial Hypotenuse</term>. The results are, respectively, the <term>Sine of Co-latitude</term> <note>original: Lambajya</note> and the <term>Sine of Latitude</term> <note>original: Akshajya</note>. The arcs of these two sines are respectively the <term>Co-latitude</term> <note>Lamba</note> and the <term>Latitude</term> <note>Aksha</note>. In both hemispheres, these are always considered in the southern direction <note>relative to the zenith</note>. The geometric proof is as follows: In the <term>Meridian Circle</term> <note>original: Yamayottara-vritta</note>, the distance between the terrestrial equator and one's own prime vertical is the Latitude. In the Meridian Circle, the distance from the southern horizon to the celestial equator is the Co-latitude. Both are south of the zenith in the upper sphere. Their sines, the Sine of Latitude and Sine of Co-latitude, are the base and upright side. From the Latitude Triangle, where the Radius is the <term>Hypotenuse</term>, and twelve and the Equinoctial Shadow are the upright and base, the <term>Sines of Co-latitude and Latitude</term> are found by proportion. Their arcs are the Co-latitude and Latitude. This is proven. || 13 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiply the <term>Gnomon</term> (12) and the <term>Shadow</term> of the <term>Equinox Day</term> separately by the <term>Radius</term> (3438) and divide by the <term>Hypotenuse</term>. This will result in the <term>Sine of Co-latitude</term> and <term>Sine of Latitude</term> respectively. By calculating the <term>Arc</term> <note>inverse sine</note> of these, the <term>Co-latitude</term> and <term>Latitude</term> are obtained. || 13 ||

### Now, the calculation of Latitude from the Midday Shadow is stated in two verses—

> **The Midday Shadow is the base; multiply it by the Sine of the Radius. Divided by its own Hypotenuse, the arc-minutes are the Zenith Distance. If the shadow is South, the Zenith Distance is North; if the shadow is North, it is South. These are combined with the minutes of the Sun's Declination: if the directions are different, add them; if the same, subtract them. The result is the minutes of Latitude. || 14-15 ||**

On any desired day, the <term>Midday Shadow</term> should be known as the "base." By that base, the <term>Radius is multiplied</term>...

# Chapter 3. With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries

The result of the arc <note>the inverse sine</note> obtained by dividing [the shadow] by the **hypotenuse of the midday shadow** is designated as the **minutes of zenith distance** <note>original: "natakala," referring to the angular distance from the zenith at noon</note>. These minutes of zenith distance are considered the "Southern Base" <note>the southern side of the right-angled triangle formed by the shadow</note> when the midday shadow, situated on the north-south line from the center of the east-west line, is in the southern direction. If the shadow is in the northern direction, the base is northern. The word "and" <note>Sanskrit: "ca"</note> is used here to define the specific conditions. These minutes of zenith distance are combined with the previously mentioned minutes of the **Sun's declination** <note>original: "surya-kranti"</note>. If the directions are different, they are added together; if the directions are the same, they are subtracted from one another. The word "and" again defines the arrangement. The result is the **minutes of latitude** <note>original: "akshakala"</note>.

The Lord <note>referring to the divine author of the Surya Siddhanta</note> has explained the logic here through the designation of the "Base" <note>bhujasanjna</note>. For instance, in a triangle where the gnomon of twelve digits is the vertical side <note>koti</note> and the hypotenuse of the midday shadow is the hypotenuse, the midday shadow itself is the base. Similarly, the distance by which the Sun is inclined in the meridian circle from the observer's zenith at midday is the zenith distance. Its sine <note>nata-jya</note> is the base in a circle where the radius <note>trijya</note> is the hypotenuse. By the rule of proportion: if the midday shadow is the base for the shadow's hypotenuse, what is the base for the radius? The result is the sine of the zenith distance. Its arc, expressed in minutes, is the zenith distance. These are related to the planet and have a direction opposite to that of the shadow.

Now, if the declination and latitude are in the same direction, the zenith distance is their sum; thus, the southern zenith distance minus the southern declination equals the latitude. If the declination and latitude are in different directions, the zenith distance is their difference. If the zenith distance is southern, then the latitude is the northern declination plus the zenith distance. If it is northern, then the latitude is the declination minus the zenith distance. This is well-proven. Some say that by taking the "Base" at any desired time—the distance the tip of the shadow is north or south of the east-west line—and treating it as the midday shadow for a small interval, one can calculate the hypotenuse and find the zenith distance to determine the latitude adjusted by the declination. || 14 || 15 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The midday shadow is the base. Multiplying this by the radius and dividing by the shadow's hypotenuse, the arc is determined as the zenith distance. If the shadow is in the south, the zenith distance is north; if in the north, the zenith distance is south. If these are in different directions, add them to the Sun's declination to find the correct latitude. If they are in the same direction, they should be subtracted. || 14 || 15 ||

### Now, the calculation of the Equinoctial Shadow from the Latitude:

->**From those [minutes of latitude], find the sine of latitude. Subtract its square**<-
->**from the square of the radius; the square root is the sine of colatitude.**<-
->**The sine of latitude multiplied by twelve and divided by the sine of colatitude**<-
->**is the equinoctial shadow.**<- || 16 ||

From those minutes of latitude comes the **sine of latitude** <note>akshajya</note>. The word "and" implies the sequence of operations. Subtracting the square of the sine of latitude from the square of the radius, the square root of the remainder is the **sine of colatitude** <note>lambajya</note>. Then, the sine of latitude is multiplied by twelve and divided by the sine of colatitude—this division is implied by the relationship of the multiplication. The result is the **equinoctial shadow** <note>akshabha or palabha</note>.

The logic is as follows: The sine of the minutes of latitude is the sine of latitude. Since this is the base in a circle where the radius is the hypotenuse, the square root of the radius squared minus the base squared is the vertical side, which is the sine of colatitude. By proportion: if the sine of latitude is the base for the sine of colatitude as the vertical side, then what is the base for a vertical gnomon of twelve digits? The result is the equinoctial shadow. || 16 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** After separating the square of the sine of latitude from the square of the radius, the resulting square root is the sine of colatitude. The sine of latitude multiplied by twelve and divided by the sine of colatitude results in the equinoctial shadow. || 16 ||

# Surya Siddhanta: Chapter 3

Now, with one and a half verses, the author explains the method for determining the Sun's position via its declination, derived from the zenith distance and the local latitude:

->The difference between the local latitude and the degrees of the Sun's zenith distance is taken if they are in the same direction; otherwise, their sum is taken. (17)<-
->The result is the declination. Its sine, multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of the maximum declination, gives the arc. This is the Sun in the signs starting with Aries. (18)<-
->In the signs starting with Cancer, subtract it from half a circle (6 signs); in those starting with Libra, add it to half a circle; in those starting with Capricorn, subtract it from a full circle (12 signs). Thus, the true Sun at noon is found. (19)<-

The plural "degrees of the zenith distance" is used because there are many degrees in the local latitude and the noon zenith distance of the Sun. If they are in the same direction, take the difference; if in different directions, otherwise—meaning a sum should be performed. The resulting figure from this calculation is the <term>declination</term> <note>original: "kranti"; the angular distance of the Sun north or south of the celestial equator</note>. The sine of that declination should be multiplied by the <term>radius</term> <note>original: "trijya"; the standard radius used in Indian trigonometry, often 3438 minutes</note> and divided by the previously mentioned sine of maximum declination. The resulting arc in degrees, etc., represents the Sun located in the first three signs starting with Aries. 

If the Sun is in the three signs starting with Cancer, subtract the calculated arc from half a circle (six signs); the remainder is the true Sun at noon. In the three signs starting with Libra, the true Sun is known by adding the arc to six signs. In the three signs starting with Capricorn, subtract the arc from twelve signs (a full circle); the remainder is the true Sun, adjusted for the <term>precession of the equinoxes</term> <note>original: "ayanāṃśa"</note>. To understand the result of the calculation, it is implied that it is adjusted for the inverse precession. This is because it was previously stated that declination is to be calculated from a planet adjusted by precession.

The logic <note>original: "upapatti"</note> here is as follows: When the declination and latitude are in the same direction, the zenith distance is southern; therefore, the latitude minus the zenith distance is the southern declination. When they are in different directions, the latitude minus the declination is the southern zenith distance; thus, the latitude subtracted from this gives the northern declination. <unclear>...</unclear> If the sine of maximum declination has the radius as its base, then what is the base for this desired sine? That is the sine of the Sun with precession; its arc is the "arm" <note>the distance from the nearest equinox</note> of the Sun with precession. Since the "arm" is equal in all four quadrants: in the first quadrant (Aries etc.), the arm itself is the Sun. In the second quadrant (Cancer etc.), the arm is subtracted from six signs. In the third quadrant (Libra etc.), the arm is added to six signs. In the fourth quadrant (Capricorn etc.), the arm is subtracted from the full circle. This inverse calculation is very easy to understand. // 17 // 18 // 19 //

<insert>
**Hindi Commentary:** If the local latitude and the Sun's zenith distance are in the same direction, take the difference; if in different directions, take the sum to find the declination. Multiply the sine of this declination by the radius and divide by the sine of maximum declination (1397). Finding the arc of this result gives the true Sun with precession in Aries etc. Subtracting from 6 signs for Cancer etc., adding to 6 signs for Libra etc., and subtracting from 12 signs for Capricorn etc., yields the true (precessed) Sun. // 17 // 18 // 19 //

# Chapter 3: Expenditure (Calculations)
## With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries — Page 77

> The *Manda-phala* <note>Equation of the Center; the correction for the eccentricity of the orbit</note> applied repeatedly in reverse to the True Sun results in the Mean Sun.

From the calculated True Sun, the *Manda-phala* (correction for anomaly) should be applied "in reverse" (subtracted if it was added, and vice versa) multiple times to arrive at the Mean Sun as derived from the *Ahargana* <note>The count of elapsed days since the start of the epoch</note>. The meaning is this: by treating the True Sun as the Mean Sun, one calculates the correction from the *Mandocca* <note>Apogee/Perihelion point</note> as previously described. By applying this correction in reverse to the True Sun, one approaches the Mean Sun. This process is repeated—calculating the correction from the new result and applying it again—until the difference becomes negligible. Thus, while the True Sun is found by a single application of the correction to the Mean Sun, finding the Mean Sun from the True Sun requires this iterative process.

**Logic:** The correction is originally derived from the Mean Sun. Since the Mean Sun is unknown when starting from the True Sun, one uses the True Sun as a proxy. Each iteration brings the value closer to the precise Mean Sun until the result is flawless.

**Hindi Commentary:** By determining the *Manda-phala* from the *Nirayana* <note>Sidereal</note> True Sun and applying it repeatedly in reverse, the Mean Sun is obtained. That is, by treating the True Sun as the Mean Sun and performing the apogee calculations, one gets a rough Mean Sun; by repeating this, the exact position is refined.

***

Now, desiring to explain the calculation of the shadow and the hypotenuse at noon, the author first describes the knowledge of the *Natamsha* <note>Zenith distance; the angular distance from the zenith</note> at that time and its sine/cosine:

> The sum of one's local latitude and the Sun's declination if they are in the same direction; otherwise, the difference.
> The remainder is the Sun's *Natamsha*; its sine is the *Bhuja-jya* and its cosine is the *Koti-jya*. || 20 ||

If the local latitude and the midday solar declination are in the same direction (both North or both South), they are added. Otherwise (if one is North and the other South), find the difference between the latitude and declination. The resulting value is the Sun's *Natamsha* (Zenith distance) at noon. The sine of these degrees is the *Bhuja-jya* <note>Sine of the zenith distance</note>, and the sine of the complement (90 minus the degrees) is the *Koti-jya* <note>Cosine of the zenith distance</note>.

**Logic:** On the meridian circle at noon, the distance from the Zenith to the Celestial Equator is the Latitude. The distance from the Equator to the Sun is the Declination. Therefore, if the Sun is South of the Equator, the Zenith distance is the sum of Latitude and Declination. If North, it is the difference. In the "shadow triangle," the sine of this distance acts as the base (*Bhuja*), the *Mahashanku* <note>Great Gnomon; the cosine of zenith distance multiplied by the radius</note> acts as the upright (*Koti*), and the Radius acts as the hypotenuse. || 20 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** If the local latitude and the solar declination are in the same direction, add them; if in opposite directions, take the difference. The result is the midday Zenith distance (*Natamsha*). From this, calculate the Sine (*Bhujajya*) and Cosine (*Kotijya*). || 20 ||

Now, he explains the method for bringing forth (calculating) the shadow and the hypotenuse:

### The sine of the zenith distance and the radius, multiplied by the digits of the measure of the gnomon,
### are divided respectively by the cosine of the zenith distance; the results are the shadow and the hypotenuse in digits. || 21 ||

The "sine of the base and the radius" means the sine of the zenith distance <note>the angular distance from the point directly overhead</note> and the total radius. These should be multiplied by the twelve digits of the gnomon's measure. In both cases, they are divided by the "cosine of the base," meaning the sine of ninety degrees minus the zenith distance. The two results obtained respectively—following the order of the sine of the zenith distance and the radius—are the midday shadow and its hypotenuse.

Here is the proof: In the triangle of the shadow, the twelve-digit gnomon is the vertical side (cosine), the desired shadow is the horizontal base (sine), and the square root of the sum of their squares is the hypotenuse. By proportion: if in the great circle the vertical side is the "great gnomon" <note>the cosine of zenith distance</note> and the horizontal base and hypotenuse are the sine of zenith distance and the radius respectively, then what will the base and hypotenuse be when the vertical side is a twelve-digit gnomon? Thus, the midday shadow and its hypotenuse are produced. This is proven because the factors used belong to the same specific moment in time. || 21 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** Multiplying the sine of the zenith distance and the radius separately by the gnomon's measure (12) and dividing by the cosine of the zenith distance results in the shadow and the hypotenuse. || 21 ||

Now, wishing to explain the calculation of the "base" (latitude-related distance), he first brings forth the "amplitude" (agra) and the "amplitude of the hypotenuse":

### The sine of declination multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse and divided by the gnomon-sine,
### is the solar amplitude. This, multiplied by the desired hypotenuse and divided by the middle-hypotenuse, is its own [hypotenuse-amplitude]. || 22 ||

The sine of the sun's declination <note>the sun's distance north or south of the celestial equator</note> is multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse <note>the hypotenuse of the shadow at the equinox</note> and divided by the "gnomon-sine." The "gnomon" here refers to the twelve-digit standard; thus, it means dividing by twelve. The result is the "amplitude" (agra) of the sun. By extension, this applies to planets as well. This amplitude is then multiplied by the shadow-hypotenuse of the desired time and divided by the "middle-hypotenuse." The "middle of the diameter" refers to the semi-diameter or Radius; thus, it means dividing by the Radius. <note>The author notes a grammatical rule regarding the term 'middle-hypotenuse' (madhyakarna) being used for Radius</note>. The result is the "own-hypotenuse-amplitude" (svakarnagra).

Here is the proof: In the triangle of the latitude, the sine of declination is the vertical side in the unmandala <note>east-west hour circle</note>, and the amplitude is the hypotenuse on the horizon. In the local latitude triangle, if the equinoctial hypotenuse is the hypotenuse for a vertical side of twelve, then by proportion, what is the hypotenuse (amplitude) for a vertical side equal to the sine of declination? Furthermore, by the proportion "if this is the value in the circle of the Radius, what is it in the circle of the [current] hypotenuse?", the amplitude of the hypotenuse-circle is proven. || 22 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** Multiplying the sine of declination by the equinoctial hypotenuse and dividing by the gnomon (12) gives the solar amplitude (Suryagra). Multiplying the amplitude by the hypotenuse of the desired day and dividing by the Radius gives the "own-hypotenuse-amplitude." || 22 ||

Now, he speaks via two verses on the calculation of the "base" (bhuja):

### In the southern hemisphere, the solar amplitude added to the equinoctial shadow is the north base.
### In the northern hemisphere, subtracting it from the equinoctial shadow gives the north base. || 23 ||
### By the reverse, the base becomes southern. This is the distance between the east-west line and the end of the shadow.
### The midday base is always known as the midday shadow. || 24 ||
