# Chapter 3 ]           With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.

The **Sun’s amplitude** <note>original: *arkāgrā*; the distance along the horizon from the East-West line to the point of sunrise</note> is the amplitude of the hypotenuse at the desired time. In the **Southern Hemisphere** <note>original: *dakṣiṇagole*</note>, when this is added to the **equinoctial shadow** <note>original: *viṣuvadbhā* or *akṣacchāyā*; the shadow cast by a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</note>, the result is the **base** <note>original: *bhuja*; the north-south distance from the east-west line to the tip of the shadow</note> in the northern direction. In the **Northern Hemisphere**, one should subtract the amplitude of the hypotenuse from the equinoctial shadow; the remainder is the base in the northern direction. 

Now, if the amplitude of the hypotenuse cannot be subtracted from the equinoctial shadow <insert>because it is larger</insert>, how is the base to be determined? To this, he says: **"By reversal."** Subtract the equinoctial shadow from the amplitude of the hypotenuse; the remainder shall be the **Southern Base**. 

If one asks why the base is sometimes southern and sometimes northern, he says: **"In the interval between East and West."** This means the base is the distance in the northern or southern direction from the East-West line. However, since the second limit was not mentioned, the distance remains undefined; to the question of "the distance of what from the East-West line is the base?", he answers under the guise of defining the **midday shadow**: **"At midday."** The base at the time of midday is always called the midday shadow. Thus, it is clarified that the base is the distance by which the tip of the shadow is north or south of the East-West line.

The rationale here is as follows: The distance by which the foot of the **gnomon** <note>original: *śaṅku*; a vertical pillar used to measure shadows</note> is north or south of the East-West line is the north-south base of the planet. The gnomon is the perpendicular line from the planet to the plane of the horizon. There, this base is produced by the combination of the **gnomon-amplitude** <note>original: *śaṅkutala*; the distance from the east-west line to the rising-setting line</note> and the **amplitude** <note>original: *agrā*</note>. The gnomon-amplitude is the southern distance of the gnomon's foot from the rising-setting line located on its own diurnal circle. The amplitude is the distance from the East-West line to the rising-setting line, being north or south according to the Northern or Southern Hemisphere. 

<margin>Slight fading on the right margin of the page.</margin>

When this is calculated for a 12-digit gnomon using proportions, the base is the distance from the East-West line to the tip of the shadow. In the latitude-triangle, if the **co-latitude** <note>original: *koṭi*</note> is 12, the base is the equinoctial shadow. By the proportion "if for the Great Gnomon this is the base, what is it for a 12-digit gnomon?", the gnomon-amplitude is derived. Because the multipliers and divisors are equal, only the equinoctial shadow remains as the component. In the Southern Hemisphere, since the amplitude is southern, they are in the same direction; thus, the sum of the equinoctial shadow and the amplitude is the Northern Base. In the Northern Hemisphere, since the amplitude is northern <note>relative to the shadow's movement</note>, they are in different directions; the difference between the equinoctial shadow and the amplitude is the base. If the equinoctial shadow remains, it is the Northern Base; if the amplitude remains, it is the Southern Base. At midday, since the shadow itself takes the form of the base, it is correct to say the midday base is the midday shadow. || 23 || 24 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In the Southern Hemisphere, the sum of the equinoctial shadow and one's own amplitude of the hypotenuse, and in the North, their difference, results in the **Northern Base**. || 23 || If subtraction from the equinoctial shadow is impossible, then subtracting the equinoctial shadow from the amplitude of the hypotenuse results in the **Southern Base**. The midday base is called the **midday shadow**. || 24 ||

Now, having described the hypotenuse of the shadow on the meridian, he describes the hypotenuse of the shadow on the prime vertical <note>the East-West vertical circle</note> in two ways:

->**Multiply the Sine of Co-latitude and the Sine of Latitude by the equinoctial shadow and by twelve,**<-
->**and divide by the Sine of Declination; these are the two hypotenuses when the Sun is on the Prime Vertical. || 25 ||**<-

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter 3]

The <term>cosine of latitude</term> and the <term>sine of latitude</term> are respectively multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and by twelve; both are then divided by the <term>sine of declination</term> <note>original: krāntijyā</note>. The results obtained when the Sun is situated on the **prime vertical** <note>the vertical circle passing exactly East and West</note> are the hypotenuses related to the observed shadow. In both cases, this results in the <term>shadow-hypenuse</term> <note>the distance from the tip of the gnomon to the tip of its shadow</note>.

The proof is as follows: The circle that follows the east-west direction directly over one's head is called the **prime vertical** <term>samamaṇḍala</term>. This describes the calculation of the shadow-hypotenuse for an object located there. If the equinoctial shadow is the base and the latitude-hypotenuse is the hypotenuse, then what is the hypotenuse when the sine of declination is the base? This yields the **prime vertical gnomon** <term>samaśaṅku</term>. Because the prime vertical gnomon and the sine of the altitude are respectively the hypotenuse and the upright... From the rule "multiplied by the digits of the gnomon measure, etc.," the **radius** <term>trijyā</term> is multiplied by twelve and divided by this. According to the rule "in division, swap the divisor and the dividend," the radius multiplied by twelve and divided by the latitude-hypotenuse is simply the <term>cosine of latitude</term>. Thus, the cosine of latitude multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by the sine of declination results in the shadow-hypotenuse at the prime vertical.

Furthermore, if the equinoctial shadow is the base and twelve is the upright, then what is the upright if the sine of latitude is the base? In taking the cosine of latitude, since the equinoctial shadows are equal and cancel out, the sine of latitude multiplied by twelve and divided by the sine of declination is the shadow-hypotenuse at the prime vertical. The hypotenuse is always established from the sine of declination. However, a planet is not always on the prime vertical. To indicate that the hypotenuse should only be calculated for a planet actually on the prime vertical and not otherwise, the text specifies "when the Sun is on the prime vertical." || 25 ||

**Commentary:** When the planet is on the prime vertical, the hypotenuse is found by multiplying the cosine of latitude by the equinoctial shadow, or by multiplying the sine of latitude by twelve, and dividing the result by the sine of declination. || 25 ||

Now, one might ask: to calculate the prime vertical gnomon—which is visibly established in the sphere at the intersection of the planet's diurnal path and the east-west circle—can the shadow-hypotenuse be calculated even if the planet is not strictly on the **prime vertical**? The phrase "when the Sun is on the prime vertical" refers to its own diurnal path and not to other times; otherwise, the method would be too broad and lead to errors. No specific qualification is known to prevent such over-application. However, when the declination is greater than the latitude, the diurnal path does not intersect the prime vertical, and the prime vertical gnomon cannot be seen on the sphere. To explain how the calculation is handled there, and while offering another method for finding the prime vertical hypotenuse, the author says:

->When the northern declination is less than the latitude, then the **midday hypotenuse**,<-
->multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by the midday amplitude, is the hypotenuse. || 26 ||<-

When the northern declination is less than the latitude, the **midday hypotenuse** <term>dyudalaśrava</term> is the noon hypotenuse calculated from the Sun's declination on the prime vertical—not necessarily the actual noon-time value. Multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by the "midday amplitude" <note>the distance of the sun from the east-west line at noon</note>, the result is the **shadow-hypotenuse** of the planet's disk when it reaches the prime vertical. By specifying "northern," it is clearly stated that this is not calculated for southern declination, as the planet's disk would not be visible on the prime vertical then. Otherwise, if the declination were less than the latitude in the southern hemisphere, the **prime vertical gnomon** would be visible and the restriction would not apply. The proof here is derived from the actual midday shadow-hypotenuse at the time of prime vertical entry...

# Chapter 3. With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.

If a 12-digit gnomon <note>the standard vertical pillar used for measuring shadows</note> has a certain hypotenuse, then what will be the **midday gnomon** <note>the vertical component of the sun's position at noon</note> relative to the radius-hypotenuse? This is the instantaneous value. If the equinoctial shadow is the base for a 12-digit perpendicular, then what is the base for the great gnomon's perpendicular? This is called the <term>Shankutala</term> <note>the distance from the center of the horizon to the rising-setting line</note>. The product of the equinoctial shadow and the radius, divided by the midday hypotenuse, is derived from the 12-digit ratio. By this base, if the midday gnomon is found, then what is the **prime vertical gnomon** <note>the gnomon's shadow when the sun is exactly East or West</note> by the amplitude-base? The product of the 12-digit amplitude and the midday hypotenuse, divided by the midday hypotenuse and the equinoctial shadow, gives the prime vertical gnomon, because the amplitude-base and the motion of that gnomon form the perpendicular and hypotenuse.

By the previous method of calculating the shadow-hypotenuse, the product of the midday hypotenuse, the equinoctial shadow, and the radius (from the 12-digit ratio) is divided by the amplitude and the midday hypotenuse. By canceling out the equal multipliers and divisors of the midday hypotenuse, the result is established. One cannot simply assign values by independent will <note>mathematical rules must be followed</note>. Even there, after reducing the dividend and divisor by the radius, the midday hypotenuse multiplied by the amplitude and divided by the radius results in the "midday-amplitude." Therefore, it is said to be divided by the midday amplitude. In the dividend, the product of the midday hypotenuse and the equinoctial shadow is not calculated for the Southern Hemisphere because the planet <note>the Sun</note> is not visible <note>in the prime vertical</note> there. Even in the Northern Hemisphere, if the declination is greater than the latitude, it is not calculated because entry into the <term>Prime Vertical</term> <note>the great circle passing through the East, West, and Zenith</note> is impossible, as the latitude exceeds the declination.

It is calculated when the declination is small enough for that to occur. Indeed, what cannot be proven in the sphere through mathematics is not accepted due to lack of evidence; thus the rule starting with "In the North..." is justified. **Bhaskaracharya** <note>the famous 12th-century mathematician</note> says: "The Sun enters the prime vertical in the Northern Hemisphere only when its declination is less than the latitude; only then is its shadow visible and calculable <insert>.</insert> The gnomon produced when the Sun is at the point of amplitude in the prime vertical is certainly used for further proportions, but it is never seen otherwise." By this, he also established the rule. || 26 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** When the declination is less than the latitude, then the midday hypotenuse multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by the midday amplitude will result in the previously mentioned hypotenuse. || 26 ||

Now, to indicate that the amplitude of the hypotenuse-circle should be calculated for the desired base at any given time, and to clarify what was previously called the "midday hypotenuse," he says:

->**The sine of the declination multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of the colatitude is the sine of the amplitude.**<-
->**Multiplied by the desired hypotenuse and divided by the radius, it becomes the amplitude in digits.**<- || 27 ||

The sine of the declination at the desired time, multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of the colatitude <note>the complement of the latitude</note>, results in the sine of the amplitude. The logic is: if the radius-hypotenuse corresponds to the colatitude-perpendicular, then what hypotenuse corresponds to the declination-perpendicular? This is the amplitude. The second half of the verse is almost a repetition of previous explanations. If, in the previous verse regarding the amplitude of the hypotenuse-circle, the term "gnomon-sine" refers to the perpendicular of the gnomon (meaning the sine and cosine of the zenith distance calculated earlier), and "midday hypotenuse" refers to the hypotenuse of the instantaneous midday shadow, then it is not a repetition. However, "amplitude" should be understood as the amplitude of the instantaneous midday hypotenuse, and "one's own" refers to the amplitude of the desired time's hypotenuse. The logic is: if the equinoctial hypotenuse is the hypotenuse for a 12-digit perpendicular, then what is the hypotenuse for a declination-sine perpendicular? This is the amplitude for that time. In the <term>Radius Circle</term> <note>the standard circle with a radius of 3438 minutes</note>, the product of 12 and the radius divided by the cosine of the zenith distance (which is the shadow hypotenuse of the midday shadow) results in the equinoctial hypotenuse multiplied by the declination-sine and divided by the cosine of the midday zenith distance, after canceling the equal 12 and radius terms. This is exactly the midday shadow hypotenuse.

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Three]

The *hypotenuse-amplitude* <note>original: "karnagra"</note> is established by asking: if the amplitude is such, then what is it by the desired shadow-hypotenuse of that time? This results in the *hypotenuse-amplitude* for the specific time. The intersection of the diurnal circle occupied by the sun and the upper meridian is the local noon; this should be understood for further proportions. || 27 ||

**Mother Commentary:** Multiply the sine of the sun's declination <note>original: "svakrantijya"</note> by the radius <note>original: "trijya"</note> and divide by the sine of the co-latitude <note>original: "lambajya"</note> to get the amplitude <note>original: "agra"</note>. Multiply that by the desired hypotenuse and divide by the radius to get the value in digits and so on. || 27 ||

Now, in five verses, he describes the "corner gnomon" <note>the gnomon's shadow when the sun is in the intermediate directions like Northeast or Southwest</note> and the sine of the zenith distance <note>original: "drigjya"</note> for the purpose of calculating the corner shadow's hypotenuse:

> From half the square of the radius, subtract the square of the amplitude; multiply this by twelve, || 28 ||
> And multiply by twelve again. The result obtained by the wise, || 28 ||
> Divided by the square of the equinoctial shadow added to half the square of the gnomon <note>72, which is half of 12 squared</note>, || 29 ||
> Is indeed called the *surd* <note>original: "karani"</note>; the wise man should set that aside. || 29 ||
> The equinoctial shadow multiplied by twelve and by the amplitude, || 30 ||
> And so divided <note>by the same divisor as before</note>, is called the *result* <note>original: "phala"</note>. The square root of the *surd* added to the square of that *result*, || 30 ||
> Diminished or increased by the *result* in the southern and northern hemispheres respectively, || 31 ||
> Is the gnomon for the two southern and two northern intermediate directions when the sun moves in the south or north. || 31 ||
> It is that gnomon. The square root of the difference between the square of the radius and the square of that [gnomon] is called the sine of the zenith distance. || 32 ||

Using the amplitude previously calculated (not the hypotenuse-amplitude, as the previous hypotenuse is not yet established): subtract its square from half the square of the radius; multiply by twelve and a second time by twelve. The word "and" implies a collection. Therefore, instead of placing the twelve-fold multiplication in two places, it means multiplying by one hundred and forty-four. The separate mention by the calculator is for the ease of multiplication. Divided by the square of the equinoctial shadow <note>original: "palabha"</note> added to seventy-two (which is half the square of the twelve-digit gnomon), the number obtained by the calculators is named the *surd* <note>original: "karani"</note>. The wise calculator should set that *surd* aside in one place. 

Then, the amplitude multiplied by twelve and by the equinoctial shadow, divided by that same sum (the square of the equinoctial shadow plus seventy-two), gives the *result* <note>original: "phala"</note>. The square root of the *surd* added to the square of that *result* is then decreased or increased by the *result* in the southern and northern hemispheres <note>original: "gola"</note> respectively. Thus, the gnomon is established. As the sun moves in the south or north, the word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> indicates the sequence: for the two southern intermediate directions (Southeast and Southwest) and the two northern intermediate directions (Northeast and Northwest). The second "but" refers to the division of the day into forenoon and afternoon. The resulting meaning is: in the forenoon, the Southeast and Northeast in southern/northern order; in the afternoon, the Southwest and Northwest in southern/northern order. That is the "corner gnomon." The radius minus the square of the corner gnomon—

# Chapter 3. | With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries
<page-num>30</page-num>

The square root of the difference between the squares of these two is called the Sine of Zenith Distance <note>original: "drgjyā"</note>. Here, the proof is provided by the method of elimination of the middle term in a single-variable algebraic equation <note>original: "bījaikavarṇamadhyamāharaṇena"</note>. Regarding this, it is said: "One should assume 'So-much' <note>original: "yāvattāvat" — the standard term for an unknown variable, like 'x'</note> as the measure of the unknown quantity and perform the operations as directed. Two equal sides (of an equation) should be diligently established by subtracting, adding, multiplying, or dividing." Following this rule, two equal sides must be established to find the value of the Corner Gnomon <note>original: "koṇaśaṅkumānam"</note>.

If the unknown variable $x$ <note>yā 1</note> is the gnomon, and the Equinoctial Shadow <note>original: "palabhā"</note> is the base when the upright is 12, then what is the base when the upright is the gnomon? This gives the "Base of the Corner Gnomon" <note>original: "koṇaśaṅkutalam"</note>: $x \cdot \text{palabhā} / 12$ <gloss>12</gloss> / <gloss>12</gloss>.

In the Southern Hemisphere <note>original: "dakṣiṇagole"</note>, the total base is this added to the Amplitude <note>original: "agrā"</note>: $(x \cdot \text{palabhā} + \text{agrā} \cdot 72) / 12$ <gloss>72</gloss> / <gloss>12</gloss>. In the Northern Hemisphere, it is the difference with the Amplitude. North of the Prime Vertical, the base is the Amplitude minus the Gnomon-base: $(x \cdot \text{palabhā} / 12) - (\text{agrā} \cdot 72 / 12)$. South of the Prime Vertical, the base is the Gnomon-base minus the Amplitude.

Because the "Corner" is the midpoint between the North-South and East-West lines, the square of the hypotenuse (the Sine of Zenith Distance) is twice the square of the base. Thus, in the Southern Hemisphere, the square of the Sine of Zenith Distance is:
$(x^2 \cdot \text{palabhā}^2 \cdot 72) + (x \cdot \text{palabhā} \cdot \text{agrā} \cdot 24) + (\text{agrā}^2 \cdot 72) / 144$.
In the Northern Hemisphere, it is:
$(x^2 \cdot \text{palabhā}^2 \cdot 72) - (x \cdot \text{palabhā} \cdot \text{agrā} \cdot 24) + (\text{agrā}^2 \cdot 72) / 144$.

This Corner Gnomon is $x$. Its square $x^2$ subtracted from the square of the Radius <note>original: "trijyā"</note> is also the square of the Sine of Zenith Distance. Setting these two sides as equal and bringing them to a common denominator <note>original: "samacchedīkṛtya"</note>, the layout for clearing the sides is as follows:

---

In the Southern Hemisphere:
{ $x^2 \cdot \text{palabhā}^2 \cdot 72$ | $x \cdot \text{palabhā} \cdot \text{agrā} \cdot 24$ | $\text{agrā}^2 \cdot 144$ }
{ $x^2 \cdot 72$ | $x \cdot 0$ | $\text{Radius}^2 \cdot 72$ }

In the Northern Hemisphere:
{ $x^2 \cdot \text{palabhā}^2 \cdot 72$ | $x \cdot \text{palabhā} \cdot \text{agrā} \cdot 24$ | $\text{agrā}^2 \cdot 144$ }
{ $x^2 \cdot 72$ | $x \cdot 0$ | $\text{Radius}^2 \cdot 72$ }

---

Now, as it is said: "Subtract the unknown from the other side, and the known constants from the opposite side," in the side of the unknowns, the sum of 72 and the square of the Equinoctial Shadow is the coefficient of $x^2$. In the place of the middle term, the product of the Equinoctial Shadow, the Amplitude, and 24 is the coefficient of $x$—positive in the Southern Hemisphere and negative in the Northern. On the side of the constants, the square of the Radius multiplied by 72 is diminished by the square of the Amplitude multiplied by 144. Since 72 times the square of the Radius is equal to 144 times half the square of the Radius, it is kept thus for ease of calculation. It is established that 144 is multiplied by the difference between half the square of the Radius and the square of the Amplitude.

If the Amplitude is greater than the Sine of 45 degrees <note>original: "sārdharāśijyā"</note>, then the difference is negative. As it is said: "When a remainder of the square of the unknown exists, multiply both sides by a suitable number and add something so the side of the unknown becomes a perfect square. By taking the square root of both sides, the value of the unknown is obtained." To find the root, we divide by the coefficient of $x^2$. By dividing the unknown side by (72 + square of Equinoctial Shadow), $x^2$ is isolated in the first place. In the second place, the coefficient is processed to find the "result" <note>original: "phala"</note>, which is added or subtracted depending on the hemisphere. Finally, the square of half the coefficient of the unknown is added to both sides to complete the square.

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter 3]

In that context, by taking the root after establishing the unknown side <note>algebraic side</note>, in the first position, there is the "as much as" <term>yāvattāvat: the standard term for an unknown variable, similar to 'x'</term>. In the second position, the result is positive or negative depending on the southern or northern hemispheres. For example: **x 1, Result 1**; **x 1, Result 1.** <note>The dot likely indicates a negative value</note>. In the northern hemisphere, for the unknown...

...because in both cases, the middle unknown can be eliminated. However, in the case of the "unit side" <note>the constant side of the equation</note>, when taking the result, it is the square root of the surd added to the square of that result. This applies when the sine of the amplitude is not greater than the sine of one and a half signs <note>45 degrees</note>. But if it is greater, it is the root of the square of the result minus the surd. Thus, even if the previously stated logic regarding "from half the square of the radius minus the square of the sine of amplitude" fails when the amplitude is greater than 45 degrees, it is not a flaw. As **Bhaskara** <note>Bhaskara II, the 12th-century mathematician</note> stated: "In any calculation of subtraction, if the quantity to be subtracted cannot be subtracted, it should be done by reverse subtraction; the rule remains as stated, but a wise man should turn addition into subtraction and vice versa." By this reasoning, the phrase "minus the square of the sine of amplitude" can mean either subtracted from or subtracting the square, depending on whether the amplitude is lesser or greater. Now, for the sake of balancing the equation—

The layout of the two sides: In the southern hemisphere { **x 1, Result 1** (Because the root of the square of the result minus the surd is less than the result).
<margin>x 0, Unit 1</margin>

The layout of those two sides as well: { **x 1, Result 1** (Here, by the rule "with one unknown," etc., and "Divide the units by the remaining unknown...
<margin>x 0, Unit 0</margin>

...the remaining unknown becomes the value of the unknown quantity"). By this, it is established that in the first position, the root is subtracted from the result. In the second position, the result is subtracted from the root; however, the Lord <note>the author of the Surya Siddhanta</note> did not mention this "negative corner gnomon." This is because the position of a negative value is reversed. Indeed, in the upper hemisphere, a reversed position is not seen even if it were visible in the lower hemisphere, making its mention unnecessary. Nor does its visibility in the lower hemisphere necessitate its mention, as the calculation is for the purpose of determining the shadow for someone in the upper hemisphere; since a shadow is impossible there <note>in the lower hemisphere</note>, it is irrelevant. # Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Three]

The terms mentioned are used to subtract from midday to find the **elapsed time from noon** <note>original: "natakala," the hour angle</note> in units of *ghatis*. From the breaths <note>units of time</note> of that duration, one calculates the minutes of arc. Following the prescribed method—using the table of versed sines <note>original: "utkramajya-pindai," segments used to calculate the versed sine</note>—one finds the versed sine. If the time from noon exceeds fifteen *ghatis* <note>6 hours</note>, one takes the sine segments of the time exceeding fifteen *ghatis* and adds them to the radius to find the versed sine.

By subtracting this from the **Antya** <note>the total diurnal arc expressed as a sine value</note>, the result is multiplied by the **radius of the diurnal circle** <note>original: "dyujya," the cosine of declination</note> and divided by the **radius** <note>3438'</note>. The result is known as the **Cheda** <note>the divisor or "corrected" diurnal sine</note>. 

Thereafter, the *Cheda* is multiplied by the **sine of colatitude** <note>original: "lambajya"</note> and divided by the **radius**; the result is the **Shanku** <note>the sine of the Sun's altitude</note> at the desired time. One should subtract the square of this *Shanku* from the square of the radius. The square root of the remainder is the **Drigjya** <note>the sine of the zenith distance</note>. From these two, the shadow and the hypotenuse are derived as previously explained. 

The reasoning <note>original: "upapatti"</note> is as follows: In the northern hemisphere, the *Antya* is the radius plus the **sine of the terrestrial amplitude** <note>original: "charajya"</note>; in the southern hemisphere, it is the radius minus the *charajya*. This is because the radius of the diurnal circle is measured from the intersection of the celestial equator and the meridian. Since the **unmandala** <note>the six-o'clock circle</note> sits above or below the horizon depending on the north/south position, the distance between it and the horizon is the *charajya*. 

The straight line from the Sun's position to the rising-setting line is the **Ishtantya** <note>the sine of the arc of the day remaining</note>. By proportion, if the radius gives the *lambajya* as the vertical side, then the *Ishtahriti* <note>the corrected diurnal sine</note> gives the **desired Shanku**. From this, the shadow and its hypotenuse are logically established. || 34 || 35 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** When the Sun is in the Northern Hemisphere, add the *charajya* to the radius; when in the Southern, subtract it—this is the *Antya*. Subtract the desired time from midday and convert to degrees to find the *Nata* <note>hour angle</note>. Subtract the versed sine of this *Nata* from the *Antya*, multiply by the radius of the diurnal circle, and divide by the radius (3438); this is the *Cheda*. Multiply the *Cheda* by the sine of colatitude and divide by the radius to get the *Shanku*. Subtract the square of the *Shanku* from the square of the radius (11,819,844) and take the square root to find the *Drigjya*. The shadow and hypotenuse are then found as before. || 34 || 35 ||

# Chapter 3. ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. ( 87 )

The gnomon <note>original: "शङ्कुः" (Shanku); the vertical pillar used in sundials</note> multiplied by the sine of the three-signs <note>original: "सत्रिभजीवा" (Sattribhajiva); equivalent to the Radius</note> and divided by its own sine of latitude <note>original: "स्वलम्बज्या" (Svalambajya); the co-latitude sine</note> results in the divisor. That divisor, multiplied by the radius and divided by the radius of the diurnal circle <note>original: "स्वाहोरात्रार्द्ध" (Svahoratrardha); the radius of the sun's daily path</note>, results in the sine of the altitude. Subtracting that from the total sine <note>original: "स्वान्त्या" (Svantya); the versed sine of the semi-diurnal arc</note>, the arc of the remainder—calculated via the versed sines <note>original: "उत्क्रमज्या" (Utkramajya)—provides the degrees of time past noon or before noon for the forenoon and afternoon respectively. **[37-38]**

The sine of the zenith distance <note>original: "दृग्ज्या" (Drigjya)</note> is obtained by multiplying the desired shadow by the radius and dividing by the hypotenuse of the shadow. The square root of the difference between the square of the radius and the square of the sine of the zenith distance is the gnomon <note>the vertical component</note>. The word "and" <note>original: "चकारो"</note> implies the constant relationship between these values. This desired gnomon, multiplied by the radius and divided by the local sine of co-latitude, yields the "divisor" <note>term: "छेद" (Cheda); a specific intermediate value in Indian astronomical computation</note>. That divisor, multiplied by the radius and divided by the diurnal radius, results in a specific sine of altitude. This is not the direct arc of time. Subtracting this from the "Antya" <note>the total versed sine from sunrise to noon</note> gives the remainder. One should find the arc of this remainder using the table of versed sines <note>the "Munayo Randhra Yamala" etc., referring to traditional mnemonic numerical tables</note>. If the remainder exceeds the radius, the arc is found by adding the sine-arc to 5400 minutes <note>90 degrees</note>. The resulting figures are the "Asus" <note>term: "असवः" (Asavah); units of time equivalent to 4 seconds or 1 minute of arc of the celestial equator</note> of the time from noon for the morning or evening. The logic here is the inverse of the previously stated rules. Because the diurnal circle's diameter is not the same as the equator's, this "sine of altitude" is treated as a close approximation. Hence, the great teacher Bhaskaracharya <note>12th-century mathematician/astronomer</note> stated: "The desired Antya should be considered equal to the sine of the altitude," etc. Otherwise, the instruction to "subtract" would be meaningless. **[36-37-38]**

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiply the desired shadow by the radius and divide by the hypotenuse to get the sine of the zenith distance. Subtract the square of this from the square of the radius; the square root is the gnomon. Multiply the gnomon by the radius and divide by the co-latitude sine to get the divisor. Multiply the divisor by the radius and divide by the diurnal radius; subtract this from the Antya to get the remaining sine of altitude. From this, calculate the arc. By the measure of the versed sine of this altitude, the time in breaths (Prana/Asu) before or after noon is established. **[36-37-38]**

**Now, he describes the calculation of the Sun via the sine of declination from the shadow at a desired time in one and a half verses:**

That sine of declination, multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of maximum declination <note>original: "परमापक्रम" (Paramapakrama); approx. 24 degrees</note>, gives the arc. This arc, adjusted by the appropriate quadrant, reveals the position of the Sun <note>original: "रविः" (Ravih)</note>. **[39]**

The sine of co-latitude is multiplied by the "Agra" <note>amplitude</note> of the hypotenuse at the desired time. The word "but" <note>original: "तु"</note> is used to exclude other types of amplitude. Dividing by the number of digits in the hypotenuse of the shadow at that moment yields the sine of declination. That sine of declination is multiplied by the radius... <unclear>multiplied</unclear>

The result obtained by dividing [the product] by the sine of the maximum declination <note>original: *paramakrāntijyā*</note> is the arc of the field, which is the base <term>Bhuja: the horizontal side of a right-angled triangle</term>. By knowing which of the four quadrants <note>the four signs of the zodiacal circle</note> it occupies, the Sun's position is determined. As previously stated, if it is in the sign of Cancer and so on, by subtracting from the half-circle, the true Sun is found. 

The proof is as follows: If at the end of the hypotenuse the amplitude <note>original: *karṇāgrā*</note> is found, what is it at the end of the radius? By the proportion: if the radius-hypotenuse has the sine of latitude <note>original: *lambajyā*</note> as its upright, what is the upright at the end of the given hypotenuse? Since the two radii (multiplier and divisor) cancel each other out, the sine of declination <note>original: *krāntijyā*</note> is equal to the given amplitude multiplied by the sine of latitude and divided by the hypotenuse. Since the method for bringing forth the Sun's position was explained earlier, this is a simpler repetition. || 39 ||

**Commentary**—Multiply the desired amplitude by the sine of latitude and divide by its own hypotenuse-fingers <note>the length of the shadow's hypotenuse measured in *angulas* or finger-breadths</note>; the result is the sine of the Sun's declination. Multiply this by the radius and divide by the sine of maximum declination. By determining the arc of the resulting sine (and knowing which quadrant of the circle it occupies), the true longitude of the Sun (including the precession of the equinoxes) <note>original: *sayana sphuṭa*</note> is found. || 39 ||

### Now, the rotation of the shadow is described:

-> On a desired day, at three different times (morning, noon, and afternoon), mark the three points of the base. <-
-> By the intersection of two "fish" figures, the path of the shadow is traced with a cord touching the three points. <- || 40 ||

On a chosen day, in the eastern part, the western part, and at three intervals of the base, marks are placed at the ends of the three bases along the East-West line. The meaning is this: From the center point of the East-West line, one mark is made at the distance of the base-fingers; a second mark in the eastern section at the distance of the base-fingers for that time; and a third mark in the western section at the distance of the base-fingers for another time. Thus, at three times in a single day, three marks are made at their respective base-distances from the East-West line. 

"By the intersection of two fish" <note>A "fish" (*matsya*) is a geometric construction where two intersecting arcs create a lens shape used to draw perpendicular lines</note> means producing a "fish" from each pair of adjacent marks. Where the two center-lines passing through the mouth and tail of each fish intersect when extended, that point is the center. With a cord <note>a compass or string</note> acting as the radius touching all three marks, the circle of the shadow's path <note>original: *bhābhrama*</note> is formed. This means the tip of the shadow at any time between the first and last marks will fall upon the circumference of that circle. 

The proof is: Having known the three shadow-tips by their distances from the East-West line, to find the center of the circle passing through them, the North-South lines are drawn through the middle of the adjacent marks using the "fish" method. Since the center must be equidistant from the points on the circumference, the intersection of these lines necessarily marks the center. Thus, the intersection of the two lines from the adjacent marks establishes the center of that circle. It is no wonder that a cord from that center touches all three points. 

However, because the shadow-tip moves according to the Sun's motion, a perfect circle is technically impossible because the diurnal circle changes every moment. Otherwise, there would be no change in declination, and the shadow-tip could not travel a single circular path. For this reason, the teacher Bhaskara stated, "The rotation of the shadow from three points is not strictly true." 

Nevertheless, <margin>it is possible for the calculated shadow-tips to reside on a single circle, and those [shadow-tips] falling between them</margin> <meta>continuity: the text likely continues to explain that for practical purposes, the arc is treated as a circle.</meta>

# Chapter 3. | With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.

Accepting that the tip of the shadow stays on the perimeter [of the circle] due to the very small difference, the compassionate Lord has explained how to know the position of the shadow's tip even without seeing it. This allows one to determine the position of the Sun in signs, etc., which depends on the shadow's arm <note>The 'arm' or *bhuja* refers to the distance from the east-west line</note>, even when the Sun is covered by clouds, by observing the positions of the shadow's tip at other times. It should be noted that if the observations are taken at a very long interval, the result is approximate; if taken at a short interval, it is somewhat precise. || 40 ||

**Hindi Commentary**—By making three marks—at midday, before it, and after it—and forming a circle that touches these three marks from the intersection point of the lines passing through the two "fish" figures <note>A geometric construction method using intersecting arcs</note>, the path of the remaining shadow is determined. <gloss>(In actual subtle calculation, the tip of the shadow moves in a different path)</gloss> || 40 ||

Now, having explained the knowledge of time, and wishing to explain the knowledge of the *Lagna* <term>Ascendant: the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</term> which is useful for predictions and results depending on that time, the author speaks two verses to establish the rising times at Lanka <note>The equator</note> for the first three signs starting with Aries, in order to calculate the rising times at one's own location:

->**The sines of one, two, and three signs are multiplied by the radius and divided by their respective diurnal radii.**<-
->**The arcs of these results are found separately.**<-
|| 41 ||
->**Then, subtracting each from the one below it, the rising times at Lanka (in respirations) starting from Aries are found.**<-
->**They are 1670, 1795, and 1935 respectively.**<-
|| 42 ||

The sines of one, two, and three signs <note>Sines of 30°, 60°, and 90°</note> are to be multiplied by the radius of the three-sign arc and divided by the diurnal radii <term>Dyujya: the radius of the day-circle for a specific declination</term> related to their respective declinations. The arcs of these results should be placed in different positions. This means they should be placed in two sets of positions. Thereafter, "each from the one below it": the result related to the sine of one sign is kept as it is; then the first result is subtracted from the second, and the second from the third. If they were not stated separately, and the first result was subtracted from the second while the second was being cleared, the third subtraction would be impossible. And since the knowledge of the first is necessary, placing the first and second separately is essential. This is why it is not said to place them separately in three ways. Starting from Aries, these are the <term>Lankodayasavas</term> <note>Rising times at the equator measured in *asus* or respirations; 6 asus = 1 sidereal minute</note> of the three signs. The first result is the rising time of Aries; the second subtracted from the third is the rising time of Gemini. Because these are fixed, he states their values: "Khagashtayah" etc. The value for Aries is 1670; the value for Taurus is 1795; the value for Gemini is 1935.

The mathematical proof here is from the <term>Siddhanta Shiromani</term> <note>A major 12th-century astronomical treatise by Bhaskara II</note>: "The sines of Aries etc. are the hypotenuses in the equatorial circle; the sines of declination are the 'arms' (verticals). Their 'roots' (horizontals) in their own diurnal circles, when converted to the scale of the Great Circle radius... the respirations of those arcs, when subtracted from the one below, are the risings at the equator." By this definition, if the radius is the hypotenuse and the diurnal radius of three signs is the side, then what are the sides for the hypotenuses of the sines of one, two, and three signs? By this proportion, the sides are calculated in the diurnal circle, and to find the hypotenuse-respirations, they must be calculated in the scale of the Great Circle radius. Therefore, by the proportion: if these are the values in the diurnal radius, what are they in the Great Circle radius...

# Surya Siddhanta - [Chapter Three]

Because the divisors are equal and cancel out, the sines of one, two, and three signs <note>zodiac signs of 30 degrees each</note> are multiplied by the radius <note>the sine of 90 degrees, or 3438 minutes</note> and divided by their respective day-radius <term>Dyujya</term><note>the radius of the diurnal circle of the planet</note>; this is the established proof. From these results, the rising times at the equator <term>Lankodayasavas</term> are found by subtracting the preceding values from the subsequent ones to find the individual rising time for each sign. This explains the text from "The radius multiplied by the half-chord..." up to "...are the rising times at Lanka." Here, the term "Lanka" should be interpreted as any place on the terrestrial equator <note>original: "niraksha-desha"</note>. Since the geometry of the sphere is identical for all points on the equator, there is no obstacle to applying this logic to any equatorial location. Otherwise, one would have to apply a longitudinal correction <term>Deshantara</term> just to calculate the rising times for one's own equatorial position. The method for finding local rising times by applying the correction for local latitude <term>Chara</term> is explained immediately following this. The calculation itself, using the numbers "six, seven, eight..." <note>referring to specific numerical constants in the Sanskrit verse</note>, serves as the proof.

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiply the sines of one, two, and three signs respectively by the radius (3438) and divide by the half-day-radius of the respective sign to determine the arc. By subtracting the first result from the second, and the second from the third, the rising times at the equator <term>Lankodaya Prana</term> <note>measured in 'pranas' or respirations; 1 prana = 4 seconds of time</note> for Aries and the following signs are found. The values in pranas are: Aries 1670, Taurus 1795, and Gemini 1935.

### Now, he describes the local rising times for these signs in half a verse:

->**The local rising times are found by subtracting the respective local segments of ascensional difference.**<-

These are now established. The "segments of ascensional difference" <term>Charakhandas</term> are derived from the local latitude. By calculating the total ascensional difference for one, two, and three signs and subtracting them sequentially, one obtains the segments for Aries, Taurus, and Gemini. When these segments are subtracted from the equatorial rising times, the results are the local rising times <term>Ishtodayasavas</term> for those three signs at that specific latitude. The proof for this is as Bhaskara stated: "The signs from Aries to Gemini rise at the equator in specific times; at a location below the equator <note>i.e., with latitude</note>, they rise in those times minus their respective ascensional differences." Thus, to know the individual rising time, one uses the individual segment of difference.

**Hindi Commentary:** By subtracting the local ascensional difference segments from the equatorial times, the rising times for the desired location are found. Later, by adding these segments in reverse order to the equatorial times, the rising times for Cancer and the following signs will be found.

### Now, he describes the rising times for the remaining signs:

->**The next three signs, Cancer and the rest, are found by adding the segments in reverse order.**<-
->**These six, when inverted, become the rising times for the six signs starting with Libra.**<-

Following this, the equatorial rising times for Aries, Taurus, and Gemini are placed in reverse order (Gemini, Taurus, Aries). By adding the respective ascensional difference segments—also placed in reverse order—one obtains the rising times for the three signs starting with Cancer (Cancer, Leo, Virgo). Having explained the first six signs, he now explains how to find the rising times for the remaining signs:

By the term **in reverse order**: These six signs ending with Virgo, when taken in reverse order—Virgo, Leo, Cancer, and so on—[are used for calculation]. The word "only" is used here to exclude the direct order of Aries, Taurus, etc. The six signs starting from Libra have rising times equal to the rising times of the signs in one's own country as determined by the reverse order. Thus, it is established that the rising time of Virgo is the same as Libra; Leo is the same as Scorpio; Cancer is the same as Sagittarius; Gemini is the same as Capricorn; Taurus is the same as Aquarius; and Aries is the same as Pisces. The mathematical rationale for this is:

> "From the end of Virgo to the end of Sagittarius, the rising times are increased by the <term>Chara-khandas</term><note>intervals of terrestrial latitude correction</note>... by the words of Bhaskara <note>Bhaskaracharya, the 12th-century mathematician</note>, this is easily understood." || 44 ||

### Now, he describes the "passed" and "remaining" breaths to be used for calculating the positive or negative Ascendant at a desired time:

-> The passed and remaining breaths should be calculated from the Sun at the desired time. <-
-> Multiplied by the rising breaths of the sign and divided by thirty. <- || 45 ||

The passed and remaining breaths are calculated from the position of the Sun at the desired time. How are they calculated? He says: **multiplied by the rising breaths.** The "passed" and "remaining" portions refer to the degrees the Sun has already traversed in its current sign. These degrees, subtracted from thirty, give the remaining degrees. These degrees, multiplied by the local rising breaths of that sign and divided by thirty, result in the "passed breaths" and "remaining breaths" respectively.

The rationale is as follows: At whatever time the Ascendant (<term>Lagna</term>) is to be calculated, the Sun's position must be determined for that exact moment; otherwise, the calculation for that specific time will not be accurate. For this purpose, the passed and remaining breaths of the sign occupied by the Sun must be found, because from sunrise until that moment, that sign is considered the rising sign. Furthermore, the knowledge of the Ascendant is easily achieved by calculating the rising breaths of the signs. Therefore, if thirty degrees equal the total rising breaths, then how many breaths do the passed/remaining degrees equal? This gives the time in breaths. 

Here, because the rising times are calculated based on the intersection of the celestial equator and the ecliptic, the Sun's position must be adjusted by the <term>Ayanamsha</term><note>precession of the equinoxes</note>. Otherwise, the calculation would be inconsistent as it wouldn't relate to the actual rising of the sign. This is why Bhaskaracharya said: "The declination should be calculated with the added precession, and the passed and remaining times should be found from the planet." 

One might ask: should these breaths not be calculated from the Sun at the moment of sunrise? If we use the Sun's position at the "desired time," it wasn't at that position at sunrise. Why then did the omniscient author say "from the Sun at the desired time"? The answer is: rising times are based on sidereal time <note>naksatra-ghati</note>, but the units we usually calculate (Ghatis) are solar/civil time <note>savana</note>. It is necessary to convert these to sidereal units, otherwise the calculation fails. For this reason, in sixty solar hours, the breaths generated by the planet's motion are added... <margin>The result of the calculation is the field...</margin>

If eighteen hundred minutes of arc correspond to the rising breaths of the three signs, then what corresponds to the given breaths? By this proportion, since the multiplier and divisor (eighteen hundred and the rising breaths) are equal, they cancel out, and the resulting value of the Ascendant is added to the Sun. The civil <term>Savana</term><note>Time measured from sunrise to sunrise</note> units remain unchanged. Thus, the Sun at the desired time and the Ascendant at that time—the civil ghatikas taken prior to that time—become sidereal <note>original: "Nakshatra"</note>. This was correctly stated by the Lord. Regarding the phrase "from the desired time of Bhaskara": with this very intention, the teacher Bhaskara said: "If the desired ghatikas for the Ascendant are civil, they should be made sidereal by the calculation of the specific time. **Commentary:** By using the rising time, and completing the elapsed and remaining degrees of the (tropical) Sun at that time to make 30, the elapsed and remaining breaths <note>original: "Asu"</note> are determined. || 45 ||

Now, he describes the calculation of the "subtractive and additive" Ascendant from the desired ghatikas in two verses:

From the breaths of the ghatikas from sunrise at the desired time, one should subtract the remaining breaths <note>original: "Bhogyasun"</note> of the sign the Sun is in. Thereafter, the breaths of the subsequent signs <note>original: "Eshya-lagna"</note>. The signs following the sign occupied by the Sun are the "coming" Ascendants. Their rising breaths should also be subtracted in sequence. In the same manner, for the elapsed time, one should subtract the rising breaths of the signs that have already passed in reverse order from the remaining breaths. The rising time of the sign that cannot be fully subtracted is the "unpurified" <note>original: "Ashuddha"</note> one; the remainder is multiplied by thirty and divided by that value. This implies that if there is no remainder, no further action is needed as the result is zero. The result in degrees, etc., is subtracted from the count of the "unpurified" sign if related to elapsed time, and added to the count of the last "purified" sign if related to the remaining time. This represents the point on the ecliptic <note>original: "Kranti-vritta"</note> intersecting the eastern part of the horizon at the desired time. For the purpose of predicting results, the position of the planets is fixed relative to the junction star of Revati; therefore, it is self-evident that the resulting Ascendant, which is measured from the equinox, should be adjusted in reverse by the precession <note>original: "Ayanamsha"</note>. It should not be argued that because the precession adjustment for the Sun was not mentioned earlier, the Ascendant should remain as it is. Because of its coarse nature, the precession adjustment is applied to the Sun for the sake of the Ascendant; this is included in the term "etc." when discussing the planet's declination, shadow, and half-duration of daylight. Now, the Lord did not explicitly state the reverse precession adjustment, so the Ascendant is taken from the equinox for the purpose of predicting results. For the Sun, however, the precession adjustment is necessary for the sake of the Ascendant, because the rising times are measured from the equinox. This is not so. "Degrees..."

The logic here is as follows: By subtracting the "to-be-traversed" time <note>original: "bhogya-asu"; the time remaining for the current sign to rise.</note> from the desired time (in <term>Ghatikas</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note>), we determine that the sign currently occupied by the Sun is not the <term>Lagna</term>. Adding these to the count of elapsed signs results in the true <term>Lagna</term>. Now, in this context, the author describes the calculation of the Midheaven to indicate a specific method of calculation:

### By the "Hour Angle" units of time from the East or West, and by the rising times at the Equator,
### subtracting from or adding to the Sun, the Midheaven is then determined. || 48 ||

The "Hour Angle" <note>original: "nata-nāḍī"; the time elapsed since the Sun was at the meridian.</note> is well known in the systems of horoscopy: it is the time remaining until noon or the time elapsed since noon (for day) or midnight (for night). Using these units of time and the position of the Sun at that moment, one uses the rising times of the signs at the Equator <note>original: "laṅkodaya"; the time it takes for zodiac signs to rise at the terrestrial equator.</note> to find the degrees and signs as previously described. By subtracting or adding these to the Sun based on whether the time is before or after the meridian, the <term>Madhya-lagna</term> (the Midheaven or 10th House cusp) for the desired time is found.

The meaning is this: For an eastern hour angle, subtract the "traversed" equatorial rising time of the Sun's sign from the hour angle units, then subtract the equatorial rising times of the preceding signs. Multiply the remainder by 30 and divide by the rising time of the incomplete sign. Subtracting these degrees and signs from the Sun gives the Midheaven. Similarly, for a western hour angle, subtract the "to-be-traversed" equatorial rising time of the Sun's sign, then the subsequent signs, and add the result to the Sun to find the Midheaven. Even for short durations, the desired time units multiplied by 30 and divided by the rising time of the Sun's sign will yield the degrees to be added or subtracted. The <term>Lagna</term> can also be calculated in this manner. The logic is: the point of the ecliptic that meets the upper meridian is the Midheaven. To calculate it, one measures the distance from the meridian at the desired time...

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter 3]

The portion of the day (measured in *ghatis* <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> and their divisions) by which the Sun has moved from the meridian is called the **Hour Angle** (*natakala*). In the eastern and western hemispheres, it is designated as eastern or western. The period from midnight until midday is the eastern hemisphere; from midday until midnight is the western hemisphere. In the case of an eastern hour angle, because the Sun is situated east of the meridian, the zodiacal sign-degree on the meridian is behind the Sun; therefore, it is calculated using the hour angle *ghatis* as a negative adjustment from the Sun's position. In a western hour angle, because the Sun is west of the meridian, the sign on the meridian is ahead of the Sun; therefore, it is calculated using the hour angle *ghatis* as a positive adjustment from the Sun's position. Since the meridian is fixed at a distance of fifteen *ghatis* from the celestial equator, this is calculated using the times of rising at the equator (*lankodaya*). The reasoning for the remaining operations is very clear and is thus stated in brief. — 48

**Hindi Commentary:** In this manner, by using the eastern and western hour angle units and the equatorial rising periods (*lankodaya*), and by subtracting from or adding to the true position of the Sun (*ravi-sphuta*), the Middle or Tenth House (*dasham lagna*) is determined. — 48

### Now, the method for determining time is stated:

-> **Add the rising units to be passed (*bhogyasu*) of the lesser, and the units already passed (*bhuktasu*) of the greater,** <-
-> **along with the rising units of the intervening signs; thus is the determination of time. — 49** <-

Now, between the Ascendant (*lagna*) and the Sun (*arka*), take the one that is lesser in longitude and calculate its *bhogyasu* <note>The time remaining for the current sign to finish rising</note>; take the one that is greater and calculate its *bhuktasu* <note>The time already elapsed since the current sign began rising</note>. Add these together along with the rising periods (*udayasu*) of the complete zodiacal signs falling between the Sun and the Ascendant. By this method, the determination of time is achieved. The logic here is: time exists between the lesser and the greater positions. Therefore, the time to be passed by the lesser position, plus the rising times of the intervening signs, plus the time already passed by the greater position, results in the time elapsed between those two points. — 49

**Hindi Commentary:** Between the Ascendant and the true Sun, take the "to-be-passed" time of the lesser and the "already-passed" time of the other; the sum of these plus the breath-counts (*prana*) <note>A unit of time; 1 prana = 4 seconds</note> of the signs situated between them will determine the time. — 49

### Now, he explains how to know if the time calculated from the Ascendant and Sun falls within day or night:

-> **If the Ascendant is less than the Sun, it is the remainder of the night; if greater than the Sun, it is day.** <-
-> **If greater than the Sun plus half the zodiac, it is after sunset. — 50** <-

When the Ascendant is less than the Sun (within a range of three signs), the time calculated by the previous method occurs at the end of the night. When the Ascendant is greater than the Sun (within a range of six signs), the time is during the day. When the Ascendant is greater than the Sun plus six signs (half the zodiac), the time calculated using the Sun's seventh-sign position and the Ascendant is after sunset—meaning during the night. By this, it is indicated that for a desired time at night, the Ascendant should be calculated from the position of the Sun plus six signs. The logic is: at sunrise, the Ascendant is equal to the Sun; therefore, if the Ascendant is less or greater, the time is respectively the end of night or during the day. Similarly, at sunset, the Ascendant is the Sun's seventh sign; if the Ascendant is greater than that, the time is proven to be at night. This is easily understood. — 50

# Now, the Fourth Chapter.

Now the Chapter on Lunar Eclipses is explained. First, the author describes the diameters of the solar and lunar orbs in yojanas <term>Yojana: a traditional unit of distance, roughly 5-9 miles</term> and their correction into "true" values in one and a half verses:

->The diameter of the Sun's orb is six thousand and five hundred yojanas.<-
->The diameter of the Moon's orb is four hundred and eighty.<-
->These, multiplied by their own true daily motion and divided by their mean daily motion, become their true diameters. || 1 ||<-

Six thousand and a half—half of a thousand being five hundred—together makes six thousand five hundred yojanas as the diameter <note>Vishkambha</note> of the Sun's spherical orb. The diameter of the Moon's spherical orb is four hundred plus eighty, or four hundred and eighty yojanas. These two diameters, multiplied by the planet's own true motion and divided by its mean motion, result in the "true" <note>corrected for distance</note> diameters. In these calculations, experts treat the diameter as the orb itself. The reasoning here is: because the planet moves in its mean orbit at a distance equal to the radius <note>Trijya</note>, the diameter measured there is the "mean" diameter. Since the mean motion is accepted there with little error, the proportion is: if this is the diameter for the mean motion, what is it for the true motion? Thus, the true orb appears larger when the planet is low <note>near Earth</note> and smaller when it is high <note>farther away</note>, corresponding to the maximum and minimum speeds of motion. || 1 ||

# Surya Siddhanta: Chapter Four

<page-num>96</page-num>
->**The Calculation of Eclipses**<-

...is in <term>yojanas</term> <note>A traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 5–9 miles</note>. By multiplying the diameter by the planet's true daily motion and dividing by its mean daily motion, the true diameter is obtained. || 1 ||

Now, while calculating the solar disk at the Moon’s orbit, the author explains the calculation of their diameters in minutes of arc in one and a half verses:

> **The Sun's diameter multiplied by its own revolutions and divided by the Moon's revolutions; || 2 ||**
> **Or multiplied by the Moon's orbit and divided by the Sun's orbit,**
> **gives the diameter at the Moon's orbit. Divided by fifteen, these become minutes of arc. || 3 ||**

The diameter of the Sun—the true diameter previously mentioned—multiplied by the Sun's own revolutions and divided by the Moon's revolutions, or alternatively, multiplied by the Moon's orbit (to be described later) and divided by the Sun's orbit, results in the true diameter of the Sun as it appears in the lunar sphere <note>the celestial path where the Moon resides</note>. Then, the number of <term>yojanas</term> of that diameter divided by fifteen gives the measure of the diameters of the Sun and Moon in <term>minutes of arc</term> <note>original: "kala"</note>.

The reasoning here is as follows: If the total minutes in a circle correspond to the total <term>yojanas</term> of the Moon's orbit, then how many <term>yojanas</term> are in one minute? In the Moon's orbit, one minute equals fifteen <term>yojanas</term>. Therefore, since the Moon stays in its own orbit, its true diameter in <term>yojanas</term> divided by fifteen gives its diameter in minutes. Similarly, in the Sun's orbit, one minute equals 250.5 <term>yojanas</term>; dividing the Sun's true diameter by that would give its minutes. 

However, because people see the Sun from a great distance as if it were in the lunar sky, and because it cannot be seen with a distinct separation <note>due to parallax and perspective</note>, the Sun's diameter is calculated according to the Moon's orbit for mathematical purposes—using the proportion: "If this is the diameter at the Sun's orbit, what is it at the Moon's orbit?" This is a mathematical construct, not a physical reality. It does not mean the Sun actually resides in the Moon's orbit; if it did, the Moon could not be described as the "coverer" <note>the obscuring body</note> during a solar eclipse. 

Furthermore, the Sun's true diameter multiplied by the Moon's orbit (which is the Moon's orbit divided by the Moon's revolutions) and divided by the Sun's orbit (the Sun's orbit divided by the Sun's revolutions) results in the cancellation of the orbital terms. Thus, it is simply multiplied by the Sun's revolutions and divided by the Moon's revolutions. This method was stated first because of its primary importance, even before the orbits were defined. Thus, the Sun's diameter at the Moon's orbit divided by fifteen yields the diameter in minutes. This is logically proven. || 2 || 3 ||

---

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiplying the Sun's true diameter by the Sun's revolutions and dividing by the Moon's revolutions—or multiplying by the Moon's orbit and dividing by the Sun's orbit—defines the Sun's diameter in the lunar sphere. That is, the measure of the Sun's diameter relative to the Moon's orbit. Dividing that Sun's diameter (and the Moon's diameter) by 15 results in the diameter in minutes and seconds. || 2 || 3 ||

Now, he calculates the necessary Earth's shadow in two verses:

> **The Earth's diameter multiplied by the Moon's true motion and divided by its mean motion;**
> **The result is the "needle" <note>the cone of the shadow</note>, the difference between the Earth's diameter and the Sun's true distance. || 4 ||**

# Chapter 4. With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries
<page-num>97</page-num>

->Multiply by the mean diameter of the Moon, divide by the mean diameter of the Sun.<-
->Subtract the result from the "Cone" <note>the *suci* or needle/cone calculation</note>; the minutes of the shadow are as before. // 5 //<-

The true motion of the Moon multiplied by the Earth's diameter and divided by the mean lunar motion results in the value called the "Cone" (*suci*). The difference between the Earth's diameter and the true diameter of the Sun's disk is multiplied by the mean diameter of the Moon's disk—which is 480 *yojanas* <note>a traditional unit of distance, roughly 5-9 miles</note>—and divided by the mean diameter of the Sun's disk—which is 6500 *yojanas*. This result is subtracted from the previously established "Cone." The remainder is the "Shadow" (*tamas*), representing the Earth's shadow in *yojanas*, for the shadow is indeed darkness. He gives its measurement in minutes of arc (*liptas*) with the word "minutes." Because the connection to the previous verse was not explicitly stated, the word "but" (*tu*) is used to make the connection to the following section easy to understand. Therefore, the word "shadow" at the end of the previous sentence does not apply here. As stated previously, "the minutes of the measure are obtained by dividing by fifteen," the minutes of the Earth's shadow should be calculated.

Here is the rationale. <term>“The Sun’s disk minus the Earth’s diameter, multiplied by the Moon’s distance and divided by the Sun’s distance; the Earth’s diameter minus that result is the width of the Earth’s shadow at the Moon’s path.”</term> <note>original: "bhūvyāsahīnaṃ ravibimbamindukarṇāhataṃ bhāskarakarṇabhaktam..."</note> This precise method is stated in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>a major 12th-century astronomical treatise by Bhaskara II</note>. The explanation is clear in its commentary. There, accepting a slight margin of error, the Sun's disk minus the Earth's diameter (4900) is multiplied by the true lunar distance in *yojanas* (which is the mean lunar distance multiplied by the mean motion and divided by the true motion). The true solar distance is the divisor. To convert this segment into minutes, the radius (*trijya*) is the multiplier and the lunar distance is the divisor. Since the true and mean motions of the Moon act as equal multiplier and divisor, they cancel out. By dividing the radius and the mean lunar distance by the radius, the divisor is separately stated as fifteen. What remains are the *yojanas* of the mean Sun's disk minus the Earth's diameter, with the Sun's true motion as multiplier and divisor. The mean distances of the Moon and Sun are also respectively multiplier and divisor. For the sake of algebraic simplicity, the diameters of the disks are used instead of the distances. Although it might seem improper to use disk diameters since they do not perfectly track with the mean distances of the Sun and Moon, it is considered acceptable due to the negligible margin of error. In the "Chapter on the Terrestrial Globe," the orbits of the Moon and Sun are said to be the Earth's diameter multiplied by the orbit and divided by the Earth's circumference. This is even more applicable to the semi-diameter of those orbits. Even there, when taking the true solar disk in *yojanas*, it is established that the mean solar disk is multiplied by the Sun's true motion and divided by the Sun's mean motion. One should not object, asking how the Earth's diameter is established here simply as "Earth's diameter" when the true and mean solar motions should technically apply to the difference between the Earth's diameter and the mean solar disk, not just the disk itself. The Lord <note>the author or the divine source of the text</note> has accepted the Earth's diameter as it is, due to the small difference. By saying "the difference between the Earth's diameter and the true solar distance," the term "true" applies to both, and because of the proximity to the solar distance, the "trueness" of the Earth's diameter is established by the same logic as the Sun's disk. Now, this calculated result subtracted from the Earth's diameter gives the Earth's shadow in *yojanas*. To convert that to minutes, the other segment of the Earth's diameter has the radius as a multiplier and the true lunar distance as the divisor. By dividing the radius and mean distance by the multiplier, fifteen becomes the divisor, and the true and mean motions of the Moon are the multiplier and divisor; thus the "Cone" calculation is explained. Because the Earth's shadow mimics a cone, the first segment is subtracted from the second segment to get the Earth's shadow in *yojanas*, which is then divided by fifteen.

# Surya Siddhanta — Chapter Four

The calculation performed in minutes of arc and other units is justified. However, if one takes the **apparent solar disk** <note>the Sun's diameter as it appears to an observer, rather than its mean size</note> right at the start—since the text "the solar disk minus the Earth's diameter" does not specify the **mean disk** <note>average diameter</note>—then the Earth's diameter is not a commonly known "apparent" value. In that case, the literal reading "the difference between the Earth's diameter and the apparent solar distance" would be correct. 

But in that scenario, the Lord <note>the author of the Surya Siddhanta</note> did not mention the multipliers and divisors for the Sun's mean and apparent motions for the remaining portion (the solar disk minus the Earth's diameter), likely because the difference is negligible. One should not argue that the **mean yojanas of the radii** <note>yojana: a traditional unit of distance, roughly 5-9 miles</note> of the Sun and Moon were used in the proportion instead of the apparent ones, and thus the multipliers/divisors for mean and apparent motion were omitted because they weren't produced. This is because it would lead to the failure to mention the **cone** <note>the shadow cone</note> produced by using the Moon's apparent distance in yojanas. 

If one argues that using the Moon's distance as a mean value causes a large error, whereas using it as an apparent value is necessary for the cone, while using the Sun's distance as a mean value only causes a small error—that is also incorrect. If one uses the yojanas of the **mean solar disk**, the calculation for the **apparent solar distance** <note>the actual distance at a specific time</note> becomes inconsistent. 

Furthermore, it cannot be argued that since both are omitted, the individual small errors add up to a large one, and therefore the Sun's motion should have been included in at least one place. There is no logical necessity for this. Previously, the multipliers and divisors for the Sun's apparent and mean motions were applied only to the solar disk, not to the Earth's diameter; but in the final calculation, they apply to both. To distinguish between the "rough" and "precise" methods, it is proper to include the Sun's motion in the final stage. 

If it is suggested that by explaining the cone using the Moon's motion for the first part of the Earth's diameter, the Sun's motion is implicitly suggested for the second part (the solar disk minus the Earth's diameter), and thus there is no harm—this is also rejected. There is no evidence for assuming the Sun's motion in this context, and it does not follow logically. Otherwise, one would be forced to use the Moon's motion here as well. 

By this, we also refute the idea that: "If the Earth's diameter corresponds to the Moon's mean motion, what is it for the apparent motion?"—calling this part the "apparent cone"—and then calculating the second part (the solar disk minus the Earth's diameter) relative to the Moon's disk. This claim that the difference between these two "apparent" parts is the "apparent Earth-shadow" is dismissed. There is no evidence that those two proportions result in "apparent" values, nor is there any occasion for such "apparentness." Furthermore, the mean disks of the Moon and Sun would become inconsistent.

The astronomer **Jnanaraja**, in his work *Siddhanta Sundara*, recognized the difficulty of the Earth's diameter not fitting the "cone-shape" perfectly. He treated the Earth's diameter itself as the first part. For the second part (the solar disk minus the Earth's diameter), because the mean distance proportion doesn't work perfectly, he derived multipliers and divisors for the mean disk. He then converted both into minutes of arc: "If the radius of the Moon's mean orbit equals the total minutes in a radian (3438), what do these two parts equal?" By this proportion, using fifteen as the divisor, he stated the difference is the Earth's shadow. 

As stated in his text:
> "The Moon's disk, multiplied by the difference between the Sun's and Earth's diameters and divided by the Sun's disk; the Earth's diameter minus that result is the Earth's shadow. That, divided by 480 <note>original: 'sharendubhaktā', literally 'divided by arrows (5) and moon (1)'? Likely a technical constant</note>, results in the value in minutes."

In this verse, the "Sun's diameter" refers to the **apparent solar disk in yojanas**, not the mean. The multipliers and divisors for the lunar and solar disks are in mean yojanas, not apparent ones—this was the view of the commentator Chintamani, but it contradicts the *Surya Siddhanta*. This is because of the reasons already stated, and because his proof fails to establish it. 

Furthermore, the commentator Chintamani's method for bringing out the "mean Earth-shadow" is also inconsistent. He suggests that if the mean shadow is found by using mean distances as multipliers/divisors, then one should calculate the "apparent" shadow using the difference in apparent motions, even if the original author didn't say so. This is incorrect because the Earth's shadow is not actually produced by the difference in motions. Otherwise, like the Sun and Moon disks which are calculated based on motion, the shadow would have to be derived solely from the minutes of the difference in motion...

# Chapter 4. With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.

...that the calculation of the Earth's shadow is achieved. This is incorrect. Because the formula established in the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>A foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy</note> states: "The true motion of the Moon multiplied by the Earth's diameter and divided by the mean motion," and because the specific "cone" <term>suci: the cone of the Earth's shadow</term> was not mentioned, the Earth's diameter is taken in its original form. Enough of elaborating on the faults of others. || 4 || 5 ||

**Hindi Commentary**—Multiply the Earth's diameter (1600) by the true motion of the Moon and divide by the daily motion of the Moon; the result will be the *suci* <note>the length of the shadow cone</note>. Multiply the difference between the Earth's diameter (1600) and the Sun's true diameter by the Moon's mean diameter (480) and divide by the mean solar diameter (6500). Subtract this result from the *suci* to find the diameter of the darkness <term>tamavyasa: the diameter of the Earth's shadow at the Moon's orbit</term> in *yojanas* <note>an ancient unit of distance</note>. As before, dividing this by 15 will give the value in minutes of arc and so on. || 4 || 5 ||

### Now he describes the occurrence of the two eclipses—

-> The Earth's shadow is six signs away from the Sun. When the Moon's node is equal to that shadow, or equal to the Sun itself, an eclipse occurs, even if it is a few degrees more or less. || 6 || <-

The Earth's shadow is at a distance of six signs <note>180 degrees</note> from the Sun because it is always opposite to the Sun. When the Moon's node <term>shashankapata: the point where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic</term> is equal to that shadow (the Sun plus six signs), or equal to the Sun itself, an eclipse of the Moon or Sun respectively occurs. Now, one might ask if an eclipse can occur even without exact equality. To this, he says: "a few degrees more or less." Even if the Moon's node is a few degrees more or less than the Sun (or the Sun plus six signs), an eclipse still occurs. Thus, there is no harm. For a lunar eclipse, these degrees are within twelve <note>the eclipse limit</note>. For a solar eclipse, however, the calculation involves the parallax of latitude <note>adjustment for the observer's perspective on Earth</note>. 

The logic here is: when the Moon's node is equal to either the Sun plus six signs or the Sun alone, the Moon's latitude <term>shara: the angular distance from the ecliptic</term> is zero. At that time, the Moon enters the Earth's shadow, causing an eclipse. Similarly, even if there is some latitude, if it is less than half the sum of the diameters <note>the combined radii of the shadow and the Moon</note>, a portion of the disk will be in the shadow and an eclipse occurs. Likewise, when latitude is zero or less than the sum of the radii, the Moon's disk covers the Sun's disk. However, in that case, the latitude is not highly refined, so what has been said is appropriate. || 6 ||

**Hindi Commentary**—The Earth's shadow is situated 6 signs away from the Sun. When the Moon's node is in the same sign as the shadow or the Sun, an eclipse will occur. An eclipse will also occur if it is slightly less or more. || 6 ||

### Now, asking when that occurs, he states the time of those two eclipses—

-> They should be equal in signs and degrees at the end of the New Moon. At the end of the Full Moon, the Sun and Moon are equal at a distance of six signs. || 7 || <-

The Sun and Moon calculated for the end of the New Moon <term>amavasya</term> are equal in signs, degrees, and minutes. At the end of the Full Moon <term>purnimanta</term>, the Sun and Moon are equal but separated by six signs. Thus, at the end of the New Moon, because the Sun and Moon are in the same spot (with only a vertical difference), a solar eclipse occurs. At the end of the Full Moon, because the Moon and the Earth's shadow are in the same spot, a lunar eclipse occurs. By this, it is indicated that in the previous verse, "Moon's node" should not be taken as two different nodes. This verse—
