It should be noted that the Moon's latitude <note>original: "chandra-vikshepa"</note> here is considered at the time of the middle of the eclipse. The rationale is as follows: since the "drkshepa" <note>the sine of the zenith distance of the ecliptic</note> is produced by the power of the "madhyajya" <note>the sine of the meridian altitude</note> in its respective direction, it is proper that the resulting values share that same direction. Now, because the "nati" <note>parallax in latitude</note> is the north-south distance from the Earth-surface observer's line of sight to the Sun up to the ecliptic in the lunar sphere, and the "vikshepa" <note>celestial latitude</note> is the distance from the ecliptic to the Moon's disk, the "apparent latitude" <note>spashta-vikshepa</note>—which is the north-south distance from the observer's line of sight to the Moon's disk—is calculated by the sum of the latitude and the parallax if they are in the same direction, or by their difference if they are in opposite directions. This is logically established. || 12 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** According to the direction of the "madhyajya," the parallax <note>avanati</note> will be North or South. If the directions are the same, it is added to the Moon's latitude; otherwise, it is subtracted to find the apparent latitude. || 12 ||

### Now, the rules mentioned in the chapter on Lunar Eclipses are applied here by extension:

-> By that [apparent latitude], the half-duration, the half-totality, the magnitude of the eclipse, etc., are as previously stated. <-
-> The scale, the deflection, and the desired magnitude at a given time are like those of the Moon <note>the Lunar Eclipse</note>. || 13 || <-

"By that" means by the apparent latitude which has been refined by the parallax. The "half-duration" <note>sthityardha</note>, "half-totality" <note>vimardhardha</note>, and "magnitude" <note>grasa</note>—and by the word "etc.," the first contact, separation, immersion, and emergence—are to be calculated exactly as described in the section on Lunar Eclipses. The word "tu" <note>but/indeed</note> is used here for emphasis to exclude any other methods. "Scale" <note>pramanam</note> means the measurement. He states the remainder: "deflection" <note>valana</note>, etc. By the word "etc.," the calculation of the magnitude at a desired time or the time for a desired magnitude is meant. These should be performed according to the rules given for the Lunar Eclipse. The underlying logic here is identical. || 13 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Using the latitude refined by the parallax, the half-duration, half-totality, magnitude, scale, deflection, and desired magnitude, etc., should be determined in the same manner as a Lunar Eclipse. || 13 ||

### Now, he describes the specific differences regarding the half-duration and half-totality in four verses:

> From the end of the lunar day <note>tithyanta</note>, decreased or increased as before, the parallax in longitude <note>lambana</note> must be calculated again ||
> for the moments of separation and first contact; then find the difference between those and the parallax at the middle of the eclipse. || 14 ||
> In the eastern hemisphere, if the parallax at the end of the eclipse is greater than at the middle, ||
> that difference is added to the half-duration of separation; if it is less, it is subtracted. In the western hemisphere, the opposite is true. || 15 ||
> Then, that difference should be added to the half-duration of separation, and likewise for the first contact, ||
> the difference in parallax should be subtracted; where the conditions are reversed, the operation is reversed. || 16 ||
> This is stated for when the phases occur in the same hemisphere; if they occur in different hemispheres, the sum of the parallaxes ||
> should be added to their respective half-durations. The same applies to the half-totality. || 17 ||

The half-duration of first contact and the half-duration of separation are calculated once according to the method described in the Lunar Eclipse chapter. Specifically: from the latitude at the time of the middle of the eclipse, the minutes of the half-duration are found, and by those, the end of the lunar day...

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Five]

The planets <note>referring here to the Sun and Moon</note> are to be calculated for the specific times. For the sake of the **half-duration of the beginning** <term>Sparsha-sthyardha: the time from the start of the eclipse to the maximum obscuration</term>, the planets should be moved backward <note>calculated for an earlier time</note>. For the sake of the **half-duration of the end** <term>Moksha-sthyardha: the time from maximum obscuration to the end</term>, they should be moved forward. Having determined the parallax in latitude <note>Nati</note> and the corrected latitude <note>Shara</note> for each of those two times, the true latitude must be calculated. 

Then, from the true latitude of the first time, the half-duration is found; by this, the planets at the end of the lunar day <term>Tithyanta: the moment of conjunction/New Moon</term> are moved as before, the true latitude is determined, and the half-duration is calculated again. This process is repeated until the **half-duration of the beginning** is consistent <note>an iterative mathematical process to find the exact moment</note>. In the same way, from the true latitude of the second time, the half-duration is found; by this, the planets at the end of the lunar day are moved forward, the true latitude is determined, and the half-duration is calculated. This is repeated until the **half-duration of the end** is consistent.

Now, with these two half-durations of beginning and end, which are respectively subtracted from and added to the time of the end of the New Moon, the **parallax in longitude** <term>Lambana</term> must be calculated again repeatedly for the moments of contact and separation. 

To explain: from the end of the lunar day minus the half-duration of the beginning, the rising sign <note>Lagna</note> and the tenth house <note>Dashamabhava</note> for that time are determined, and from these, the parallax is calculated. By correcting the time with this parallax, the process is repeated until the **parallax for the time of contact** is fixed. Similarly, from the end of the lunar day plus the half-duration of the end, the rising sign and tenth house are determined, and the parallax is calculated. By correcting the time with this parallax, the process is repeated until the **parallax for the time of separation** is fixed.

In the **eastern hemisphere** <term>Prak-kapala</term>, when the Sun is at a higher longitude than the "meridian ecliptic point" <term>Tribhonalagna: the point 90 degrees behind the rising sign</term>, the parallax is calculated from the middle time. Due to the variation in the division of the aforementioned parallax, the contact <note>Pragrahana: the beginning of the eclipse</note> is determined. Here too, the rule of parallax applies. If the parallax at the time of contact is greater, and the parallax at the time of separation <note>Maukshika</note> is less; or in the **western hemisphere** <term>Pashcharda</term>, when the Sun is at a lower longitude than the meridian ecliptic point—the word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> here implies "and"—the reverse occurs. This means the parallax at contact is less than the middle parallax, and the parallax at separation is greater. 

In such cases, the **difference in parallax** <term>Harijantara: literally 'difference born of the horizon'</term>—that is, the difference between the middle parallax and the parallax of contact or separation—must be added to the half-duration. For the contact, the difference between the contact parallax and middle parallax is added to the half-duration of the beginning. For the separation, the difference between the separation parallax and middle parallax is added to the half-duration of the end. 

Where the reverse occurs—meaning in the eastern hemisphere the contact parallax is less and the separation parallax is greater than the middle, or in the western hemisphere the contact parallax is greater and the separation parallax is less—then this difference in parallax must be **subtracted** <note>original: "shodhyam"</note>. This difference is added or subtracted when there is **unity of the hemisphere** <term>Kapalaikye</term>, meaning both the contact/middle or middle/separation points fall on the same side of the meridian ecliptic point. This has been explained. If there is a **difference in hemisphere** <term>Tad-bhede</term>, such as when the Sun at the time of contact is beyond the meridian ecliptic point of that time, but at the middle time...

# Chapter 5: Solar Eclipses
## Sanskrit Commentary and Hindi Exposition (Page 119)

If the <term>instantaneous Sun</term><note>The position of the Sun at the specific moment of calculation.</note> is less than the <term>meridian ecliptic point</term><note>The *tribhonalagna*, or the point of the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the ascendant; used to calculate parallax.</note> at the middle of the eclipse, or if the instantaneous Sun is less than the meridian ecliptic point at the time of clearance (end of eclipse), this indicates the direction of parallax. 

**The Unity of Parallax** means the sum of the parallaxes. When there is a difference between the contact (start) and the middle, the two instantaneous parallaxes are added together. Similarly, when there is a difference between the middle and the clearance, those two instantaneous parallaxes are added. 

These sums are to be applied to their respective **half-durations** (*sthityardha*). 
- To the **half-duration of contact**, add the sum of the parallaxes for the contact and middle times. 
- To the **half-duration of clearance**, add the sum of the parallaxes for the clearance and middle times. 

By doing this, the half-durations of contact and clearance become **corrected** (*sphuta*). From these, following the rules established in the section on Lunar Eclipses, the actual times of contact and clearance are determined by subtracting or adding them to the time of the middle of the eclipse.

The text now extends this logic of correction to the **half-duration of total darkness** (*vimardardha*): 
In the case of the half-duration of total darkness at contact and clearance, one should calculate them using the corrected latitude as described in the Lunar Eclipse chapter. Just as before, one uses the rule: <insert>"From the end of the lunar day (*tithi*), corrected by the half-duration, calculate the parallax again..."</insert> 

In this context, where the text previously discussed the "half-duration of the eclipse," one should now substitute the "half-duration of total darkness." Where it mentioned "contact and clearance," one should substitute **immersion** (*sammilana*)<note>The moment totality begins.</note> and **emergence** (*unmilana*)<note>The moment totality ends.</note>. The word "also" implies that the times for immersion and emergence should be calculated relative to the middle of the eclipse, just as the contact times were.

### The Rationale (Upapatti)
The time of the middle of the eclipse, minus or plus the half-duration, gives the times of contact and clearance. This requires the application of parallax at the middle of the eclipse. However, the parallax at the specific moments of contact and clearance is also required. A time corrected by parallax at one moment cannot be considered accurate for a different moment because the parallax changes. 

Since the exact times of contact and clearance are not known initially, one cannot know the instantaneous parallax for those moments. Therefore, to find the middle time, one repeatedly calculates the parallax from the end of the *tithi* (lunar day) until it stabilizes. Similarly, for contact and clearance, one calculates the parallax repeatedly for those specific moments. The difference between these corrected times and the middle time is the **corrected half-duration**.

<margin>If the parallax is negative (subtractive):</margin>
When the parallax at contact is greater than the parallax at the middle, and the parallax at clearance is less, then the difference is added to the half-duration. Conversely, if the parallax at contact is less than at the middle, the difference is subtracted. 

<margin>If the parallax is positive (additive):</margin>
When the parallax at contact is less than at the middle, and the parallax at clearance is greater... <note>The text continues to explain the mathematical logic for adding or subtracting the difference in parallax to ensure the timing of the eclipse phases is precise to the observer's specific location.</note>

<page-num>( 120 )</page-num>
<header>The Surya Siddhanta</header>
<header>[Chapter Five]</header>

## The Surya Siddhanta

Since the end of the lunar day <note>tithi</note> is considered the middle of the eclipse, the difference in parallax between those two points must be added to the half-duration of the beginning <term>sparśa-sthyardha: the time from the start of the eclipse to its peak</term>. Similarly, since the time of the end <note>mokṣa</note> is defined by the end of the lunar day plus the increased parallax, the difference in parallax between the middle and the end must be added to the half-duration of the end <term>mokṣa-sthyardha: the time from the peak to the end</term> according to the previous rule. However, when the parallax at the beginning or end is less than the parallax at the middle, then—because the time of the beginning is defined by the addition of a greater parallax and the middle by a lesser one—the difference in parallax is subtracted from the half-duration of the beginning. Thus, it is established that the difference in parallax is subtracted from the half-duration of the end when the parallax at the end is less than at the middle.

Now, one might object: "This case of subtracting the parallax difference is inconsistent. It is obstructed by logic. For instance, because negative parallax <note>parallax in longitude that shifts the perceived time earlier</note> decreases sequentially, and the times of the beginning, middle, and end occur one after the other, it is impossible for the parallax at the beginning and end to be respectively less or greater than the middle parallax. Similarly, because positive parallax increases sequentially, it is impossible for the parallax at the beginning and end to be respectively greater or less than the middle parallax. It never happens that the beginning and end times occur in reverse order relative to the middle time; such a claim is obstructed by reality." Furthermore, if the rule "the difference in parallax must be added" is already sufficient, why this elaborate explanation?

If you ask, "How then does the statement of the All-Knowing Lord <note>referring to the divine origin of the Surya Siddhanta</note>—

> "The difference in parallax <note>original: harijāntarakaṃ</note> should be subtracted where the opposite occurs" 

—hold true?" The answer is: Not so. Although the actual, corrected times of the beginning and end (after parallax is applied) must always follow the sequence of before and after the middle time, the *formal* times of the beginning and end (defined simply as the end of the lunar day plus or minus the half-duration) are artificial and not the physical reality. Because of the positive parallax at the middle time, it is possible for the formal beginning and end times to occasionally appear in reverse order relative to the middle, and thus the rule is maintained. However, in cases of purely negative or purely positive parallax, it is impossible for the end and beginning parallaxes to exceed the middle in that specific way. Since this is not explicitly stated, the word "opposite" <note>viparyaya</note> refers to a specific technical reversal. The previous general explanation was given because the word itself is general; thus, there is no error.

One might further object: "Even so, if parallax is calculated through repeated approximation <note>asakt-sādhana</note>, the parallax at the beginning will certainly be less than the negative parallax at the middle. In positive parallax, the end parallax will never be less. Since the actual beginning and end times cannot logically occur after or before the middle respectively, a fixed parallax would be impossible. Furthermore, if a stable parallax is found for a specific time through repeated calculation, that time is already the precise beginning or end; therefore, calculating the 'corrected half-duration' is useless, as the half-duration is only needed to find that very time."

If you say, "The corrected half-duration is taught so we can know the beginning and end times just like in a lunar eclipse," we say no. That would be unnecessarily cumbersome, and the rule "the difference should be subtracted" would remain illogical. The truth is: we do not accept the necessity of repeated approximation for parallax. Even if a single calculation of parallax leaves a small margin of error, the Lord has accepted it because the difference is negligible. Therefore, in the phrase "parallax again," the interpretation of "again" as "repeatedly" (as said previously) is not ideal. Rather, it means: "Having calculated parallax for the sake of the middle time, calculate parallax a *second* time for the sake of the beginning and end times." Or, "again" is simply a poetic ornament. Now, when the middle time occurs during negative or positive parallax at the approximate time of the beginning...

<page-num>121</page-num>
<header>Chapter 5. | Including Sanskrit Commentary and Hindi Translation.</header>

Since the end of the lunar day <note>tithi</note> minus the parallax is the time of contact <note>sparśa</note>, and the lunar day plus the parallax is the middle time, the difference between them—the half-duration of contact—is justified as being combined with the parallax of that specific time. Similarly, when the parallax is negative at the middle time and the rough time of release <note>mokṣa</note> has a positive parallax, the half-duration of release is justified as being combined with the sum of the parallaxes. 

One should not ask: "How could the Lord, who is omniscient, be intent on this method which contains slight errors due to accepting a single parallax calculation, when precise contact and release times are achieved through repeated <term>asakṛt</term><note>iterative calculation</note> parallax calculations?" It is said that the Omniscient Lord, fearing the excessive effort required for repeated parallax calculations, accepted a very small margin of error for the sake of simplicity and to follow the method used in lunar eclipses; thus, the calculation of the corrected half-duration <term>sphuṭa-sthityardha</term> was taught. 

In reality, if the contact occurs before sunrise and the middle time after, then the contact parallax—calculated from the fourth house <note>pātāla</note> and the sign plus three signs <note>sattribhalagna</note>—is sometimes less than the middle parallax. Where the middle is before sunrise and the release after, the release parallax is sometimes greater than the middle parallax. Where contact is before sunset and the middle after, the contact parallax is sometimes greater due to the connection with the night. Where the middle is before sunset and the release after, the release parallax is not less than the middle parallax. The phrase "sometimes" refers to eclipses occurring at sunrise or sunset. Because a reversal is possible, the instruction "subtract the difference of the two" is not invalid. By this, the solution stating that parallax should not be calculated repeatedly is refuted. The same logic applies to the half-duration of total obscuration <term>vimardārdha</term>. 

**Bhāskarācārya**, however, states:

> "From the calculated end of the lunar day, subtract or add the half-duration; calculate the parallax for those times.
> By adding or subtracting the half-duration resulting from the latitude and parallax to the calculated end of the New Moon, 
> and by performing this repeatedly <term>asakṛt</term>, the times known as contact and release become successively clear.
> The difference between those and the middle time results in the two corrected half-durations.
> Similarly, by subtracting or adding the half-duration of total obscuration to the end of the New Moon, the times of immersion and emersion are found."

By this, he implies a method even more precise than that spoken by the Lord <note>referring to the Sun God in the Surya Siddhanta</note>; enough of this elaboration. || 14 || 15 || 16 || 17 ||

**Hindi Translation:** By performing repeated operations <term>asakṛt</term> after adding or subtracting the half-duration to the end of the lunar day, one should calculate the parallax for the contact and release times. When the Sun is east of the meridian <term>madhyalagna</term>, the contact parallax will be greater than the middle parallax, and the middle greater than the release. If it is in the western direction, it is the reverse. At that time, if it is east of the meridian, the difference between release parallax and middle parallax is added to the release half-duration, and the difference between contact parallax and middle parallax is added to the contact half-duration; otherwise, do the opposite to find the corrected half-duration. If contact and middle, or middle and release, are on opposite sides of the meridian, the parallaxes should be added and the sum applied to the half-duration. In this way, the half-duration of total obscuration <term>vimardārdha</term> is determined. || 14 || 15 || 16 || 17 ||

# Chapter Six

Now the Chapter on Graphical Representation <note>Sanskrit: *Parilekhadhikara*</note> is explained. First, the author declares the purpose of this topic:

> Because the distinct variations of the two eclipses cannot be clearly
> understood without a diagram, I shall therefore describe the 
> excellent knowledge of graphical projection. || 1 ||

Because the variations of the two eclipses—namely the lunar and solar eclipses—cannot be known without a <term>diagram</term> <note>Sanskrit: *Chedhyaka*, literally "that which is to be cut or divided"; a geometric projection</note>. By using the dual form "two eclipses," the idea that the previous two chapters were a single subject is refuted. The "variations" refer to the directions of the beginning and end of the eclipse, the points of total obscuration and emergence, and the magnitude of the eclipsed portion. These are "clear" when they are established through the reality of the celestial sphere. Without this projection—a constructed method used to demonstrate the position of the spheres—these details are not understood. Therefore, for the sake of knowing these variations, I, the personified rays of the Sun, shall speak and declare this superior <term>knowledge of projection</term>, which is the means of achieving the graphical representation. || 1 ||

*Hindi Commentary:* Without a diagram, the directions of contact and separation or the variations in magnitude of both eclipses do not become clear; therefore, I now speak of the knowledge of projection. || 1 ||

First, he explains that one should draw the <term>circle of deflection</term> <note>Sanskrit: *Valana-vritta*</note>:

> On well-leveled ground, having made a central point, one should first 
> draw a circle for the deflection with a radius of forty-nine digits. || 2 ||

First, on ground that has been made as level as the surface of water, one should make a point to mark the center of the circle. From that mark, with a radius measuring the square of seven (forty-nine) digits <note>An *angula* or "digit" is a traditional unit of measurement, roughly the width of a finger</note>, the mathematician desiring to know the eclipse variations should draw a circle <term>dependent on the deflection</term>. This means the circle is used for applying the previously calculated "clear deflection" <note>The *valana* is the variation between the ecliptic and the local horizon/vertical</note>. The reasoning for this was stated previously. || 2 ||

*Hindi Commentary:* Having marked a point on prepared level ground, one should construct a circle for the purpose of deflection with a radius of 49 digits. || 2 ||

Now, he speaks of the second and third circles:

> A second circle is drawn with a radius equal to half the sum of the 
> eclipsed and eclipsing bodies; this is called the "summation" circle. 
> A third is drawn with the radius of the eclipsed body. || 3 ||

Chapter 6 | Including Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries | (123)

One should draw a second circle with a radius equal to half the sum of the diameters of the eclipsed body <note>the Moon or Sun</note> and the eclipser <note>the Shadow or the Moon</note>, measured in digits <term>angulas: a traditional unit of measurement based on finger-breadth</term>. This circle is called the **Circle of Conjunction** <note>Samāsa-vṛtta</note> because it is produced by the union of the two measurements. A third circle should be drawn with a radius equal to half the diameter of the eclipsed body. 

**The Rationale:** In an eclipse, the deflection <term>vikṣepa: celestial latitude</term> is less than the sum of the radii; therefore, the Circle of Conjunction is drawn to apply this deflection. Since the circle drawn with the radius of the eclipser from the center of the perimeter of the eclipsed body must meet the eclipsed circle, it is called the Circle of Conjunction. The eclipsed circle itself is extremely useful for understanding the different types of eclipses, as such knowledge is impossible without it. // 3 //

**Hindi Commentary:** Taking a radius equal to half the sum of the digits of the eclipsed and eclipser bodies, make a second circle (the Circle of Conjunction), and taking half the diameter of the eclipsed body, make a third circle. // 3 //

Now, he describes the method for establishing the directions in those circles and the rules for the directions of contact and separation to apply the deflection <term>valana: the angle between the ecliptic and the equator</term>:

### The determination of South, North, East, and West is as before.
### For the Moon, contact is in the East and separation in the West; for the Sun, it is the opposite. // 4 //

Among the eight directions, the determination of South, North, East, and West should be done "as before," following the method described in the chapter on the Three Problems <note>Tripraśna-adhikāra</note> starting with "On a stone surface cleaned with water..." To explain: with a twelve-digit gnomon <term>śanku: a vertical pillar used to cast shadows</term> placed at the center, mark the shadow's position in the forenoon and its exit in the afternoon. From these two marks, produce a "fish" <note>matsya: an almond-shaped intersection of two arcs</note> to find the North-South line, which should be extended outside the circle. The other line passing through the center of the circle is the North-South line within the circle. From the head of that "fish," the East-West line is drawn, extending outside the circle on both sides. This becomes the East-West line in the circle. 

The "contact" <term>sparśa: the beginning of the eclipse</term> of the Moon occurs in the East. The "separation" <term>mokṣa: the end of the eclipse</term> occurs in the West. For the Sun <note>Arka</note>, the contact and separation are known to be the opposite. This means the contact (the start of the eclipse) is in the West and the separation (the end) is in the East. 

**The Rationale:** By establishing directions in the circle, the directions are marked according to the prime vertical. Because of the difference in deflection from these marks, the directions of the ecliptic exist. To regulate the directions of contact and separation, they are determined according to the East and West of the ecliptic, as the motion of the planets follows that path. The faster-moving Moon enters the Earth's shadow (which is 180 degrees from the Sun) from the West, moving toward the East; thus, the contact occurs on the Eastern side of the Moon's disk. When the Moon moves forward, surpassing the Earth's shadow, the separation from the shadow occurs on the Western side of the Moon; hence, separation is in the West. In the case of the Sun, the Moon comes from the West and covers it; therefore, the Sun's contact is on the Western side and separation is on the Eastern side. // 4 //

**Hindi Commentary:** One should determine the lines going to the four directions—South, North, East, and West—as before. In a lunar eclipse, contact is in the East and separation is in the West. But in a solar eclipse, it is the opposite of this. // 4 //

Now he describes applying the deflection in the Deflection Circle:

### Apply the deflection for the contact of the Moon <note>Himadīdhiti: "the cool-rayed one"</note> according to its direction;
### But for the separation, it is reversed; for the Sun <note>Ravi</note>, this is entirely the opposite. // 5 //

<page-num>124</page-num>
# Surya Siddhanta
## [Chapter Six]

For the Moon, which is the body being eclipsed, the **deflection at contact** <note>original: *sparshika valana*; the angle at the beginning of the eclipse</note> should be applied from the eastern mark according to its direction. If it is south, it is directed southward; if north, it is directed northward. This is applied like a half-chord <note>sine</note> on the circle known as the "deflection-dependent circle" <note>original: *valanashrita-vritte*</note> relative to the east-west line. Therefore, that circle is named the "deflection-dependent" circle. The **deflection at separation** <note>original: *maukshika valana*; the angle at the end of the eclipse</note> of the Moon, however, is applied in reverse from the western mark. This means if it is south, it is directed toward the north; if north, it is directed toward the south, relative to the east-west line.

Now, he states the specific rule for a solar eclipse: **"In reverse."** For the Sun, which is the body being eclipsed, these deflections at contact and separation are inverted. The deflection at separation is applied from the eastern mark relative to the east-west line like a half-chord—if south, then southward; if north, then northward. The deflection at contact is applied from the western mark—if south, then northward; if north, then southward.

The reasoning <note>original: *upapatti*</note> here is: In a lunar eclipse, contact occurs on the eastern side; therefore, contact deflection is applied according to its direction from the eastern mark of the prime vertical <note>term: *samamandala*; the great circle passing through the zenith and the east/west points</note>. Because the western-northward direction is southern, and the southward is northern, the deflection at separation is applied in reverse from the western mark. In a solar eclipse, however, because contact occurs on the western side, the contact deflection is applied in reverse from the western mark. Since separation occurs on the eastern side, the deflection at separation is applied according to its direction from the eastern mark. || 5 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** In the case of a lunar eclipse, one should draw the deflection in the form of a chord <note>sine</note> on the eastern part of the deflection-dependent circle according to the contact deflection. However, at the time of separation, one should draw the chord on the western half of the circle in the direction opposite to the deflection's direction. In a solar eclipse, the opposite of this will occur. || 5 ||

### Now, he describes the application of the latitudes at contact and separation on the second circle:

->**From the end of the deflection, one should draw a line to the center;**<-
->**wherever it touches the circle of addition, the latitudes of contact and separation are applied. || 6 ||**<-

From the points in the first circle where the end of the contact deflection and the end of the separation deflection are known, one should draw a "sutra"—meaning a line—to the center, which is the middle point of the circle. Where these lines touch the circumference of the second circle, called the "circle of addition" <note>term: *samasa-vritta*; the circle whose radius is the sum of the radii of the eclipsing and eclipsed bodies</note>, the **latitudes** <note>term: *vikshepa*; celestial latitude or the distance of a planet from the ecliptic</note> of contact and separation should be applied as half-chords from those lines along the circle of addition, according to their respective directions.

The reasoning here is: Where the line from the end of the deflection meets the circle of the half-sum of the diameters <note>original: *manaikya-khanda-vritte*</note>, that represents the east-west direction of the ecliptic. Since the Sun and Moon are separated by their latitude, the latitude is applied from the deflection-line on the circle of addition to find the center of the eclipsing body. This applies to solar eclipses. In lunar eclipses, however, because the Moon moves on its own latitude circle, and after applying the parallax-deflection <note>original: *nati-valana*</note>, the Sun (as the obscurer of the Moon) is located at a distance of the latitude in the direction opposite to the latitude's direction. Thus, it is established that the latitude is applied in reverse as a half-chord on the circle of addition from the deflection-line. This is why it is said later that "for the Moon, they are reversed." || 6 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** Draw a line from the end of the deflection to the center point. At the spot where this line touches the circle of addition, construct a chord of the magnitude of the contact and separation latitudes upon that same line within the circle of addition. || 6 ||

# Chapter 6. | With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. (125)

Now, he describes the method for knowing the locations of the beginning (contact) and end (separation) of the eclipse on the circle of the eclipsed body:

> **From the tip of the latitude, one should again extend a cord to the center point.**
> **From the intersection of that with the eclipsed circle, one should indicate the contact and separation. || 7 ||**

Where the latitude meets the circle, from that point one should draw a cord—meaning a line. Here, the word "cord" is used throughout to suggest that because a straight line might be difficult to draw accurately by hand, one should first hold a string between the two endpoints and then draw the line according to it. "Again" means for a second time; just as a line was previously drawn from the tip of the deflection (<term>valana</term>: the angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator), one now draws a line from the tip of the latitude (<term>vikṣepa</term>). The calculator should "extend" it toward the center point, which is the middle of the circle. From the intersection of that line and the circumference of the eclipsed body's circle (<term>grāhya-bimba</term>), the calculator should "indicate"—that is, declare—the contact and separation. 

<note>The "eclipsed body" is the Sun in a solar eclipse and the Moon in a lunar eclipse.</note>

Where the cord from the tip of the latitude at the start of the eclipse (<term>sparśika-śara</term>) touches the eclipsed circle, that is the point of contact. Where the cord from the tip of the latitude at the end of the eclipse (<term>maukṣika-śara</term>) touches the eclipsed circle, that is the point of separation. 

The geometric proof is as follows: On the circle of the sum of the radii (<term>mānaikya-khaṇḍa</term>), where the center of the eclipsing body is located, a circle drawn with the radius of the eclipser will touch the eclipsed circle at the points of contact and separation. For the sake of simplifying the drawing (to avoid drawing many circles), a cord representing the sum of the radii is drawn from the center of the eclipser; where this touches the eclipsed circle, the contact and separation of the two circumferences occur due to the joining of their respective radii. || 7 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** From the tip of the latitude on the combined circle, where the cord going to the center point touches the eclipsed circle, those two places are the locations of contact and separation. || 7 ||

Now, with two verses, he describes the rule for the direction of latitude in an eclipse and the application of the deflection at the middle of the eclipse for the sake of knowing the middle state:

> **For the Sun, latitudes in the projection are always according to their actual direction.**
> **For the Moon, they are reversed. Based on that, the middle... || 8 ||**
> **...deflection should be applied facing East if it is of the same direction as the latitude.**
> **If they differ, it should be applied facing West; for the Moon, it is the opposite of the Sun. || 9 ||**

In a solar eclipse (<term>arka-grahaṇa</term>), the latitudes of the Moon in the projection (the method of showing the different parts of the eclipse) are always to be known "according to their direction"—that is, in their actual direction. In a lunar eclipse (<term>candra-grahaṇa</term>), the latitudes of the Moon are "reversed": if they are South, they are drawn North; if North, they are drawn South. The latitudes for the contact and separation should be applied following this rule. It should be understood that they are not drawn in the direction they are calculated. 

Then, "based on that"—meaning based on the direction of the latitude at the time of the middle of the eclipse—from the direction of the corrected latitude at the middle of a solar eclipse, or from the opposite direction of the latitude at the middle of a lunar eclipse: if "the latitude is the same," meaning the deflection (<term>valana</term>) and the latitude at the middle of the eclipse have the same direction... <note>The text continues to explain the orientation of the deflection arc.</note> ...it is applied "facing East" (toward the front mark). On the circle used for deflection, like a half-sine, the middle deflection of the Moon at the time of the middle of the eclipse...

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Six]

The true deflection <term>valana; the angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator</term> must be applied. If the directions of the deflection and the latitude <term>vikshepa; the celestial latitude of the moon</term> are different, it is applied facing westward. On the circle representing the deflection, like a half-chord <term>ardhajya; a sine value</term>, the deflection of the Moon at the time of the middle of the eclipse should be applied facing the western mark. 

Regarding the specific case of a solar eclipse, he says: **"Of the Sun..."** In a solar eclipse, the deflection of the Sun is applied in the reverse of the aforementioned rule. This means if they are in the same direction, it is applied facing the western mark; if in different directions, it is applied facing the eastern mark. 

The practical result is this: In a lunar eclipse, if both the direction of the middle deflection and the calculated latitude are South, then from the North mark on the deflection circle, the middle deflection should be applied like a half-chord facing the East mark. If both are North, the deflection should be applied from the South mark facing East. If the deflection is South and the latitude is North, then from the South mark, the deflection should be applied like a half-chord facing the West mark. If the deflection is North and the latitude is South, then from the North mark on the deflection circle, the deflection should be applied like a half-chord facing the West mark. 

However, in a solar eclipse, if both are South, the deflection should be applied from the South mark on the deflection circle facing the West mark. If both are North, it should be applied from the North mark facing West. If the deflection is South and the latitude is North, then from the North mark it faces East. If the deflection is North and the latitude is South, it should be applied from the South mark facing East. 

The teacher Bhaskaracharya <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> stated this result more concisely: the South and North deflections should be applied clockwise and counter-clockwise respectively. 

The reasoning here is as follows: The logic for the first verse was explained in the context of applying the latitude for the contact <term>sparshika; the beginning of the eclipse</term> and the separation <term>maukshika; the end of the eclipse</term>. The center of the eclipsing body is at a distance of the latitude from the center of the eclipsed body. Since the "arrow" <term>shara; another term for celestial latitude</term> faces the pole of the ecliptic <term>kadamba</term>, it is necessary to know the position of the pole on the deflection circle to apply the latitude from the center toward the pole. Therefore, because the directions of the ecliptic exist relative to one's own directions through the difference in deflection, the poles—which are the North and South points of the ecliptic—are placed South and North by the middle deflection. Thus, applying this in accordance with East and West is most appropriate. 

Although in a lunar eclipse the latitude has an opposite direction, one could simplify the statement by saying: for both Sun and Moon, if the latitude and deflection are in the same direction, face West; if different, face East. Nevertheless, because the eclipses of the Sun and Moon differ, such a single statement might cause confusion for those of dull intellect <note>A common pedagogical phrase in Sanskrit commentaries to justify detailed explanations</note>. To prevent that, the explanation is given separately. Furthermore, an independent author is not subject to the commands of others. || 8 || 9 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In a solar eclipse, one should do the same: extend two lines emerging from the mouth and tail of those two "fish" <note>matsya; a geometric construction using intersecting arcs to find directions</note> so that the lunar latitude is in the appropriate direction. For a lunar eclipse, it should be taken in the opposite direction. In the middle of the eclipse, the latitude is treated in the same way. || 8 ||

In the middle of a lunar eclipse, if the deflection and latitude are in the same direction, the deflection is said to face East; if in different directions, it faces West. It will be North or South according to the latitude. However, in a solar eclipse, this is reversed. || 8 || 9 ||

---

Now, he shows the middle of the eclipse in the diagram with two verses:

## From the tip of the deflection, again, one should enter a line to the center point. ||
## Along that middle line, one should lead the latitude toward the deflection. || 10 ||

### ### From the tip of the deflection, one should draw a circle with half the diameter of the eclipsing body.
### ### Whatever portion of the eclipsed circle is covered by that, that much shall be seized by darkness. || 11 ||

From the tip of the deflection <note>original: *valanāgra*; the angular deflection of the ecliptic from the celestial equator</note>—specifically the tip of the deflection at the middle of the eclipse as mentioned in the previous verse—the calculator should draw a line toward the center point of the circle. This means the construction of the line is the same as previously described for the tips of the deflection at the beginning and end of the eclipse. Along this central line, one should measure the latitude <note>original: *vikṣepa*; the celestial latitude or distance from the ecliptic</note> of the middle of the eclipse, moving toward the tip of the deflection. This measurement starts from the center point of the circle. At the end of this latitude measurement, one should mark a point. From this "tip of the latitude," the calculator should draw a circle with a radius equal to half the diameter of the eclipsing body <note>the Moon in a solar eclipse, or the Earth's shadow in a lunar eclipse</note>. Whatever portion of the eclipsed circle <note>the Sun or Moon</note> is encompassed or pervaded by that circle is the part "seized" or covered by the darkness of the obscurer. One should represent that portion as smeared with ink or a dark substance.

**The underlying logic:** In the circle, the central line faces the pole of the ecliptic <note>original: *kadamba*</note>. The center of the eclipsing body is placed at the distance of the latitude from the center of the eclipsed body. The circle drawn with the eclipsing body's radius shows how much of the eclipsed body is covered at the middle of the eclipse. Because this is how it appears in the sky, it is said to be "seized by darkness." || 10 || 11 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Draw a line from the tip of the deflection to the center point. On this line, mark the latitude from the center point toward the deflection. By imagining a circle around this point with a radius equal to half the diameter of the eclipsing body, whatever part of the eclipsed circle is covered is the part obscured by darkness. || 10 || 11 ||

Now, a doubt arises: all that has been said applies if the eclipse occurs in the eastern hemisphere. If the eclipse occurs in the western hemisphere, the diagramming would be reversed. For instance, the direction where the start or end of the eclipse appears in the diagram would be seen as the opposite in the sky because the observer is facing west. To address this, he says:

### ### When drawing the projection on the ground or on a board, the wise man
### ### should reverse the directions for the eastern and western hemispheres. || 12 ||

On the ground or on a board <note>made of wood</note>. The word "or" indicates an alternative. Since a drawing on the ground cannot be moved around, the use of a board is mentioned. The "wise man"—the calculator who knows the underlying principles—when drawing the projection <note>original: *chedyaka*; a diagram created by "cutting" or intersecting circles</note> described earlier, must reverse the directions (East, etc.) depending on whether the eclipse is in the eastern or western hemisphere. Just as one writes East etc. in a clockwise order for the eastern hemisphere, one should not do the same for the western hemisphere. Instead, East should be placed where West was, and West where East was. North and South should be written in their respective places. The idea is that even if the eclipse occurs in the western hemisphere, the diagram will then match the observation.

**The underlying logic:** Because the directions appear reversed in the sky, by reversing them on the diagram beforehand, the projection will match the actual appearance. However, the great teacher Bhaskara did not state this. His view was that the purpose of the diagram is simply to know "in such a direction, such a thing happens," and that logic remains undisturbed. It is not strictly necessary for the drawing on the ground to look exactly like the sky.

On a wooden board, because of the absence of actual space and other <unclear>physical elements</unclear>. <note>The text notes that a diagram on a board is only a representation, as it lacks the three-dimensional reality of space.</note> Therefore, one should keep in mind that this is only a partial illustration due to slight differences from reality. || 12 ||

<gloss>Commentary: On a level wooden board, after drawing the intersecting lines, one should swap the eastern and western halves of the circle. || 12 ||</gloss>

### Now, he describes eclipses that are not visible:

> Because of its brightness, even if a twelfth part of the Moon is eclipsed, it is not seen.
> Because of its intensity, even if three minutes of the Sun are eclipsed, they are not seen. || 13 ||

A twelfth part of the Moon's disk being eclipsed means it is covered. The word "even" implies that although the loss of light might suggest visibility, it is not actually seen. He gives the reason: "Because of its brightness." This refers to the remaining fully visible portion of the Moon being clear and full of moonlight. Thus, due to the abundance of that moonlight, even a small eclipsed portion does not appear in its true shape; it appears as if it were part of the moonlight due to the distance. Even if three minutes <term>minutes (liptā): 1/60th of a degree</term> of the Sun are eclipsed, it is not seen. The reason given here is: "Because of its intensity." This means the intensity of the Sun's light is such that it overpowers the human eye. However, the Elder Vashistha stated: <quote>“If two digits of the Moon are eclipsed, or three digits of the Sun, they are not perceived. Yet, slightly less than that may be perceived at the time of rising or setting, because then the two are deprived of their piercing rays.”</quote> Therefore, one should keep in mind that the best visibility occurs at the time of rising or setting. || 13 ||

<gloss>Commentary: Due to the Moon's clarity, even a twelfth-part eclipse is not visible. Due to the sharpness of the Sun's rays, even a three-minute eclipse is not seen. || 13 ||</gloss>

At the ends of the latitudes <term>latitudes (vikṣepa): the celestial latitude of the Moon</term>—namely the contact, middle, and separation latitudes previously given to determine the timing of the start, middle, and end of the eclipse—three points should be made, marked with their respective names. The calculator should place three points: a point marked for "contact" at the end of the contact latitude, a point marked for "separation" at the end of the separation latitude, and a point marked for the "middle" at the end of the middle latitude. Among these three points, between the first (contact) and the middle...

# Chapter 6. Including Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.

Between the center point and the points designated as the middle and the end of the eclipse <note>the "moksha" or release point</note>, the calculator should draw a "fish" <note>a *matsya* is a geometric construction using two intersecting arcs to find a perpendicular bisector</note> for each interval. From the center of these two "fish"—that is, from the intersection of the mouth and the tail—two lines should be drawn. By extending these two lines along their own paths to the point where they intersect, that intersection should be designated as the center. With a string fixed at this center and extending to any of the three points <note>the radius</note>, one should draw an arc—a segment of a circle—that touches all three points. This arc is declared to be the path of the "grāhaka" <note>the seizer or eclipsing body; in a lunar eclipse, this is the Earth's shadow</note>. This is the path along which the eclipser will travel to cover the body being eclipsed. This construction is necessary because the diagram of the eclipse must account for the time before and after the maximum point. The mathematical proof for this, involving the positions of East and West on a given day, was previously explained in the chapter on the three problems of direction, place, and time.

**Hindi Commentary:** Mark three points at the tips of the latitude lines <note>the *vikshepa*</note> corresponding to the contact, the middle, and the release. Construct two "fish" figures between the contact and middle points, and between the release and middle points. Using the intersection of these as a center, draw an arc that touches the three previously mentioned points. That arc is the path of the eclipsing body; it follows this path during the eclipse.

-> Now, the method for diagramming the eclipse at a desired time is described in three verses: <-

With the remaining digits, place a rod from the center point of the three circles toward the arc representing the path of the contact and release points. How? Before the maximum eclipse, the rod should touch the path leading to the contact point. For a desired time during the clearing of the eclipse <insert>1</insert> <note>original: "tada" (at that time) is a variant reading</note>, it should touch the path toward the release point. # Chapter 6 ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries ( 131 )

For the purpose of understanding the **emergence** <note>Sanskrit: *unmīlana*; the moment the eclipsed body begins to reappear</note>. In this manner, one should extend a pointer <note>Sanskrit: *śalākā*; a physical or geometric rod used for measurement in a diagram</note> measuring half the sum of the diameters from the center point toward the direction of liberation <note>The exit point of the eclipse</note>. Just as a circle was previously drawn for the **immersion** <note>Sanskrit: *sammīlana*; the start of total eclipse</note> based on the path of the pointer, the same should be done here. One should draw the obscuring circle from the point where the pointer meets the path of liberation. Then, in that direction where the intersection of the obscuring and obscured circles occurs, the emergence of the eclipsed orb takes place. The logic here is that at the moment of emergence, the distance between the centers of the two orbs is equal to half the sum of their diameters, acting as the hypotenuse. The reasoning for the direction of liberation is identical. || 22 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In this way, by placing the pointer in the direction of liberation, the spot where it touches the orb as before will be the direction of emergence. || 22 ||

-> Now, he describes the colors of the Moon during an eclipse: <-

When less than half the orb is eclipsed, the eclipsed part appears **smoky** <note>Sanskrit: *dhūmra*</note> in color. When more than half is eclipsed, it appears **black** <note>Sanskrit: *kṛṣṇa*</note>. As it begins to be released—meaning when it is nearing the end of the eclipse but still more than three-quarters covered—the color is **black-red** <note>Sanskrit: *kṛṣṇa-tāmra*; a dark coppery hue</note>. In a total eclipse, the orb appears **tawny** <note>Sanskrit: *kapila*; a brownish-orange or golden-brown</note>. These colors occur because the Earth's shadow, being an absence of light, covers the Moon. However, in a solar eclipse, the Moon (which is a watery sphere) is the coverer; on the day of the new moon, the half visible to us is always black, so the eclipsed portion of the Sun is always black. Therefore, because it does not change, the Lord <note>The author of the text</note> has not described different colors for the Sun. || 23 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** If the lunar eclipse is less than half, it is smoky; if more, it is black. When three-quarters eclipsed, it is coppery-black, and when total, it is tawny. (The eclipsed part of the Sun is always black). || 23 ||

This **graphic projection** <term>Chhedyaka: The method of drawing and calculating eclipses geometrically</term> of eclipses is a thing to be kept secret even by the gods. The idea is that by living together for a year, one gains true knowledge of the student's character. || 24 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** This truth is a secret even for the gods. It should not be given to just anyone.

# Now, the Seventh Chapter.

Now begins the explanation of the Section on Planetary Conjunctions <note>original: "grahayutyadhikara"</note>, undertaken because it was brought to mind by the description of the "apparent" conjunctions. Here, the author describes the different types of conjunctions:

> Between the star-planets <note>the five planets: Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn</note>, there occur "Conflict" and "Association."
> "Association" is with the Moon; with the Sun, it is "Disappearance." || 1 ||

When the star-planets—the five beginning with Mars—meet each other, it results in "Conflict" <note>original: "yuddha"</note> or "Association" <note>original: "samagama"</note>, which differ according to the characteristics to be described later. The meeting of any of the five star-planets with the Moon is termed "Association." The meeting of any of the five star-planets, or the Moon, with the Sun is "Disappearance" <note>original: "astamana"</note>, meaning total combustion. This does not mean mere setting, as that occurs daily before and after the actual conjunction. || 1 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The mutual meeting of planets is called Conflict or Association. The meeting of planets with the Moon is called Association. The meeting with the Sun is called Disappearance. || 1 ||

Now, the author explains the mathematical determination of the conjunction in one and a half verses:

> When the faster planet is ahead of the slower, the conjunction is past; otherwise, it is in the future.
> This is the case for two planets moving eastward; for two retrograde planets, it is the reverse.
> If one is moving eastward and is ahead of a retrograde planet, the association is past; otherwise, it is to come. || 2 ||

Between the two planets whose conjunction is desired, if the fast-moving planet is "greater" <note>at a higher longitude</note> than the slow-moving planet, their union, termed conjunction, is "past" <note>it has already occurred</note>. Otherwise—meaning if the slow planet is at a higher longitude than the fast one—their union is "to be" <note>in the future</note>. This rule for past and future applies to two planets that are "eastward-moving" <note>original: "praggayin," i.e., direct motion</note>. For two "retrograde" <note>original: "vakrin"</note> planets, the rule is reversed...

# Chapter 7: With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries

<page-num>133</page-num>

...due to the reversal of the previously stated conditions. The word "but" implies that the conjunction is "to come" (future). When the faster-moving planet has a higher longitude than the slower-moving planet, the conjunction is "past." If the slower-moving planet has a higher longitude than the faster-moving one, the conjunction is "to come." Now, regarding the case where one planet is in retrograde motion: among the two, if one is retrograde and the longitude of the direct-moving planet is greater, the conjunction is "past." However, if the longitude of the retrograde planet is greater than that of the direct-moving planet, the conjunction is "to come." 

**The Rationale:** Among two direct-moving planets, if the faster one is ahead, a future conjunction is impossible, so the conjunction is "past." If the slower one is ahead, the faster one will eventually catch up, so the conjunction is "to come." In the case of retrograde motion, if the faster planet is ahead, its speed will decrease <note>relative to the other's direction</note> allowing for a future meeting. If the slower is ahead, the gap will only increase, meaning the conjunction is "past." Furthermore, if the direct-moving planet's longitude is greater than the retrograde planet's, they are moving away from each other (past); if the retrograde planet's longitude is greater, they are moving toward each other (future) || 2 ||

*Hindi Commentary* — When the longitude of the fast-moving <term>Graha</term> <note>Planet</note> is greater than the slow-moving one, the <term>Samagama</term> <note>Conjunction</note> is past; otherwise, it is yet to occur. If both are retrograde, the rule is reversed. If only one is retrograde, the conjunction is past if the direct planet is ahead, and future if the retrograde planet is ahead || 2 ||

Now, the method for calculating the equal longitudes of two planets at the time of conjunction, and the calculation of the days elapsed or remaining until that time, is described in three and a half verses:

> Multiply the minutes of the difference between the two planets by their respective daily motions <note>Bhukti</note> || 3 ||
> Divide this by the difference of their daily motions if both are moving in the same direction (both direct or both retrograde) ||
> If one of the two is retrograde, divide by the sum of their daily motions || 4 ||
> The resulting minutes should be subtracted from the current positions if the conjunction is past, and added if it is in the future ||
> In the case of two retrograde planets, this is reversed. If only one is retrograde, addition and subtraction are applied accordingly || 5 ||
> Thus, the two planets will reach equal minutes of longitude within the zodiac.
> By dividing the difference in the same way, the result in days and time units is obtained || 6 ||

The minutes of the difference between the two planets involved in the conjunction at the desired time are multiplied separately by their own daily motion minutes. In both cases—whether the planets are moving "with the hair" <note>Anuloma: direct motion</note> or "against the hair" <note>Viloma: retrograde motion</note>—the calculator should divide by the difference of their true daily motions. He mentions a specific case: if one of the two is retrograde, divide by the *sum* of their motions. The resulting minutes should be subtracted from the planets' positions if the conjunction is "past" and they are moving direct. If the conjunction is "to come," the result should be added. For two retrograde planets, the rule is reversed: add if past, subtract if future. If only one is retrograde, the results for the direct and retrograde planets are respectively added or subtracted <note>to bring them to the same point in the zodiac</note>.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of planetary conjunctions and the mathematical adjustments required for direct and retrograde motion, transitioning into the calculations for visibility corrections (drkkarma).</meta>

<page-num>134</page-num>
<header>Surya-Siddhanta — [Chapter Seven]</header>

The values should be added or subtracted. Specifically: in a past conjunction, for a planet in direct motion <note>original: "marga-grahe"</note>, its result is subtracted; for a retrograde planet <note>original: "vakrini"</note>, it is added. In a future conjunction, it is subtracted from the retrograde planet and added to the direct planet. By doing this, those two planets involved in the conjunction become situated in the zodiac <note>original: "bhagana"</note>—meaning their position in the circle of signs, degrees, and minutes—at the same minute of arc <note>original: "samaliptau"</note>. Since the word "minute" <note>original: "lipta"</note> refers to a part of the zodiacal circle, it means they are equal.

Now, he describes the knowledge of the time of conjunction: "The difference" <note>original: "vivaram"</note>. The difference in minutes between the two planets involved in the conjunction at the desired time is taken. To find the result used for making them equal in minutes, just as the difference is multiplied by the motion and divided by the sum of the motions or the difference of the motions, so it is here. By dividing by that divisor, the result in days and so on is said to be past or future from the desired time, depending on the nature of the conjunction. At that time—the time of their conjunction—those two planets are equal.

The reasoning <note>original: "upapatti"</note> here is: If the difference in motion gives one day, then what do the minutes of the planets' interval give? In a past conjunction, the result is subtracted from the planets. In a future conjunction, it is added. If both are retrograde, the result of the division by the difference in motion is added to the planets in a past conjunction and subtracted in a future one, because the value of a retrograde planet decreases over time. If one is retrograde, then their interval increases daily by the sum of their motions. Therefore, the result obtained using the sum of motions as the divisor is subtracted from the direct planet in a past conjunction (because it was previously less) and added to the retrograde planet (because it was previously greater). In a future conjunction, it is added to the direct planet (as it increases) and subtracted from the retrograde planet (as it will decrease). Whether by the sum of motions or the difference of motions, one day is obtained; by that proportion, the past or future days etc. are found. || 3 || 4 || 5 || 6 ||

**Commentary Translation:** Having taken the minutes of the interval between two planets, multiply them respectively by their motions. If both are direct or both retrograde, divide by the difference of their motions. If it is a past conjunction, subtract the result from the direct planets and add to the retrograde. If it is a future conjunction, do the opposite. If only one is retrograde, use the sum of motions as the divisor; add for retrograde and subtract for direct in the past, and vice versa for the future. Then both planets will be at the same minute in the zodiac. To know the time, divide the interval minutes by the aforementioned divisor; the resulting days etc. are the interval between the desired time and the time of equal minutes. || 3 || 4 || 5 || 6 ||

->Now, he states that the tools for the visibility correction <term>Drkkarma: calculations to find the actual visible position of a planet</term> must be prepared:<-

For those two planets at that time, one should calculate the measure of the day and the measure of the night respectively, and then the minutes of celestial latitude <note>original: "vikshepa-liptika"</note>. This is the meaning. Here, the Lord <note>the author/divinity of the text</note> mentioned calculating the latitude after mentioning the day and night measures. The day and night measures are calculated by the ascensional difference <note>original: "chara"</note> derived from the corrected declination. However, it is suggested here that they should be calculated using the ascensional difference derived from the simple declination, uncorrected by the planet's latitude. The remainder of the sentence is that the visibility correction <note>drkkarma</note> mentioned immediately after must be performed. <meta>This page continues the technical discussion of planetary conjunctions and the calculation of time since rising. It follows the previous page's focus on determining the exact moment when two planets share the same longitude.</meta>

Because the rising of a planet is unknown, the measure of time elapsed since that rising is also unknown. It is not possible to achieve this result using only the total measures of day and night without knowing the specific time the planet has spent above or below the horizon. Therefore, the author says: **"By means of its own rising sign (Lagna), etc."** This means the calculation is performed by means of the rising sign at the specific time when the two planets reached the same longitude <note>the moment of conjunction</note>, as determined by the previously described method. From that simultaneous position of the planets, one must calculate the "elevated" <term>Unnata: the time elapsed since rising or remaining until setting</term> and "inclined" <term>Nata: the hour angle or time from the meridian</term> times for each.

The meaning is as follows: designate the rising sign at the time of conjunction as the "greater" and the position of the planet as the "lesser." Then, applying the rule from the *Chapter on the Three Problems* <note>Tripraśnādhikāra</note>: "Add the remaining breaths of the lesser sign to the elapsed breaths of the greater sign, and add the breaths of the intervening signs; thus is the time calculated." By this, one determines the time elapsed during the day or night for the planet. In the daytime, the smaller value between the time elapsed since sunrise and the time remaining until sunset is the *Unnata*. The half-day (or half-night) minus that *Unnata* is the planet's *Nata*. By using the singular term "measure of day and night" and "Nata-Unnata," it is indicated that for two planets in conjunction, the day-measure, night-measure, and the Nata/Unnata are considered identical; thus, the time interval does not need to be calculated separately for each. Furthermore, it is clarified that the day and night measures cannot be determined beforehand solely by the ascensional difference <note>Chara</note> derived from the true declination, as the rising sign itself is not yet established.

The logic here is: just as the time elapsed since sunrise is determined by the Sun's position and the current rising sign, so too is the time since a planet's rising determined by the planet's position and the rising sign. Although this method is strictly accurate for the Sun (since the Sun always stays on the ecliptic), it is technically "incorrect" for a planet because planets usually deviate from the ecliptic <note>due to celestial latitude</note>. Therefore, the time derived this way refers to the point on the ecliptic where the planet is marked, not the actual physical disk of the planet. However, since this "ecliptic-point time" is exactly what is required for the visibility corrections <term>Drkkarma</term> to be explained later, there is no error in this approach. // 7 //

**Hindi Commentary:** Calculate the day and night measures for the planets at the time they share the same longitude. Having determined their specific latitude <term>Vikshepa</term> at that moment, calculate the *Nata* and *Unnata* from the rising sign corresponding to the planets' positions. // 7 //

### Now, with two verses, the author describes the Visibility Correction for Latitude (Aksha-Drkkarma) and its application to the planet:

> Multiply the latitude by the equinoctial shadow and divide by twelve. // 8 //
> Multiply the result by the planet's own Nata-hours and divide by its own half-day.
> The result is subtracted in the east if the latitude is north, and added in the west. // 9 //
> If the latitude is south, it is added in the eastern hemisphere and subtracted in the western.

The latitude of the planet is multiplied by the equinoctial shadow <term>Akshabha</term> and divided by twelve. The result is then multiplied by the *Nata* hours of the planet and divided by its half-day (or half-night, if at night). Although the day-measure and *Nata* are the same for both planets in a conjunction, the Lord <note>the author, Surya</note> uses the word "own" <insert>each planet's own</insert> to ensure the rule remains applicable to other visibility calculations where the planets are not in conjunction. In reality, the Lord describes the conjunction after the two visible positions are made equal...

Once the mid-rising time is fixed, the Nata and Unnata are easily known through the difference in desired time units.

<header>Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter 7]</header>

Because of the equality of the two, for the sake of calculating the <term>visibility correction (Drkkarma)</term>, the use of the term "own" is appropriate since the hour angle and the length of the day are different. 
One might ask: since there is a difference in the length of the day produced by the <term>apparent declination</term> and a difference in the hour angle, why was "own" specified? It should be understood that this is because the calculation would otherwise be inconsistent. According to the stated rule, if the <term>celestial latitude (Vikshepa)</term> is North, the resulting minutes of arc are subtracted from the planet in the eastern hemisphere (before the meridian). In the western hemisphere, they are added. The opposite applies if the latitude is South. By the word "but" (in the original verse), the resulting fruit should be added in the eastern hemisphere and subtracted in the western hemisphere. || 8 || 9 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** Multiply the <term>latitude (Vikshepa)</term> by the <term>equinoctial shadow</term> and divide by 12. Multiply the result by the planet's own <term>hour angle (in Nadis)</term> and divide by its own <term>half-day duration</term>; this gives the <term>latitude-visibility correction (Aksha-drkkarma)</term>.
If the latitude is North: before the planet reaches the meridian (middle-rise), subtract this from the planet's longitude; after the meridian, add it. If the latitude is South: before the meridian, add it; after the meridian, subtract it. This is a significant adjustment. || 9 ||

### Now, the Ecliptic-Visibility Correction (Ayana-drkkarma) —

> The minutes of the planet's <term>latitude (Vikshepa)</term> multiplied by the degrees of the <term>declination</term> of the planet plus three signs <note>original: "sattribha-graha" — adding 90 degrees to the longitude</note> result in seconds of arc. These are added or subtracted depending on whether the declination and latitude are of different or the same direction. || 10 ||

The minutes of latitude previously calculated, when multiplied by the degrees of declination arising from the planet's longitude plus three signs (90°), become seconds of arc. These are applied to the planet already corrected by the <term>latitude-visibility correction</term>. Regarding the declination of the planet-plus-three-signs and the latitude of the planet: if these two are of different directions or the same direction, they are respectively added or subtracted. 

**The geometric derivation (Upapatti):** Where the <term>secondary to the equator (Dhruvaprota-vritta)</term> <note>a great circle passing through the celestial poles</note> touches the planet's orb on the circle of latitude and meets the <term>ecliptic (Kranti-vritta)</term> near the planet, the interval on the ecliptic between those points constitutes the "Ayana" minutes. To calculate this, the "field" or triangle is formed: the planet's latitude is the hypotenuse directed toward the <term>pole of the ecliptic (Kadamba)</term>. The base is the interval on the diurnal circle between the intersection of the diurnal circle and the polar circle. In the polar circle, the apparent latitude is the perpendicular side between the planet's orb and that intersection. 

Thus, if the <term>sine of the ecliptic deviation (Ayana-valana-jya)</term> is the base for a <term>radius (Trijya)</term> hypotenuse, then by proportion, what would the base be for a latitude hypotenuse? One might object that the base minutes are on the ecliptic, and because the ecliptic is slanted, that region cannot strictly function as a linear base. However, the triangle—where the sine of deviation is the base, the radius is the hypotenuse, and the "staff" is the perpendicular—is visible in the sphere. Therefore, the proportion holds. 

Here, the Lord <note>the divine author of the text</note>, out of compassion for the world and for ease of calculation, accepted the base minutes of the diurnal circle as being on the ecliptic due to the very small difference between them. Therefore, while the rule should be "multiply the latitude by the sine of deviation and divide by the radius," the Lord accepted the degrees of declination of the planet-plus-three-signs as the deviation. These degrees, multiplied by 58, become the sine. Since the maximum declination is 24 degrees, 24 multiplied by 58 (minus 5) equals the <term>maximum sine of declination</term>. 

To get the result in seconds, the latitude is multiplied by these degrees and a factor of 60. It is established that the planet's latitude multiplied by the declination degrees of the planet-plus-three-signs, then multiplied by 3480 (which is 58 times 60, minus 20), and divided by the radius, gives the result. Here too, for the sake of simplification, since the multiplier is close to the value of the radius, the difference is negligible—

<meta>catchword: negligible— (svalpāntaratvād-)</meta>

These corrections ensure the calculated position of a planet matches its observed position on the horizon.</summary>
