# Chapter 7: Including Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries (Page 137)

Because of the acceptance <note>of the mathematical principles</note>, the destruction of the additive and subtractive factors is established, starting from the phrase "with three signs added" up to "deficient." However, according to **Bhaskaracharya** <note>A celebrated 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note>:

-> "The ecliptic visibility correction (*Ayanavalana*), multiplied by the true latitude and divided by the radius of the diurnal circle, results in the ecliptic correction minutes when multiplied by 1/180th of the planet's position." <-

This has been stated by us as a more precise method. The reasoning for the additive and subtractive corrections is as follows: In the northward progression (*Uttarayana*) starting from Capricorn, the south celestial pole is below the south ecliptic pole, and the north celestial pole is above the north ecliptic pole. In that situation, when the latitude is North, the planet's disk is inclined toward the north ecliptic pole, causing the north pole to be elevated. Consequently, the intersection of the circle passing through the ecliptic poles and the planet's position—which represents the corrected planetary position—falls behind the planet's position on the ecliptic. Therefore, if the ecliptic correction minutes are subtracted from the true planet, the longitude of the corrected planet is known.

Similarly, with South latitude, because the planet's disk is inclined toward the south ecliptic pole, the pole is elevated, and the corrected planetary position on the ecliptic falls ahead of the planet's position; thus, the ecliptic correction minutes are additive.

However, in the southward progression (*Dakshinayana*) starting from Cancer, the south celestial pole is above the south ecliptic pole, and the north celestial pole is below the north ecliptic pole. In that case, if the planet's latitude is South, then because the planet's disk is inclined toward the south pole, the corrected planetary position on the ecliptic is behind the planet's position; hence the ecliptic correction is subtractive. If the latitude is North, then because the planet's disk is inclined toward the north pole, the corrected planetary position is ahead of the planet's position on the ecliptic; thus the ecliptic correction is additive.

Thus, by the positioning of the celestial sphere (*Gola*), it is established: if the direction of the progression (*Ayana*) and the latitude (*Shara*) are the same, it is subtractive; if the directions of the progression and latitude are different, it is additive. Since the direction of the planet's progression is equal to the direction of the celestial sphere of the planet plus three signs, it is established that if the declination of the planet plus three signs and the planet's latitude have the same direction, it is subtractive; if different directions, it is additive.

Now, the explanation of the terrestrial latitude correction (*Akshadrikkarma*): When the planet's disk is attached to the vertical circle passing through the intersection of the terrestrial horizon and the meridian, the point where the ecliptic is nearest to the planet is the planet corrected by the terrestrial latitude minutes. The distance on the ecliptic between that and the ecliptic-corrected planet constitutes the terrestrial latitude correction minutes (*Akshadrikkala*). Since the maximum difference occurs when the planet's disk is on the horizon, and there is no difference when the planet is on the meridian (where the ecliptic-corrected point coincides with the latitude-corrected point), the correction is absent there.

Therefore, when the planet's disk is on the horizon, the vertical circle is different from the horizon circle passing through the intersection of the meridian and the horizon. There, the intersection of the ecliptic and the circle passing through the poles attached to the planet's disk represents the ecliptic-corrected position. The minutes by which this is separated above or below the point of the ecliptic on the horizon are the terrestrial latitude correction minutes. To calculate these, the time degrees (*Asu*) situated in the segment of the diurnal circle of that intervening region, born of the terrestrial latitude, are calculated.

To explain: On the circle passing through both poles and the planet's disk, the distance between the celestial equator and the planet's disk is the true declination (*Sphuta Kranti*). The distance between the celestial equator and the ecliptic at the ecliptic-corrected position is the mean declination. The distance between the ecliptic-corrected position and the planet's disk is the true latitude (*Sphuta Shara*). When both declinations are in the same direction, the true declination is greater. In that case, in the northern hemisphere, the ecliptic-corrected position is below the horizon in its own diurnal circle by the time degrees of the difference between the two declinations.

# Surya Siddhanta - [Chapter Seven]

The planetary marker on its own diurnal circle moves above or below by equal time-breaths <note>Asu: a unit of time equal to 4 seconds, or one sidereal breath</note> relative to the two **declinations** <term>Kranti: the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</term>. Because the planetary marker at the solstice is situated above or below the celestial equator by an interval equal to the ascensional difference of the true declination in the northern and southern hemispheres. And because of the nature of the celestial equator's distance from the horizon. Bhaskaracharya <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> has stated the precise understanding of the terrestrial visibility correction: "**When the two ascensional differences of the true and mean declinations have the same direction, the time-breaths produced by their difference or sum are called the terrestrial correction for the inhabitants of the heavens.**" 

However, the Lord <note>Referring to the divine origin of the Surya Siddhanta</note>, following the previously mentioned method, accepted that the time-breaths of the terrestrial visibility correction are nearly equal to the actual latitude, arising from the correction of the true and mean declinations. This was done by the proportion: if the **Equinoctial Shadow** <note>Palabha: the shadow of a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</note> is the base for a gnomon of twelve digits, then what will it be for the sine of the latitude? By discarding the arc of the result of the sine of the latitude and assuming the sine of the amplitude and the sine of the ascensional difference to be identical due to the small difference, these breaths were held as **terrestrial breaths** <term>Akshasava: time-breaths related to the local latitude</term>. For a planetary disk located elsewhere than the horizon, these minutes are transformed by the desired hour angle, as stated in the section **"By the equinoctial shadow..." up to "...divided by half the day."** 

Here, the **ecliptic visibility correction** <term>Ayana Drkkarma: correction for the deviation of the ecliptic from the celestial equator</term> must be applied to the planet. Therefore, after calculating the hour angle from the length of the day and night, the terrestrial visibility correction is performed; then it becomes somewhat precise. This is self-evident in the seventh verse of the text beginning with "The sine of the planet with three signs added..." There is no room for doubt regarding the uselessness of the proportion of the hour angle, because the difference in the length of the day and the hour angle is established by the correction of the planet's longitude and its ecliptic visibility. 

The logic of the addition and subtraction is as follows: the vertical circle passing through the planetary disk meets the **ecliptic** <term>Kranti-vrtta: the sun's apparent path</term> at a point of longitude corrected by the **terrestrial visibility correction** <term>Aksha-drkkarma</term>, as said before. In the eastern hemisphere, the solstice-marker of that planet on the ecliptic is in the forward part if the latitude is north, and in the rear part if the latitude is south; thus addition is prescribed accordingly. In the western hemisphere, it is in the rear for north latitude and in the forward part for south latitude; thus, by applying addition and subtraction to the solstice-planet, the planet becomes **corrected by both visibility corrections** <term>Drkkarma-dvaya-samskrta</term>. All is thus proven. || 10 ||

**Commentary:** By multiplying the **minutes of latitude** <term>Vikshepa-kala</term> by the **declination degrees** <term>Krantyamsha</term> derived from the **true planet with three signs added**, the **seconds of the ecliptic visibility correction** will be produced. If the aforementioned **declination** and **latitude** are in different directions, **add** them to the planet; otherwise, **subtract** them. || 10 ||

->Now, he states the occasions for applying the visibility corrections:<-

### In the conjunction of stars and planets, and in calculating the rising and setting of planets;
### And in the elevation of the Moon's horns, this visibility correction is prescribed. || 11 ||

The locative case here indicates the cause. The plural is used because there are many planets and stars. For the **conjunction of a star and a planet** <term>Nakshatra-graha-yuti</term>, these two **visibility corrections** <term>Drkkarma</term> mentioned before are prescribed to be done first. This means the operation should be performed after them. Here, since the **polar longitudes of the stars are already corrected for ecliptic visibility**, it should be understood that the ecliptic correction is not to be done for them. The rising and setting of planets refers to both the daily rising/setting and the rising/setting caused by proximity to the Sun <note>Heliacal rising and setting</note>. By implication, this applies to stars as well. For the purpose of calculating these, the correction must be given to the planet or the star. Here, for the sake of the terrestrial visibility correction, only the **latitude** <term>Shara</term> is to be calculated, not the length of the day, night, or the hour angle. Since the rising and setting points are necessarily connected to the horizon, the transformation for an hour angle away from the horizon is useless.

# Chapter 7. | With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries | ( 139 )

In a conjunction, it is necessary to calculate the result for simultaneous visibility on the secondary circle <note>original: "samaprotacalavṛtte" - a vertical circle passing through the planet</note>. This applies to the elevation of the Moon's horns <note>the "shringonnati" or the phase/tilt of the crescent</note>. The word "but" <note>Sanskrit: "tu"</note> here is used in the sense of "and" to include both concepts. In this verse, one should keep in mind that the visibility correction <note><term>Drik-karma</term>: the calculation to find a planet's position on the horizon</note> mentioned in the first half of the verse has not yet been applied. || 11 ||

<gloss>Hindi Commentary</gloss> — In the conjunction of stars and planets, and in determining the rising and setting of planets, or the elevation of the Moon's horns, one should first calculate this visibility correction. || 11 ||

Next, he describes the time of conjunction for two planets already adjusted by the visibility correction, and the north-south distance between the two planets based on their latitudes at that moment:

->**The latitudes of the two planets must be calculated again for that specific moment. ||**<-
->**If they are in the same direction, the difference is taken; if in different directions, the sum is the distance between the planets. || 12 ||**<-

For a second time, using those planets—determining whether the conjunction is past or yet to come based on whether the faster planet has exceeded the slower one—the two planets, adjusted by the visibility correction, become equal at the time of their conjunction. The time of conjunction for the adjusted planets should be known from the time of the "clear" <note>mathematically true</note> planets. At that time, the positions of those two planets should be calculated through the standard operations for mean and true positions. The latitudes <note><term>Vikshepa</term>: celestial latitude</note> of these two calculated planets must then be found. The "and" implies that these planets are now perceived as equal once adjusted by the visibility correction. If not, the process should be repeated until the time is fixed and the perception is clear. Then, after calculating the latitudes of the planets at the precise moment of conjunction: if they are in the same direction <note>both North or both South</note>, the difference between the two latitudes is taken. If they are in different directions, the sum of the latitudes is taken. The result is the distance between the planets produced by this calculation. This represents the north-south interval between the centers of the two planetary disks during conjunction.

The logic here is: for two planets adjusted by the visibility correction, there is no east-west distance between them on the secondary circle, so they are "equal." Since the centers of the planetary disks are at the ends of their latitudes, if they are in the same direction, the difference between the latitudes is the north-south distance. If they are in different directions, the sum of the latitudes is the distance. The great teacher Bhaskaracharya <note>12th-century Indian mathematician</note> stated this precisely: "The planets moved by the days of conjunction are equal; from them, like a solar eclipse, the latitudes are adjusted by their own parallax. When these are clear, the latitudes should be handled as before: the difference if in the same direction, the sum if in different directions." The Compassionate Lord <note>the author of the original Surya Siddhanta</note> has simplified this because the difference is very slight. || 12 ||

<gloss>Hindi Commentary</gloss> — From this, one should again determine the equal minutes of arc and the time. One should calculate repeatedly until the position is stable; once stable, determine the latitude of both planets. If they are in the same direction, subtract; if in different directions, add. This result is the distance between the planets. || 12 ||

Next, he describes the measurement of the diameters of the disks of the five star-planets in two verses:

->**For Mars, Saturn, Mercury, and Jupiter, the diameters at the Moon's orbit are thirty, increased by half of half [seven and a half] successively. ||**<-
->**For Venus, the diameter is declared to be sixty. || 13 ||**<-

<header>Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Seven]</header>

# Divided by the sum of the third and fourth chords, multiplied by twice the radius,
# the diameters become clear; divided by their own distance, they become the angular diameters in minutes. || 14 ||

The diameters <note>original: *vishkambha*</note> of Mars, Saturn, Mercury, and Jupiter are stated in terms of the Moon's orbit—meaning the Moon's celestial sphere—increasing by half and half-of-a-half of thirty. Specifically: thirty for Mars; thirty-seven and a half for Saturn; forty-five for Mercury; and fifty-two and a half for Jupiter <insert>[</insert>. Following this same sequence, the diameter for Venus <note>original: *Bhrigu*</note> is sixty. By stating sixty for Venus, the interpretation that "half and half-of-a-half" applies to each previous value is rejected, and the intended meaning is clarified. These stated diameters, doubled and multiplied by the radius <note>original: *trijya*</note>, are divided by the "sum of the third and fourth chords." 

The traditional commentary explains this as the sum of the "slow" chord <note>term: *manda-karna* — the distance adjustment for the planet's elliptical eccentricity</note> and the "fast" chord <note>term: *shighra-karna* — the distance adjustment for the Earth's motion relative to the planet</note> used in the third and fourth steps of calculation. However, modern scholars <note>original: *navya*</note> disregard the previous explanation because the third step does not explicitly mention a chord ratio, and the "third chord" is not well-established, leading to logical contradictions. They interpret "three" to mean the radius and "four" to mean the "fast" chord of the fourth step; thus, the sum of the radius and the fast chord is the divisor. 

The "clear" diameters are the actual diameters of the planetary bodies. When divided by fifteen, they become the angular diameters in minutes <note>original: *mana-liptika*</note>. 

The reasoning <note>original: *upapatti*</note> is as follows: The five star-planets, though situated in their own respective orbits, appear to people as if they are in the Moon's celestial sphere due to their great distance <insert>]</insert>. Therefore, their true diameters in leagues <note>original: *yojana*</note> are determined just as the Sun's diameter was calculated in the chapter on Lunar Eclipses—by calculating the distance relative to the Moon's orbit based on their revolutions. 

As stated in the *Shakalya Samhita*:
> "Just as tall trees in the distance appear to be at the edge of a forest, all the planets, due to their distance, appear to be in the Moon's orbit. Their diameters are seen through the eyes of the scriptures as thirty, increasing by half and half-of-a-half."

These values are stated for a "fast" chord equal to the radius. Therefore, when the fast chord is greater, the planet is near its furthest point <note>apogee</note> and the disk appears smaller; when the chord is smaller, the planet is near its closest point <note>perigee</note> and the disk appears larger. While a simple inverse proportion might seem appropriate, the Lord <note>the divine source of the text</note> observed that the disk size varies according to the average of the radius and the actual chord. By rearranging the fraction, it is proven that the diameters are multiplied by twice the radius and divided by the sum of the radius and the fast chord.

As also stated in the *Shakalya*:
> "The average of the sum of the third and fourth chords is the 'clear' chord at the top. The diameters multiplied by the radius and divided by the clear chord are known as the 'clear' diameters."

Because the disk's appearance depends on its position in the fast epicycle—which relates to its distance from the Earth's center—the connection to the "fast" chord is logical, while the "slow" chord is irrelevant here. In the geometric diagrams <note>original: *chedyaka*</note>, it is not demonstrated that the planet's disk exists at the average of the slow and fast chords. If that were the case, it would have to be accepted in the calculation of the "fast" result as well. 

However, the Great Teacher Bhaskara <note>historical note: Bhaskara II, 12th-century mathematician</note> states: Five minus a quarter, six and a quarter, six and a third, two, nine, and five and a third—these are the mean angular diameters in minutes for Mars and the others, when the radius is divided by the difference of the chords...

# Chapter 7. ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. ( 141 )

...multiplied. "The results of the three-fold multiplication are divided by the sine of the distance; the results, when added or subtracted respectively from the separate positions, become the true positions when the hypotenuse is less or greater than the radius." This is stated as a general rule. The followers of Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, the 12th-century mathematician</note>, however, say that by the logic of the "three-four hypotenuse," this means dividing by the sum of the radius and the fourth-operation hypotenuse <term>Sheeghra-karna: the distance from the earth to the planet in its second epicycle</term>. || 13 || 14 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In the lunar orbit, the diameters of the disks <term>Bimba-vyasa</term> are: Mars 30, Saturn 37 1/2, Mercury 45, Jupiter 52 1/2, and Venus 60. By multiplying these diameters by twice the radius and dividing by the sum of the radius and the hypotenuse obtained in the fourth operation (in the calculation of true positions), the true diameter of the disk is found. Dividing the true diameter by 15 gives the value in minutes of arc <term>Kaladiman</term>. || 13 || 14 ||

### Now, he describes how two planets involved in a conjunction should be observed at the time of their meeting:

->**On the ground where the shadow falls, reversed, at the tip of one's own shadow, one should show it.**<-
->**The planet, situated within one's own mirror, is seen at the tip of the gnomon.**<- || 15 ||

On the "ground where the shadow falls," meaning on earth leveled like water to make it suitable for casting shadows. "Reversed" means placed in the opposite direction at the "tip of one's own shadow," which is the location of the tip of the planet's shadow. The word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> is used here for emphasis to exclude other methods. "Situated within one's own mirror" means the reflection of the planet is located in the center of a mirror placed there. The astronomer <term>Ganaka</term> should show this to his student.

The meaning is as follows: Having determined the directions on level ground, one should measure the digits of the shadow at the time of conjunction from the intersection of the direction lines. This is done in the direction opposite to the "arm" <term>Bhuja: the north-south sine</term> and at a distance equal to the "arm," in the direction of the celestial hemisphere <term>Kapala</term> occupied by the planet. A mirror is placed there. The astronomer, standing at the intersection of the direction lines, shows the reflection of the planet to the student.

The mathematical proof <term>Upapatti</term> is this: Where a plumb line dropped from the planet's disk—acting as a "great gnomon"—hits the ground, that is the location of the planet's reflection. To know this: if for the "great gnomon's" base (the distance from the zenith to the planet in the sky), the "arm" is the sine of the zenith distance <term>Drig-jya</term>, then for a gnomon of twelve digits, what will the "arm" be? By this proportion, the shadow is brought to the hemisphere occupied by the planet. Just as the shadow of a twelve-digit gnomon at the intersection of directions falls in the planet's hemisphere, so would the shadow of a gnomon placed at the planet's reflection-point fall at the intersection of directions. Therefore, by marking the shadow from the intersection point into the planet's hemisphere, the location of the planet's reflection is known. This explains the text from "on the ground where the shadow falls" to "situated within one's own mirror."

Now, since shadows usually fall in the hemisphere opposite to the planet, a simple-minded person might doubt how a shadow can be cast in the same hemisphere as the planet. To resolve this, he says: "at the tip of the gnomon." The astronomer sees the planet in the sky at the top (head) of the gnomon placed at the intersection of directions. || 15 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Having fixed a gnomon <term>Shanku</term> on leveled ground, one should mark the tip of the shadow in the other direction using the planet's sine of zenith distance. By placing a mirror at the tip of the shadow, the planet situated within the mirror and the tip of the gnomon will be seen in a straight line. || 15 ||

<header>The Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Seven]</header>

Now, explaining how they are seen, he describes the method of observing the two planets involved in a conjunction using one and a half verses:

> Two gnomons <note>shanku: a vertical staff used for measurement</note>, each five cubits <note>hasta: a unit of length, approx. 18-24 inches</note> high, should be placed according to their respective directions.
> They are to be separated by the distance between the two planets and buried one cubit deep in the ground. || 16 ||
> Then, one should apply the hypotenuses of the shadows <note>chāyā-karṇa</note> so they meet the tops of the gnomons.
> To an observer situated at the intersection of the tips of the shadow-hypotenuses, ||
> the two planets will appear in the sky as if resting upon the tips of their respective gnomons, appearing equal in height. || 17 ||

The two planets involved in the conjunction are adjusted by the "ecliptic intersection" <note>āyana-dṛkkarmā</note> and the "latitude intersection" <note>akṣa-dṛkkarmā</note> mentioned previously. They are at the same point, or very close to it, at the rising sign <note>udaya-lagna</note>. When increased by six signs <note>180 degrees</note>, they are at the setting sign <note>asta-lagna</note>. At the time one desires to see the planets, if the rising and setting signs at that moment during the night are respectively less or more <note>than the planets' positions</note>, and if they are visible due to the absence of the Sun's glare, then:

Two gnomons five cubits high—a cubit being twenty-four digits <note>angulas</note>—should be used. Thus, two straight wooden poles five cubits long are placed according to the "direction-rotation" <note>digbhrama</note> at the time of conjunction. Depending on whether the planets are in the eastern or western hemisphere <note>kapāla</note> due to the diurnal rotation, they should be placed in the direction of the hemisphere occupied by the planets, not the unoccupied one.

By the "distance between the planets" <note>grahāntara</note>—calculated as the north-south difference in minutes of arc as per the rule "in difference, a conjunction," etc.—they are placed apart. Here, by the rule "with the elevation," etc., the planetary latitudes are converted into digits, and the distance between the planets is determined.

"Below" means inside the earth. "Buried one cubit deep" means they are placed in a pit the size of a cubit; by planting one cubit of the gnomon in the ground, the portion above the ground remains four cubits long. Then, from the base of each gnomon, in the direction of the hemisphere where the planets are located, the "hypotenuses of the shadows" <note>chāyā-karṇa</note> belonging to each, reaching the "head" or the top of its own gnomon, should be provided by the calculator <note>gaṇaka: the astronomer/mathematician</note>.

This is what is meant: Having determined the rising sign at the time of conjunction, the time interval between the rising sign and the desired sign is the "civil" <note>sāvana</note> time of the planets' rising. Thus, at the time of the planets' conjunction, the shadow should be calculated using the method taught in the "Chapter on the Three Inquiries" <note>Tripraśna-adhikāra</note> using the corrected declination. Then, whichever direction the planet is in (North or South), the shadow is laid out in that direction from the base of the gnomon, toward the hemisphere not occupied by the planet, along the north-south line.

However, the shadow brought forth is for a gnomon of twelve digits; it must be recalculated for a gnomon of four cubits, and a line of that length should be drawn from the base of the gnomon. A mark should be made at the end of the line to indicate the tip of the shadow. A string should be tied there with a peg and stretched to touch the tip of the gnomon. At the "intersection of the tips of the shadow-hypotenuses"—that is, where the tip of the shadow and the base of the hypotenuse meet—the student, seated in a pit made at that spot, will see the two planets in the sky through the eyes of the calculator, aligned with the tops of their respective gnomons...

# Chapter 7: With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries (Page 143)

...standing, he should show them as they have come into the range of vision. The reasoning here is as follows: To facilitate viewing from a height, two <term>gnomons</term><note>Sanskrit: *shanku*; vertical rods used for measurement</note> of five cubits in length are prepared. One cubit is buried in the ground for stability. The remaining four cubits, roughly the height of a man, remain above ground; the gnomon is often referred to by terms synonymous with "man" for this reason. Because the line from the gnomon is connected to the <term>planetary disk</term><note>Sanskrit: *graha-bimba*</note>, it is said they are positioned according to the directions. Since the rule is that the planetary disk aligns with the tip of the gnomon, the two gnomons are placed separated by the north-south distance between the planets. 

In this context, although one could calculate the exact <term>declination</term> and the <term>hypotenuse-distance</term> and then find the "arm" (base) using the <term>equinoctial shadow</term><note>Sanskrit: *palabha*; the shadow cast by a gnomon at noon on the equinox</note> to find the precise distance between the gnomons, the Lord <note>referring to the divine source of the *Surya Siddhanta*</note> has instead used the apparent visual distance in the sky to avoid excessive mathematical labor. From the tip of the shadow, the line of the "shadow-hypotenuse" is the line of sight to the planet; therefore, a person looking from the base of this hypotenuse will surely see the planetary disk at the tip of the gnomon. This is the method. || 16 || 17 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** One should place two gnomons, each five cubits long, along the north-south line at a distance measured in digits <note>Sanskrit: *angula*</note>, burying them one cubit deep. From the tip of the shadow to the top of the gnomon, determine the two "shadow-hypotenuses." A person positioned at the end of this hypotenuse line should be shown the planet; he will see the planet exactly at the tip of the gnomon. || 16 || 17 ||

Now, in two verses, the author describes the "battles" and "unions" of the five planets previously promised:

->**Grazing (*ullekha*) occurs from the touching of the stars; piercing (*bheda*) is described by the ancients. || 18 ||**<-
->**A battle called "clashing of rays" (*anshu-vimarda*) occurs when their rays intermingle.**<-
->**When the distance is less than a degree, it is "sinister" (*apasavya*) if one planet is smaller.**<-
->**It is a "union" (*samagama*) if the distance is more than a degree and both are bright. || 19 ||**<-

Among the five planets (Mars, etc.), when two meet, if their disks merely touch at the edges, experts in planetary conflict call this **Grazing** (*ullekha*). If the north-south distance is such that one disk appears to overlap or "pierce" the other, it is called **Piercing** (*bheda*). This occurs when the distance is less than half the sum of their diameters. 

On this point, the great teacher **Bhaskaracharya** says: <note>The following is a translation of a technical Latin-style citation of Bhaskara's *Siddhanta Shiromani*</note> "When the distance between two heavenly bodies is less than half the sum of their diameters, a conjunction occurs. One should calculate everything like a solar eclipse, including <term>parallax</term><note>Sanskrit: *lambana*</note>, for the sake of accuracy. Imagine the lower planet as the Moon and the upper as the Sun to determine the overlap..." However, it should be noted that the Lord <note>the author of the *Surya Siddhanta*</note> ignored these extreme refinements because, in the sky, the tiny disks cannot be seen distinctly from a distance, and such effort would be futile. 

When there is a meeting of their rays, it is the battle called **Clashing of Rays** (*anshu-vimarda*). If the north-south distance is...

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Seven]

<page-num>( 144 )</page-num>

When the distance is less than or equal to one degree (sixty minutes of arc), it is called an **Apasavya** <note>literally "contrary" or "from the left"</note> encounter. Here, the author provides a specific detail:

If, in this Apasavya encounter, one of the two planets is small (**Anu**) <note>referring to the size of the planetary disc</note>, then the encounter is considered "distinct" or "manifest" (**Vyakta**). Otherwise, it is "indistinct" (**Avyakta**). Regarding the results of these four types of encounters, the **Bhargaviya** <note>An ancient astrological treatise attributed to the sage Bhrigu</note> states: "In an *Apasavya* encounter, one should predict discord; in a *Rashmi-sankula* (clash of rays), a battle; in *Lekhana* (grazing), distress to ministers; and in *Bheda* (piercing), the loss of wealth."

Having described the types of warfare, he now describes **Samagama** (union/conjunction): When the latitudinal distance between two planets is greater than one degree (sixty minutes), it is called **Samagama**. Here too, he adds a detail:

If the two planets involved in the conjunction are endowed with strength (**Bala**) and possess large, clear discs, the union is "manifest." Otherwise, it is "indistinct." As the text says: "In a union, if both are radiant, large, and bright, there is mutual affection; if the opposite, they destroy their own sides. If the warfare or union is indistinct by these characteristics, the results for the kings of the earth are likewise declared to be indistinct." This is all consistent with the teachings of **Kashyapa** <note>Another revered Vedic sage and astronomer</note>, who says: "Piercing, grazing, clashing of rays, and the contrary encounter—these occur when planets come within one degree."

**Hindi Commentary:** The mutual touching of the stars is called *Ullekha* (grazing). If the discs overlap, it is called *Bheda* (piercing). When their rays mingle, it is called *Anshuvimarda* (clashing of rays). If the separation is no more than one degree, it is *Apasavya* warfare; in that case, if one star is small, it is a "bright" (manifest) battle, and if they are equal, it is "dim" (indistinct). If the separation is more than one degree and both planets are strong, it is called *Samagama* (union). || 18–19 ||

### Now, the characteristics of a planet defeated in warfare are described:

-> **In an Apasavya encounter, the one who is covered, small, lusterless, rough, colorless, or situated to the south is considered struck down and defeated.** || 20 || <-

Between the two, the one who is "struck down" by the other is known as the conquered or defeated (**Vijita**). The characteristics of being "struck" are: In an *Apasavya* encounter, the one who lacks the signs of victory. (By this, it is implied that in the other three types—grazing, etc.—the specific names of the encounters apply rather than the result of "defeat"). **Covered** means obscured or indistinct. **Small** means having a smaller disc than the other planet. **Lusterless** means lacking brilliance. **Rough** means not bright or "oily." **Colorless** means lacking its natural, inherent color. **Situated to the south** means being located to the south relative to the other planet. As the **Bhargaviya** states: "A planet that is dark, devoid of its circle of rays, rough, thin, or overtaken and placed to the south is to be known as 'struck' by the other planet." || 20 ||

**Hindi Commentary** — In an "Apasavya" <note>original: "अपसव्य" - a type of planetary conflict where planets move in an unnatural or counter-clockwise fashion</note> encounter, the planet that is covered, possesses little radiance, and has a small disk is the loser. Such a planet appears rough, deformed, and is situated to the south. || 20 ||

Now, with half a verse, the author describes the characteristics of the victorious planet —

### Situated to the north, radiant, and large; even in the south, that which is powerful is the victor. || 21 ||

Compared to the other planet, the one situated in the northern direction; radiant (endowed with brilliance); and large (having a broader disk compared to the other planet's disk) is the victor. Now, regarding the idea that victory and defeat are not strictly determined by the north-south division, he says: "In the south." A planet that is powerful, radiant, and possesses a large disk even while in the southern direction is the victor. The word "even" <note>original: "api"</note> is used to include the northern direction as well. The implication is that the specific direction (north or south) is secondary to the actual strength and brilliance of the planet when determining victory or defeat. || 21 ||

**Hindi Commentary** — A radiant planet situated in the north with a large disk is the victor. Even if situated in the south, if it is powerful, it is the victor. || 21 ||

Now, he describes special cases in planetary warfare —

### If both are near and both are radiant, it is a "Samagama" (Meeting); if both are small and lusterless, it is a "Kuta-vigraha" (Deceptive War). || 22 ||

"Both" refers to the two planets. "Near" means they are within one degree of each other. The word "even" implies they are characterized by the conditions of warfare. If both are radiant (endowed with brilliance), then because they both possess strength, this specific type of encounter is called *Samagama* <term>Samagama: A peaceful 'meeting' or conjunction where both planets retain their power</term>. If both planets are small (having minute disks) and lusterless (both showing signs of defeat), then they are respectively termed *Kuta-vigraha* <term>Kuta-vigraha: A 'hidden' or 'miserable' conflict where both parties appear defeated or weakened</term>. || 22 ||

**Hindi Commentary** — If both planets become radiant and come close together, it is *Samagama*. If both have very little brilliance and appear destroyed, it is called *Kuta-vigraha*. || 22 ||

Now, stating that Venus generally possesses the characteristics of a victor, and extending the previously mentioned rules of conjunction to the Moon, he says —

### Whether situated in the north or the south, Venus is generally the victor; one should calculate the conjunction of these planets with the Moon in the same manner. || 23 ||

Whether situated to the north or the south relative to the other planet—meaning in either direction—Venus <note>original: "Bhargava"</note> is generally the victor due to its inherent nature of possessing victorious characteristics. The intent is that it only rarely exhibits signs of defeat. The mathematician/astronomer should calculate the "union" or conjunction of these five planets (Mars and the others) with the Moon <note>original: "Shashanka"</note> using the methods described above. Regarding a specific technical point: "In a conjunction with the Moon, the latitude should be known as clarified by parallax." This half-verse appears in some manuscripts but not all; considering it an interpolation, it has been disregarded here, as it would also result in an incomplete verse for this section. By stating this, the prohibition of the parallax adjustment in other types of planetary conjunctions is established...

<header>Surya-Siddhanta — [Chapter 8]</header>

It should be noted that if a specific rule is not mentioned, the general method described for solar eclipses applies everywhere, as the specific details are established by the context of the calculation. || 23 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** Whether in the north or the south, Venus usually emerges victorious <note>In planetary "war" (yuddha), the brighter or more northern planet is often considered the winner</note>. One should determine the time of the Moon's conjunction with the planets using the previously established rules. || 23 ||

Now, an objection arises: since these planets always have a vertical distance between them (being at different heights), and a physical meeting is impossible, how can a "conjunction" be consistent with reality? To answer this, the author says:

> **This conceptualization is shown for the well-being or ill-fortune of the world. ||**
> **Moving in their own paths, these planets remain far from one another. || 24 ||**

These planets move in their own paths—that is, they stay within their respective orbits. At the time of a conjunction, they appear as if joined because there is no perceived horizontal distance, even though they are separated vertically. Thus, this "conjunction" is a conceptualization <note>kalpana: a mental construct or model</note> rather than a physical collision, and it has been described in the preceding text as it appears from a distance. If it is not a physical reality, why was it mentioned? The purpose is stated: "For well-being or ill-fortune." This means the conjunction was described, even if not physically real, for the purpose of predicting the good and bad fortunes of the living beings on Earth. || 24 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** The planets move in their own respective orbits, situated far from each other. Because they appear together to the observer, conjunctions and other phenomena are described for the sake of determining the auspicious and inauspicious fates of men. || 24 ||

Now, to prevent any inconsistency in the upcoming text, the conclusion of the chapter is stated clearly: In the commentary on the Surya-Siddhanta composed by Ranganatha, this Chapter on Planetary Conjunctions is completed in the *Gudartha-Prakashaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings"</note>. Thus ends the Chapter on Planetary Conjunctions in the *Gudartha-Prakashaka* composed by the mathematician Ranganatha, son of the priest Ballala, the sovereign of all calculators.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the Surya Siddhanta, specifically focusing on the calculation of the polar longitudes (dhruvaka) of various lunar mansions (nakshatras) and refuting alternative opinions from other astronomical traditions.</meta>

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Eight]

The reading is incorrect because it contradicts the *Shakalya Samhita* <note>An ancient astronomical treatise</note>. By this, the claim made by Narmada—that the *dhruvaka* <term>Dhruvaka: The polar longitude of a star, measured along the ecliptic</term> accepted by all people is 15 degrees minus 10 minutes in Gemini, and the *dhruvaka* favored by Parvata is 13 degrees plus 10 minutes—is rejected. 

The value for **Punarvasu** is 78; for **Pushya**, 76; for **Ashlesha**, 14. The word "likewise" is used in the text to complete the poetic meter. For **Magha**, it is 54; for **Purva Phalguni**, 64; for **Uttara Phalguni**, 50; for **Hasta**, 60; for **Chitra**, 40; for **Svati**, 74; for **Vishakha**, 78; for **Anuradha**, 64; and for **Jyeshtha**, 14. 

Following these, for **Mula**, it is 6; for **Purva Ashadha**, 4. 

He then states the *dhruvaka* for **Uttara Ashadha**: "Of the Universal Gods" <note>original: *Vaishvam*</note>. The junction star of the Uttara Ashadha constellation is located at the midpoint of the portion of **Apya** (Purva Ashadha). It should be understood to be situated at 20 degrees of the sign Sagittarius. This means the *dhruvaka* of Uttara Ashadha is 8 signs and 20 degrees. 

By this, the view that the junction star of Uttara Ashadha is separated from the junction star of Purva Ashadha by 7 degrees minus 20 minutes—which would make the *dhruvaka* of Uttara Ashadha 8 signs, 14 degrees, plus 7 degrees minus 20 minutes (resulting in a *dhruvaka* 40 minutes greater than stated)—is dismissed, as it contradicts the *Brahma Siddhanta*.

He states the *dhruvaka* for **Abhijit**: "Of the Waters" <note>original: *Apyasya*</note>. At the end of Purva Ashadha, at 27 degrees minus 20 minutes of Sagittarius, the junction star of Abhijit is to be known. This means the *dhruvaka* of Abhijit is 8 signs, 26 degrees, and 40 minutes. The word "only" <note>original: *eva*</note> is used to exclude other positions. Thus, the position of **Shravana** at 15 degrees, or the position at 9 signs, 14 degrees, 13 minutes, and 20 seconds, is rejected.

He states the *dhruvaka* for **Shravana**: "At the end of the Universal Gods" <note>original: *Vaishvante*</note>. The position of the Shravana junction star is at the end of Uttara Ashadha. This means the *dhruvaka* of Shravana is 9 signs and 10 degrees.

He states the *dhruvaka* for **Dhanishtha**: "In the third and fourth quarters" <note>original: *trichatuh-padayoh*</note>. At the junction of the end and beginning of the third and fourth quarters of Shravana respectively, at 20 degrees of Capricorn, <term>Shravishtha or Dhanishtha</term> is to be known. This means the *dhruvaka* of Dhanishtha is 9 signs and 20 degrees. By the use of the word "but" <note>original: *tu*</note>, the position of Dhanishtha within the sign Aquarius at 7 degrees minus 20 minutes is rejected.

He states the portion for **Shatatara**: "From its own portion" <note>original: *svabhogatah*</note>. This means from the end of the portion of Dhanishtha up to 7 degrees minus 20 minutes of Aquarius. The portion of Shatatara is 80. Therefore, to indicate that the *dhruvakas* are as before, he says "from its own portion." This results in the position of Shatatara being its *dhruvaka*.

He states the portions of the remaining constellations: "The square of six" <note>original: *shat-kriti*, meaning 36</note>. The portion of **Purva Bhadrapada** is 36 minutes; of **Uttara Bhadrapada**, 22; of **Revati**, 79.

Now, the method for calculating the *dhruvaka* is as follows:
The portion of **Ashwini** is 48. Multiplied by ten, it is 480. Since there are no preceding constellations, there is no addition of portions. Therefore, the *dhruvaka* of Ashwini in minutes is 480. In signs and degrees, it is 0 signs, 8 degrees.
The portion of **Bharani** is 40. Multiplied by ten, it is 400. Since there is one preceding constellation, adding 480 gives 880 for Bharani. By the standard definition, the *dhruvaka* in signs and degrees is 0 signs, 20 degrees <note>880 minutes = 14 degrees 40 minutes; the text here seems to be summarizing or using a specific technical shorthand</note>.
Similarly, the portion of **Ardra** is 4. Multiplied by ten, it is 40.

The <term>Dhruva</term><note>The polar longitude or fixed point of a star</note> in minutes of arc is 4040, obtained by adding the five-fold value of the preceding <term>Nakshatras</term><note>Lunar mansions/star clusters</note> to eight hundred multiplied by five (4000). In signs and degrees, this is 2 signs, 7 degrees, and 20 minutes. Similarly, for *Purvashadha*, the <term>Bhoga</term><note>The portion or longitudinal extent</note> is multiplied by ten, resulting in 40. When added to eight hundred multiplied by nineteen (15200), the <term>Dhruva</term> in signs and degrees becomes 8 signs and 14 degrees. For *Shatabhisha*, the ten-fold <term>Bhoga</term> is 800. Added to eight hundred multiplied by twenty-three (18400), it results in 19200, making the <term>Dhruva</term> 10 signs and 20 degrees. For *Purva Bhadrapada*, the ten-fold <term>Bhoga</term> is 360. Added to eight hundred multiplied by twenty-four (19200), it becomes 19560, making the <term>Dhruva</term> 10 signs and 26 degrees. Because *Uttara Ashadha*, *Abhijit*, *Shravana*, and *Dhanishta* are situated behind their respective <term>Bhoga</term> positions, the previously mentioned method is not possible; therefore, their <term>Dhruvas</term> are stated using a different method. The distances from their starting points to the <term>Yogatara</term><note>The junction star or principal star of a Nakshatra</note> in minutes are divided by ten to define the <term>Bhoga</term>. Thus, it is said in the *Brahmasiddhanta*:

> "Eight, twenty, <unclear>dhau</unclear>, seven-born-fire <note>37</note>, five-less-half <note>4.5</note>. Three-six <note>63</note>, seven-with-a-third <note>7.33</note>, six-serpent-limbs <note>686</note>, and six hundred. Nine-parts, nine-suns <note>108</note>, and four-moons <note>14</note>, five-five-earth <note>155</note>. Void-seven-sixteen <note>1670</note>, self-eighteen <note>18</note>, nine-beyond-eighteen <note>19</note>, twenty-two. Four-form <note>44</note>, nine-eye-hands <note>229</note>, poet-ten-hands <note>210</note>, age-half-eyes <note>24.5</note>. Void-twenty-six <note>260</note> minus a third, four-three-hands <note>234</note>, void-elephant-eyes <note>280</note>. Void-mountain-twins <note>207</note>, void-teeth <note>320</note>, six-teeth <note>36</note>, mountain-three-fires <note>337</note>. From Aries onwards, the middle degrees are sixty minus six <note>54</note>."

Now, he states the <term>Vikshepa</term><note>Celestial latitude; the distance north or south of the ecliptic</note> degrees of the <term>Nakshatras</term>. "Of these" refers to the stars starting from *Ashwini* associated with the aforementioned <term>Dhruvas</term>. "In order" means sequentially. "From their own" means from their own declination or from the position of the <term>Dhruva</term> on the <term>Ecliptic</term><note>The sun's apparent path</note>. The <term>Vikshepa</term> degrees are either South or North. There, in the North direction, for the three starting with *Ashwini*, the values are ten, twelve, and five respectively. In the South direction, for the three starting with *Rohini*, they are five, ten, and nine. In the North, for *Punarvasu*, it is six degrees. For *Pushya*, it is zero, meaning an absence of <term>Vikshepa</term>. <note>The author notes a technical poetic fault here: "The heaviness of the fifth syllable breaks the meter, but as it is an archaic/sage-authored text, it is not a flaw."</note> In the South, for *Ashlesha*, it is seven. In the North, for the three starting with *Magha*, they are zero, twelve, and thirteen. In the South, for the three starting with *Hasta* and *Chitra*, they are eleven and two. Thereafter, for *Swati* in the North, it is thirty-seven. In the South, for the six starting with *Vishakha*, they are one-and-a-half, three, four, nine, five-and-a-half, and five respectively. Similarly, in the North, the <term>Vikshepa</term> degrees for *Abhijit* are sixty. For *Shravana*, thirty. For *Dhanishta*, thirty-six. The word "only" is used to exclude more or less. The word "and" is for completion. In the South, the word "but" is used similarly. For *Shatabhisha*, it is half a degree. In the North, for *Purva Bhadrapada*, it is twenty-four. In that same direction, the <term>Vikshepa</term> degrees for *Uttara Bhadrapada* are twenty-six. For *Revati*, there is an absence of <term>Vikshepa</term>. The word "and" is for completion. || 2 || 3 || 4 || 5 || 6 || 7 || 8 || 9 ||

Now, the polar longitudes and latitudes of the stars Agastya <note>Canopus</note>, Lubdhaka <note>Sirius</note>, Vahni <note>Alpha Arietis</note>, and Brahmahridaya <note>Capella</note>, along with their explanations, are stated in three verses:

<page-num>151</page-num>
<header>Chapter 8. ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. </header>

# With eight and thirty respectively, these two are situated to the north. ||
# Having constructed the globe, one should examine the latitude and the precise polar longitude. || 12 ||

From its own position on the ecliptic <note>the path of the sun</note>, the brightest star **Agastya** <note>Canopus</note> is situated at the end of Gemini <note>Mithuna</note> or the beginning of Cancer, eighty degrees to the south. The polar longitude <term>Dhruvaka</term> <note>the degree of the ecliptic which rises or culminates with the star</note> of the star Agastya is three signs <note>90 degrees</note>. This means the southern latitude <term>Vikshepa</term> is eighty degrees. **Mrigavyadha** <note>Sirius, the "Deer-Hunter"</note>, also called **Lubdhaka**, is situated at the twentieth degree of the sign Gemini. The word "and" implies a collection. The polar longitude of the star Lubdhaka is two signs and twenty degrees <note>80 degrees</note>. Its latitude is measured as forty degrees to the south from the ecliptic. In the sign of Taurus <note>Vrisha</note>, **Vahni** <note>El Nath / Beta Tauri</note> and **Brahmahridaya** <note>Capella</note> are both situated at twenty-two degrees. The polar longitude of the stars Vahni and Brahmahridaya is one sign plus twenty-two degrees <note>52 degrees</note>. Regarding those two, Vahni and Brahmahridaya: "with eight and thirty." The word "and" indicates the sequence. The word "certainly" is used to exclude any more or less. They are "situated to the north," meaning in the northern direction, possessing latitude. The latitude of Vahni is eight degrees north. The northern latitude of Brahmahridaya is thirty degrees.

Now, one might ask whether these polar longitudes and latitudes are fixed or variable over time. To this, he says: "The globe..." Having constructed the globe <note>an armillary sphere</note> using bamboo strips and the like, one should examine the precise latitude—which is fit for declination transformation—and the precise polar longitude directed toward the pole, which has been processed by the precession of the equinoxes <term>Ayanakarma</term>. One should accept what is proven by observation in one's own time. Thus, because the latitude fit for declination and the polar longitude processed for precession are unstable due to the influence of the precession of the equinoxes <note>Ayana</note>, I have stated these fixed polar longitudes and latitudes processed for precession for the sake of simplicity, in accordance with the present time. In other times, they should be known through observation with the globe instrument. This is the intent.

As for observation with the globe instrument: the globe instrument should be made according to the method described in the construction of the globe. There, upon the celestial sphere <term>Khagola</term>, place the starry sphere <term>Bhagola</term>, and upon the supporting circle, place the equinoctial circle <note>celestial equator</note>. Having fixed the ecliptic marked with degrees as described, there should be another movable observation circle <term>Vedha-valaya</term> attached to the two pole-pins of the axis. That too should be marked with degrees. Then, having stabilized that globe instrument so that the axis is correctly facing the pole and the horizon circle is level with water, one should look at the star **Revati** <note>Zeta Piscium</note> through a sight-hole in the center of the globe at night. Having placed the end of Pisces <note>the vernal equinox</note> on the ecliptic—displaced by the degrees of precession—upon the star Revati, one should look at the junction-star <term>Yogatara</term> of a constellation like Ashvini through that same central sight and align the observation circle over it. When this is done, the intersection of the observation circle and the ecliptic shows how many degrees it is from the end of Pisces; those are to be known as the polar longitude degrees of that star. On the observation circle itself, the number of degrees between that intersection and the junction-star are the degrees of latitude, to be known as south or north. However, if observing with an observation circle passing through the poles of the ecliptic <term>Kadamba</term>, the polar longitudes processed for precession would always be fixed. But since that is impossible due to the absence of stars at the ecliptic poles, the polar longitudes and latitudes processed for precession, as determined by the stated observation method, are established as precise and directed toward the celestial poles. This is the direction <note>general guidance</note>. || 10 || 11 || 12 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The polar longitude of Agastya is 3s 0° and latitude 80° South. Mrigavyadha polar longitude 2s 20° and latitude 40° South. Agni <note>Vahni</note> polar longitude 1s 22° and latitude 8° North. Brahmahridaya polar longitude 1s 22° and latitude 30° North. One should examine the precise latitude and all polar longitudes while constructing the globe. || 10 || 11 || 12 ||

<header>The Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Eight]</header>

### Now, he describes the piercing of the "Cart of Rohini"—

> **In the seventeenth degree of Taurus, that planet whose southern**
> **latitude is greater than two degrees, pierces the Cart of Rohini. || 13 ||**

In the zodiac sign of Taurus, at the seventeenth degree, whichever planet possesses a southern latitude <note>distance north or south from the ecliptic</note> exceeding two degrees, that planet "pierces" the Cart of Rohini—meaning it enters the middle of the cart-like formation of the stars. The word "but" (tu) in the verse implies a specific distinction: if the planet's latitude is less than Rohini's latitude, it behaves differently. If the southern latitude were significantly greater than Rohini's, the planet would be situated outside the Cart to the south and would not "pierce" it. Here, the longitude of the leading star of the Cart is one sign and seventeen degrees <note>47 degrees total</note>, and its southern latitude is two degrees; this is a clear logic established by observation. || 13 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** A planet that pierces the Cart of Rohini is located at 17 degrees of Taurus with a southern latitude of two degrees. || 13 ||

---

### Now, he describes the method for calculating the conjunction of planets and stars—

> **One should perform the visibility correction for the stars according to their day and night, just as for the planets.**
> **The rest is like the conjunction of planets; the days are found by the planet's motion. || 14 ||**

Just as the measures of day and night are used for planets to perform the <term>Visibility Correction (Aksha-Drikkarma)</term> <note>a calculation to adjust the celestial position to the observer's local horizon</note>, the calculator should do the same for the fixed longitudes of the stars. After that, having calculated the daily rising and setting of the stars as before, and having determined the "natam" <note>zenith distance</note> from the remaining time of day or night using the equinoctial shadow, one should perform the <term>Visibility Correction (Drikkarma)</term>. 

<margin>Note: Some examples apply the polar longitude correction to the star's fixed position, but this is improper as it is already inherent in the fixed position.</margin>

Following this, the remaining calculation for the union of a star and a planet—making the planet's position equal to the star's—should be done according to the <term>Method for Planetary Conjunction (Graha-melaka)</term>, using the minutes of distance between them. Now, one might ask: since the rule for planets says "multiply the minutes of distance by the respective motions and divide by the difference in motions," what motion should be used for a star? To this, he says: <term>By the planet's motion (Graha-bhuktya)</term>. Using only the planet's daily motion, the result is applied to the planet's position until it equals the star's longitude. Because stars have no forward motion, their fixed position remains as it is. To the slight doubt of how to calculate the time of conjunction when there is no "difference in motion" (since the star is stationary), he says: "The days." The days of conjunction between the planet and the star are to be calculated from the distance using only the planet's motion. The word "and" (cha) indicates the inclusion of this logic because stars lack motion. || 14 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** One should perform the <term>Visibility Correction (Drikkarma)</term> for stars following the day-night measures of the planets. Treat it the same as a conjunction of all planets. By taking the <term>Planet's Motion (Graha-bhukti)</term> in place of the "difference in motions," everything will be correct. || 14 ||

<page-num>153</page-num>
<header>Chapter 8. ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. ( 153 )</header>

Now, to avoid confusion, the author explains whether the time of conjunction between a planet and a star has passed or is yet to come, relative to the desired time:

### If the planet's position is less than the star's longitude, the conjunction is yet to come; if greater, it has passed.
### In the case of a planet in retrograde motion, the opposite is understood to be true regarding the conjunction. || 15 ||

When the planet—specifically the planet processed by the two-fold visibility corrections <note>referring to āyana-drkkarma and ākṣa-drkkarma, calculations used to find the apparent position of a celestial body on the ecliptic</note>—is at a lower longitude than the fixed star's longitude, the conjunction between the star and the planet is "future" or yet to occur from the desired time. If the planet's longitude is greater, the conjunction has already occurred. If the planet is in retrograde motion <note>vakra-gati: appearing to move backward in the sky</note>, the opposite of what was just stated should be understood: if the retrograde planet's longitude is less, the conjunction has passed; if greater, it is yet to come. The logic here is very simple: since the stars are considered stationary due to their lack of motion, the conjunction occurs solely through the movement of the planet. || 15 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** If the corrected planet is less than the star's longitude, the conjunction will happen later; if more, it has already happened. For a retrograde planet, this meeting is the opposite. || 15 ||

Now, since constellations like Ashvini consist of many stars, one might wonder: "Which specific star do these coordinates belong to?" or "Which is the junction star?" Keeping this in mind, and wishing to describe the junction stars <term>Yogatārā: the principal star of a lunar mansion used for astronomical calculations</term> of Ashvini and the others, the author first identifies the junction stars for these specific groups:

### Of the two Phalgunis, the two Bhadrapadas, and likewise the two Ashadhas,
### as well as Vishakha, Ashvini, and Mrigashirsha, the northern star is considered the junction star. || 16 ||

Among the stars belonging to each of these mentioned constellations, the one situated to the north is declared by those learned in the celestial sphere <note>the "Gola-vid," or experts in spherical astronomy</note> to be the junction star. || 16 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** For both Phalgunis, both Bhadrapadas, Purva-ashadha, Uttara-ashadha, Vishakha, Ashvini, and Mrigashirsha, the stars located to the north are called the junction stars. || 16 ||

Now, the author speaks of the junction stars for the following two:

### The star situated to the west of the second north-western star
### is the junction star of Hasta; and for Shravishtha, it is the western one. || 17 ||

The constellation Hasta <note>meaning "the hand"</note> consists of five stars arranged in the shape of a hand with five fingers. Among those, there is a star situated to the north of the westernmost star (which is in the southwest); the star situated to the west of that (in the northwest) is to be known as the junction star of Hasta. The result is that the star situated to the west, near the northern star, is Hasta's junction star. Regarding the junction star of Dhanishtha (Shravishtha): among the stars of Dhanishtha, the one situated in the western direction is its junction star. The word "and" indicates the inclusion of both. || 17 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** In the five-starred constellation of Hasta, the star situated to the west of the north-western star is the junction star of Hasta; and the star situated to the west of Dhanishtha is the junction star of Dhanishtha. || 17 ||

### Now he speaks of others among these:

> The middle star of Jyeshtha, Shravana, Maitra (Anuradha), and Barhaspatya (Pushya) is the junction star.
> For Bharani, Agneya (Krttika), Pitrya (Magha), and Revati, it is the southern star. || 18 ||

Since Jyeshtha, Shravana, Anuradha, and Pushya each consist of three stars, the middle star among them is the <term>Yogatara</term> <note>The "junction star" or principal star of a constellation used as a reference point for astronomical calculations</note>. For Bharani, Krttika, and Magha, as well as Revati—the word "and" implies the grouping—the star situated to the south among their respective clusters is the junction star. || 18 ||

**Commentary:** The middle stars of Jyeshtha, Shravana, Anuradha, and Pushya, and the southernmost stars of Bharani, Krttika, Magha, and Revati are their respective junction stars. || 18 ||

### Now he speaks of the remaining ones among these:

> For Rohini, Aditya (Punarvasu), and Mula, it is the eastern star; likewise for Sarpa (Ashlesha).
> For the remaining ones, the largest star shall be the junction star. || 19 ||

For Rohini, Punarvasu, Mula, and Ashlesha, the star situated to the east within their respective clusters is the junction star; this is the meaning of the particle "hi" (indeed). For the remaining constellations—namely Ardra, Chitra, Svati, Abhijit, and Shatataraka—the star which is the most "gross" or largest (brightest) among their stars is the <term>Yogatara</term>. || 19 ||

**Commentary:** The eastern stars of Rohini, Punarvasu, Mula, and Ashlesha, and the largest (brightest) stars of the remaining constellations are the junction stars. || 19 ||

### Now he describes the position of the star named Brahma:

> Situated five degrees to the east of Brahma-hrdaya is Prajapati.
> He is at the end of Taurus, thirty-eight degrees to the north. || 20 ||

At a distance of five degrees to the east from the position of <term>Brahma-hrdaya</term> <note>Literally "The Heart of Brahma," identified with the star Capella</note>, the star-form Brahma, known as Prajapati, is situated on the ecliptic. To the question "Where?", he replies: "At the end of Taurus." This means near the end of the sign Taurus. The longitude (dhruvaka) of Brahma is thus 1 sign and 27 degrees (57°). Regarding its latitude (vikshepa), he says: "He is situated thirty-eight degrees to the north." This means its latitude is 38 degrees north. || 20 ||

**Commentary:** Prajapati is situated 5 degrees east of Brahma-hrdaya. Its longitude is at the end of Taurus, i.e., 1s 27° (57°), and its latitude is 38° North. || 20 ||

### Now he describes the positions of the two stars Apamvatsa and Apas:

> Apamvatsa is five degrees north of Chitra.
> Slightly larger than this is Apas, likewise six degrees to the north. || 21 ||

The star named Apamvatsa is situated five degrees to the north of Chitra (Spica). The first "tu" <note>a grammatical particle</note> indicates it shares the same longitude as Chitra. The second "tu" refers to the latitude of Chitra, which is two degrees south...

# Chapter Nine

Now the Chapter on Risings and Settings is explained. One might ask: since it was previously mentioned that planets set along with the Sun, shouldn't the chapter on Risings and Settings have been described immediately after the Chapter on Planetary Conjunctions, and before the Chapter on Star-Planet Conjunctions? To show the proper connection here, the author first introduces the chapter:

> **Now, the knowledge of the rising and setting**
> **of those bodies of little luster, whose forms are overcome by the rays of the Sun, is proclaimed. || 1 ||**

Now, after the <term>Chapter on the Conjunction of Stars and Planets</term>, [we discuss] the rising and setting of the planets like the Moon and the stars, whose forms or disks are overwhelmed by the Sun's rays. Because of this, they have "little luster" or diminished power. In the coming time, due to the possibility of moving closer or further from the Sun, their rising and setting occur in sequence. "Rising" is the first visibility at a certain distance after emerging from the Sun. "Setting" is the first disappearance at a certain distance when approaching the Sun. By this, the daily rising and setting [due to Earth's rotation] are excluded; this refers to heliacal phenomena. <term>Knowledge</term> means the method of precise calculation is proclaimed. The meaning is: "It is spoken by me with great precision." Although "setting" was mentioned previously in the context of planetary conjunctions, it was discussed there only because it occurs when planets are near the Sun. The conjunction of stars and planets was discussed next because it is similar to planetary conjunctions. Therefore, since the curiosity regarding the obstacles [to visibility] must be addressed, this is the appropriate opportunity. Following that logic, after the Chapter on Star-Planet Conjunctions, the previously mentioned "setting" and its counterpart "rising" are now propounded. || 1 ||

# Surya Siddhanta
## [Chapter Nine]

**Commentary:** Now the knowledge of rising and setting is described. Planets with lesser brilliance, when overcome by the rays of the Sun, undergo setting <note>astamana; becoming invisible in the solar glare</note>. || 1 ||

First, he describes the setting in the west and rising in the east for the five star-planets:

> ->Jupiter, Mars, and Saturn, when their longitude is greater than the Sun’s, set in the west.<-
> ->When their longitude is less, they rise in the east; so too Venus and Mercury when in retrograde motion.<- || 2 ||

When Venus and Mercury are in retrograde motion <term>Vakri; appearing to move backward against the stars</term>, and their longitude is greater than the Sun's, they go to their western setting. When their longitude is less than the Sun's, they attain their eastern rising. The rest is clear. || 2 ||

**Commentary:** If the true longitude of the planet is greater than the true longitude of the Sun, then Jupiter, Mars, and Saturn set in the west. If their longitude is less than the Sun's, they rise in the east. Retrograde Venus and Mercury behave in the same way. || 2 ||

Now, he describes the eastern setting and western rising of the Moon, Mercury, and Venus:

> ->When their longitude is less than the Sun’s, the Moon, Mercury, and Venus set in the east.<-
> ->When their longitude is greater, these fast-moving planets rise in the west.<- || 3 ||

"Fast-moving" <term>shighrayayinah</term> means those whose daily motion is greater than the Sun's motion. It is stated here that when Mercury and Venus move slower than the Sun <note>when not retrograde</note>, they do not follow this rule of eastern setting and western rising. The rest is clear. 

The reasoning <term>upapatti</term> is as follows: If a planet moving slower than the Sun has a longitude less than the Sun's, it deserves to be visible in the east. Because the Sun has greater longitude and greater speed, the distance between them increases daily. Due to the force of the Provector wind <note>Pravaha; the cosmic wind believed to drive the celestial spheres</note>, the one with lesser longitude rises first in the east. If the distance <term>viprakarsha</term> is sufficient after the planet's disk has cleared the horizon but before the Sun rises, visibility is possible. 

Conversely, when a slow-moving planet has a longitude greater than the Sun's, the Sun rises first due to the Provector wind, making the later-rising planet invisible. However, at sunset, the Sun (having lesser longitude) sets first, and the planet (having greater longitude) sets later. Even if the planet is visible in the west after sunset, because the faster-moving Sun is behind it and catching up, the distance decreases <term>sannikarsha</term> daily until the planet disappears in the west. These planets are Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn; and also Mercury and Venus when their motion is reduced by retrogradation. 

Now, if a planet moving faster than the Sun has a longitude less than the Sun's, the distance decreases daily, leading to its disappearance (setting) in the east. When its longitude is greater than the Sun's, the distance increases daily, leading to its appearance (rising) in the west. These are the fast-movers: Moon, Mercury, and Venus. Thus, the statement is proven. || 3 ||

**Commentary:** If these three fast-moving planets—Moon, Mercury, and Venus—are at a position less than the Sun's, they set in the east; if they are at a greater position, they rise in the west. || 3 ||

Now, to find the timing of these events on a desired day, he states that the positions of the Sun and the visible planet must be calculated for the time of sunrise and sunset:

It distinguishes between slow-moving planets (Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) and fast-moving ones (Moon, Mercury, Venus).</summary>

# Chapter 9. | With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.

<page-num>157</page-num>

->For the west, the Sun and planet are calculated at sunset; for the east, at sunrise.<-
->During the day, calculate the Sun and planet; then perform half of the visibility correction for the planet. || 4 ||<-

When calculating the rising and setting in the west, the astronomer should calculate the positions of the Sun and the planet at the time of sunset on the desired day. For rising and setting in the east, they should be calculated at the time of sunrise. The word "and" (ca) implies an alternative. Thereafter, one must perform the <term>Visibility Correction (Dṛkkarma)</term> <note>Dṛkkarma refers to the mathematical adjustment made to a planet's longitude to account for its latitude and the tilt of the ecliptic, ensuring its position is relative to the observer's horizon.</note>. Both the Ecliptic and Polar visibility corrections should be applied. The word "but" (tu) signifies a specific distinction regarding the first half of the verse on visibility correction.

**The logic here is:** For calculating western rising and setting, the observation occurs in the west; therefore, the Sun and planet at sunset are precise for determining the <term>Time-Degrees (Kālāṃśas)</term> <note>Kālāṃśas are units of time expressed in degrees (1 degree = 4 minutes) used to measure the distance between the Sun and a planet to determine visibility.</note>. For eastern rising and setting, the observation is in the east; thus, the positions at sunrise are precise. While positions calculated at other times might be slightly approximate, the planet must be processed with the visibility correction because a corrected planet is capable of touching the horizon just like the Sun. || 4 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** For events in the west, determine the true positions of the Sun and planet at sunset; for the east, at sunrise. Thereafter, calculate the planet's visibility correction. || 4 ||

Now, he describes the calculation of the desired Time-Degrees:

-><gloss>1</gloss> Then, the breath-intervals between the rising signs divided by sixty are the Time-Degrees.<-
->In the west, the same is done for the two with six signs added. || 5 ||<-

Then, from those two—the Sun and the planet corrected for visibility—the <term>Rising-Interval Breaths (Lagnāntara-prāṇas)</term> <note>Prāṇa is a unit of time equivalent to 4 seconds; it is the time taken for one sidereal minute of arc to rise at the equator.</note> are found using the method of "the portion to be passed and the portion already passed." These breaths, divided by sixty, become the desired Time-Degrees. For eastern rising/setting, this is done directly; for western rising/setting, the Sun and the visibility-corrected planet are both increased by six signs (180 degrees), and then the rising-interval breaths are calculated. Those breaths, similarly divided by sixty, result in the desired Time-Degrees.

**The logic here is:** Using the visibility-corrected planet and the Sun, the interval of time at sunrise represents the time elapsed in the day for the purpose of eastern rising/setting. Similarly, for western rising/setting, the interval between the Sun and the planet at sunset represents the remainder of the day. To calculate this using the rising times of the signs, the Sun and planet are increased by six signs. This time is expressed in breaths. Since the breaths of a full day and night are equal to the minutes of a circle (21,600), we seek the degrees. By the rule of proportion, dividing by sixty converts these breaths into degrees.

One should note: For the east, the planet is moved backward by the time elapsed since sunrise. For the west, using the values increased by six signs, the planet is moved forward by the time remaining in the day. Thus, the planet's position at the moment of rising or setting in the east or west is found. From these and the Sun (or Sun + 6 signs), the interval of time at the moment of rising/setting is found in sidereal breaths; these divided by sixty are the precise Time-Degrees.

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Nine]

The time of rising and setting, calculated from the positions of the Sun and the planets at the eastern and western horizons, is considered precise even when using sidereal time <note>time measured by the stars rather than the sun</note>. Because these calculations do not rely on the actual moment of sunrise or sunset, the resulting degrees of visibility <term>Kālāmśas: degrees of time/arc required for a planet to become visible or invisible</term> are accurate. However, if one calculates these degrees using only a single instance of sunrise or sunset, the results are coarse; if calculated from an arbitrary desired time, they are extremely imprecise because the day is measured in solar time <note>Sāvana time</note>. A full circle of the heavens is not completed in exactly sixty solar ghatis <note>a ghati is 24 minutes</note>, which is why such methods fail to achieve precision. || 5 ||

**Commentary:** In the eastern horizon, determine the difference in rising times <note>Prānas</note> between the true positions of the Sun and the planet, then divide by 60 to find the degrees of visibility. For the western horizon, calculate the difference using the positions increased by six signs <note>180 degrees</note>. || 5 ||

Now, desiring to explain the specific degrees at which rising or setting occurs, the author first states the degrees for Jupiter, Saturn, and Mars:

->**Jupiter's degrees are eleven, and those of the Sun's son (Saturn) are fifteen.**<-
->**The degrees of the Earth's son (Mars) are ten plus seven.**<- || 6 ||

After understanding the desired degrees of visibility, one learns the setting degrees. These degrees, which define the point of setting, are also understood to define the point of rising. The degrees of visibility for Jupiter <note>original: "Amarejya"</note> are eleven. For Saturn <note>original: "Arkaja"</note>, the number is fifteen. For Mars <note>original: "Bhumiputra"</note>, it is ten plus seven, meaning seventeen degrees. || 6 ||

**Commentary:** Jupiter 11, Saturn 15, and Mars 17; these are their respective degrees of setting (visibility). || 6 ||

Next, he speaks of Venus:

->**In the west, setting and in the east, rising occur at eight degrees due to its greatness.**<-
->**Setting in the east and rising in the west occur at ten degrees for Venus, due to its smallness.**<- || 7 ||

Because of the "greatness" of Venus—meaning its large disk <term>Bimba: the visible disk of a planet</term> when it is retrograde and near its perigee—its setting in the west and rising in the east occur at only eight degrees of visibility. Not more. However, when Venus is "small" (having a minute disk), the calculator should reckon its setting in the east at ten degrees. Not less. Its rising in the west, when the disk is minute, is likewise known to be at ten degrees. || 7 ||

**Commentary:** Due to its thickness (large disk), the western setting and eastern rising of Venus occur at 8 degrees. But for the eastern setting and western rising, 10 degrees must be taken because the disk is smaller. || 7 ||

Next, he speaks of Mercury:

->**Similarly, Mercury, at twelve and fourteen degrees,**<-
->**being retrograde or fast-moving, undergoes setting and rising from the Sun.**<- || 8 ||
