<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of planetary visibility (heliacal rising and setting) relative to the Sun, specifically focusing on Mercury and the general rules for determining if an event has already occurred or is yet to come.</meta>

<page-num>159</page-num>
<header>Chapter 90 ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. (159)</header>

When retrograde <note>Sanskrit: *vakri*; moving backward against the stars</note>, Mercury is fast-moving. The word "and" implies a combination of conditions. Mercury undergoes setting and rising at 12 and 14 degrees of time <term>time-degrees (kala-bhaga): a measure of the Sun's distance below the horizon required for a planet to become visible</term> from the Sun. Mercury follows the pattern of Venus: it sets in the west and rises in the east at 12 time-degrees due to its large disk <note>original: *mahabimbataya*; when the planet appears larger and brighter</note>. Conversely, it sets in the east and rises in the west at 14 time-degrees because of its small disk <note>original: *anubimbatvat*; when the planet appears smaller and fainter</note>. || 8 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In this manner, Mercury, when retrograde, attains its rising or setting at 12 degrees from the Sun, and when fast-moving, at 14 time-degrees. || 8 ||

Now, the author explains how to know whether the rising or setting has already passed or is yet to occur, based on the calculated time-degrees:

### When the time-degrees are greater than these, the planets are visible; when less, they are invisible. ###
### In this world, the celestial bodies have their forms swallowed by the radiance of the Sun. ### || 9 ||

If the calculated time-degrees at the desired time are greater than those specified in the previous three verses (starting with "eleven for Jupiter"), the planets are capable of being seen. Thus, in calculating the setting, if the planet is visible, the setting is yet to come <note>future event</note>. In calculating the rising, if it is visible, the rising has already occurred <note>past event</note>. If the time-degrees are fewer, the planets are "invisible" in this world—meaning they are not within the range of sight. Why are they invisible? The text says: "their forms are swallowed by the radiance of the Sun." Because of their proximity to the Sun, their bodies (disks) are overwhelmed by the brilliance of the solar rays, which strikes the eyes of people in the world. Therefore, in calculating the setting, if the planet is invisible, the setting has already passed. In calculating the rising, if it is invisible, the rising is yet to occur.

This aligns with the statement of the teacher Bhaskaracharya: "If the calculated degrees are less or more than those stated, the rising of the planet is respectively future or past; the opposite is understood for the setting." The logic here is: the rising or setting caused by the Sun occurs exactly when the planet reaches the stated time-degrees. Since these degrees are the cause for the planet's disappearance due to solar proximity, if the degrees are less than required, the planet is definitely in a state of being "set." || 9 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** When situated at a distance greater than the time-degrees mentioned above from the Sun, the planets are visible. When the distance is less, the disk is surrounded by the Sun's splendor, and the planets are not visible to people. || 9 ||

Now, he describes how to calculate the days and other units for the past or future rising and setting:

### The difference in minutes between the required time-degrees and the actual degrees, divided by the difference in daily motions, ###
### yields the result in days and so on; for a retrograde planet, use the sum of the motions. ### || 10 ||

# Surya Siddhanta: Chapter Nine

<page-num>160</page-num>
<header>Surya Siddhanta — [Ninth Chapter]</header>

The difference between the stated <term>degrees of time</term><note>Kālāṃśa: units of time expressed as degrees, where 1 degree equals 4 minutes, used to determine visibility</note> and the desired degrees of time is converted into minutes of arc and divided by the difference between the daily motions of the Sun and the planet. The resulting value in days and fractions of days indicates the time elapsed or remaining until the rising or setting. Regarding the specific case of a planet with <term>retrograde motion</term><note>Vakragati: the apparent backward motion of a planet against the stars</note>, the author says: *The result is obtained.* For a retrograde planet, one must divide by the **sum** of the daily motions of the Sun and the planet to find the days past or remaining.

The reasoning here is as follows: If one day is equivalent to the difference in the daily motions of the Sun and the planet, then how many days correspond to the difference between the desired and stated degrees of time? This proportion reveals the time until the rising or setting. In the case of a retrograde planet, because the distance between the Sun and the planet increases or decreases by the sum of their motions each day, using the sum in the proportion is logically sound. || 10 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Subtract the desired degrees of time from their respective visibility degrees and convert to minutes. Divide this by the difference in daily motions to get the days. If the planet is retrograde, the sum of the motions should be used. || 10 ||

Now, considering that the daily motions of the planets occur along the <term>ecliptic</term><note>Krāntivṛtta: the sun's apparent path</note> while the degrees of time are measured along the <term>equatorial circle</term><note>Ahorātravṛtta: the circle of daily rotation</note>, a direct proportion might be considered inaccurate due to the different "species" of measurement. To resolve this and make the motions compatible with the time-units, the author explains how to transform the daily motions:

->**Multiply the two daily motions by the rising time of the sign and divide by 1800.**<-
->**These become the "time-motions"; use them to find the days past or remaining.**<- || 11 ||

The daily motions of the Sun and the planet (in minutes) are multiplied by the <term>rising time</term><note>Udayāsava: the time it takes for a zodiac sign to rise at a specific latitude, measured in breaths or 'asuns'</note> of the zodiac sign in which the planet is currently situated. This product is divided by 1800 <note>The number of minutes in a single zodiac sign (30 degrees × 60 minutes)</note>. The results are the "time-motions" of the Sun and planet, now equivalent to the degrees of time. Using these adjusted motions, the days past or remaining for rising and setting should be calculated as previously described. This is more accurate than using the raw motions, which would result in significant error. The logic is: if the total minutes in a sign (1800) correspond to the rising time of that sign, then the planet's daily motion in minutes corresponds to how much "time-motion"? || 11 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiply the two daily motions by the rising time of the sign (Prāṇa) and divide by 1800 to get the "time-motion." Use this to determine the days past or remaining as per verse 10. || 11 ||

Next, to determine the rising and setting of fixed stars based on their proximity to the Sun, the author begins by stating their required <term>degrees of time</term>:

->**Swati, Agastya, Mrigavyadha, Chitra, Jyeshtha, Punarvasu,**<-
->**Abhijit, and Brahmahridaya become visible at thirteen degrees.**<- || 12 ||

<margin>Mrigavyadha is Sirius (the Hunter).</margin> These stars become visible when they are separated from the Sun by thirteen degrees of time. The rest is clear. || 12 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The visibility degrees (Kālāṃśa) for Swati (Arcturus), Agastya (Canopus), Mrigavyadha (Sirius), Chitra (Spica), Jyeshtha (Antares), Punarvasu (Pollux), Abhijit (Vega), and Brahmahridaya (Capella) are 13 degrees. || 12 ||

# Chapter 9 | Including Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries ( 161 )

Now he speaks of others:

> **Hand (Hasta), Ear (Shravana), the two Phalguni, the Wealthy (Shravishtha/Dhanishtha), the Red One (Rohini), and the Mighty (Magha);**
> **Also the Branched (Vishakha) and the Twin Horsemen (Ashwini) are visible at fourteen degrees.** || 13 ||

<note>The verse lists specific Nakshatras or lunar mansions.</note> *Phalguni* refers to the pair of both Purva-Phalguni and Uttara-Phalguni. *Ashwini-daivatam* refers to the Ashwini Nakshatra, whose presiding deities are the Ashwini Kumaras. These are "visible" <note>original: "drishya"</note>, which by implication also defines when they are "invisible" <note>original: "adrishya"</note>. The grammatical gender should be understood as appropriate to the context; the rest is clear. || 13 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The time-degrees <term>Kalansha; the degrees of solar separation required for a star to become visible</term> for Hasta, Shravana, Uttara-Phalguni, Purva-Phalguni, Dhanishtha, Rohini, Magha, Vishakha, and Ashwini are 14 degrees. || 13 ||

Now he speaks of others:

> **The Pleiades (Krittika), the Friendly (Anuradha), the Root (Mula), the Serpent (Ashlesha), and the Moist (Ardra);**
> **These are seen at fifteen degrees, as are the two Invincible ones (Ashadha).** || 14 ||

Krittika, Anuradha, and Mula Nakshatras are seen at fifteen time-degrees. By implication, this also refers to their disappearance. The word "only" <note>original: "eva"</note> is used to exclude any more or less. *Sarpa* refers to Ashlesha and *Raudra* to Ardra. The word "and" <note>original: "cha"</note> serves as a conjunction. The "two Ashadhas" refers to both Purva-Ashadha and Uttara-Ashadha; these are also seen at fifteen time-degrees. || 14 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Krittika, Anuradha, Mula, Ashlesha, Ardra, Purva-Ashadha, and Uttara-Ashadha have 15 degrees. || 14 ||

Now he speaks of the remaining ones:

> **The Bearer (Bharani), the Flower (Pushya), and the Soft (Mrigashira), due to their minuteness, at twenty-one degrees;**
> **The remaining stars are visible or invisible at seventeen degrees.** || 15 ||

*Tishya* is Pushya. *Saumya* is the Mrigashira Nakshatra, which has the Moon as its deity. These Nakshatras, due to their "minuteness" <note>original: "saukhshmya"</note>—meaning they have very small disks or faint light—become visible or invisible at "three-times-seven" or twenty-one time-degrees. This means they rise or set <note>heliacally</note> at that point. The "remaining" stars, other than those previously mentioned, are Shatabhisha, Purva-Bhadrapada, Uttara-Bhadrapada, and Revati; also those named Agni, Brahma, Apa, and Vatsa <note>referring to specific coordinates or minor stars</note>. These become visible or invisible at seventeen time-degrees. The word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> in the text serves to connect the states of visibility and invisibility. || 15 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Because Bharani, Pushya, and Mrigashira are subtle/faint, they appear at 21 degrees; all other remaining Nakshatras appear at 17 degrees. || 15 ||

Now, for the purpose of calculating the visibility and other factors, he explains the conversion of the "desired" degrees into the "standard" measure:

> **The visibility degrees multiplied by eighteen hundred and divided by the respiration-units of their own rising;**
> **The result is the degrees of the ecliptic, which determine visibility or invisibility.** || 16 ||

The "visibility degrees" <note>time-degrees</note> are multiplied by 1800. Dividing that by the "rising-breaths" <term>Udayasu; the time taken for a sign to rise at a specific latitude, measured in sidereal respirations</term> of the planet's sign yields the "ecliptic degrees" <term>Kshetransha; the actual arc of the zodiac</term>. By these degrees, visibility and invisibility are determined. Rising and setting are thus calculated by another method...

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Nine]

<page-num>162</page-num>
<header>Surya Siddhanta — [Ninth Chapter]</header>

The two should be known according to the stated method. Having derived the degrees of the ecliptic <note>kshetransha</note> from the degrees of time <note>kalansha</note>, the difference in minutes between them is divided by the sum or difference of the actual motions. The result gives the elapsed or remaining time of the rising or setting, just as previously described. The logic here is: if the rising time of a zodiac sign in breaths <note>prana</note> corresponds to the minutes of one sign, then what would the breaths equal to the minutes of the degrees of time correspond to on the ecliptic? These are the degrees of time divided by sixty. For simplicity, the degrees of time themselves were held in the place of the desired quantity. Thus, what was stated is proven. || 16 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** By multiplying the degrees of time by 1800 and dividing by the rising breaths of the sign <note>lagnaprana</note>, the ecliptic degrees are obtained. From that, one should determine the rising and setting. || 16 ||

Now, it has been stated in which direction the planets set and in which they rise. However, this has not been stated for the stars <note>nakshatras</note>. Because they lack motion, it is impossible to calculate the elapsed or remaining days through the combination of two motions. Therefore, the author says:

->**Their rising is in the east and setting in the west; the visibility correction is as before. ||**<-
->**The determination of elapsed or remaining days is always through the motion of the Sun. || 17 ||**<-

The rising of these stars is in the east and their setting is in the west, because like a very slow-moving planet, they lack independent motion. The visibility corrections <note><term>Drik-karma</term>: mathematical adjustments to find the true visibility of a celestial body on the horizon</note> for these stars should be performed as previously described. However, it should be noted that this refers to what was stated in the first half of the verse. "Always" means constantly; the word "indeed" <note>original: "eva"</note> implies it is never otherwise. Certainly, the acquisition of the elapsed or remaining days is through the Sun's motion alone, because the stars lack motion. In the case of a conjunction, it would be like the motion of a planet. || 17 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The rising of the stars occurs in the eastern direction and the setting in the west. After performing the visibility corrections as before, one should always determine the days using the Sun's motion (as per verse 10). || 17 ||

Now, he explains that certain stars do not set due to their proximity to the Sun:

->**Abhijit, Brahmahridaya, Svati, Shravana, Dhanishtha, ||**<-
->**And Uttara Bhadrapada, due to their northern position, are not obscured by the Sun's rays. || 18 ||**<-

Abhijit, Brahmahridaya (this also includes the region of Brahma), Svati, Shravana, and Dhanishtha. Also "Ahirbudhnya," which is Uttara Bhadrapada. These stars, because of their northern position—meaning their large northern latitude <note>vikshepa</note>—are not obscured by the Sun's rays. This means they do not undergo heliacal setting. The logic here is as stated by <term>Bhaskaracharya</term> <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note>: "When the Sun of setting for a star is greater than the Sun of its rising, due to the great length of its northern latitude, that star never sets despite its proximity to the Sun." This is stated in the *Ashtakshama*. Otherwise, Purva Bhadrapada would also be subject to this, which is the point. || 18 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Abhijit, Brahmahridaya, Svati, Shravana, Dhanishtha, and Uttara Bhadrapada, because of their position far to the north, are never obscured by the Sun's rays. || 18 ||

<summary>This page details the mathematical methods for calculating the heliacal rising and setting of stars, noting that unlike planets, stars are fixed and their visibility depends solely on the Sun's motion. It also identifies specific northern stars that never set due to their high celestial latitude.</summary>

Now, to prevent any inconsistency in the upcoming text, the conclusion of the section is stated with a brief explanation: The "Chapter on Risings and Settings" <note>original: "Udayāstādhikāra"</note> was so named because it described the rising and setting of both stars and planets in a general manner. Thus, in the commentary on the *Surya Siddhanta* composed by Ranganatha: "This Chapter on Risings and Settings is completed in the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* (Illuminator of Hidden Meanings)." Thus ends the Chapter on Risings and Settings in the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* composed by the mathematician Ranganatha, son of the venerable Ballala, the emperor of all calculators. || 19 ||

->Thus ends the Chapter on Risings and Settings.<-
->The Ninth Chapter is finished.<-

# **Chapter Ten**

Now, a doubt arose in the previous chapter: when Mars and other planets are near the Sun at their rising or setting, their entire disks are visible due to their brilliance. Similarly, the Moon's entire disk is not visible as white (illuminated) at the time of its own rising and setting; rather, only a portion of the disk is seen as white. Why is the Moon dissimilar to Mars and the others? Since this question was established in the previous section, the "Chapter on the Elevation of the Moon's Horns" <note>original: "Śṛṅgonnatyadhikāra"; referring to the cusps of the crescent moon</note>, which serves as the answer, is necessarily commenced and explained. Because the elevation of the horns is seen a few days before the time of rising or after the time of setting, and because the previous chapter mentioned the Moon's "time-degrees" <term>Kālāṃśa: the arc of separation from the sun required for a celestial body to become visible</term> but did not explicitly state its rising and setting, the author first directs the calculation for the Moon's rising and setting:

->The rule for rising and setting should be performed for the Moon <note>original: "śītagora", literally 'the cold-rayed one'</note> just as before.<-
->At twelve degrees, it becomes visible in the west and invisible in the east. || 1 ||<-

<margin>Bracket and arrow mark</margin> Regarding the Moon, the word "also" <note>implied in the Sanskrit 'api'</note> is used to group it with the planets and stars mentioned in the previous chapter. The method for calculating the rising and setting should be performed by the mathematician in the same manner as described in the preceding section. If one asks how this is achieved since the time-degrees were mentioned previously, the text says: "By degrees." With twelve degrees [of separation from the Sun], the Moon becomes visible (risen) in the west. In the east, it attains invisibility (setting). Here, although "west" and "east" are repeated, it should be understood that this is to prevent the confusion of a dull-witted person who might think—because the Moon's rising and setting were mentioned earlier alongside Mercury and Venus—that the Moon sets in the west and rises in the east in the same manner as they do. || 1 ||

**Hindi Commentary**—The calculation for the Moon's rising and setting should also be done according to the previously stated method. By being 12 degrees away, it shows itself in the west, and by being within 12 degrees in the east, it becomes invisible. || 1 ||

Now, following the topic of rising and setting, and wishing to explain the calculation of the Moon's daily setting and rising, the author first describes the Moon's daily setting in three verses:

->The time-breaths <term>Asu: a unit of time equal to four seconds</term> of the interval between the ascendant and the Sun and Moon, increased by six signs, are found as before.<-
->When the Sun and Moon are in the same sign, the calculation of their power should be made. || 2 ||<-
->The daily motions of the Sun and Moon are multiplied by those minutes and divided by sixty...<-

<summary>This page marks the conclusion of the 9th chapter on planetary visibility and the beginning of the 10th chapter concerning the Moon's phases (elevation of the horns). It establishes that the Moon requires 12 degrees of separation from the Sun to be visible.</summary>

# The Surya Siddhanta

> With the results of those [calculations] applied, the time-interval in breaths (*asūs*) must be calculated again. || 3 ||
> This process is repeated until the interval in breaths between the Sun and the Moon becomes stable.
> By those breaths, the Moon reaches its setting in the bright fortnight after the setting of the Sun. || 4 ||

In the bright fortnight (*shukla-paksha*), on the desired day, the true positions of the Sun and Moon are to be calculated at the time of sunset. The two visibility corrections <term>Drik-karma<note>Calculations to adjust a planet's longitude to its actual visible position on the horizon, accounting for the ecliptic's tilt and the observer's latitude.</note></term> must be applied to the Moon. Among these, the "latitude-visibility correction" (*aksha-drik-karma*) is as stated in the first half of the verse. The time-interval in breaths (*asūs*) between the Sun and the Moon, each increased by six signs <note>Adding six signs (180 degrees) shifts the calculation from the eastern horizon (rising) to the western horizon (setting).</note>, should be calculated as previously described using the method of "breaths of the remaining portion of the sign."

If the Sun and Moon, both increased by six signs, are in the same zodiac sign, then the difference in minutes of arc between them should be taken. The word "and" (*ca*) is used here to define the specific application. The breaths derived from the minutes of that difference are divided by 360. The resulting ghatikas <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note> are multiplied by the rising breaths of the sign and divided by the total minutes in a sign (1800) to find the breaths; these are then divided by 360 to get the time in ghatikas. 

With these, the daily motion of the Sun and Moon (the multiplicands) is divided by 60, and the resulting values are added to the Sun and Moon (each increased by six signs). Again, the interval in breaths (*vivara-asūs*) must be calculated as before. In this way, using those time units, the Sun and the Moon (corrected for visibility and increased by six signs) are adjusted until the interval between them becomes stable (unchanging). By those stabilized breaths, the Moon reaches its setting after the Sun has set.

**The Logic (Upapatti):**
At the time of sunset, the Sun plus six signs is the descendant point (the western horizon). The Moon, corrected for visibility and increased by six signs, represents the descendant at the time of the Moon's setting. However, the position at sunset is not the same as the position at the actual time of setting. The principle is that the western visible planet is calculated at sunset. The interval breaths are the "civil" (*savana*) time remaining in the day for the Moon. 

However, because technical definitions often rely on sidereal (*nakshatra*) time, the Moon must be moved by that interval. To show a consistent method and to remove the doubts of the slow-witted as to how an accurate time can be established from the Sun and Moon at different times, the Sun (plus six signs) is also calculated at the time of the Moon's setting. The interval breaths between them, though sidereal, are more accurate than those calculated from the sunset position. 

**Translator's Critique:**
In reality, if one accepts the civil (*savana*) measurement, there is only one verse in the *Surya Siddhanta*: *"The interval in breaths of the Sun and Moon increased by six signs is found as before; by those breaths the Moon sets after the Sun."* The two verses starting with "in one sign" and ending with "interval breaths of the Sun and Moon" were likely inserted by someone of dull intellect who thought the time must be calculated repeatedly. This was perhaps taken from the *Shishyadhivriddhida* <note>A famous astronomical treatise by Lalla (c. 8th century).</note> and included here by someone who considered it logical, even though it is unnecessary. How else could the instruction for repeated calculation be consistent with the words of the All-Knowing Lord after the pure civil time is already known? Furthermore, the instruction to "calculate the difference in minutes" is already implied by the rules in the chapter on the Three Problems (*Triprashna*) and is redundant here. If sidereal time is accepted, moving the Moon by the civil time is necessary to find its setting, but moving the Sun serves no purpose...

...due to the state [of the calculation]. Indeed, the ascendant <note>Lagna</note> at the time of sunset is not perfectly established by adding six signs to the sun at the time of moonset, which would make the adjustment of the sun's position appropriate. Furthermore, if the precise sidereal time <term>Nakshatra-kala: time measured by the stars</term> can be established by adjusting the moon just once, why would the All-Knowing One <note>referring to the author of the Surya Siddhanta</note> describe a repetitive process for finding sidereal time? That would be illogical and unnecessarily burdensome. There is no logical basis for achieving precise sidereal time through repetitive calculation here. Therefore, the statement of the teacher Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, the 12th-century mathematician</note> is correct: "When one desires to know the rising sign of a planet at a specific time, the difference in time-units <term>Nadikas</term> between the two are the civil <term>Savana</term> time-units elapsed for that planet." This is the essential truth. || 2 || 3 || 4 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In the bright fortnight <term>Shukla-paksha</term>, at the time of twilight, one should determine the fixed breaths <term>Prana: a unit of time</term> of the difference between the ascendants of the sun (with six signs added) and the moon (corrected by visibility calculations <term>Drik-karma</term>). After sunset, the moon will set after the lapse of that specific number of breaths. || 2 || By adding six signs to the true sun, determine the measure of the interval from the moon. That is the time of the moonrise in the dark fortnight <term>Krishna-paksha</term> after sunset. || 3 || When the declinations <term>Kranti-jya</term> of the sun and moon are in the same direction, subtract them; if in different directions, add them. The result will be designated South or North according to the position of the moon relative to the sun. || 4 ||

### Now he describes the method for calculating the rising:

> Adding half a revolution to the sun, the breaths of their difference should be calculated.
> By those breaths, in the dark fortnight, the moon <note>literally: "the cold-rayed one"</note> shall reach its rising. || 5 ||

In the dark fortnight, "adding half a revolution" means adding six signs to the sun. By the word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note>, it implies *not* adding them to the moon. "The breaths of their difference" refers to the breaths of the interval between the moon (corrected by visibility calculations) and the sun (with six signs added). These should be calculated as previously described. By those calculated breaths, the moon shall rise after sunset.

The reasoning <term>Upapatti</term> is as follows: Since the sun with six signs added represents the ascendant at the time of sunset, six signs are added to the sun to calculate the rising. Because the planet's position is required, the moon is taken as it is, corrected by visibility calculations, without adding six signs. The interval breaths between the moon and the sun (with six signs added at sunset) are sidereal. To calculate the elevation of the moon's horns <term>Shringonnati</term>, the sun and moon must be calculated at the time they are visible. To indicate this, the daily rising and setting of the moon are described. The rising and setting of other <unclear>...</unclear> planets and stars are not mentioned because they serve no purpose here, or they are implied by the moon's description. Note that in that case, the distinction between bright and dark fortnights does not apply. || 5 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiply the shadow-hypotenuse of the moon at that time (located on its own fish-line) by the previously mentioned result. If the product is South, add it to the equinoctial shadow <term>Aksha-jya</term> multiplied by twelve; if North, subtract it. || 5 ||

### Now, wishing to speak of the subject at hand, he describes the field consisting of the base, perpendicular, and hypotenuse in three verses:

> The difference of the declinations of the sun and moon [is taken] if they are in the same direction; otherwise, their sum.
> That sine, and the moon's [position] from the sun's amplitude, should be known as South or North. || 6 ||
> If the moon's shadow-hypotenuse at midday is multiplied...

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter 10]

## Then, from the product of the Sun's [shadow] and the sine of latitude, the southern [value] should be subtracted or added. || 7 ||
## The remainder, divided by the sine of co-latitude, results in the Base (side), oriented in its own direction. ||
## The Gnomon is the Perpendicular; the square root of the sum of their squares shall be the Hypotenuse. || 8 ||

If the clear declinations <note>original: "spashta-krānti"</note> of the Sun and Moon are in the same direction, take their difference; if in different directions, take their sum. Here, the word "declination" should be understood as the *sine* of declination <note>original: "krānti-jyā"</note>, as this avoids contradiction in the proof. This sine, refined by the necessary calculations, represents the north-south distance. One must determine the direction of this sine based on the Moon's position relative to the Sun. If the Moon's declination is greater than the Sun's in the same direction, the direction of the sine follows the declination. If less, it is the opposite. If they are in different directions, the direction is that of the Moon's declination.

That sine is multiplied by the hypotenuse of the Moon's shadow at midday. For the purpose of calculating the elevation of the Moon's horns <note>the visible points of the crescent</note>, one must calculate the shadow-hypotenuse of the Moon at that specific time, just as one would for the midday shadow. By subtracting the Moon's clear declination from the latitude if they are North, or adding them if South, and dividing the product of twelve and the radius by the sine of the resulting co-latitude, the value is found.

According to the logic of the proof, the term "midday" refers to the specific time in question. At the time the Moon is observed, one should calculate the elapsed or remaining part of the day, determine the Gnomon <note>term: Śaṅku; a vertical pillar used to measure shadows</note> using the rules from the "Three Questions" chapter, and thus find the shadow-hypotenuse. This is the intent of the Lord <note>the divine author of the text</note>. Otherwise, how would the previous statement regarding the "two-fold visibility correction for the elevation of the Moon's horns" make sense? The use of the visibility correction is specifically for calculating the shadow beyond midday; it has no other use in the mathematics of the Moon's elevation. The shadow-hypotenuse is established by the clear declination itself.

Here too, the latitude-correction mentioned in the first half of the verse must be applied. This means multiplying by the shadow-hypotenuse. If that sine is Northern, it is subtracted from the product of twelve and the sine of latitude. If the product of twelve and the sine of latitude is smaller, the subtraction still works in reverse without error. If it is Southern, it should be added. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> serves as a separator of these conditions. The result of this calculation, divided by the local sine of co-latitude <note>term: lambajyā; the sine of the angle complementary to the latitude</note>, gives the **Base** (side) <note>term: bhujā</note>. "Oriented in its own direction" means the direction resulting from the calculation.

Since the Base requires a Perpendicular and a Hypotenuse, the text says: "The Gnomon is the Perpendicular." A gnomon of twelve digits is the **Perpendicular** <note>term: koṭi</note>. The square root of the sum of the squares of the Base and Perpendicular is the **Hypotenuse** <note>term: karṇa</note>. Here is the proof:

> "When the Gnomon-ends of the Sun and Moon are in the same or different directions, the sum or difference becomes the base. The difference of like parts or sum of different parts is the clear Base of the Moon. If the Moon's base is subtracted from the Sun's, the direction is reversed."

This method for finding the precise Base was stated by the teacher Bhāskara in the *Siddhānta Śiromaṇi*. The proof is clear in his commentary. By this method, to find the Base, the sines of the amplitudes <note>agra</note> must first be found. The proportion is: if the sine of co-latitude is the Perpendicular to the Radius-hypotenuse, then what is the hypotenuse for the sine of declination? The specific form for the Sun and Moon is the sine of declination multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of co-latitude: <insert>$\left\{ \frac{\text{Sun's Sine Declination} \times \text{Radius}}{\text{Sine Co-latitude}} \right\}$</insert>

<vocab>Surya Siddhanta, Krāntijyā (Sine Declination), Lambajyā (Sine Co-latitude), Bhujā (Base/Side), Koṭi (Perpendicular), Karṇa (Hypotenuse), Bhāskarācārya, Siddhānta Śiromaṇi, Śṛṅgonnati (Elevation of the Horns), Akṣajyā (Sine Latitude)</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical derivation of the Moon's elevation (shringonnati), specifically focusing on the calculation of the "base" or "arm" (bhuja) used to determine the orientation of the Moon's horns.</meta>

<page-num>167</page-num>
# Chapter 10: Including Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries

The sine of the Moon's true declination <note>original: "chandra-spashta-kranti-jya"</note> multiplied by the radius <note>original: "trijya"</note> and divided by the cosine of latitude <note>original: "lamba-jya"</note> {Moon's Decl. Sine × Radius / Cosine Lat.}. To these results, one's own **gnomon-base** <term>shanku-tala: the distance from the center of the horizon to the point where the gnomon's shadow falls</term> must be applied as a correction. In this context, for the sake of the **elevation of the Moon's horns** <term>shringonnati: the visual orientation of the illuminated crescent</term>, the Lord Sun has accepted only the calculation for the time of sunrise or sunset. At those times, because the Sun's gnomon is absent <note>since the Sun is on the horizon</note> and its gnomon-base is therefore absent, the Sun's amplitude <note>original: "surya-agra"</note> itself is established as the **Sun's base** <note>original: "surya-bhuja"</note>.

However, for the Moon, because a gnomon exists at that time <note>as it is above the horizon</note>, a gnomon-base is produced. This is calculated by the proportion: if the sine of latitude <note>original: "aksha-jya"</note> is the base for a hypotenuse of the cosine of latitude <note>original: "lamba-jya"</note>, then what will the base be for a hypotenuse of the Moon's gnomon? Thus, the **Moon's great gnomon** <note>calculated via the three-question chapter methods for the specific time of the Moon's altitude</note> multiplied by the sine of latitude and divided by the cosine of latitude results in the southern gnomon-base:
{ Sine Lat. × Moon's Gnomon / Cosine Lat. }
This should be added to the Moon's southern amplitude. This constitutes the **Moon's southern base**.

In the case of the Moon's northern amplitude, this value is subtracted to find the northern base. If the value is subtracted from the Moon's northern amplitude and the result is negative, it becomes the Moon's southern base. For example, the southern base is:
{ (Moon's Decl. Sine × Radius / Cosine Lat.) + (Sine Lat. × Moon's Gnomon / Cosine Lat.) }
Or:
{ (Moon's Decl. Sine × Radius) + (Sine Lat. × Moon's Gnomon) } / Cosine Lat.
{ Northern Base: } { (Moon's Decl. Sine × Radius) - (Sine Lat. × Moon's Gnomon) } / Cosine Lat.

Now, the **corrected base** <note>original: "spashta-bhuja"</note> used for the elevation of the horns is the difference between the Moon's base and the Sun's amplitude if they are in the same direction, and their sum if they are in different directions.
For instance, when the Sun is in the **Southern Hemisphere** <note>original: "dakshina-gola"</note>:
{ (Sun's Decl. Sine × Radius / Cosine Lat.) - [(Moon's Decl. Sine × Radius + Sine Lat. × Moon's Gnomon) / Cosine Lat.] }

{ (Sun's Decl. Sine × Radius / Cosine Lat.) + [(Moon's Decl. Sine × Radius + Sine Lat. × Moon's Gnomon) / Cosine Lat.] }
These two bases become the corrected base. It is southern if the Moon's base is subtracted from a smaller Sun's base. However, if the Sun's base is larger:
{ (Sun's Decl. Sine × Radius / Cosine Lat.) - [(Moon's Decl. Sine × Radius + Sine Lat. × Moon's Gnomon) / Cosine Lat.] }
{ These two bases are northern. As stated: "from the Sun's base, in the opposite direction of the Moon's purified base." }
In the case of addition, the base is northern:
{ (Sun's Decl. Sine × Radius + Moon's Decl. Sine × Radius + Sine Lat. × Moon's Gnomon) / Cosine Lat. }
(Even when the Sun is in the **Northern Hemisphere** <note>original: "uttara-gola"</note>):
{ (Sun's Decl. Sine × Radius / Cosine Lat.) + [(Moon's Decl. Sine × Radius + Sine Lat. × Moon's Gnomon) / Cosine Lat.] }

{ (Sun's Decl. Sine × Radius / Cosine Lat.) - [(Moon's Decl. Sine × Radius + Sine Lat. × Moon's Gnomon) / Cosine Lat.] }
These two bases are southern. In the case of a difference where the Sun's base is smaller, the base is northern:
{ (Sun's Decl. Sine × Radius / Cosine Lat.) - [(Moon's Decl. Sine × Radius + Sine Lat. × Moon's Gnomon) / Cosine Lat.] }

# The Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Ten]

->**The Surya Siddhanta**<-

If the sine of the Sun’s declination is greater, then:
{ (Sun's Sine Declination × Radius / 1) ± (Moon's Sine Declination × Radius / 1) × Sine Latitude × Moon's Gnomon / 1 } / Cosine Latitude

This is the southern **bhuja** <note>The 'bhuja' here refers to the side of a right-angled triangle, specifically the north-south distance between the Sun and Moon in this astronomical context</note>. Because it was stated that the **bhuja** is derived from the Moon's subtraction. Here, among the nine cases, in the first case: the difference between the sines of the Sun's and Moon's declinations (when in the same direction) is multiplied by the Radius. If this relates to the Sun's declination, then the product of the Sine Latitude and the Moon's Gnomon is subtracted from it and divided by the Cosine Latitude. If it relates to the Moon's declination, then that product is added and divided by the Cosine Latitude. This is established.

There, because the degrees of latitude are southern, for the sake of addition in the same direction, the remainder of the Moon is considered southern, and the remainder of the Sun is considered northern for the sake of subtraction in different directions. This is appropriate. When the Sun's declination is greater, the Moon is north of the Sun. In the elevation of the horns (**shringonnati**), the Moon's position is primary.

In the second case, by adding the sines of declination in different directions, one should subtract that product and divide by the Cosine Latitude. Here too, for the sake of the difference of the tips, the northern direction is taken because the Moon's declination is northern; thus the Moon is even further north of the Sun situated in the south.

In the third case, when the sines of declination are in the same direction, the difference relates to the Sun; that product is subtracted, and the difference is northern. Even if both are in the southern hemisphere, the Moon (being less) is north of the greater Sun.

In the fourth case, when adding sines of declination in different directions, that product is subtracted; the sum is northern because the Moon is situated in the northern direction. The fifth case is identical to the fourth. In the sixth case, the sum of the sines of declination in different directions is southern; it is added to the product because the Moon is in the southern hemisphere.

In the seventh case, the difference of sines of declination in the same direction relates to the Sun; it is added to the product, and the difference is southern. Even if both are in the northern hemisphere, the Moon (being less) is south of the Sun. If it were greater, it would be northern and subtracted from the product. In the eighth case, the difference of sines of declination in the same direction relates to the Moon; it is northern and the product is subtracted, because the Moon (being greater) is situated to the north. In the final case, the difference of sines of declination in the same direction relates to the Sun; it is added to the product and is southern, because the Moon (being less) is situated to the south. Thus, what was stated in the first verse is proven.

Here, some have taken the word "declination" (**kranti**) to mean the arc-declination and performed the calculation, then said the sine should be taken. This contradicts the logic. Arc-declinations are not suitable as causes for proving the **bhuja**. Therefore, that explanation is incorrect. Nor are the sum and difference of the sines of declination equal to the sine of the sum and difference of the arc-declinations, which would make such a statement consistent. Otherwise, one would fall into the error of trying to calculate the sine of zenith distance (**natamsha-jya**) by adjusting sines of declination and latitude without using the actual degrees.

Now, this **bhuja** is in the circle of the Radius. For simplicity, if this **bhuja** is calculated in the circle of the Radius, then what is it in the circle of the Moon's shadow-hypotenuse? By proportion, the first part (the adjustment of the sines of declination) is multiplied by the Moon's shadow-hypotenuse. Since the previous multiplier (Radius) and the current divisor (Radius) are equal, they cancel each other out.

Then the second part, consisting of the product of the Moon's Gnomon and the Sine Latitude, must be multiplied by the Moon's shadow-hypotenuse and divided by the Radius. Here, since the shadow-hypotenuse is equal to (Radius × 12) divided by the Moon's Gnomon, the Gnomon and Radius in the multiplier and divisor cancel out respectively. Thus, the second part is established as (Sine Latitude × 12). If both parts are in the same direction, they are added; if different, they are subtracted.

The result obtained from the previous calculation, when divided by the <term>sine of colatitude</term><note>Sanskrit: *lambajya*; the sine of the angle between the zenith and the celestial equator</note>, becomes the <term>base</term><note>Sanskrit: *bhuja*; the horizontal side of a right-angled triangle</note> oriented in its own direction. Taking the Moon's <term>gnomon</term><note>Sanskrit: *shanku*; the vertical pillar or altitude of the celestial body</note> as the <term>perpendicular</term><note>Sanskrit: *koti*</note>, the base is derived from the hypotenuse circle of the Moon's shadow. In that same circle, the perpendicular must also be calculated. However, that is fixed at twelve <insert>units</insert>. The base is calculated in the hypotenuse circle of the Moon's shadow using this fixed perpendicular. At sunrise and sunset, because the Sun's gnomon is absent, there is no correction for the Sun's gnomon. At other times, the process cannot be completed without this method. The square root of the sum of the squares of the perpendicular and the base is the <term>hypotenuse</term><note>Sanskrit: *karna*</note>; this is the logic explained in the previous two verses. — 6, 7, 8.

**Hindi Commentary:** This remaining result, when divided by the sine of colatitude, will be the base indicating its own direction. By knowing the Moon's gnomon as the perpendicular, and taking the square root of the sum of their squares, the hypotenuse is found. — 6, 7, 8.

### Now, the calculation of the illuminated part (Phase) is described:

->**The minutes of the Moon's longitude minus the Sun's, divided by nine hundred, gives the illuminated part.**<-
->**Multiplied by the Moon’s diameter in digits and divided by twelve, it becomes accurate. — 9**<-

The minutes of the Moon's position minus the Sun's position, divided by 900, results in the illuminated portion. When this is multiplied by the Moon's diameter in digits (calculated as described in the section on Lunar Eclipses) and divided by twelve, the result is the accurate illuminated portion (<term>shukla</term>). 

**The Logic:** At the end of the New Moon (<term>amavasya</term>), there is no distance between the Sun and the Moon; therefore, the Sun's rays do not reflect on the half of the lunar sphere visible to us, resulting in no brightness. As the Moon moves eastward away from the Sun, the brightness gradually increases on the western part of the lunar sphere visible to us. Thus, at a distance of six signs (180 degrees) at the end of the Full Moon (<term>purnima</term>), the entire visible half of the lunar sphere becomes white. 

Here, the proportion is: if the minutes in six signs (10,800 minutes) result in a white portion for a disk with a diameter of twelve digits, then what will the desired minutes of the Moon minus the Sun produce? By simplifying the ratio, we get 900 in the place of the divisor. Therefore, the minutes of the Moon minus the Sun divided by 900 gives the brightness based on a standard twelve-digit diameter. To adjust this for the specific diameter of the Moon's disk at that time, the second proportion is used. By this method, it is proven that at a distance of three signs (90 degrees), half of the visible lunar sphere is white. 

The great teacher **Bhaskaracharya** stated in his explanation of the "Elevation of the Horns" (<term>shringonnati</term>): <note>original: "कक्षाचतुर्थस्तरणेर्हि..."</note> "Because the Moon is at a distance of one-fourth of its orbit from the Sun, the Sun's rays fall obliquely; therefore, at a distance of roughly 90 degrees, half the Moon is visible to man and half of that is illuminated." In the chapter on the Elevation of the Horns, he further calculates the specific position of the Moon for this illumination calculation. This is sufficient for now. — 9.

**Hindi Commentary:** Subtracting the Sun's position from the Moon's and converting it to minutes, then dividing by 900, gives the illuminated fraction. Multiplying by the Moon's diameter in digits and dividing by 12 gives the accurate illuminated part. — 9.

### Now, the diagram of the Elevation of the Horns is described in four verses:

->**Having marked the point designated as the Sun, draw the base in its own direction.**<-
->**Then draw the perpendicular facing West, and the hypotenuse between the tip of the perpendicular and the center. — 10**<-

## Surya Siddhanta

-> From the point where the base and hypotenuse meet, one should draw the disk as it appears at that moment. <-
-> First, one should establish the directions using the line of the hypotenuse. || 11 || <-
-> Along the hypotenuse, from the point where it meets the disk, one should measure the illuminated part inward. <-
-> Between the end of the illuminated part and the north and south points, one should construct two "fish" figures. || 12 || <-
-> From the intersection of the central lines of those figures, one should draw an arc touching the three points. <-
-> Just as the disk is drawn there, so the Moon appears on that day. || 13 || <-

Having determined the directions at a desired spot on level ground, one should draw an east-west line and a north-south line. At the intersection of these directions, one should mark a point designated as the "Sun" <note>original: *arkasañjñitam*</note>. Then, from that point, one should lay out the "arm" <term>bhuja: the side of a right-angled triangle representing the latitude/deviation</term> previously calculated, facing its own direction—either north or south—and mark the point after counting the digits <note>units of measure</note> of the arm. From the tip of the arm, one should lay out the "base" <term>koti: the perpendicular side of the triangle</term> consisting of twelve digits, facing westward along the east-west line. Then, the "hypotenuse" <term>karna: the diagonal connecting the Sun-point to the tip of the base</term> previously calculated should be placed so it touches the center and the tip of the base. This means one should lay out the digits of the hypotenuse in that interval.

Taking the intersection of the base and hypotenuse lines as the center, one should draw the disk of the Moon as calculated for the specific time of sunrise or sunset. On that drawn lunar disk, one should first establish the "determination of directions" <note>original: *diksiddhi*</note> using the line of the hypotenuse. Where the lunar disk meets the hypotenuse line, that is the East on the lunar circle. By extending the hypotenuse line forward along its path to where it meets the opposite side of the lunar circumference, that is the West. The north and south points are found where a line drawn from two "fish" figures <note>a geometric method using intersecting arcs to find a perpendicular</note> meets the lunar circle.

The "white portion" <note>the illuminated part of the moon</note> previously calculated should be measured along the path of the hypotenuse from the intersection of the disk and the hypotenuse (the East point). It should be brought "inward," meaning toward the center of the lunar circle, to mark the "tip of the white" <note>original: *shuklagra*</note>. This means one should count the digits of the illuminated part from the western mark on the hypotenuse toward the interior of the lunar circle.

Between the tip of the white and the north-south points—meaning the point where the illuminated tip sits inside the circle and the two points on the circumference marking north and south—one should construct two "fish" figures in the intervening space. One fish is made from the illuminated tip and the south point, and another from the illuminated tip and the north point, following the method previously described.

From the intersection of their central lines: the central line of those "fish" (the line touching the mouth and tail) should be extended. Where they meet—either inside or outside the lunar circle—depends on whether the illuminated tip is toward the west or east. From that point of intersection, one should draw an arc that "touches three points" <note>original: *vindutrisprig*</note>. These three points are the tip of the illuminated part and the north and south marks. Using the distance from the intersection to the illuminated tip as the radius, one should draw a portion of a circle (an arc) inside the lunar disk.

The lunar disk as drawn previously: "just as" it appears when cut by the drawn arc on its western side, "so" it truly is. The word "exactly" <note>original: *eva*</note> emphasizes this...

This section serves to clarify the calculation. On this day, at the time of twilight—which is the basis for calculating the elevation of the horns—the Moon is positioned in the sky. Here is the <term>rational proof<note>Sanskrit: upapatti; a logical or mathematical demonstration of a rule.</note></term>. The <term>base<note>Sanskrit: bhuja; the horizontal side of a right-angled triangle.</note></term> represents the distance between the Sun and the Moon. Having established the Sun's position, one should draw the base line according to the direction. From that, because the Moon is in the western direction during the <term>bright fortnight<note>Sanskrit: shukla-paksha; the waxing phase of the moon.</note></term>, the elevation of the horns occurs. The vertical distance between the Sun and Moon is given as the <term>perpendicular<note>Sanskrit: koti; the vertical side of a right-angled triangle.</note></term>. The distance between the Sun and Moon is the <term>hypotenuse<note>Sanskrit: karna; the diagonal connecting the base and perpendicular.</note></term>, drawn from the tip of the perpendicular to the Sun's disk. The hypotenuse is drawn to ensure the straightness of the perpendicular. Because the Moon is located at the junction of the perpendicular and the hypotenuse, the lunar circle is drawn with that point as its center. Since the illuminated part is seen along the path of the hypotenuse, the East-West and North-South lines are fixed on the lunar disk according to that hypotenuse-line. In the bright fortnight, the western part of the Moon is white because it faces the Sun; therefore, the measure of the illuminated portion is marked along the hypotenuse from the western edge toward the center. There, in the lunar circle, an arc forming part of a circle bounded by the North and South points and touching the tip of the white portion must be drawn to show the Moon's shape. To find the center of the circle touching these three points, one should create two <term>"fish" figures<note>Sanskrit: matsya; a geometric construction method using intersecting arcs to find a perpendicular bisector.</note></term> from the three points as previously described. The intersection of those lines is the center, and the arc is drawn from there; thus, the appearance of the Moon becomes visible to the eye.
॥ 10 ॥ 11 ॥ 12 ॥ 13 ॥

**Hindi Commentary:** Mark the point named "Sun" and draw a line for the <term>base</term> according to its direction. At the end of that line, draw a line for the <term>perpendicular</term> facing West. The line from the tip of the perpendicular to the center point will be the <term>hypotenuse</term>. Draw a circle according to the size of the lunar disk around the point where the perpendicular and hypotenuse meet. Whichever direction the hypotenuse-line points should be understood as East. From the spot where the lunar circle and hypotenuse meet, place a point at the distance of the illuminated portion toward the center. By creating two "fish" figures between that point and the North point, and that point and the South point, use the intersection of the lines from their "mouths and tails" as a center to draw an arc touching the three points. The Moon will appear on that day exactly as the lunar disk was constructed. ॥ 10 ॥ 11 ॥ 12 ॥ 13 ॥

Now, someone might object that the knowledge of the "elevation of the horns"—the very purpose of this effort—has not been explicitly stated. To this, he says:

->**By establishing the directions via the perpendicular, the horn is shown elevated at the end of the transverse line.**<-
->**By making the perpendicular elevated, that becomes the actual shape of the Moon. ॥ 14 ॥**<-

By the "perpendicular line," one establishes the directions like the hypotenuse-line on the lunar circle; in the diagram, by making the "perpendicular" (the tip of the white arc) elevated or high, one observes it. At the "end of the transverse line," meaning at the extremity of the North-South line, one should show the elevated or high horn. This is established through the diagram. The "shape" or "form" refers to the Moon as it exists in the sky; the meaning is that the form established in the diagram matches the direct observation of the Moon in the heavens. The proof is as follows: just as the directions of the Moon are determined by the hypotenuse-line on the lunar circle, the directions of the Sun are determined by the perpendicular line. The distance between them is the base transformed into the lunar circle. Now, because the two tips of the arc are attached to the North and South points of the Moon, the horns (in the form of the perpendicular) become tilted or elevated relative to the Sun's North and South...

# Surya Siddhanta: [Chapter Ten]

The horn is lowered. The other horn is raised. Therefore, the teacher Bhaskaracharya <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> said: "The raised horn shall be in the direction opposite to the deflection." || 14 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Having determined the direction from the "koti" <note>the vertical side of a right-angled triangle</note>, one should show the raised horn of the Moon in the remaining part of the north-south transverse line. That indeed is the shape of the Moon in the sky. || 14 ||

Now, an objection arises: if the Sun is six signs away from the Moon, the calculated white portion (the illuminated part) might exceed the Moon's disk. How is this possible, as it seems contradictory? To answer this, he states the following specific rule:

**In the dark fortnight, subtract the Moon from the Sun increased by six signs to find the dark portion. ||**
**One should apply the "arm" (the base of the triangle) in the opposite direction; there, the dark part of the Moon's disk is on the west. || 15 ||**

In the dark fortnight <term>Krishna Paksha: the waning half of the lunar month</term>, one should subtract the Moon's position from the Sun's position increased by six signs <note>original: "shadrashibhih sahitamarkam"</note>. Then, the dark portion <note>the "asita" or black part</note> should be calculated by dividing the minutes by nine hundred, as per the previous method. The previously mentioned calculation for the white portion <note>the "shukla" or bright part</note> was specifically for the light fortnight <term>Shukla Paksha: the waxing half of the lunar month</term> to show the increase in brightness. In the dark fortnight, because brightness decreases and darkness increases, calculating the dark portion is appropriate, not the white portion. This is why a month is composed of two fortnights, light and dark.

Now, regarding the specific method for drawing the dark phase: he says "one should apply." In the context of drawing the dark phase, the "arm" <note>the "bhuja" or horizontal side of the triangle</note> should be applied in the opposite direction. The calculator should place the northern arm to the south of the Sun's mark, and the southern arm to the north. One should show the dark portion on the western side of the Moon's disk. Just as in the light fortnight the brightness is on the western side of the Moon's disk, in the dark fortnight, one should show the increase of darkness on the western side of the Moon's disk.

The reasoning <note>upapatti</note> is as follows: At the start of the dark fortnight, there is a difference of six signs between the Sun and the Moon. From then on, until the difference is six signs again, the darkness increases. Therefore, it is proper to calculate the dark portion using the Sun increased by six signs. Furthermore, where the white horn was lowered, the dark horn is raised; where it was raised, it is now lowered. Thus, for drawing the dark phase, the "arms" are given in reverse. That darkness also increases from the western side. Therefore, it should be marked from the side of the Moon's disk on the hypotenuse line. Then, the elevation of the dark horn is determined as before. || 15 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In the dark fortnight, after adding 6 signs to the Sun and subtracting the Moon's true position, determine the dark portion <note>asita</note> just as the white portion was determined. By reversing the direction of Rahu <note>the lunar node, here used for directional calculation</note>, show the dark portion on the western side of the Moon's disk. || 15 ||

Now, to prevent any doubt about the existence of the following text, he concludes the section with a statement: Since the rising and setting of the Moon are discussed in the context of the elevation of the horns, they are included right here and do not constitute an independent chapter; otherwise, they would have been mentioned in the chapter on the rising and setting of planets. By this, the idea that the rising and setting of the Moon belongs to the Full Moon chapter is refuted. There is no evidence for such a designation; otherwise, one could just as easily argue it belongs to the New Moon chapter. This should be kept in mind.

Thus ends the "Commentary on the Elevation of the Moon's Horns" in the *Surya Siddhanta* composed by Ranganatha. This chapter on the Elevation of the Horns is completed in the *Gudartha Prakashaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings"</note>. Thus ends the Chapter on the Elevation of the Horns in the *Gudartha Prakashaka* composed by the astronomer Ranganatha, son of the venerable astronomer Ballala, the sovereign of all calculators. || 10 ||

## ->Chapter Eleven<-

Now the Chapter on the Nodes <note>Sanskrit: *Pātādhyāya*; refers to specific astronomical latitudinal alignments</note> is explained. Desiring to describe the occurrence of the two types of nodes, the author first explains the occurrence of the node named *Vaidhrita*:

**When the Sun and the Moon are situated in the same solstice,**
**and their sum equals twelve signs (one circle), if their declinations are equal, it is called *Vaidhrita*. || 1 ||**

The Sun and the Moon. This usage follows the Vedic scripture: "The Creator fashioned the Sun and the Moon as before." *In the same solstice*: situated in the same northern or southern path. At that time, when the sum of the longitudes of the Sun and Moon equals twelve signs <note>360 degrees</note>, and their declinations <note>distance from the celestial equator</note> are equal, then the great node named *Vaidhrita* occurs. || 1 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** When the Sun and the Moon are in the same solstice (*Ayana*), their combined sum is 12 signs, and their declinations are equal, then *Vaidhriti-pata* occurs. || 1 ||

Next, he explains the occurrence of the node named *Vyatipata*:

**When the Moon and Sun are in opposite solstices,**
**and their declinations are equal, or when their sum is half a circle (six signs), it is *Vyatipata*. || 2 ||**

The Moon and Sun are in opposite solstices (situated in different paths). When the sum of the longitudes of the Sun and Moon equals half a circle (six signs), and their minutes of declination are equal, then at that time the node named *Vyatipata* occurs.

The rationale here: The time of the "Great Node" is the moment of equal declination. Because there is no fixed rule for the increase or decrease of the distinct differences between the true declinations, the exact time is difficult to perceive. Therefore, determining that the equality of declinations (adjusted for celestial latitude) occurs either before or after the time when the mean declinations are equal, one must first find the proximity to that mean equality.

The equality of declination for the Sun and Moon occurs when their "arms" <note><term>Bhujas</term>: the arc of a planet from the nearest tropical or equinoctial point</note> are equal, as declination is produced from the *Bhuja*. If you ask how the *Bhujas* can be equal when the sum is six or twelve signs, or when the difference is six signs or zero, listen: When there is no difference (zero), the two are identical, so there is no dispute regarding the equality of the *Bhujas*. Similarly, with a difference of six signs, they are in opposite quadrants, and their respective elapsed or remaining arcs in those quadrants are equal, so the *Bhujas* are indisputably equal. When the sum is six or twelve signs, because they are in odd/even quadrants respectively, their elapsed and remaining arcs are equal, making the *Bhujas* equal.

When they are at the solstitial points of the solar sphere, the declination is at its maximum; there too, the equality of declination occurs naturally. Therefore:
1. In the same solstice but different hemispheres: equality occurs when the sum is 12 signs.
2. In the same hemisphere and same solstice: equality occurs when there is no difference between them.
3. In opposite solstices but the same hemisphere: equality occurs when the sum is 6 signs.
4. In different hemispheres: equality occurs when the difference is 6 signs.
Thus, the term "sum" is an implication; "difference" should also be understood. Not only when their sum is a full circle or half a circle—

<meta>This page continues the eleventh chapter of the Surya Siddhanta, focusing on the astronomical and astrological phenomenon of Patas (nodes or conjunctions of celestial influence), specifically Vyatipata and Vaidhriti.</meta>

<page-num>174</page-num>
<header>Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Eleven</header>

The explanation provided in the prescribed order is intended to resolve the differences arising from the variations in the celestial spheres; however, even there, it is unavoidable due to the equality of declination <note>original: "krantisamya"</note>. It should be noted that the descriptions of "moving in opposite solstitial directions" or "moving in the same solstitial direction" are formal descriptions and not strictly necessary for the core calculation. In reality, when the sum or difference of the longitudes of the Sun and Moon equals twelve signs <note>360 degrees</note>, the equality of declination is called *Vaidhrita*. When their sum or difference equals six signs <note>180 degrees</note>, the equality of declination is called *Vyatipata*. This is the essential meaning. Therefore, the subsequent statements regarding the Sun and Moon are philosophically sound. || 2 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** When the minutes of declination of the Moon and the Sun—which have moved into opposite solstitial points—become equal, and their combined longitude equals 6 signs <note>180 degrees</note>, the *Vyatipata Pata* occurs. || 2 ||

Now, one might ask: how does a *Pata* <note>literally "fall" or "node," here a malignant astronomical aspect</note> occur simply from the equality of declinations? To answer this, it is said:

### From the contact of their equal webs of rays, and fanned by the Provahe wind,
### a fire born of the wrath of their gaze arises for the destruction of the world. || 3 ||

"Of those two" refers to the Moon and the Sun. The word "but" <note>Latin/Sanskrit: *tu*</note> emphasizes the time of equal declination. "From the contact of their equal webs of rays" means the meeting of the clusters of similar rays as they face one another. Because they become unified, a "wrath born of their gaze" occurs—this is the anger resulting from the two gazes of the centers of their discs facing each other, an excess of brilliance. The resulting "fire" is "fanned by the Provahe" <note>the *Pravaha* is the great celestial wind in Indian cosmology that keeps the planets moving</note>. This "arises for the destruction of the world," meaning it produces inauspicious results for people. || 3 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** From the meeting of the rays of both, a fire produced by the "wrath of their gaze" is ignited by the *Pravaha* wind, giving inauspicious results to mankind. || 3 ||

Next, it is explained whether this fire is called *Vyatipata* or *Vaidhriti*:

### Because this *Pata* repeatedly destroys people,
### it is famous as *Vyatipata*, or by another name, *Vaidhriti*. || 4 ||

"In this" refers to the time of equal declination. "Famous" refers to the nature described in the previous verse. The *Pata* is the fire. "Because" it "repeatedly"—meaning again and again whenever it occurs—"destroys people" or causes ruin. For this reason, this fire is named *Vyatipata*; this same fire, by a "difference of name" <note>a different technical designation</note>, is known as *Vaidhriti*. Thus, in both cases, the fire called *Pata* exists. || 4 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** At the time of equal declination, the *Pata-vahni* (fire of the node) always destroys people; for this reason, it is called *Vyatipata*, or it is given the name *Vaidhriti*. || 4 ||

Now, its physical form is described:

### He is black, with a terrible body, red-eyed, and big-bellied;
### a doer of all evils, fierce, he is born again and again. || 5 ||

That "Fire-Personified" called *Pata*, produced at the time of equal declination and bearing both names, is "black" or dark-hued. He has a "terrible body" (a harsh or frightening physique) and "red eyes" (bloodshot eyes). He is "big-bellied" (having a large stomach). For these reasons, he is the "doer of all evils"...

...causing misfortune for all people. Fierce and destructive. Again and again—meaning many times. Each time the period of equal declination <note>original: "kranti-samya-kala"</note> arises or is produced. || 5 ||

**Hindi Translation:** Yellow or black in color, with a hard body, red eyes, and a large belly; it brings misfortune to all people, is destructive, and occurs many times. || 5 ||

Now, wishing to explain the knowledge of the precise time, he first speaks of the Sun and Moon when their declinations are equal, adjusted for the precession of the equinoxes:

### When the Sun and Moon are situated within the circle of the zodiac, or within half the circle, ||
### and are joined with degrees etc. calculated to match observation, their declinations [should be found]. || 6 ||

"Of the Sun and Moon joined with degrees etc. calculated to match observation"—this means they are refined by the degrees of precession <note>original: "ayanansha"</note> so that they are visible to the eye, according to the rule "the circle moved forward..." etc. By this, the previous general statement is also clarified, since declinations arise from the tropical <note>original: "sayana"</note> positions. "Within the circle"—the zodiac consists of twelve signs; "situated within" means those two whose sum is twelve signs. "Within half the circle"—half the circle is six signs; "situated within that limit" means those two whose sum is six signs. "Their own"—meaning their respective declinations <note>original: "apagramau"</note> are to be calculated. The declination of the Sun is to be found, and the declination of the Moon, refined by its celestial latitude <note>original: "vikshepa"</note>, is to be found. || 6 ||

**Hindi Translation:** When the sum of the Moon and Sun, refined by degrees calculated to match observation (refined by the precession of the equinoxes), is near 12 or 6 signs, then the declination <note>original: "apagrama"</note> of that time should be determined. || 6 ||

Now, with the two calculated declinations, he explains the past or future status of the precise moment of the node <note>term: Pata; the astronomical alignment of Sun and Moon</note> from the calculated time, and its specific nature, in two verses:

### Now, if the Moon is in an odd quadrant and its declination, refined by latitude, ||
### is greater than the declination of the Sun, then the Pata has passed. || 7 ||
### If it is less, then it is yet to come; the opposite is true for an even quadrant. ||
### If the Moon's declination is subtracted from its latitude, there is a change in quadrant. || 8 ||

Now, regarding the calculation of the declinations of the Sun and Moon: If the Moon is in an odd quadrant <note>term: Vishamapada; the 1st and 3rd quadrants of the celestial circle</note>, its declination refined by latitude—meaning its "clear" or precise declination—if it is greater than the calculated declination of the Sun (whether the Sun is in an odd or even quadrant), then the *Pata*—the moment of equal precise declination—is "past." This means it occurred before the time the declination was calculated. If the precise declination of the Moon in an odd quadrant is less than the Sun's declination, then the *Pata* is "future," meaning it will occur after the calculated time. But what if the Moon is not in an odd quadrant? To answer how to know if it is past or future then, he says: "the opposite." For an even quadrant <note>term: Yugmapada; the 2nd and 4th quadrants</note> of the Moon...

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Eleven]

The word "and" implies that the <term>True Declination</term> <note>spashta-kranti: the actual angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</note> may be greater or less than the <term>Sun's Declination</term> <note>surya-kranti</note>. "Reverse" means the opposite of the previously mentioned order of "past" and "future." This applies to the movement of the Node <note>Pata</note>. Now, the author explains a specific rule regarding the Moon:

The "change of quadrant" <note>pada-anyatvam</note> occurs in the calculation of the Moon's true declination. If the Moon's <term>latitude-adjusted</term> <note>vikshepa-samskrita</note> simple declination is subtracted from a latitude of a different direction—meaning it is less than the latitude—then the resulting true declination (formed by the latitude minus the declination) requires a change of quadrant. This means the Moon should be understood to be in a different quadrant than the one indicated by its longitude. For a Moon that appears to be in an even quadrant according to its tropical longitude <note>sayana-rashi</note>, it should be treated as being in an odd quadrant, and vice versa. The true declination must be understood through the relationship of that adjusted quadrant.

The mathematical proof <term>Upapatti</term> is as follows: In an <term>odd quadrant</term> <note>vishama-pada: the 1st and 3rd quadrants of the zodiac</note>, the declination is increasing; in an <term>even quadrant</term> <note>sama-pada: the 2nd and 4th quadrants</note>, it is decreasing. Therefore, if the Moon's declination in an odd quadrant is greater than the Sun's declination, it will become even greater moving forward. Because the increase in declination is greater than the small change in the Sun's position, the Moon's declination cannot equal the Sun's in the future. Thus, it is inferred that the equality occurred in the past, when the Moon's declination was less. Similarly, if the Moon's declination in an even quadrant is less than the Sun's, it will decrease further, making future equality impossible; therefore, equality must have occurred in the past when it was greater. 

Conversely, if the Sun's declination is greater than the Moon's in an odd quadrant, equality will happen in the future. If the Moon's declination in an even quadrant is greater than the Sun's, it will decrease and reach equality in the future. This is why the text speaks of "being equal." Here, the <term>Node</term> <note>gola-sandhi: intersection of the celestial equator and the ecliptic</note> is where the Moon's <term>orbit of latitude</term> <note>vikshepa-vritta</note> meets the <term>equator</term> <note>vishuvad-vritta</note>, where true declination is zero. Three signs (90 degrees) away on the orbit of latitude is the <term>Solstice</term> <note>ayana-sandhi</note>. 

When the Moon's mean declination is in a different direction than its latitude and is less than the latitude, then by subtracting it from the latitude, the true declination belongs to a quadrant different from the mean declination's quadrant. Therefore, it is correctly stated: **"There is a change of quadrant for the Moon if the declination is subtracted from the latitude."**

As stated by the great mathematician <term>Bhaskaracharya</term>:
> "At the full circle (360°) and half circle (180°), minus the precession, is the Sun's <term>Equinoctial Point</term>. Similarly, at three and nine signs is the Solstice. Take the <term>cosine</term> <note>kotijya</note> of the Node minus precession... [technical calculation involving sines and multipliers]... When the Sun is in the signs starting with Aries, the <term>Equinoctial and Solstitial points</term> are as stated. For the Moon, when in the six signs starting with Libra, they are added. The wise should know the Moon's quadrant ends at these points. Like the Sun's sphere, the Moon's true and mean declinations follow the direction of its own sphere."

This is how the quadrants are known. The quadrant of the Moon's true declination must be known this way because it relates to the orbit of latitude, not the standard zodiacal quadrants, otherwise, determining the quadrant would be impossible. By accepting this, the half-verse regarding "change of quadrant" is explained by the Sage to ensure this specific quadrant logic is understood. // 7-8 //

<term>Hindi Commentary-</term> If the Moon is in an odd quadrant and its latitude-adjusted declination is greater than the Sun's declination, the event is past. If it is less, it is in the future. In an even quadrant, the opposite is true. If the declination must be subtracted from the latitude, it reaches the <unclear>limit</unclear> and changes quadrant. // 7-8 //
