Now, desiring to explain the method for calculating the time that has passed or is yet to come <note>The "past and future" time of an astronomical event</note>, he first describes the method for bringing the clear declinations into equality in three verses:

> The sines of the two declinations are multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of the maximum declination.
> The difference between those two arcs, or half of it, should be added to the Moon if the node is in the future; || 9 ||
> It should be subtracted from the Moon if the node has passed. That [result] multiplied by the Sun’s motion
> and divided by the Moon’s motion, gives the result in minutes etc. for the Sun, just like the Moon. || 10 ||
> Similarly, the result for the Node <note>Rahu</note> should be applied in reverse.
> This process should be repeated until the two declinations become equal. || 11 ||

The sines of the calculated declinations of the Sun and Moon should be taken and multiplied by the radius <term>Trijya (Radius)</term>. They are then divided by the sine of the maximum declination <note>original: "paramakrantijya"</note>. The "maximum sine" refers to the value 1397 previously mentioned. The arcs <note>inverse sines</note> of those two results should be calculated. When the Moon's result exceeds the radius, making it impossible to find the arc in the standard way, one must use a proportion: if the radius gives 90 degrees, what does the desired sine give? Or, one should consider that the arc is 5400 minutes <note>90 degrees</note> plus the arc of the excess. The difference between them, or half the difference <note>the text offers "half" as an alternative depending on the magnitude of the error</note>, is used. If the node <term>Pata (Node)</term> is in the future, this value in minutes is added to the Moon's position. If the node has passed, it is subtracted from the Moon.

To calculate the Sun's adjustment, he says: "That..." The adjustment related to the Moon is multiplied by the Sun's true motion and divided by the Moon's true motion. The resulting minutes are added to or subtracted from the Sun in the same way as they were for the Moon.

To calculate the Node's adjustment, he says: "Similarly..." The adjustment for the Moon's node <note>Rahu</note> is found by multiplying the Moon's adjustment by the node's motion and dividing by the Moon's true motion, but it is applied in reverse <note>if added to the Moon, subtract from the node</note>.

Regarding the repetition of this process, he says: "This process..." This mathematical operation must be done "not once" <note>repeatedly/iteratively</note>. From the adjusted Sun, calculate the solar declination; from the adjusted Moon and Node, calculate the Moon's true declination. From these two declinations, find the difference of the arcs (or half) again. Apply this to the second Moon to get a third Moon. Using the initial motions, find the adjustments for the Sun and Node to get a third Sun and Node. From these third positions, repeat the process to get a fourth, and so on. He gives the limit: "Until..." The process must be repeated until the calculated declinations of the Sun and Moon are exactly equal.

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Eleven]
Page 178

The explanation is as follows: From the apparent declinations <note>spashta-kranti</note> at the time of the *Pata* (node alignment), which is characterized by the equality of the mean declinations, the actual time of the *Pata*—defined by the equality of the apparent declinations—is known as either past or future. However, to determine that specific time precisely, the apparent declinations of the Sun and Moon must be calculated until they are equal. In this regard, one must calculate the positions of the Sun, Moon, and the Node <note>Pata</note> at the desired time based on whether the *Pata* is past or future relative to the mean time, and then derive their declinations. Only when these calculated declinations are exactly equal is it considered the "apparent *Pata*." 

Now, because there is no fixed rule, for the purpose of calculating the Moon's position at the initial or subsequent time, certain fixed degrees—calculated as described—are added or subtracted from the Moon's position; these are assumed as the "desired degrees" <note>ishtamsha</note>. To illustrate: if the sine of the Sun's declination is divided by the sine of the maximum declination <note>paramakranti-jya</note>, which is 1397 <note>original: "chaturdasha-shatamitaya" - approximately 1400</note>, and multiplied by the radius <note>trijya</note>, the result is the sine of the arc <note>dorjya</note>. The arc of this value is the tropical longitude of the Sun. Similarly, the arc of the Moon's apparent declination will be either less than or greater than the tropical longitude of the Sun because their declinations are not yet equal. 

Even if the apparent declination exceeds the sine of 24 degrees <note>the maximum declination</note>, making it impossible to find the arc using standard sine tables because the sine value exceeds the radius, one should follow the rule from the **Siddhanta Shiromani**:

> "If the sine exceeds the radius, the arc of the excess is found using the versed sine <note>utkramajya</note>... adding 5400 minutes to the arc."

Thus, there is no error in deriving the arc. This refutes the doubt that an arc is impossible when the declination reaches 28.5 degrees <note>the maximum possible lunar declination</note>. The text does not explicitly state these as "maximum declinations" here. Furthermore, if one does not follow this iterative method, it would be impossible to stop the calculation even after the declinations are equal. Even if the declinations are equal, a difference in the arcs may persist due to different divisors, potentially stalling the operation. In iterative calculations <note>asakrit-karma</note>, once the desired result is achieved, no further operation is possible; otherwise, it would contradict the very nature of the proof. 

The difference between these two arcs constitutes the "desired degrees" <note>ishtamsha</note>. These are added to or subtracted from the Moon's position depending on whether the *Pata* is past or future. If these degrees are large, the result is achieved through many iterations; to achieve it faster, half of these degrees are taken. These are the "desired degrees" for the Moon. Then, by proportion—if these are the degrees for the Moon's motion, what are they for the Sun and the Node?—the Sun's position is adjusted like the Moon's to synchronize them. However, since the Node <note>Pata</note> moves in reverse <note>retrograde</note> through the zodiac, the adjustment for the Node is applied inversely. 

From these adjusted positions, the apparent declinations of the Sun and Moon are calculated again. If they are still unequal, the "desired degrees" must be applied to the *newly* calculated Moon, not the original one, because the new declination arises from the updated position. Otherwise, if the original positions were used, the declinations would remain unchanged, leading to an infinite loop and a failure of the mathematical process. By applying the adjustment to the immediately preceding result, the calculation succeeds. The adjustments for the Sun and Node should be made using their apparent motions from the previous step, as the exact motion at the precise future moment is not yet known. By repeating this process <note>iteration</note>, the equality of declinations is eventually achieved in subsequent steps. This explains the three verses beginning with "The sines of the two declinations..."

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiply the sine of the declination of both [Sun and Moon] by the radius and divide by the sine of the maximum declination. Find the difference between the two resulting arcs. If the *Pata* is in the future, add half of that difference to the Moon. If the *Pata* is past...

# Chapter 11. ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.

...upon occurring, one should separate it from the Moon. The result mentioned above, which is obtained by dividing by the Sun's motion, should be applied to the Sun just as it was to the Moon. According to the rules for the Sun, apply the correction inversely to the calculated *Pata* <note>The Pata refers to the astronomical node or the moment when the declinations of the Sun and Moon are equal</note>. In this manner, perform the calculation repeatedly until the declinations become equal. || 9 || 10 || 11 ||

Now, explaining clearly that the equality of declination is the *Pata*, and to determine that specific time, the author describes whether the time of the *Pata* has passed or is yet to come, based on the midnight closest to the calculated Moon at the time of declination equality:

->**When the two declinations are equal, it is the Pata. If the Moon, adjusted by the added degrees, is—**<-
->**less than the midnight Moon, the Pata has passed; if greater, it is yet to come. || 12 ||**<-

When the clear declinations <term>Sphuta-Kranti: the precisely calculated declination</term> of the Sun and Moon are equal, it is the "Clear Pata." Now, following this: the Moon calculated in relation to the clear *Pata*—which becomes <unclear>determined</unclear> through previous calculation—should have its clear position at the nearest midnight calculated according to the method for finding the true position from the mean. If that calculated Moon (associated with the declination equality) is less than the Moon at midnight (after being adjusted by the arc of declination or half of it), then the time of the *Pata* has already passed relative to that midnight. If the Moon at the time of declination equality is greater than the midnight Moon, it means the time of the *Pata* is in the future.

The reasoning here is as follows: Although the time elapsed or remaining in *ghatis* <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> from the moment of mean declination equality can be known through the methods described later using the Moon at the clear declination equality and the Moon at mean declination equality, calculating it from the nearest midnight Moon and then stating the elapsed/remaining time is considered "heavy" (complex) due to the extra steps in calculating the clear midnight Moon. However, because the Moon's motion is very rapid and its velocity changes every moment, a calculation based on a long interval of time would be too imprecise. Because the difference is smaller when using a time close at hand, the text specifies the clear midnight Moon. This requires the use of the clear daily motion. Therefore, it is correctly stated that the clear *Pata* is past or future based on whether the Moon at declination equality is less or greater than the midnight Moon. This aligns with the statement of the teacher Bhaskaracharya: <note>original: "समीप तिथ्यन्तसमीपचालनं विधोस्तु तत्कालजयैव युज्येत्"</note> "The movement of the Moon near the end of a *tithi* (lunar day) should only be calculated using its velocity at that specific time." || 12 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The equality of the declinations of the Sun and Moon is the *Pata*. If the Moon, corrected by the added degrees, is less than the midnight Moon, the *Pata* has passed at midnight; if the Moon at that time is greater, the *Pata* is yet to occur. || 12 ||

### Now, the method for knowing the precise time of the Pata is stated:

->**Take the difference in minutes between the fixed midnight Moon and the other;**<-
->**multiply by sixty and divide by the Moon's motion to find the ghatis of the Pata time. || 13 ||**<-

The "fixed midnight Moon" refers to the Moon calculated for the nearest midnight, and the other is the Moon determined at the moment of clear declination equality. The word "two" is used to clarify these two specific values.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of calculating the precise timing of astronomical conjunctions (specifically the Pāta or 'aspect') from the previous section. It focuses on the mathematical derivation of the duration of this phenomenon.</meta>

# Surya Siddhanta: Chapter Eleven

Because of the confusion caused by an error in the final singular case <note>a grammatical point regarding the Sanskrit text</note>, the difference in minutes of arc multiplied by sixty and divided by the true motion of the Moon at midnight (in minutes) gives the result. These are the ghatikas <term>ghatika: a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term> of the time of the aspect, representing the equality of the true declination to be reached after midnight. This means that by the sequence of time following midnight, the aspect—defined as the equality of true declination—will occur earlier or later by the resulting ghatikas. 

The reasoning here is as follows: If sixty solar ghatikas are obtained by the true motion of the Moon, then how much time is obtained by the minutes of arc representing the difference between the Moon at midnight and the Moon at the time of equal declination? This is the calculation provided. It should be noted that since the initial motion of the Moon and the calculated Sun are taken as gross (approximate), the calculation of the time of the aspect using the true Sun at midnight is not described here as being perfectly precise. || 13 ||

**Hindi Commentary:**
The difference in minutes between the Moon at the time of equal declination and the Moon at midnight, multiplied by 60 and divided by the Moon's daily motion, will give the difference in time from midnight to the true moment of the aspect. || 13 ||

### Now he describes the calculation of the half-duration of the aspect—

-> Multiply half the sum of the diameters of the Sun and Moon by sixty and divide <-
-> by the difference of their daily motions; the result is the half-duration in ghatikas. || 14 || <-

Following the method described in the chapter on Lunar Eclipses, one should take the minutes of the diameters of the Sun and Moon produced by their respective motions. Half of their sum should be multiplied by sixty and divided by the difference between the true motions of the Sun and Moon in minutes. The resulting ghatikas and their fractions represent the "half-duration" <term>sthityardha: literally 'half-stay', the time from the start to the middle, or middle to the end</term>. This means the aspect remains in effect for the duration of this half-period both before and after the precise moment of the aspect.

The reasoning is this: 1. When the centers of the solar and lunar disks are on the same diurnal circle, or are at an equal distance from the celestial equator on either side, the "middle of the aspect" occurs due to the equality of the centers. The region of the circumference of the disk situated on the line of declination nearest to the equator is the inner edge of the disk. The one furthest away is the outer edge. The aspect is defined by this north-south movement. 

The beginning of the aspect occurs when the outer edge of the faster-moving body and the inner edge of the slower-moving body reach that state. The end of the aspect occurs when the outer edge of the Sun and the inner edge of the Moon reach that state. Therefore, before and after these two times, no part of the solar or lunar disks overlaps in this specific alignment, and thus the aspect does not exist. The duration of the aspect is the period from the beginning to the end during which the Sun and Moon are in this state. At the middle of the aspect, there is no difference in declination; at the beginning and end, the difference in declination is equal to half the sum of the diameters. 

Therefore, the time taken for that difference to decrease (before the middle) or increase (after the middle) is the half-duration of the beginning and end. The calculation is stated as a proportion: if the difference in the motions of the Sun and Moon corresponds to sixty ghatikas, then what time corresponds to the minutes of half the sum of the diameters? 

Although this proportion might seem inconsistent because the quantities (declination vs. longitudinal motion) are not of the same nature—since the increase and decrease of the north-south declination is very different from the increase and decrease of the east-west longitudinal motion—nevertheless, for the sake of mathematical simplicity and out of compassion for people, the Lord <note>referring to the divine source of the Surya Siddhanta</note> accepted this proportion as having only a small margin of error. Thus, it is not a flaw. 

The Great Teacher Bhaskara <note>Bhaskaracharya, the famous 12th-century mathematician</note> rightly said: "Half the sum of the diameters multiplied by the true ghatikas and divided by the first [motion]... the resulting ghatikas give the beginning and end of the aspect from the middle." Some others say that the declination should be calculated by moving the planets by sixty ghatikas, and the difference or sum of those results is the difference in motion, according to their own preference. || 14 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiply the sum of the semi-diameters <note>the combined radii</note> of the Sun and the Moon by 60, and divide that by the difference of their daily motions; the result will be the *Sthityardha* <term>Sthityardha: half-duration of the astronomical event</term> in *Dandas* <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>. || 14 ||

### Now, the beginning, middle, and end times of the Pata are described:

> The calculated time of the *Pata* is known as the "Middle." Subtracting the half-duration from it gives the "Beginning" time; adding the half-duration to it gives the "End" time. || 15 ||

The precise time of the *Pata*—which is the moment of *Kranti-samya* <term>Kranti-samya: equality of declination between the Sun and Moon</term>—calculated through the previously mentioned midnight methods, is to be understood as the "Middle" time. That middle time, when diminished by the calculated half-duration (*Sthityardha*), marks the "Beginning" or commencement of the *Pata*. The word "also" implies inclusion. That same middle time, when increased by the half-duration, becomes the "End" time of the *Pata*. The logic here is as clear as the calculation for the contact and separation phases of a lunar eclipse. Its essential nature was previously explained. || 15 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The time of the *Pata* itself is the Middle. Subtracting the half-duration from it gives the Beginning time, and adding the half-duration gives the End time. || 15 ||

### Now, regarding the purpose of this knowledge, it is stated that the duration of the Pata is forbidden for auspicious acts:

> The period between the beginning and end times should be known as extremely terrible. Like a blazing fire, it is condemned for all auspicious works. || 16 ||

The interval of time residing between the start and the completion of the *Pata* is exceedingly harsh. It should be known as prohibited for all *Mangala-kritya* <note>auspicious ceremonies like weddings or initiations</note>. The adjective "like a blazing fire" provides the reasoning: it is of the nature of a glowing flame. The implication is that any auspicious work performed during this time would be reduced to ashes. || 16 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The time from the Beginning to the End is extremely dreadful; it is like a brilliant fire and is condemned for all auspicious deeds. || 16 ||

### One might argue that since Pata is defined by the exact equality of declination—a momentary point in time—only that calculated middle moment should be forbidden, not the entire duration, as exact equality does not exist throughout. To answer this, it is said:

> As long as the distance between the disks of the Sun and Moon remains within the same path, the Pata exists, destroying the fruits of all actions. || 17 ||

As long as any portion of the disks of the Sun and Moon remains within the same path <margin>Another reading: "situated in the same direction"</margin>—meaning as long as their bodies overlap in declination—that entire duration is meant. The word "only" is used to exclude any time more or less than this. During this time, the *Pata* destroys all performed auspicious acts. "Existence" here refers to the total duration. It is not just the moment of exact equality of the centers, because the *Pata* persists as long as there is a connection between the disks. Therefore, the statement by *Bhaskaracharya* <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> is most appropriate: "The difference in declinations exists as long as it is less than half the sum of the diameters, due to the equality of declinations of the portions of the disks." || 17 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** As long as any portion of the solar and lunar disks occupy the same position <note>in terms of declination</note>, this *Pata* <term>Pata: a malignant astronomical aspect or node</term>, which destroys the fruits of all worldly actions, is possible. || 17 ||

Lest one thinks this is only a destroyer of auspiciousness and not a bringer of good, the author says:

### Through bathing, charity, chanting, ancestral rites, vows, and fire sacrifices, etc. ||
### Great spiritual merit is obtained by knowing the exact time of its occurrence. || 18 ||

*Vows* refers to the worship of one's chosen deity. The word *etc.* refers to other religious duties. Through these holy acts performed at that specific time, humans obtain excellent welfare. This is possible through the knowledge of the duration and timing of that *Pata*. The word *and* implies the accumulation of merit. The meaning is that great excellence is attained thereby. || 18 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** By knowing the time of the *Pata* and performing bathing, charity, chanting (*Japa*), ancestral rites (*Shraddha*), vows, and fire sacrifices (*Homa*), etc., one attains great and superior results. || 18 ||

Now, he describes the specific types of *Pata*:

### When the declinations of the Sun and Moon are equal near the equinox, ||
### Then the Pata occurs twice in its two variations; otherwise, there is an absence of it. || 19 ||

At whatever time [the Sun] is near the equinox <term>Vishuvat: the celestial equator or equinoctial points</term>, where declination is nearly zero—here, the proximity of the Moon's apparent declination to zero should also be considered—and the declinations of the Sun and Moon become equal, then at that approximate time, the *Pata* consisting of the two variations, *Vyatipata* and *Vaidhrita*, occurs twice. "Twice" means each occurs two times. "Otherwise" refers to the opposite case: when they are near the solstice <note>the point where the Sun or Moon reaches its highest or lowest declination</note>, and their declinations are equal. Here, it should be understood that "absence" occurs if the Sun's declination is greater than the Moon's maximum apparent declination. In such a case, the *Pata* (equality of declination) cannot manifest during that period. By this, the statement of Bhaskaracharya <note>a famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> is consistent:

> "At the solstice of the Moon, as long as its declination is less than the Sun's declination at that time, equality of their declinations does not exist."

The calculation for this is found by repeatedly adding or subtracting the desired degrees (derived from the initial arc difference) to the Moon's position to find the two moments of the *Pata*. The rationale is as follows: In *Vyatipata*, the *Pata* occurs when the Sun and Moon are at equal distances on opposite sides of the equinoctial circle. Due to the equality of declination, even in *Vaidhrita*, the *Pata* occurs when they occupy the same diurnal circle. Similarly, in the variations of *Vyatipata* and *Vaidhrita*, the *Pata* status is achieved when they are on the same diurnal circle or at equal distances from the equinoctial circle. This is proven by the principles of the sphere regarding the equality of declination, and is visible near the nodes of the lunar orbit. The reason for "absence" is: at the Moon's solstice, its maximum northward or southward movement from the equinoctial circle is equal to its apparent declination. As the Moon moves forward or backward from this point on its inclined orbit, its declination can only decrease. Therefore, if the Sun's declination at that time is greater than the Moon's maximum apparent declination at its solstice, the equality of declinations is impossible. Because the Sun moves slower than the Moon, the decrease in the Sun's declination [cannot compensate for the difference]...

...because of the possibility of its smallness. However, when the solar declination <note>original: *suryakanti*</note> increases, that impossibility is even more certain. Thus, the solar declination there is less, and due to the increase in its decrease, the Moon's clear declination becomes equal to it in the subsequent period. But if the solar declination increases, it is even more impossible. And so, near the junction of the second solar hemisphere when the Moon's node is near the solstice and the Sun is also near the solstice, this impossibility lasts for some days; elsewhere, as stated, the possibility exists—this is the result of the logic of the spheres <note>original: *golayukti*</note>. Even in the definition of possibility, if the difference in declination is less than the sum of the semi-diameters, then according to the previously stated rule—"as long as the distance between the disks of the Sun and Moon is within one degree"—the *Pata* <note>an astronomical alignment or "node" often considered inauspicious</note> is possible. There, for the sake of determining the middle of the *Pata* at that time, one should calculate using the difference between the declination and the sum of the semi-diameters, instead of the "half-sum of the solar and lunar diameters" as previously mentioned. This should be kept in mind. || 19 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** When the Moon's declination becomes equal to the Sun's declination near the equinox, the two *Patas* occur twice; otherwise, there is an absence of both. || 19 ||

Now, following the mention of the prohibition of the "Great Alignment" <note>Mahapata</note> for auspicious works, the author explains the knowledge of the *Vyatipata* <note>a specific astrological yoga</note> which falls within the five limbs of the calendar <note>Panchanga</note>:

### The sum of the minutes of the Moon and Sun, divided by the portion of a constellation <note>800 minutes</note>, ###
### if the result is the end of the seventeenth, it is the third Vyatipata. || 20 ||

The sum of the positions of the Moon and Sun, adjusted for the precession of the equinoxes <note>Ayanamsha</note>, converted into minutes and divided by eight hundred, gives a result. If this result is within the seventeenth—meaning after the sixteenth and up to the seventeenth—that is also called *Vyatipata*. This is "another" one, distinct from those mentioned previously in this chapter. The "third" refers to the third type, as *Vyatipata* and *Vaidhriti* are derived from the sum and difference of the Sun and Moon. By this same logic, if the result is twenty-seven (after the twenty-sixth), then it is the third *Vaidhriti*. This is because the *Pata* known to experts is of two types based on sum and difference. The underlying logic here is that the seventeenth *Yoga* <note>astrological division of time</note> in the sequence starting with *Vishkambha* is *Vyatipata*. || 20 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Adding the minutes of the Moon and Sun and dividing by 800; if the quotient is at the end of (near) 17, it is the third *Pata* named *Vyatipata*. || 20 ||

Now, intending to describe the "Junction of Constellations" <note>Bhasandhi</note> and "Node's End" <note>Gandanta</note>, which are similarly prohibited for auspicious acts, he explains their nature:

### The final quarters of the constellations Ashlesha, Jyeshtha, and Revati are the "Star-Junctions"; ###
### The first quarters of the stars following them are called "Gandanta." || 21 ||

The final (fourth) quarters <note>padas</note> of the constellations Ashlesha, Jyeshtha, and Revati are the junctions of the constellations <note>Nakshatra-sandhi</note>. In the stars following them—meaning in the constellations Magha, Mula, and Ashvini—the first quarter is famously called *Gandanta*. Although the final two *ghatikas* <note>units of 24 minutes</note> of Ashlesha, Jyeshtha, and Revati, and the first two *ghatikas* of Magha, Mula, and Ashvini—making four *ghatikas* in total—constitute the *Gandanta*. Any other junction of constellations consists of two *ghatikas* (the last of the previous and first of the next), or two and a half *ghatikas* regarding the Moon's disk; though this might seem to contradict some traditions, the word of the Sun <note>referring to the Surya Siddhanta text</note> is self-evident...

# Surya Siddhanta: [Chapter Eleven]

There is no harm in following the authoritative texts. Alternatively, to maintain consistency in the sentence, the word *pada* <note>literally "foot" or "quarter"</note> refers to the number two, as in the eyes or limbs of a person. The word "Ghatika" <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> is understood here. Thus, the "junctions of the stars" (*Nakshatra-sandhi*) consist of the final two Ghatikas. The meaning is that the period measuring the first two Ghatikas is the *Ganda-anta* <note>a spiritual "knot" or transitional danger zone in the zodiac</note>. Even here, describing the junction of two signs as *Ganda-anta* might seem improper since *Ganda-anta* is technically the interval between them; however, because the intent is to state that this time is forbidden, describing it in two parts serves to indicate that the interval is increasingly forbidden, so there is no error. || 21 ||

**Commentary:** The fourth quarter of the stars Ashlesha, Jyeshtha, and Revati is the *Bha-sandhi* <note>stellar junction</note>, and the first quarters of Ashwini, Magha, and Mula are the *Ganda-anta*. || 21 ||

Now, he speaks of the equal forbidden nature of those things mentioned in this chapter:

> The three *Vyatipatas* are terrible, as are the three *Ganda-antas*.
> One should avoid these three *Bha-sandhis* in all ceremonies. || 22 ||

The "three *Vyatipatas*" refer to: two forms of *Vyatipata* consisting of the alignment of declination <term>Kranti-samya: when the sun and moon have equal declination</term> through addition and subtraction, and the third being the *Vyatipata* occurring near the equinox due to a difference in declination. These are not distinct but variations. The third is the *Vyatipata* included within the five limbs of the calendar (*Panchanga*). By implication, the three *Vaidhritis* are also included. Two are named *Vaidhriti* based on declination alignment through addition and subtraction near the equinox. The one named *Vaidhriti* is included within those; it is not separate. The third is the *Vaidhriti* yoga found in the *Panchanga*. Some say the "three *Vyatipatas*" are as follows: the two types of *Vyatipata* and *Vaidhriti* (previously called *Vaidhriti* by a different name) and the *Vyatipata* of the *Panchanga*. These are "terrible" or wicked. Likewise, the three *Ganda-antas* and the three *Nakshatra-sandhis* are terrible. For this reason, one who desires auspiciousness should abandon these wicked times in all marriage or festive ceremonies. || 22 ||

**Commentary:** The three *Vyatipatas*, the three *Ganda-antas*, and the three junction periods (*Sandhi-kala*) are extremely defiled. One should abandon them in all works. || 22 ||

Now the Man-of-the-Sun-Fragment <note>the incarnation of the Sun God</note> concludes his remaining speech:

> Thus, this supreme, merit-bestowing, and beneficial history of the stars has been told.
> It is a great secret; what else do you wish to hear? || 23 ||

O Maya, this is for you. "Listen with a focused mind," etc., up to "avoid in all ceremonies"—this history of the lights (planets and stars), meaning the knowledge of mathematics and astronomy, is beneficial and brings fame in this world. It is "supremely meritorious," leading to excellent Dharma in the next world. Therefore, I have told you this "great secret," which is to be kept very private. Now, [the speaker] inferred from the trembling of Maya's lower lip that the settled meaning of this, which was explained without logical proofs, had not yet reached Maya's mind. Thinking, "I must speak with logic after waiting for his question, as he is unable to grasp my essence due to my brevity," he says: "What?" That is, "Beyond this, what other thing do you wish to hear or know?" As I previously said to you...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the student and the teacher (the Sun-god's representative) regarding the cosmography of the Surya Siddhanta. It follows the introductory verses of the 12th chapter (Bhugola-adhyaya) concerning the structure of the universe.</meta>

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Twelve]

O Lord, what is the **size** of the Earth? What is its **shape**? What is its **support** (what does it rest upon)? How is it **divided**? Furthermore, how do the seven **underworld regions** <note>Sanskrit: *patala*, the seven subterranean realms in Hindu cosmology</note> exist as divisions within this Earth? This is the intention of the question: Since you previously mentioned the Earth's measure as "eight hundred yojanas" and so on, yet it is also known to be fifty million <note>Sanskrit: *panchashat-koti*</note> in extent, there is doubt regarding the true measurement. Otherwise, the question would be useless if the answer were already known. 

Similarly, since the calculation of the "sine of latitude" <note>Sanskrit: *lambajya*</note> implies a specific circumference, and the common perception of the Earth as flat like a mirror <note>Sanskrit: *adarshakara*</note> makes such calculations impossible, your intended shape must be different; hence the question "What is its shape?" Furthermore, since you suggested that the planets revolve around the Earth, they could not revolve if the Earth were supported by something like the world-serpent *Shesha*. Because it is impossible for a supportless object to remain stable, there is doubt regarding its foundation; hence the question "What is its support?" Thus, the questions in the second half of the verse are raised to clarify the true nature of the Earth, which differs from common worldly understanding. || 2 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** O Lord! What is the measurement of this Earth? What is its shape? Upon whose support does it stay? What are its divisions? And in what manner are the seven underworlds and the Earth situated? || 2 ||

Now, regarding the cause of the question about the Earth's support, the following is asked using the Sun as an illustration of the planets' movement around the Earth:

->**How does the Sun establish the arrangement of day and night?**<-
->**How does he wander around the Earth, illuminating the worlds? || 3 ||**<-

How, or by what means, does the Sun create the **arrangement of day and night** (the distinction between day and night)? The idea is this: If the Earth were flat like a mirror with Mount Meru in the middle, and the Sun moved clockwise above the Earth, day would occur when the Sun is visible and night when he is hidden. But if your intended solar motion is different, how does the Sun create day and night without a physical barrier? How do other planets create their own day and night? This is implied by using the Sun as an example. If one accepts the revolution around the Earth, then the Earth itself acts as the barrier, making the day-night arrangement logical. Therefore, he asks another question: How does the Sun, while illuminating the **worlds** <note>Sanskrit: *bhuvanani*, referring to the various spheres of existence</note>, travel around the Earth? Since a supportless Earth seems impossible, if it had a support, the revolution of planets *around* it would be blocked by that support. || 3 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** And in what manner does the Sun-God <note>Sanskrit: *Suryanarayana*</note> arrange the day and night? How does he travel around the Earth while illuminating the groups of worlds? || 3 ||

A further question:

->**Why is the day and night of the Gods and Demons mutually reversed?**<-
->**How does this occur through the Sun’s completion of a revolution? || 4 ||**<-

<note>The "Gods" are traditionally situated at the North Pole (Meru) and the "Demons" (Asuras) at the South Pole. Their days and nights last six months each and are opposite to one another.</note>

The first half of the verse was explained previously. The phrase "for what purpose" <note>original: *kimartham*</note> refers to the intent behind the specific definition of a day and night. The underlying thought is: why was it not said that the day and night of the Gods and Demons are identical, given there is a governing rule for their inversion? That day and night of the Gods and Demons is determined by the Sun’s passage through the twelve signs of the Zodiac. How and from what? The word "or" <note>original: *vākāra*</note> here functions as a conjunction. My doubt remains on both sides because of the governing principle. Since the day and night are regulated by the visibility or invisibility of the Sun: where the Gods see the Sun for a period of six months, the Demons do not see it. Where the Gods do not see it for six months, the Demons do see it. This is the point the Lord <note>referring to the Sun God or the teacher of the Surya Siddhanta</note> must clarify. || 4 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Why are the days and nights of the Gods and Demons mutually opposite? And why is this equal to the Sun’s revolution through the 12 signs? || 4 ||

Now, regarding another question, he states the intent of the previous two verses and asks:

### A day of the Ancestors <term>Pitrya: relating to the Pitris or spirits of departed ancestors</term> consists of a month, while that of Humans <term>Manusha: relating to mankind</term> consists of sixty ghatis <term>Nadi-shashtya: 60 nadis/ghatis, equivalent to 24 hours</term>. 
### Why is it that the same [measurement] does not prevail everywhere? || 5 ||

This day and night of the Ancestors is defined by a month—specifically a lunar month, which is longer than a solar year <note>The commentator is clarifying the specific lunar-sidereal calculations used for the Pitris</note>—by what cause? This question applies to each case. By what reason does it happen? Otherwise, the question would be illogical. By what reason is the human day and night composed of sixty civil <term>Savana: terrestrial or civil day from sunrise to sunrise</term> units of time? One should not argue that because the "Divine Day" was mentioned previously, and the Ancestral and Human days were not explicitly defined, the question is inconsistent. By saying "That is called a Divine Day," the previously mentioned civil day and lunar month were already implied to be their respective days. Since the Ancestors were not mentioned in the "Divine" category, and since the solar-civil day is perceived by humans as their own day, it is established by elimination that the month is the day of the Ancestors. 

However, a question regarding the human day—which is proven by direct perception—might still seem unnecessary. Thus, he asks the "intent" question: "Why is it that the same..." The word "same" <note>original: *tadeva*</note> refers to the human day. The word "only" <note>original: *eva*</note> excludes others. Why, with certainty, is this not the case in all worlds? How is the imperceptible day and night of the Ancestors, Gods, and Demons accepted? And why is the human day, which is proven by perception, not also attributed to them? || 5 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** An Ancestral day is one month long, and the human day is 60 ghatis. Why are day and night not the same for everyone? Why are the lords of the day, year, month, and hour <term>Hora: an hour or 1/24th of a day</term> not of one type? || 5 ||

Now, regarding the lords of the day, month, and year known from the calculation of elapsed days <term>Ahargana: the heap of days elapsed from a fixed epoch</term>, he asks about the lord of the hour <insert>and regarding the verse "moving westward with great speed"</insert>, he poses two questions:

### Why are the lords of the day, year, month, and hour not the same? 
### How does the circle of asterisms <term>Bhagana: the zodiac or revolution of signs</term> revolve, and what is the support of this planet? || 6 ||

Why are the masters of the day, year, month, and hour not identical? Just as the lordship of the day belongs to the Sun and others in sequence, it would be logical for the lordship of the months and years to follow the Sun and others in the order of the first month and year onwards.

<vocab>Pitrya (Ancestral), Manusha (Human), Ahoratra (Day and Night), Hora (Hour), Adhipa (Lords/Regents), Bhagana (Zodiacal revolution), Savana-ghati (Civil time unit), Chandramasa (Lunar month)</vocab>

<summary>This page discusses the varying definitions of a "day" for different beings—gods, demons, ancestors, and humans—and questions why the planetary regents (lords) of time divisions like hours and months are not uniform.</summary>

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Twelve]

<page-num>188</page-num>

<note>The commentator explains that while the calculation of the 'Lord of the Hour' (Hora) was not explicitly mentioned before, the student asks about it because it is a well-known concept in worldly astrology.</note> How does the "Circle of Asterisms" <note>original: "Bhagana"; the 360 degrees of the zodiac including the stars</note>, along with the planets, revolve? By what means are the stars and planets impelled to wander around the Earth? Furthermore, regarding their position in space, he asks: What is the support <note>original: "āśraya"</note> of this visible celestial circle? Since staying in the atmosphere without a support seems impossible, what holds them up? || 6 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** How does the circle of stars revolve along with the planets, and what is their foundation? || 6 ||

Now, one might suggest that the "orbits" <term>Kakshas: the specific paths or circular shells in which planets travel</term> are the supports, as it was previously stated that they move in their own paths. To clarify this, he asks four questions regarding these orbits:

## What are the heights of the orbits of the planets and stars, one above the other?
## What are the distances between them, what are their sizes, and in what order are they situated? || 7 ||

Starting from the Earth, moving upwards, what is the height <note>original: "utsedha"</note> of the orbits of the planets and stars in the sky? That is, at what distance from the Earth do these paths exist? What is the interval <note>original: "antara"</note> between them? Even as they get higher and higher, what is the space separating one from the next? What is their "measure" <note>original: "mātrā"</note>—meaning, what is their nature, their form, or their specific magnitude? Finally, in what order are they arranged? The student implies that the sequence—which one comes first, which one follows—is not yet understood. || 7 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** How high are the orbits of the planets from the Earth? What is the distance between them? What is their measurement, and how are they positioned? || 7 ||

Next, he asks a question based on observation, and in that context, a question about the spread of the Sun's rays, followed by two questions regarding the systems of measurement previously mentioned:

## Why is the Sun fierce-rayed in Summer, but not so in Winter?
## How far do those rays reach? How many "measures of time" are there, and what is their purpose? || 8 ||

Why is it that in the Summer season <note>original: "Grishma"</note> the Sun has such sharp, hot rays, but in the Winter <note>original: "Hemanta"</note> it is not like that? What is the extent or the method of the reach of the Sun's rays? Regarding the "measures" <note>original: "mānāni"</note>—the Sidereal, Civil, Lunar, and Solar systems previously mentioned—how many are there exactly? Although they were mentioned briefly at the beginning, their true essence is not fully understood. And what is the specific use or purpose of each of these measures? || 8 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** In summer the rays of the sun are intense, and in winter they are not so; what is the rule of the reach of these rays? How many types of measurements are there, and what is their utility? || 8 ||

# Chapter 12. ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.

Now, he concludes his question:

> **O Blessed Lord, Creator of Beings, please sever this doubt of mine.**
> **Other than You, O All-Seeing One, there is no one who can destroy it. || 9 ||**

O Blessed Lord <note>Sanskrit: *Bhagavan*; one endowed with the six divine opulences</note>, meaning the Awakener of all. O Creator of Beings <note>Sanskrit: *Bhuta-bhavana*</note>, one who contemplates the past (*Bhuta*). By implication, this means you are the knower of the present and future as well. You must sever—meaning destroy—this doubt of mine. The singular "doubt" is used here to represent the entire class of questions I have asked. If you were to say, "I cannot speak now, go to another to remove your doubts," he responds: "Other than You." Without you, there is no other "All-Seeing One" <note>Sanskrit: *Sarva-darshin*; omniscient</note> who can remove these doubts. The intent is: "Just as you have spoken until now, please kindly explain the rest." || 9 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** O Creator of Beings, Blessed Lord! Please remove all these doubts of mine; besides You, there is no other all-seeing destroyer of doubt. || 9 ||

Now, after the sage <note>the narrator</note> repeats the questions asked by Maya to the other sages, he describes how the Man-of-the-Sun <note>Sanskrit: *Suryansha-purusha*; a partial incarnation or representative of the Sun God</note> spoke again to Maya:

> **Having heard these words spoken by Maya with devotion,**
> **He then spoke to him again regarding the supreme, secret spiritual knowledge. || 10 ||**

He, the Man-of-the-Sun, having heard the words uttered by Maya—which arose from devotion and the knowledge of worship—spoke again to Maya. He spoke of the "Supreme" <note>referring to the second section or the latter part of the book</note> which is the "Secret" <note>Sanskrit: *Rahasya*</note>, the essential truth of the preceding part of this text. || 10 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Hearing the words of Maya spoken with a spirit of devotion, the Man-of-the-Sun again spoke the supreme spiritual secret. || 10 ||

Now, repeating the words of the Man-of-the-Sun, he tells Maya that he must listen to what is said with great care:

> **Listen with a focused mind to the secret known as the Spiritual Wisdom.**
> **I shall proclaim it; for to those who are deeply devoted, there is nothing I cannot give. || 11 ||**

Because for those who are "Deeply Devoted"—those like you who perform my worship—there is nothing that I, the Man-of-the-Sun, should withhold. Therefore, I shall proclaim to you the "Secret" known as "Spiritual Wisdom" <note>Sanskrit: *Adhyatma-sangyitam*</note>. You must "Listen with a focused mind"—meaning your mind should be fixed solely on my words—and perceive this directly through the union of the self and the sense of hearing. || 11 ||

<summary>Maya concludes his plea for knowledge, acknowledging the Sun's representative as the only one capable of resolving his doubts. The Sun's representative agrees to reveal the most guarded spiritual and astronomical secrets due to Maya's intense devotion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the twelfth chapter of the Surya Siddhanta, transitioning from the introductory dialogue to the metaphysical explanation of the universe's origin.</meta>

# Surya Siddhanta
## [Chapter Twelve]

**Commentary:** "Well then, I shall speak of the secret spiritual truth; listen with a focused mind. There is nothing that I cannot give to my most devoted followers." || 11 ||

Regarding the statement "I shall speak of the secret," he says:

->Vasudeva is the Supreme Brahman; His form is the Supreme Spirit (Purusha).<-
->He is unmanifest, devoid of qualities (Nirguna), peaceful, beyond the twenty-fifth principle, and imperishable.<- || 12 ||

The name *Vasudeva* <note>original: "Vāsudeva"</note> is derived from the root *vas*, meaning that the entire universe dwells in Him, or He dwells in the entire universe. *Deva* comes from the root meaning to shine or illuminate. Thus, He is Vasudeva. As it is said: "Because everything dwells in Him and He dwells everywhere, He is sung of by the wise as Vasudeva." This is not merely a reference to being the son of Vasudeva <note>Krishna's father</note>, as that would be irrelevant in the context of describing the cause of the universe. In our view, He is the material cause, as the effect is supported by the cause and the cause permeates the effect. This is confirmed in the Upanishads: "All this is pervaded by the Lord" <note>Isha Upanishad 1</note>. And in the Bhagavata: "That from which the world is born is inseparable from it." To distinguish Him from individual souls, who are also of the nature of Brahman, the word "Supreme" (Param) is used, meaning the highest of all. As the Smriti says: "Since I transcend the perishable and am higher than even the imperishable, I am celebrated in the world and in the Vedas as the Supreme Spirit (Purushottama)."

"His form" <note>Tanmurti</note> refers to a portion or manifestation of Vasudeva. This adjective describes Samkarshana <note>the first expansion of the divine in this cosmology</note>, who is about to be mentioned. The reading "Form of Consciousness" (Chinmurti) is an error, as it fails to convey the intended meaning that Samkarshana originates from Vasudeva. "Unmanifest" (Avyakta) means beyond the reach of the senses. As the scripture says: "You do not know Him who created these things; something else has come between you... enveloped in mist, the talkers wander." And: "His form does not stand within the range of sight; no one perceives Him with the eye." The reason for being unmanifest is that He is "devoid of qualities" (Nirguna). He is "peaceful" because He is free from the six waves of worldly existence <note>hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death</note>. "Beyond the twenty-fifth" refers to the twenty-four principles of Samkhya philosophy (the sixteen transformations, the seven nature-transformations, and primordial nature); the twenty-fifth is the individual soul (Jiva), and He is beyond even that. If the reading "consisting of the twenty-five" is taken, it means He is the soul of the universe. || 12 ||

**Commentary:** Vasudeva, the Supreme Brahman, His form the Supreme Spirit, unmanifest, without qualities, peaceful, imperishable, and beyond the twenty-five principles. || 12 ||

Since the pure Brahman cannot [directly] be the cause of the material world, he says:

->The Deity, dwelling within Nature (Prakriti), pervading all both outside and in,<-
->is this Samkarshana; at the beginning of creation, he cast his seed into the waters.<- || 13 ||

"Dwelling within Nature" means associated with the power of illusion (Maya). He "pervades all outside and in" because He is the material cause of the universe. All these attributes of Samkarshana, though he is a portion of Vasudeva, should be understood as being identical to Vasudeva in essence. Samkarshana, as a portion of Vasudeva, first created the waters and then "cast his seed"—a specific power—into those waters. || 13 ||

<summary>This page provides a metaphysical foundation for Hindu astronomy, identifying Vasudeva (Brahman) as the ultimate source of the universe and Samkarshana as the active creative principle who initiates the material world.</summary>
<keywords>Vasudeva, Brahman, Samkarshana, Purusha, Samkhya, twenty-five principles, Prakriti, creation, cosmology, Surya Siddhanta</keywords>

# Chapter 12 ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries ( 191 )

**Hindi Commentary—** As the material cause of the universe, these aspects are contained within Nature <note>Prakriti</note>. Sankarshana <note>A form of Vishnu associated with ego and strength</note> exists both externally and internally and is all-pervading. At the beginning of creation, he casts his seed into the waters of the causal ocean. || 13 ||
What happens after that? It is said:

->That egg became golden, surrounded everywhere by darkness. <-
->There, Aniruddha, the eternal one, first became manifest. || 14 ||<-

The water, combined with those respective powers, became a golden <note>Sanskrit: *haimam*</note> egg, spherical in shape, covered everywhere—inside and out—by darkness. The meaning is that a golden egg was produced in the space accompanied by darkness. In that golden egg, at the beginning, Aniruddha <note>The grandson of Krishna, representing the mind or the conscious manifestation</note>—who is eternal and constant—became manifest. Because he is a portion of Sankarshana (who is himself a portion of Vasudeva), he is described as "manifested" rather than "born." This is because of the doctrine of *Satkaryavada* <note>The philosophical theory that the effect pre-exists in its cause</note>. Just as oil is always present in sesame seeds and is merely expressed/manifested rather than newly created, so too was he manifested. || 14 ||

**Hindi Commentary—** That water turned into the form of a golden egg covered by darkness. In that, the eternal Aniruddha first became manifest. || 14 ||
Now, for the sake of understanding the worlds within this egg, it is said:

->He is celebrated in the Vedas as the Lord Hiranyagarbha. <-
->He is called Aditya because he is the first being, and Surya because of his procreative power. || 15 ||<-

This Lord Aniruddha, endowed with the six divine glories <note>Sanskrit: *shad-guna-aishvarya*</note>, is described in the Vedas <note>Sanskrit: *chhandasi*</note> as Hiranyagarbha <note>The "Golden Womb" or "Golden Embryo"</note> because he stayed within the womb-like interior of the golden egg. This means Hiranyagarbha is his well-known alternative name in the Vedas. He is certainly called Aditya because he was the first to be manifested. Because of the birth or manifestation of the world from him, this Aniruddha is called Surya <note>The Sun</note>. The Scripture <note>Shruti</note> says: "In the beginning, Hiranyagarbha existed; once born, he was the sole lord of all beings." || 15 ||

**Hindi Commentary—** In the Vedas, he is called Hiranyagarbha; he is called Aditya because he was there in the beginning, and Surya because he is the cause of creation. || 15 ||
His form and status are described:

->This Sun, also called Savita, is the supreme light beyond the darkness. <-
->The creator of beings, he moves through the worlds, bringing them to life. || 16 ||<-

This Aniruddha, named Surya, is also known by the name Savita. The word "and" <note>Sanskrit: *cha*</note> implies his various famous attributes. He is the supreme, excellent light <note>Sanskrit: *jyoti*</note> at the end of darkness. The intended meaning is that he is the destroyer of darkness. The Scripture <note>Shruti</note> says: "I know that great Person of the color of the Sun, beyond the darkness." This Savita, the creator of beings <note>Sanskrit: *bhuta-bhavanah*</note>—the cause of the birth, maintenance, and destruction of living beings—moves through the worlds (which will be described later), illuminating them. He constantly revolves within the golden egg. || 16 ||

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Twelve]

**Commentary:** This very Aniruddha <note>A form of Vishnu associated with the mind and cosmic preservation</note> is the supreme, most luminous Sun. Crossing the realm of darkness, he wanders through all the worlds with his life-giving rays. || 16 ||

Now, explaining the phrase "Supreme Light," the author describes his nature in two further verses:

->He is renowned as the Soul of Light, the Destroyer of Darkness, and the Great One.<-
->The Rig-Veda verses are his orb, the Sama-Veda verses are his rays, and the Yajur-Veda verses are his form. || 17 ||<-
->This Lord consists of the Three Vedas; he is the Soul of Time, the Maker of Time, and the All-pervading.<-
->He is the Soul of All, the All-going, the Subtle; everything is established within him. || 18 ||<-

He is the form of light and the destroyer of darkness; therefore, this Sun, named Aniruddha, is called "The Great One" or the *Mahat-tattva* <note>The first principle of cosmic evolution in Samkhya philosophy</note>. Thus he is renowned in the Vedas and Puranas. Of this described Sun: the *Riks* (Rig-Veda mantras) constitute his physical disk or orb; the *Samans* (Sama-Veda mantras) are his *Usras* or rays; and the *Yajus* (Yajur-Veda mantras) are his *Murti* or embodied form. The word "and" implies their collective union. For this reason, the described Lord is endowed with the six divine fortunes <note>The six 'Bhagas': lordship, might, glory, splendor, dispassion, and liberation</note>. He is composed of the three Vedas. He is the form of Time and the cause of Time. He is the Lord (*Vibhu*), capable of the creation, preservation, and destruction of the universe. Therefore, he is the Soul of All, the form of the world, all-pervading (present everywhere), and yet subtle (possessing an unmanifest form). In this described Sun, the entire universe is established. By this, it is shown that there is no contradiction between his pervading and non-pervading aspects. || 17 || 18 ||

**Commentary:** Known by the names Light-form, Darkness-destroyer, and The Great, the Sun is famous. The Rig-Veda is his orb, the Sama-Veda his rays, and the Yajur-Veda his image. This Lord, embodying the three Vedas, is the Soul of Time, the Creator of Time, possessed of qualities like atom-sized subtlety, the Soul of All, the All-pervader, the Subtle, and within him alone everything is stationed. || 17 || 18 ||

Now, the author explains the half-verse "He wanders through the worlds":

->Having fashioned a wheel made of the Year upon his chariot composed of the universe,<-
->And having yoked the seven Meters as his horses, he wanders eternally. || 19 ||<-

On the chariot which is the three worlds, having fixed the "Year-Wheel" consisting of the twelve months, and having yoked the seven Vedic meters—*Gayatri, Ushnih, Anushtubh, Brihati, Pankti, Trishtubh,* and *Jagati*—as his horses. <margin>1. An alternative reading is: "He wanders thus, always in control."</margin> In the reading "The meters are yoked there as horses," it means having joined the seven horses to the chariot. Always, eternally, this one named Aniruddha wanders or revolves. || 19 ||

**Commentary:** On a chariot made of the universe, with the wheel of the Year, he makes the seven Vedic meters his horses and wanders forever. || 19 ||

Now he describes his essential nature and the birth of Brahma:

->Three-quarters of him are immortal and secret; one quarter has become manifest.<-
->That Lord created Brahma, the Ego-principle, for the sake of creating the universe. || 20 ||<-

Three-quarters of this soul of the Vedas, the immortal three steps, are to be known as residing in the heavens. Therefore, this is secret and inaccessible. The fourth step or quarter became manifest and perceptible in the form of the world, consisting of both the stationary <note>plants and minerals</note> and the moving <note>animals and humans</note>. The Scripture <note>original: "Shruti," referring to the Purusha Sukta of the Rig Veda</note> also clearly states: "The three-footed Purusha rose high above; one foot of his was here again." That Lord, named Aniruddha <note>a manifestation of Vishnu representing the cosmic intellect</note>, is capable of all production. He created the personified Brahma, who is the embodiment of the principle of Ego <note>term: Ahamkara - the "I-maker" or principle of individual identity</note>, for the purpose of world-creation. || 20 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Three of his steps remain hidden like nectar. The manifest world exists only in the fourth step. That Lord produced Brahma, in the form of Ego, for the creation of the universe. || 20 ||

Now, having appointed the created personage Brahma for the sake of world-creation, the Lord himself remains circulating. Thus it is said:

### Having given him the excellent Vedas, and having established
### the Grandfather of all worlds within the Egg,
### He himself then moves about, illuminating all. || 21 ||

Now, after the production of Brahma, the Lord named Aniruddha himself, having given those excellent and superior Vedas to the created personage Brahma so that he might create according to the path prescribed in the Vedas, and having established that Brahma—the "Grandfather" of all worlds—within the Golden Egg <note>original: "suvarnanda," the Hiranyagarbha or cosmic womb</note>, He moves about while illuminating and manifesting the creation. || 21 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Having given the supreme Vedas to that Brahma and establishing him in the Egg as the Grandfather of all worlds, He Himself moves about in a state of radiance. || 21 ||

### From his mind the Moon was born, and from his eyes
### the Sun, the storehouse of splendors. || 22 ||

Now, after attaining his authority, Brahma, who holds the form of the principle of Ego, directed his mind <note>inner faculty</note> toward creation. This means the desire arose: "I shall perform creation." Subsequently, from that mind, the Moon was born. The meaning is that by the thought "Let there be a Moon," the Moon was produced. From his two eyes, the Sun—the source and storehouse of all lights—was produced. This is because the sense of sight is composed of the element of fire/light. || 22 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** After that, when Brahma, the embodiment of Ego, set his mind to create, the Moon was born from his mind, and the Sun, the treasury of light, was born from the brilliance of his eyes. || 22 ||

### Great Elements were born. || 23 ||

By the desire "Let there be Space" from the mind, Space <note>original: "Kham/Akasha," the ether or void</note> emerged from the Self. From Space, in successive order, came Wind—

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Twelve]

...water, and earth. "From space came air, from air fire, from fire water, and from water earth." In this way, by the increase of one quality <note>original: "guna"</note> at each step, the five great elements <note>The Mahabhutas: Space, Air, Fire, Water, and Earth</note> were produced. The word "only" in the original verse excludes any number less or more than five. To be clear: Space possesses the quality of sound; Air possesses two qualities, sound and touch; Fire possesses three qualities, sound, touch, and form; Water possesses four qualities, sound, touch, form, and taste; and Earth possesses five qualities, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. || 23 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** From the mind first came space, then air, fire, water, and earth; by the increase of one quality, the five great elements were produced. || 23 ||

### Now, describing the nature of the Moon and Sun, he explains the origin of the five planets:

->**The Sun and Moon are Fire and Soma; from them, Mars and the others,**<-
->**were produced from fire, earth, space, water, and air respectively. || 24 ||**<-

The Sun and Moon, whose origins were mentioned previously, are of the nature of fire and soma <note>Soma here refers to the cooling, watery principle</note>. The Sun is of the nature of fire, a globe of light, because it is visible to the eye. The Moon is of the nature of soma; since the word "soma" refers to the nectar in the middle, it is a globe of water. The grammatical usage of "Agni-shomau" <note>Fire and Soma</note> follows Vedic rules. After that, the five "star-planets" <note>the visible planets excluding the Sun and Moon</note> beginning with Mars were produced respectively from fire, earth, space, water, and air. The word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> implies that in each planet, its respective element is predominant while the other elements are present in equal, smaller portions. Mars was produced from fire, which is why it is called "the glowing coal" <note>original: "Angaraka"</note>. Mercury from earth. Jupiter from space. Venus from water. Saturn from air. || 24 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Of the nature of fire and soma are the Sun and Moon; thereafter the group of planets starting with Mars were produced from fire, earth, space, water, and air in that order. || 24 ||

### Now he describes the Zodiac signs and the Lunar Mansions:

->**Again, the Controller divided himself into twelve parts called Signs,**<-
->**and further into the form of the twenty-seven Lunar Mansions. || 25 ||**<-

Furthermore, he divided himself into twelve parts in twelve places known as the Signs <note>original: "Rashi"; the Zodiac signs</note>. This means he divided the circle imagined by the mind into twelve parts to create the Zodiac. A second time, he divided himself into the form of the Lunar Mansions <note>original: "Nakshatra"</note> consisting of twenty-seven parts. This means he made that same mentally-conceived circle into twenty-seven divisions. If one asks why he did not make more or fewer divisions, or what the governing rule for these numbers was, the text says: "The Controller" <note>original: "Vashi"</note>. One who has his will under his own control is "Vashi"; because he is independent, he is not subject to the commands of others. The sense is that he created these specific numbers of divisions by his own will. It follows that the stars which manifest these twenty-seven divisions were then created. || 25 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The Controller, Brahma, then divided the mentally-conceived circle into 12 parts as Signs and again into 27 parts as Lunar Mansions. || 25 ||

# Chapter 12. Including Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. (195)

Now, he describes how the Creator made the world of moving and non-moving beings:

> ### Then he fashioned the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings, beginning with the gods;
> ### Creating the primordial natures from the upper, middle, and lower streams. || 26 ||

**Sanskrit Commentary:** After the creation of the planets and the righteous beings, he created the universe—the world consisting of conscious and unconscious beings—beginning with the gods, humans, and demons. He did this by creating the "primordial natures" <note>Prakriti</note> characterized by the divisions of the three qualities: Lucidity, Passion, and Inertia <note>Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas</note>, arising from the upper, middle, and lower streams (representing the superior, middling, and inferior manifestations). || 26 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** After that, having created the superior, inferior, and following natures, he constructed the moving and non-moving universe, including gods and humans. || 26 ||

Now, he describes how he established the positions of the created objects:

> ### Having created them according to the divisions of qualities and actions, in the same sequence as before;
> ### He ordained their respective divisions according to the vision of the Vedas. || 27 ||

**Sanskrit Commentary:** "Qualities" refers to Lucidity, Passion, and Inertia. "Actions" refers to the good and evil deeds accumulated in previous births. By the division and combination of these two, and following the sequence of creation mentioned previously (such as the Sun and Moon), he created the moving and non-moving world—gods, humans, demons, the earth, mountains, and so on. He then ordained their "divisions"—their specific locations and states—according to their respective places and times, following the methods declared in the Vedas <note>The ancient sacred scriptures</note>. || 27 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Having performed the creation in the previous order according to the divisions of qualities and actions, he established the divisions according to the methods stated in the Vedas. || 27 ||

He specifies for whom these divisions were made:

> ### For the planets, constellations, and stars; for the earth and the entire universe;
> ### For the gods, demons, and humans, as well as the perfected beings, in their proper order. || 28 ||

**Sanskrit Commentary:** The Lord <note>Vibhu</note>, namely Brahma, who is capable of such arrangement, established the positions in space for the spheres of the planets and constellations, for the earth, and for the three worlds. The word "or" <note>Sanskrit: vā</note> here is used in a cumulative sense (meaning "and"). There, the planets and constellations have positions that vary according to time, while the earth has a fixed position. Within the earth, the three worlds are positioned according to their respective regions. There, in the proper order and as is fitting, he established the locations for the gods, demons, humans, and perfected beings <note>Siddhas</note>. The word "and" is used to include all these together. || 28 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Lord Brahma, endowed with supernatural powers like atomization <note>Anima</note>, caused the planets, constellations, stars, the earth, the universe, and the gods, demons, and perfected beings to be situated in their respective assigned orders. || 28 ||

Now, a question arises: since space exists everywhere, did Brahma, situated in the middle of the Cosmic Egg, place the planets, stars, and earth in the space outside the Cosmic Egg or within it? To this, he says:

> ### This Cosmic Egg is hollow; within it are the Earth, the Atmosphere, and the Heavens.
> ### It is like the joining of two shallow bowls, forming a spherical shape. || 29 ||

<summary>This page describes the creation of the physical and spiritual inhabitants of the universe based on their past karma and inherent qualities, and begins to define the structure of the "Cosmic Egg" (Brahmanda) as a hollow sphere containing all realms.</summary>

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Twelve]

This previously mentioned Golden Egg <note>original: "suvarnandam," the cosmic egg of creation</note>, presided over by Brahma, is hollow and consists of space. Within that space, this world—comprising the Earth, the atmosphere, and the heavens—is situated, and not outside of it. Now, one might ask how the Egg can contain an internal space if it is not spherical; to this, the author says: "of two hemispheres." A *kataha* <note>a shallow bowl or cauldron</note> is a hemispherical vessel with space inside. Two of these, being equal—the word "equal" is used to exclude any difference in size—joined face-to-face in a pair, form a spherical shape. Thus, there is no contradiction. || 29 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** The Earth, atmosphere, and heavens are situated within the spacious Universe. It is spherical in shape, like two bowls joined together. || 29 ||

Now, while stating the inner circumference of the Universe, he explains in two verses how the planets and other bodies wander in their respective places within space:

### The circumference within the Universe is called the Orbit of the Sky.
### Within that, the stars revolve, and beneath them, one under the other in order: || 30 ||
### Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.
### Below them are situated the Siddhas, the Vidyadharas, and the clouds. || 31 ||

The inner circumference of the Universe, measured as a circle, is called the "Orbit of the Sky" <term>Vyomakaksha: the outermost limit of the astronomical universe</term>, which will be described later. In the middle of that, in the space of the Universe, occurs the revolution of the stars—all of them being at an equal distance from the center in every direction. Likewise, at equal intervals below them, one under the other in sequence, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon revolve below. The *Siddhas* and *Vidyadharas* <note>semi-divine celestial beings</note> are situated below the Moon, one under the other in space. Because these latter groups are not situated within the *Pravaha* wind <note>the celestial wind believed to drive the planets</note>, they do not revolve like the Moon. || 30 || 31 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** In the Universe, the name of the circumference is the Orbit of the Sky; within it is the revolution of the stars. Below that, in order, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, the Sun, Mercury, and the Moon revolve. Below those are the groups of Siddhas and Vidyadharas, and at the very bottom, all the clouds are situated. || 30 || 31 ||

Now, he describes the position of the Earth:

### In the very middle of the Universe, the Earth-globe stands in space,
### Bearing the supreme power of Brahma, which has the nature of support. || 32 ||

In the middle of the Egg—that is, the Universe—at the central point in space, the Earth-globe stands. Now, since it is impossible for an object without a support to remain in space, one might ask how the Earth-globe remains fixed; to this, he provides a description of the Earth: "Bearing..." It stands bearing <insert>holding</insert> the supreme power of Brahma, which is characterized by "support"—the power of remaining in place without a visible foundation. Thus, there is no contradiction. By this, the two questions—"What is the shape of the Earth?" and "What is its support?"—are answered. || 32 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** By the strength of the supreme supporting power of Brahma, the Earth-globe is situated in the midst of space, in the very center of all regions of the Universe. || 32 ||

Now, the author provides the answer to the question: "What are the seven subterranean realms?"—

> **Within its interior are seven layers, the abodes of Serpents and Demons.**
> **Endowed with divine medicinal herbs and elixirs, these subterranean realms are enchanting. || 33 ||**

Within the interior layers of this terrestrial globe <note>the Earth</note>, there are seven cave-like divisions known as Atala, Vitala, Sutala, and so on. These subterranean regions are beautiful and captivating. One might ask: "If humans and others live on the surface of the globe, who lives there?" To answer this, the author provides the description: <term>abodes of Serpents and Demons</term> <note>original: "nāgāsura-samāśrayāḥ"</note>. These regions serve as the home for serpents led by Vasuki <note>the King of Serpents in mythology</note> and for the Daityas <note>a race of giants or demons</note>. Furthermore, since the sun does not travel there, one might wonder how the inhabitants conduct their lives in darkness. To this, the second description is given: <term>endowed with divine medicinal herbs and elixirs</term> <note>original: "divyauṣadhi-rasopetāḥ"</note>. These are divine plants that are self-luminous. Their light allows for daily activities, and the sight of them sustains the lives of the people there. || 33 ||

**Hindi Commentary—** At the interior of the Earth globe are the seven realms such as Patala, inhabited by Serpents and Demons; they are enchanting and filled with self-luminous trees. || 33 ||

Now, having described the globe, the author explains the position of Mount Meru, which exceeds the diameter of the Earth to the North and South—

> **A mountain composed of gold and a collection of many gems,**
> **Meru passes through the middle of the Earth globe and emerges on both sides. || 34 ||**

The mountain situated in the middle of the Earth globe is named Meru. It is a <term>collection of many gems</term>, meaning it is composed of various types of jewels like rubies and diamonds. It is also <term>made of Jāmbūnada gold</term>. As stated by the teacher <term>Bhaskaracharya</term> <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note>: "From the juice dripping from the ripe Jambu fruit flows the Jambu river; the mud of its banks becomes gold. The hosts of Gods and perfected beings constantly drink from it, as it has the power of nectar." Thus, it is made of gold. It emerges from both sides of the Earth's surface, extending beyond the radius. The Earth globe is pierced through the middle by this rod-shaped golden mountain. Therefore, the name <term>Earth-bearer</term> <note>original: "bhūbhṛt," a common Sanskrit word for mountain</note> is literally meaningful. || 34 ||

**Hindi Commentary—** Located in the center of the Earth and emerging from both poles is Meru, made of various gems and beautified by the Jambu river gold. || 34 ||

Next, he explains that Gods and others live on the upper part of Meru, while Demons live on the lower part—

> **Upon the upper part of it stay the Gods with Indra, and the Great Sages.**
> **Below them are the Demons; likewise, they stay there hating one another. || 35 ||**

On the upper part of Meru stay the Gods including Indra, as well as the Great Sages. The word "and" should be understood to connect them. They are stationed there. Below, in the lower region of Meru, are the Demons. "Likewise" means they stay there just as the Gods stay in the upper part. If one asks why the Gods and Demons do not stay together in one place, the author says: "hating." They harbor mutual hatred toward one another. Thus, between the Gods and Demons there is a constant...
