# The Surya Siddhanta – [Chapter Ten]

Because of their mutual hatred, it is impossible for them to reside in the same place. Therefore, the exalted gods and the great sages <note>Maharshis</note>, fearing the demons, reside in the upper portion. The inferior demons are situated in the lower portion. This is the intended meaning. || 35 ||

**Commentary:** In the upper part (the northern direction), the gods led by Indra and the assembly of great sages are located. In the lower part (the south) is the abode of the demons <note>Asuras</note>. Due to their mutual hostility, they have taken refuge in opposite directions. || 35 ||

### Now, the placement of the oceans on the globe is described:

> Then, all around the circumference, the Great Ocean gradually covers half the globe.
> It stands like a girdle <note>mekhala</note> around the Earth, creating the division between gods and demons. || 36 ||

From the staff-like Meru <note>the central axis of the Earth</note>, this visible Great Ocean extends in every direction. In a continuous sequence, it forms a circumference like a waistband or girdle for the Earth. It acts as the boundary line dividing the spheres of the gods and the demons on the terrestrial globe. This establishes that the half of the globe north of the ocean is Jambu-dvipa <note>the island-continent of the humans/gods</note>, and the half of the globe south of the ocean—comprising the other six islands and six oceans—belongs to the demons. The salt ocean exists as a circumference in the middle of the globe, aligned with the axis of Meru. Since a girdle sits below the waist, the implication is that the northern hemisphere touches the edge of the ocean that encompasses the southern hemisphere. || 36 ||

**Commentary:** Within this, the Great Ocean is situated in the shape of a circle, like a girdle. The ocean has divided the globe between the gods and the demons. || 36 ||

### Now, it is stated that there are four cities in the four divisions at the beginning of Jambu-dvipa, on the northern shore of the ocean's circumference:

> All around the center of Meru, at equal distances in the directions of the ocean,
> in the island-continents, there are cities built by the gods in the East and other quarters. || 37 ||

"From the center of Meru" means from the middle region of the staff-like Meru, which is the core of the globe. "All around" means on the surface of the globe. At equal parts of the ocean that forms the circumference, at the starting points of the island of Jambu-dvipa, in the four cardinal directions (East, South, West, and North), there are four cities built by the gods. The essential meaning is that on the northern shore of the ocean, at the very beginning of Jambu-dvipa, four cities exist at equal intervals in the designated East, South, West, and North directions of the globe. || 37 ||

**Commentary:** In the four directions—East and so on—around the central region of Meru, within the encircling ocean, there are four cities constructed by the gods. || 37 ||

### Now, the names of these cities and their positions within the technical divisions known as "Varshas" (regions) of Jambu-dvipa are clarified in the following three verses—

# Chapter 12 | With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries ( 199 )

> On the eastern quarter of the Earth's circle, in the region of Bhadrasva, is the famous city known as Yamakoti, featuring ramparts and arches of gold. || 38 ||
> To the south, in the region of Bharata <note>India</note>, is the great city of Lanka; to the west, in the region called Ketumala, the city known as Romaka is celebrated. || 39 ||
> To the north, in the region of Kuru, the city named Siddhapuri is renowned. In that place dwell the Great-Souled <term>Siddhas</term> <note>Perfected beings or masters of yoga</note>, free from all suffering. || 40 ||

On the globe, where the rod-like Meru <note>The celestial North Pole or central axis</note> emerges at both poles, the Earth is divided. By a vertical circular line, the globe is split into two halves, East and West; by a horizontal circular line, it is split again. Thus, like the walls of a fortress, there are four quarters of the Earth. On the eastern boundary of the upper section, at one-fourth of the ocean's circumference, in the region named Bhadrasva, at the junction of the upper and lower sections, lies a city famous by the name **Yamakoti**. It is renowned for having palaces and gateways fashioned from gold. To the south, at the junction of the two upper sections—being south of Meru—in the region named Bharata, is the great city named **Lanka**, similarly famous for its golden walls and arches. To the west, at the junction of the western and lower sections, in the region named Ketumala, the city of **Romaka** is described. To the north, at the junction of the two lower sections, in the region named Kuru, the city named **Siddhapuri** is proclaimed. The author explains that the name "Siddhapuri" is literal: in that city, the *Siddhas*—those who practice yoga and whose souls are greater and more excellent than ours—dwell eternally, free from all pain. || 38 || 39 || 40 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In the eastern direction, at one-fourth of the Earth's circle, is the Bhadrasva region; within it is the city of Yamakoti. It is said to be surrounded by golden walls and ceremonial arches. In the southern direction is Bharata-varsha; in its center is the great city of Lanka. In the middle of the west, in Ketumala-varsha, is the city of Romaka. In the north, within Kuru-varsha, is situated Siddhapuri. There, the Great-Souled Siddhas reside, liberated from all hardships. || 38 || 39 || 40 ||

Now, the distance between these four cities and their distance from Meru is described:

> These cities are situated at intervals of one-fourth of the Earth's circumference from one another. To the north of them is Meru, the abode of the gods, located at that same distance. || 41 ||

These aforementioned cities are established at intervals of one-fourth of the Earth's total circumference from each other. The word "and" connects this to the previous description. From these cities, Meru—the previously mentioned "abode of the gods" inhabited by celestial beings—is located to the north, at a distance equal to one-fourth of the Earth's circumference.

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Twelve]

...situated at a distance of a quarter <note>original: "panchashat" - referring to 90 degrees or a quadrant of the Earth's circumference</note> of the Earth's circle. The word "only" is used to exclude any greater or lesser distance. The word "and" is used to connect this with the first half of the verse. || 41 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** These cities are situated at a distance of one-fourth of the Earth's circumference from each other. Directly to the north of them is that Mount Meru, where the gods reside. || 41 ||

Now, he states that these cities are located on the equator <term>Niraksha-desha: "land without latitude," referring to the equator</term>:

> The Sun, moving along the equinoctial circle, passes directly above them.
> In those cities, there is no equinoctial shadow, nor is any elevation of the pole observed. || 42 ||

Above those aforementioned cities, the Sun moves while situated on the equator <note>the celestial equator</note>. This means on the day when day and night are equal, the path the Sun follows is the equinoctial circle. For this reason, in those cities, there is no "equinoctial shadow" <term>Vishuvat-chhaya: the shadow cast by a vertical gnomon at noon on the day of the equinox</term>, because the east-west circle of those cities is identical to the equinoctial circle. At midday, when the Sun is positioned there, no shadow is observed. Therefore, in those cities, the "elevation of the pole" <note>the height of the North Star above the horizon</note>, which constitutes the degrees of latitude, is not accepted or acknowledged. The meaning is that due to the absence of latitude, their status as equatorial regions is established. || 42 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** The Sun, situated at the equator, travels directly over them. For this reason, there is neither an equinoctial shadow nor an elevation of the pole there. || 42 ||

Now, wishing to demonstrate the absence of colatitude and latitude respectively at Meru and the equatorial cities, he first describes the position of the two Polar Stars:

> At the two poles of Meru, the two Polar Stars are fixed in the sky.
> For those staying in the equatorial regions, both stars appear on the horizon. || 43 ||

At the two ends of Meru, the North and South, the two Polar Stars situated in the sky are respectively directly overhead in the center of the sky <note>zenith</note>. For those staying in the equatorial regions—the people in the cities mentioned previously—both the North and South Polar Stars are "resting on the horizon," meaning they appear on the horizon line of those locations. || 43 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** In the sky at the center of both poles <note>Meru</note>, two Polar Stars are situated in the South and North. Because of being in an equatorial region, both are situated on the horizon line. || 43 ||

Now, explaining that for this very reason there is an absence of latitude and a maximum of colatitude in those cities, he describes the maximum latitude at Meru:

> Therefore, there is no elevation of the pole in those cities, as the two Polar Stars sit on the horizon.
> At Meru, the degrees of colatitude are ninety, and the degrees of latitude are the same. || 44 ||

In those aforementioned cities, because both stars rest on the horizon, there is no "elevation of the axis" <note>latitude</note>. Since latitude is defined as the height of the Pole Star above the horizon, its absence follows from the star being on the horizon. Furthermore, in those cities where the poles are on the horizon, the degrees of colatitude <term>Lambamsha: the complement of latitude (90 minus latitude)</term> are ninety, because ninety minus zero latitude equals ninety. From the zenith to the poles on the horizon is the nature of colatitude. Similarly, at Meru, the latitude is [ninety]...

This is established by the facts. By this, the answer to the first question posed by the Great Teacher Bhaskara is indicated: "If one city is north of another, what is the difference in their latitudes? By the proportion of the degrees of the circle, the measurement of the circumference is rightly declared." Now, wishing to answer the question regarding the arrangement of day and night, he first describes the beginning of the day for the Gods and the Demons:

### When the Sun is at the beginning of Aries, in the section of the Gods, it becomes visible to the Gods.
### Likewise, when it moves to the beginning of Libra, it becomes visible to the Demons. || 45 ||

The circumference circle at the boundary of the ocean characterized by Jambu-island <note>the terrestrial world</note> is in the middle of the globe; the circle in the sky aligned with it is the Equator <term>Vishuvad-vritta: the celestial equator</term>. There, the Ecliptic <term>Kranti-vritta: the sun's path</term> is attached at two points six signs apart; these are the locations of Aries and Libra. It revolves via the Provector wind <note>Pravaha-vayu: the cosmic wind believed to drive celestial motion</note> along the path of the Equator. From the position of Aries, the position of Cancer is twenty-four degrees to the north of the Equator. The position of Capricorn is twenty-four degrees to the south of the Equator. It revolves in its own place by the Provector wind. Thus, the regions of the Ecliptic remain in their respective places by the Provector wind. 

There, at the beginning of Aries, the Sun is in the "Section of the Gods"—as previously stated, Jambu-island is divided into sections for Gods and Demons. The zodiac signs connected to that, from Aries to Virgo, constitute the Northern Hemisphere <term>Uttara-gola</term>. The Sun situated there, at the beginning of Aries, goes to—meaning attains—its first appearance after six months to the Gods residing at the northern tip of Meru. This is because the Equator serves as their horizon. Similarly, for the Daityas <note>Demons</note> residing at the southern tip of Meru, it is said: "Likewise, its movement in the section of the Daityas." The signs from Libra to Pisces, situated in the southern division starting from the ocean, constitute the Southern Hemisphere. The Sun, moving in such a manner, attains its first appearance after its disappearance at the beginning of Libra. For them also, the Equator is the horizon. || 45 ||

**Hindi Commentary—** When the Sun is situated in the section of the Gods starting with Aries, it is visible to the Gods. When it is situated in the section of the Demons starting with Libra, it is visible to the Demons. || 45 ||

Now, in this context, he provides the answer to the previously asked question regarding why the rays are fierce in summer:

### Because of extreme proximity, the rays of the Sun are fierce in summer
### In the section of the Gods; but for the Demons, it is the opposite—faintness in winter. || 46 ||

"Because of that"—meaning because of the cause consisting of the Sun's movement in the northern and southern hemispheres. "In the section of the Gods"—in Jambu-island. Because of extreme proximity, meaning the Sun being very close, in the summer season, the rays of the Sun's orb of light are sharp and very hot. For the Demons, [the opposite occurs] in the section of the Gods... <note>The text cuts off here, explaining the inverse relationship for the southern hemisphere</note>

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Twelve]

Because of the alignment, in the portion belonging to the demons <note>the Southern Hemisphere</note>, in the southern regions beyond the ocean during the winter season, the rays of the sun are extremely hot because the sun is very close. Otherwise, if the sun were far away, the rays would be dull and lack extreme heat. In the portion belonging to the gods <note>the Northern Hemisphere</note>, the rays are dull during the winter season. Therefore, there is an excess of cold there. In the portion belonging to the demons, during their summer, the rays are dull and there is an excess of cold <note>referring to the inverse relationship of the hemispheres</note>. Thus, for the portion of the gods, the sun is distant in the southern hemisphere and near in the northern hemisphere; the meaning is that the noon zenith distances are respectively greater and smaller. || 46 ||

**Commentary:** For this reason, due to extreme proximity, the sun's rays are intense for the gods in their region. Otherwise, in winter, they attain dullness. || 46 ||

Now, having stated that the portion of the gods begins with Aries <note>the vernal equinox</note>, the author clarifies this under the guise of describing the day and night of the gods and demons:

->**At the equinox, the gods and demons behold the sun**<-
->**situated upon the horizon. For them, the left and right**<-
->**halves of the year are day and night respectively. || 47 ||**<-

At the time of the equinox, the gods and demons see the sun situated on the horizon. This is because the celestial equator, being in the middle of the sphere relative to their positions, serves as their horizon. For these gods and demons, what are mutually "left and right" (counter-clockwise and clockwise) become respectively day and night. The idea is this: The northern part of the earth is the gods' own, hence "right" <term>Savya: auspicious or clockwise</term> to them, while it is "left" <term>Apasavya: inauspicious or counter-clockwise</term> to the demons as it is not their own. Similarly, the southern part of the earth is the demons' own and "right" to them, but "left" to the gods. Therefore, the "left and right" parts of the demons—the northern and southern hemispheres—are respectively the day and night of the gods. The "left and right" parts of the gods—the southern and northern hemispheres—are the day and night of the demons. Otherwise, the consistency of the phrase "mutually left and right" would not be established. Therefore, it was previously said "beginning with Aries," etc. || 47 ||

**Commentary:** On the day of the equinox, the gods and demons see the sun on the horizon line. In this manner, due to the north and south directions, there is a mutual reversal of day and night. || 47 ||

Now, suspecting ambiguity in the latter half of the previous verse, the author clarifies the meaning through two verses by describing the first and second halves of the day:

->**Rising at the beginning of Aries, the sun, moving through**<-
->**three signs northward, completes the first half of the**<-
->**day for the inhabitants of Mount Meru. || 48 ||**<-
->**Moving through Cancer and the following signs, he likewise**<-
->**completes the latter half of their day. In the same way,**<-
->**through Libra and the following three, and Capricorn and the**<-
->**following three, he does the same for the enemies of the gods. || 49 ||**<-

At the beginning of Aries, at the part of the ecliptic situated on the celestial equator near the star Revati, the sun rises and becomes visible. Moving "northward"—meaning gradually and sequentially—through the three signs situated in the northern quarter (Aries, Taurus, and Gemini), he completes the "first half of the day" for the gods residing on Mount Meru <note>the North Pole</note>. This means he makes it full. At the end of Gemini...

The result is that when the Sun is at the meridian of those staying at Meru <note>The North Pole</note>, it is midday. Passing through the three signs beginning with Cancer—namely Cancer, Leo, and Virgo—in that order, the Sun completes the second half or the latter part of the day. The word "only" is used to exclude any other connection. The result is that at the end of Virgo, sunset occurs for those staying at Meru.

Now he speaks of the Daityas <note>The demons or Asuras residing at the South Pole</note>. "Beginning with Libra": for the enemies of the gods staying at the southern tip of Meru, the Sun passes through the three signs beginning with Libra—Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius—and then through Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces in that order. The word "and" implies the first and second halves of the day in the order of Libra and Capricorn. The word "only" excludes anything other than what was stated. This means the Sun completes their day. The result is that when the Sun is at the end of Sagittarius, it is midday for the Daityas, and when the Sun is at the end of Pisces, it is sunset for them. || 48 || 49 ||

<term>Hindi Commentary</term> — For the inhabitants of the North Pole, when the Sun is in Aries and the following signs, sunrise occurs for three signs in order towards the north; then it is the first half of the day for the gods living at Meru. When the Sun is in Cancer and the following northern signs, it is the latter half of the day. Similarly, in Libra and Capricorn, it is the first and second halves of the day for the Asuras. || 48 || 49 ||

Now, the answer to the question regarding the gods and demons is established:

->**Therefore, their day and night are mutually reversed.**<-
->**The measure of a day-and-night is from the Sun's completion of a revolution. || 50 ||**<-

"Therefore," due to the stated reason, for those gods and Daityas, day and night exist "mutually" or reciprocally by "reversal" or inversion. This result has been explained many times before. How does this happen? He gives the answer to the question "from the Sun's completion of a revolution" by saying: "the measure of a day-and-night." The measure of a day-and-night for the gods and Daityas comes from the Sun's passage through the twelve signs beginning with Aries. The word "and" connects this with the first half of the verse, making it clear that the previously mentioned cause is the same for both. || 50 ||

<term>Hindi Commentary</term> — Therefore, their day and night are mutually swapped. The time taken for the completion of the Sun's <term>Bhagana</term> <note>A full revolution through the zodiac</note> is indeed their day-and-night. || 50 ||

Now he explains the result and the logic of the two verses beginning with "Rising in Aries":

->**The halves of day and night for these are reversed at the end of the solstices.**<-
->**The Gods and Demons each consider themselves to be on top. || 51 ||**<-

For these gods and Daityas, at the "end of the solstices" <note>the solstitial points</note>, the halves of the day and night are "reversed" or inverted. The result is that when it is midday or midnight for the gods, it is respectively midnight or midday for the Daityas; and where it is midday or midnight for the Daityas, it is respectively midnight or midday for the gods. He gives the reason for this: "On top." The gods and Daityas, residing at the northern and southern tips of Meru, "consider" or accept "themselves" to be in the "upper part" or the higher portion. In reality, because of the <term>spherical nature of the earth</term>, everything is equal, and absolute "upper" and "lower" parts are impossible. Thus, the gods, thinking of themselves as being above relative to the Daityas, consider the Daityas to be below. And the Daityas, thinking of themselves as being above relative to the gods' position, place the gods below. This is the intended meaning.

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Twelve]

Because of the opposite positions of the Gods and the Demons <note>The "Gods" reside at the North Pole (Meru) and "Demons" at the South Pole (Meru-adhas)</note>, it follows that their days and nights are likewise reversed. || 51 ||

**Commentary** — Midday and midnight occur at the southern and northern solstices. This happens in an opposite manner for the Gods and the Demons. Furthermore, each group considers their own location to be "upward." || 51 ||

Now, the author applies this principle of "up" and "down" to others on the globe by way of an illustration:

->Others also, situated on the same diameter, consider each other to be "below."<-
->Such is the case for those in Bhadrasva and Ketumala, as well as those in Lanka and Siddhapura. || 52 ||<-

"Others" refers to humans on the globe other than the Gods and Demons. The word "also" is used to include them in the same logic. Those who are <term>situated on the same diameter</term> <note>original: "sama-sutra-stha"; literally "standing on the same string," referring to antipodes</note>, being separated by the diameter of the earth, consider one another to be underneath. He gives an example: <term>those in Bhadrasva and Ketumala</term>. These names specifically refer to the cities of Yamakoti and Romaka-pattana <note>Yamakoti is traditionally placed 90 degrees east of Lanka, and Romaka 90 degrees west</note>. Because they are separated by the earth's diameter, they naturally view each other as being "below." The final part of the verse regarding Lanka and Siddhapura is self-explanatory. || 52 ||

**Commentary** — Similarly, those on the same diameter consider each other to be underneath. For example, <term>Bhadrasva</term> and <term>Ketumala</term>, or the inhabitants of <term>Lanka</term> and <term>Siddhapura</term>, are situated at opposite ends of a diameter. || 52 ||

Now, to confirm that these directions are merely conceptual, he says:

->Everywhere on this terrestrial globe, people regard their own place as being "on top."<-
->Since this globe stands in the void, where can there be an "up" or a "down" for it? || 53 ||<-

Everywhere on the globe, in all regions, people consider the place where they stand to be the "upper" part. Because of this, everyone on the globe is "up." There is no one who is truly "down." The reality is that "up" and "down" are relative to one's position and not absolute. Otherwise, if one were truly "down," there would be a fear of falling, which would make the habitation of humans on the globe impossible. He gives the reason for this: "in the void." Because the globe of the Earth is situated in the center of the space of the universe <note>the "Akasha" or ether</note>, and because space is equal in all directions around the globe, absolute "up" and "down" are impossible. He clarifies his view: for a globe suspended in the middle of space, in what direction could "up" be? Or in what direction could "down" be? Since space is uniform all around, it is impossible to define "up" and "down" for the Earth itself. || 53 ||

**Commentary** — Because the Earth is a globe, everyone everywhere considers their own place to be situated "upward." In a globe situated in the middle of the void, what is "low"? And where is "high"? || 53 ||

But if this Earth appears flat like a mirror to our eyes, how can it be said to be global? To this, he replies:

->Because of the smallness of their bodies, people see this circular Earth as a flat disk,<-
->looking out toward the horizon from their own position. || 54 ||<-

# Chapter 12 | With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries

People, from the place where they stand, see this visible Earth as circular and flat like a disc in every direction. <note>The text uses the word 'mandala' (disc/circle) to describe the perceived flatness.</note> The word "even" is used here for emphasis. Therefore, although the Earth is actually spherical in reality, there is no contradiction in it appearing as a flat mirror-like surface. The reason for this is given: "due to the smallness of the body." This means because of the short stature of humans. Thus, to a very small human standing on the surface of the massive Earth, the sphere does not appear as a globe because their range of vision is so limited; instead, it appears as a flat circle, because a hundredth part of a great circle's circumference appears straight. Otherwise, the calculations of arcs in the first chapter would be inconsistent. || 54 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Because they have small bodies, people see this Earth as a circular shape all around them. || 54 ||

Now, wishing to explain the measurement of day and night in places other than the North Pole (Meru), such as the equator, the author describes the rotation of the celestial sphere at the poles and the equator:

->It rotates clockwise for the Gods, and counter-clockwise for the enemies of the Gods.<-
->Above the equator, this celestial sphere always moves toward the west. || 55 ||<-

This visible celestial sphere—the physical globe inhabited by the stars—rotates "clockwise" for the Gods who reside at the North Pole (Meru). This means it moves in the order of East and so on. <note>original: "savyam" - clockwise/rightward</note>. It rotates "counter-clockwise" for the demons (Daityas) who reside at the South Pole. This means it moves in the reverse order of the directions, starting from the East. <note>original: "apasavyam" - counter-clockwise/leftward</note>. At the equator <term>Niraksha: the place with no latitude</term>, the celestial sphere directly overhead always rotates toward the west. This is because the celestial sphere rotates on an axis fixed by the two Poles, and at the equator, those Poles lie on the horizon. || 55 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** This celestial sphere rotates clockwise (from south to north-west) for the Gods, counter-clockwise for the demons, and for people at the equator, it moves westward directly overhead. || 55 ||

Now, while stating the measurement of day and night at the equator, he explains that elsewhere the measurements become longer or shorter:

->Therefore, there the day is thirty ghatikas, and the night is the same.<-
->Increase and decrease are always opposite in the regions of the Gods and Demons. || 56 ||<-

Because the celestial sphere rotates directly overhead at the equator, the day there is thirty <term>ghatikas: a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term> <note>30 ghatikas = 12 hours</note>. The night is likewise thirty ghatikas. Since the horizon circle there passes through both poles and bisects the sphere, it is logical that day and night are equal. In the regions of the Gods and Demons—meaning the northern continent of Jambu-dvipa and the southern regions beyond the ocean—the increase and decrease of day and night are always "opposite" to one another (except when the sun is on the equator). This means: when the day decreases and the night increases in Jambu-dvipa, then in the southern region, the day increases and the night decreases respectively. In Jambu—

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Twelve]

When there is an increase in the day and a decrease in the night in the Island <note>Jambudvipa, the northern hemisphere</note>, then in the southern region, there is a corresponding decrease and increase in the day and night respectively. Thus, the increases and decreases in the southern region are the opposite of the increases and decreases in the day or night in the Island of the Rose-Apple <note>Jambudvipa</note>, as appropriate. The mathematical rationale here is: because the horizon circle is connected to the poles, it does not pass through the center of the celestial sphere <note>except at the equator</note>; therefore, the day and night are never equal except on the day of the equinox. However, the total duration of a full day and night remains sixty *ghatikas* <term>Ghatika: a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term>. — 56

**Commentary:** At the equator <note>literally "the region without latitude"</note>, the day is always thirty *ghatikas* and the night is also thirty. In the division between the Gods and Demons <note>the North and South poles/hemispheres</note>, the increase and decrease occur in a manner opposite to the passage of the day. — 56

->Now, he clarifies the meaning of the latter half of this verse with two subsequent verses:<-

> From the beginning of Aries, there is always an increase [of the day] which becomes greater toward the north.
> In the portion of the Gods, there is a decrease in night; the opposite is true for the Demons. — 57
> From the beginning of Libra, the decrease and increase of day and night are reversed for both.
> This knowledge is always determined by the latitude of the place and the declination, as stated previously. — 58

When the sun is in the six signs starting from Aries <note>the northern hemisphere</note>, as one moves further north, there is always a greater increase in the day within the portion of the Gods (the Island of the Rose-Apple) compared to the day at the equator. As the sun moves further north, the day increases until it reaches its northern limit and then turns back. This means the increase gradually diminishes. "Decrease in night" refers to the shortening of the nighttime. The word "and" implies a combination. In the portion of the Demons—the southern part including the oceans—the increase and decrease of day and night are "opposite" or inverted. This means there is a decrease in the day and an increase in the night.

When the sun is in the six signs starting from Libra <note>the southern hemisphere</note>, for both regions (the Island of the Rose-Apple and the southern oceanic region), the decrease and increase of day and night are "reversed." The meaning is this: in the Island of the Rose-Apple, the decrease and increase follow the pattern of the northern hemisphere's increase and decrease. In the southern region, the increase and decrease of day and night are [similarly] present.

Now, if one asks how much this increase or decrease amounts to, he reminds us of what was said before: "by the latitude and declination." The "knowledge of that"—the numerical understanding of those increases and decreases—is always determined daily by the latitude and declination of the place. By considering both the local shadow <note>equinoctial shadow</note> and the declination, it was stated previously in the section on clear motion: "The sine of declination multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by twelve is the earth-sine. This, multiplied by the radius and divided by the day-radius, gives the sine of the ascensional difference. Its arc [is the ascensional difference in breaths]." By this, the half-day and half-night are determined. Doubling that results in the full day and night.

The rationale is as follows: At the equator, the horizon circle is attached to both poles. North of that, the horizon is not at the center of its own terrestrial sphere; it is lower than the North Pole and higher than the South Pole. Therefore, in the northern hemisphere, the half-day at the equator (fifteen *ghatikas*) is increased or decreased by the "ascensional difference" <term>Chara: the difference between the equatorial and local rising times</term> depending on the hemisphere, and the half-night is the opposite. Similarly, in the desired location in the southern part, the horizon is raised toward the North Pole and depressed toward the South Pole; thus, relative to the equatorial horizon, it is the inverse of the northern part. — 57–58

**Hindi Commentary—** As the sun moves through the signs starting from Aries (up to Cancer), the length of the day increases and the night decreases in the portion of the Devas <note>The Northern Hemisphere/North Pole</note>; however, the opposite occurs in the portion of the Asuras <note>The Southern Hemisphere/South Pole</note>. From Libra onwards, the increase and decrease of day and night are reversed. The specific nature of this increase and decrease according to the latitude <term>declination; original: "kranti"</term> of a country is the highest knowledge, which has been explained previously (in Chapter 2). || 57 || 58 ||

Now, wishing to explain the boundary limits of the aforementioned, he first states the distance in <term>yojanas; ancient Indian unit of distance</term> corresponding to the degrees of declination—

->**The Earth's circumference multiplied by the degrees of declination, divided by the degrees of a circle (360),**<-
->**gives the yojanas by which the sun moves above the equator. || 59 ||**<-

The measure of the Earth's circumference <note>original: "bhuvrittam"</note> previously mentioned, multiplied by the desired degrees of declination and divided by the 360 degrees of the twelve zodiac signs, results in the distance in yojanas. By this distance, the sun, situated in the sky, moves either to the south or to the north. In the absence of declination, it revolves directly over the equatorial line <note>original: "niraksha-desha"; literally 'the place without latitude'</note>. The proof is as follows: From the equator toward the North or South Poles <note>original: "meru"</note>, the sun moves by degrees of declination. To know that distance in yojanas, the proportion is: if the degrees of a full circle correspond to the yojanas of the Earth's circumference touching the equator, then what distance corresponds to the degrees of declination? Thus it is proven. || 59 ||

**Hindi Commentary—** Multiplying the Earth's circumference (Verse 59) by the sun's declination and dividing by 360 gives a number in yojanas. At a place located that many yojanas away from the equator, the sun will be directly overhead at noon. || 59 ||

Now, with two verses, he explains the knowledge of the boundary regions for the calculation of day-length—

->**From the maximum declination, one should subtract the yojanas in this manner**<-
->**from a quarter of the Earth's circumference; whatever yojanas remain, || 60 ||**<-
->**at the end of the solstice, in the reversed regions of the Devas and Asuras,**<-
->**there is once a day of sixty ghatis, and likewise once a night. || 61 ||**<-

From the degrees of maximum declination <note>obliquity of the ecliptic</note>, which are twenty-four. The yojanas are produced according to the previously stated method. One should subtract these from a fourth part of the previously mentioned Earth's circumference. The remaining yojanas represent the distance to two places in the regions of the Devas and Asuras—that is, north and south of the equator. At the end of the solstice <note>original: "ayananta"</note>—when the sun is at the beginning of Cancer (Summer Solstice) or the beginning of Capricorn (Winter Solstice)—by reversal, there occurs once a day of sixty <term>ghatis; a unit of 24 minutes, 60 ghatis = 24 hours</term>. In such a place, near that same solstice, there is likewise once a night of sixty ghatis by reversal. The word "also" <note>original: "api"</note> is used to include the day. This is what is meant: When the sun is at the beginning of Cancer, in the place separated by those yojanas to the north of the equator, there is a day of sixty ghatis; at that same time, in the place separated by those yojanas to the south of the equator, there is a night of sixty ghatis. When the sun is at the beginning of Capricorn, in that northern part, there is sixty ghatis <unclear>.</unclear>

In such a southern part, the night is sixty <term>ghatis</term><note>A ghata or ghati is 24 minutes; 60 ghatis make a full 24-hour day.</note> long, and the day is likewise. The mathematical proof is as follows: The <term>yojanas</term><note>A measure of distance, roughly 5-9 miles depending on the system.</note> of maximum declination are less than one-fourth of the Earth's circumference in yojanas. The distance from the equator to the north or south poles is gradually separated by these yojanas of maximum declination. Therefore, at that location, the latitude is 66 degrees and the obliquity is 24 degrees. In that region, the horizon follows the <term>ecliptic</term><note>The sun's apparent path; original: "kranti-vritta"</note>. This is appropriate because at the solstice, the diurnal circle touches the horizon at only one point rather than two; thus, the completion of the Sun's revolution driven by the <term>provector wind</term><note>The celestial force believed to rotate the stars; original: "pravaha"</note> results in sixty ghatis of either constant visibility or invisibility, as is directly evident from the position of the sphere. || 60 || 61 ||

In the interval between the equator and the aforementioned boundary in the northern and southern regions, the increase and decrease (waxing and waning) of day and night occur appropriately within the sixty-ghati limit. This is because the calculation of the <term>ascensional difference</term> cannot be performed when the sine exceeds the radius. || 62 ||

In that region, in the southern area from the equator <note>original: "nirakṣadeśād," literally "the place without latitude"</note>. The word "and" is used for conjunction. The word "but" implies that in a region separated by those specific <term>yojanas</term> <note>a traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note>, the Sun situated in the signs of Gemini or Cancer (at the beginning of Cancer) is not seen by the inhabitants of that land. "Shadow-loss at the quarter-circle of the Earth" means that at a distance of one-fourth of the Earth's circumference where the Earth's shadow <note>night</note> is absent, one should say the Sun is always visible. The meaning is that where there is no night consisting of the Earth's shadow, there is day. Thus, the result is that in the northern region separated by those yojanas from the equator, the Sun in Cancer and Gemini is visible; in the southern region separated by those yojanas, the Sun in Sagittarius and Capricorn is visible. Therefore, the statement of the teacher **Bhaskaracharya** <note>a famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> is consistent: "Where the latitude degrees are sixty-six and a third, there sometimes Capricorn and Sagittarius are not seen, while Cancer and Gemini are always risen." || 63 || 64 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** When the yojanas derived from the declination of two signs are subtracted from a quarter of the Earth's circumference, at that distance in the <term>Devabhaga</term> <note>the "Land of the Gods," referring to the Northern Hemisphere/North Pole</note>, the Sun situated in Sagittarius or Capricorn is never seen. Similarly, in the <term>Asurabhaga</term> <note>the "Land of the Demons," referring to the Southern Hemisphere/South Pole</note>, at the same distance, the Sun in Gemini and Cancer is never seen. In the place where the Earth's shadow does not reach, the Sun is visible. || 63 || 64 ||

Now, he shows the opposite situation in other places with two verses:

## By the yojanas brought from the sine of one sign's declination, subtracted ##
## from the quarter of the Earth's circumference, by the remaining yojanas from the equator— ## 65 ##
## The Sun situated in Sagittarius, Capricorn, Scorpio, and Aquarius is not seen ##
## in the Land of the Gods; but for the Demons, it is not seen in the four signs starting with Taurus. ## 66 ##

When the quarter of the Earth's circumference is reduced by the degrees of declination from the sine of one sign, in the northern region (Land of the Gods) at a distance of the remaining yojanas from the equator, the Sun situated in the signs of Sagittarius, Capricorn, Scorpio, and Aquarius is not seen by the inhabitants of that land. In the southern region (Land of the Demons) at the same distance from the equator, the Sun situated in the four signs starting with Taurus <note>Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo</note> is not seen by the inhabitants. Conversely, in the northern region, the Sun in the four signs starting with Taurus is visible, and in the southern region, the Sun in the four signs starting with Scorpio is visible. Therefore, the statement of **Bhaskaracharya** is consistent: "Where the latitude is seventy-eight degrees, there the four signs starting with Scorpio are not seen, and the four signs starting with Taurus are observed to be always risen." || 65 || 66 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** When the yojanas derived from the declination of one sign are subtracted from a quarter of the Earth's circumference, from that distant place in the Land of the Gods, the Sun situated in Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, and Aquarius is not seen; likewise, in the Land of the Demons, the Sun in the four signs starting with Taurus is not seen. || 65 || 66 ||

Now, he speaks of the unique situation at the two poles, understood from the yojanas brought from the declination of zero signs:

## At Meru, the Gods see the Sun in the half-cycle starting with Aries ##
## risen only once; likewise, the Demons see it in the half starting with Libra. ## 67 ##

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Twelve]

The gods residing on the northern half of Meru <note>The North Pole</note> see the sun only once <note>original: "sakrit-eva-varam"</note> when it is situated in the first half of the zodiac, beginning with Aries <note>the six signs from Aries to Virgo</note>. The word "only" is used to emphasize that it does not happen multiple times. They see it continuously after its first appearance following a period of invisibility. Similarly, the Asuras <note>demons/titans</note> residing at the southern tip of Meru see the sun continuously when it is situated in the six signs beginning with Libra <note>the southern hemisphere's summer</note>. || 67 ||

**Commentary:** The gods dwelling on Meru always see the sun when it is in the northern half of the zodiac, and the Asuras see the sun similarly when it is in the southern half. || 67 ||

### Now he describes how many yojanas <note>a traditional unit of distance, roughly 5-9 miles</note> above the equator the sun is at the solstice:

->**At the fifteenth part of the Earth's circumference, in the region of the gods or the Asuras,**<-
->**the sun passes directly overhead at the end of its northern or southern course.**<- || 68 ||

In the region of the gods (North) or the Asuras (South), at a distance of one-fifteenth of the Earth's circumference from the equator <note>original: "Niraksha-desha"</note>, the sun passes directly overhead <note>at the zenith</note> when it reaches the end of its northern or southern progress <note>the Summer and Winter solstices</note>. The meaning is that just as the sun is overhead at the equator during the equinoxes <note>original: "Gola-sandhi"</note>, it is overhead at these two specific latitudes during the solstices. The mathematical proof is as follows: At the solstice, the maximum declination <note>original: "Kranti"</note> is 24 degrees. Using the rule "Multiply the Earth's circumference by the degrees of declination and divide by the degrees of a circle (360)," we multiply by 24 and divide by 360. Reducing this fraction (24/360) gives 1/15. Thus, the statement "at the fifteenth part of the Earth's circumference" is proven. || 68 ||

**Commentary:** At a distance of one-fifteenth of the Earth's circumference, the sun passes directly overhead in the northern region (of the gods) during the northern solstice and in the southern region (of the Asuras) during the southern solstice. || 68 ||

### Having described the sun's movement up to the fifteenth part of the circumference from the equator, he now explains the movement of the shadow:

->**In the interval between those two, the shadow may fall both south and north;**<-
->**Beyond that, in their respective regions, it always moves toward Meru.**<- || 69 ||

In the regions situated between the equator and the fifteenth-part markers (the tropics), the midday shadow of a twelve-digit gnomon <note>a vertical pillar used for measuring shadows</note> or the shadow at any desired time may fall either to the south or to the north. This means: in the northern region within that fifteenth-part interval, if the sun's zenith distance is south, the shadow falls north; if the zenith distance is north, the shadow falls south. Similarly for the southern region. However, *beyond* that fifteenth-part interval, in the respective northern or southern zones, the shadow always moves toward Meru—meaning it points toward the pole <note>northward in the north, southward in the south</note> because the sun is always on the opposite side. The word "also" <note>original: "api"</note> connects this to the previous discussion of the solstices. || 69 ||

**Commentary:** In the places located between these two points, the shadow can fall either south or north. Beyond those points, in their respective hemispheres, the shadow always falls facing toward Meru. || 69 ||

<meta>This page continues the cosmological discussion regarding the movement of the Sun across the different regions (Varshas) of the world, specifically addressing the simultaneous times of day in different longitudes.</meta>

<page-num>211</page-num>
<header>Chapter 12. ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. </header>

Now, he answers the question of how the Sun wanders through the worlds, illuminating them, with two verses:

->**When the Sun is above Bhadrasva, it causes sunrise in Bharata;**<-
->**At that time, it is midnight in Ketumala and sunset in Kuru. || 70 ||**<-
->**Wandering in the same way through the regions of Bharata and the others,**<-
->**It creates the times of midday, sunrise, midnight, and sunset in a clockwise direction. || 71 ||**<-

When the Sun is positioned directly above the region of *Bhadrasva* <note>The eastern continent in Puranic geography</note>, it causes its own sunrise in *Bharatavarsha* <note>India/the southern continent</note>. By the use of the word "but" (tu), it is implied it creates midday in *Bhadrasva*. At that same time, it creates midnight in the region of *Ketumala* <note>the western continent</note> and sunset in the region of *Kuru* <note>the northern continent</note>. By the word "but," it is meant that in the intervals between these mentioned regions, it creates the corresponding elapsed or remaining portions of the day and night as appropriate. 

If one takes these as very large general regions, the literal meaning holds; however, if one takes more precise locations, these names should be understood as referring to the cities of *Yamakoti*, *Lanka*, *Romaka*, and *Siddhapura*. As the great teacher Bhaskaracharya stated in his *Geography* <note>original: "Bhugola"</note>: "When there is sunrise at the city of Lanka, it is midday at the city of Yamakoti. At that same time, it is sunset at Siddhapura and midnight at Romaka." This is consistent because these cities are separated by one-fourth of the Earth's circumference. 

Now, regarding the three regions starting with Bharata—namely *Bharata*, *Ketumala*, and *Kuru*—the Sun acts just as it did when above *Bhadrasva*. The word "exactly" (eva) excludes any variation. Wandering—that is, moving with effort to stay above its intended locations—the Sun moves in a clockwise <term>Pradakshina: a circumambulation keeping the object to one's right</term> manner, following the sequence of its positions. In these four regions, it creates the times known as midday, sunrise, midnight, and sunset. 

The meaning is this: When the Sun is above *Bharatavarsha*, then in *Bharata*, *Ketumala*, *Kuru*, and *Bhadrasva*, there will be midday, sunrise, midnight, and sunset respectively. When the Sun is above *Ketumala*, then in *Ketumala*, *Kuru*, *Bhadrasva*, and *Bharata*, there will be midday, sunrise, midnight, and sunset respectively. When the Sun is above *Kuru*, then in *Kuru*, *Bhadrasva*, *Bharata*, and *Ketumala*, there will be midday, sunrise, midnight, and sunset respectively. || 70 || 71 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** At the time when the Sun is overhead in *Bhadrasva*, it is at sunrise in *Lanka* (within *Bharata*); in *Ketumala* it is midnight, and in *Kuru* it is mostly sunset. In the regions of *Bharata* etc., the Sun similarly wanders to create the clockwise rotation of midday, sunrise, midnight, and sunset. || 70 || 71 ||

Now, one might object: "Since the planets have motion, their movement toward the north or south might appear different at every moment in every country. However, since the stars <note>the Nakshatras</note> lack their own motion, even if they do not stay in one place due to the constant rotation of the celestial sphere, why is their position not seen as identical in every country? Furthermore, since the two Poles <note>Dhruvas</note> do not wander, why is it not the case that they are seen in the same position everywhere at all times?" To this, he says:

->**The elevation of the Pole and the depression of the circle of stars increase for one going toward Meru;**<-
->**For one going toward the Equator, the depression and elevation are reversed. || 72 ||**<-

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the celestial sphere's movement and the relative positions of the poles as observed from different locations on Earth, following the Surya Siddhanta's cosmological model.</meta>

<page-num>212</page-num>
-> Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter 12] <-

As a person travels toward Meru <note>The sacred mountain at the North Pole</note>, either toward the northern or southern tip, the elevation of the Pole Star <term>Dhruva: the fixed point of the celestial axis</term> gradually increases in the north or south respectively. Simultaneously, the depression of the celestial sphere <term>Bhachakra: the circle of the fixed stars</term>—which is the central circle of the sphere where the stars reside—gradually increases in the south or north. For a person traveling toward the equator <term>Niraksha: the "place without latitude"</term>, the aforementioned elevation and depression are reversed. For a person in the northern part moving toward the equator, the North Pole appears lower compared to their previous position, and the celestial sphere appears higher. Similarly, for a person in the southern part moving toward the equator, the South Pole appears lower and the celestial sphere appears higher. **72**

**Commentary:** By moving toward the Pole, the elevation of the Pole Star and the depression of the celestial sphere are observed in sequence; by moving toward the equator, the opposite is seen—namely, the depression of the Pole and the elevation of the celestial sphere. **72**

Now, explaining why this is so, and answering the question "How does the circle of stars revolve with the planets, and what is its support?", the author describes the actual state of the celestial sphere's rotation:

### **The celestial sphere, bound at the two poles, is impelled by the Pravaha winds.**
### **It revolves constantly; attached to it are the orbits of the planets in their respective order. 73**

The celestial sphere, which is the physical embodiment of the globe of fixed stars, is bound by the Creator at the two fixed northern and southern poles. It is held fast by the circular motion of the regulated winds. Impelled by the parts of the <term>Pravaha: the great cosmic wind that drives the stars</term> acting upon their respective positions, it revolves constantly. This means it rotates toward the west. 

One might ask: "The circle of stars is moved by the wind, but how do the planets, which are situated further and further below, revolve since they lack that direct connection?" To this, he says: "Attached to it." The orbits or paths of the planets—Saturn and the others—which are composed of wind-elements and situated in the space within the celestial sphere, are attached below it in their respective order. They are bound by "wind-threads" to the celestial sphere, which is itself established within the great globe of the Pravaha wind. Therefore, they revolve along with the celestial sphere. What wonder is there, then, that the planets situated therein also revolve? 

Furthermore, at the equator—the east-west line in the middle of the globe of Pravaha wind—the two poles are on the horizon. Because the celestial sphere revolves directly overhead there, as one travels toward the tip of Meru, the Pole becomes higher. Consequently, the celestial sphere appears depressed because it is closer to the horizon, and higher when further from it. All this is logical. **73**

**Commentary:** Bound at the two poles, the celestial sphere, impelled by the Pravaha wind, revolves constantly; and the planetary orbits bound to it move along with the celestial sphere in their proper order. **73**

Now, he answers the questions regarding why a day of the Fathers <note>The Manes or ancestors</note> lasts a month:

### **The Gods and Demons see the sun risen once for half a year.**
### **The Fathers, residing on the Moon, see it for a fortnight; and humans on Earth for their own day. 74**

Just as the Gods and Demons see the sun, once it has risen, for half a solar year, so too the Fathers, who reside on the upper part of the lunar sphere, see the sun for a fortnight (fifteen lunar days). Humans on Earth see the sun for the duration of their own day. Therefore, the statements "A day of the Fathers consists of a month" and "A day of humans consists of sixty nadis" are entirely consistent.

> “The Ancestors <note>Sanskrit: Pitris</note> dwelling on the upper part of the Moon <note>Sanskrit: Vidhu</note> churn the nectar from its lower part. They see the Sun directly above their heads, and therefore that is their midday. Because they are separated by half a circle <note>180 degrees</note>, the Sun is not below the Moon; therefore, midnight for them occurs on the Full Moon. In the dark fortnight, the Sun rises for them at the midpoint of the lunar phase, and in the bright fortnight, it sets; this is established by logic.”

->This agrees with what was stated in detail by the teacher Bhaskara. <note>Bhaskara II, a 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer.</note> || 74 ||<-

<term>Hindi Commentary</term>—Just as the Gods and Demons see the Sun for six months once it has risen, the Ancestors—due to being situated on the Moon—see the Sun for a fortnight <note>two weeks</note>, and humans on Earth see the Sun for the duration of a day. || 74 ||

Now, by way of context, to demonstrate the reasoning why those situated higher have fewer revolutions <note>Sanskrit: bhaganas</note> and those situated lower have more revolutions, he first describes the greatness or smallness of the <term>Orbit</term> <note>Sanskrit: Kaksha; the circular path of a planet</note> in order of height:

## The orbit of the one situated above is great, and that of the one below is small. ||
## In a great orbit, the degrees are great; likewise, in a small one, they are small. || 75 ||

The orbit of a planet situated higher, which takes the form of a path in the circle of the wind, is "great," meaning it has a large circumference. The orbit of a planet situated lower has a "small" circumference. The word "and" <note>Sanskrit: cha</note> is used for emphasis. Because small orbits are contained within large orbits, and large orbits contain small ones, the two orbits situated above and below have large and small circumferences respectively. Otherwise, the described nature of the universe would be impossible. Thus, when the <term>Twelve Signs</term> <note>The Zodiac</note> are marked equally on a large circumference, the individual portions of each degree are "great" because of the large orbit, meaning they occupy more physical space. In a small circle, when marked similarly, the portions are "small" because of the small orbit, occupying less space. Consequently, the measure of each degree is respectively more or less and not equal in physical length, as otherwise the completion of the parts of the circle would not be achieved. This is the intended meaning. || 75 ||

<term>Hindi Commentary</term>—The orbit situated above is large, and the orbit situated below is small; for that reason, the degrees <note>Sanskrit: amsha</note> within the orbit are large and small respectively. || 75 ||

->Now he describes the greatness and smallness of the time taken for a planet's revolution and its movement, in order of height:<-

## A planet resting in a small rotation completes a revolution in a short time. ||
## Moving in a great circle, a planet [completes it] in a long time. || 76 ||

"Resting in a small rotation" refers to the lower orbit whose circumference measure is small. A planet situated there completes or traverses a "revolution"—consisting of the twelve signs—in a "short time." "In a great circle" refers to the upper orbit. Moving there, it traverses the twelve signs in a "long" or significant amount of time. This is because the speed in <term>Yojanas</term> <note>A traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note> is considered to be the same for all planets. || 76 ||

<term>Hindi Commentary</term>—A planet resting in a small orbit experiences its <term>Revolution</term> <note>Sanskrit: Bhagana; one full trip through the zodiac</note> in a short time. And a planet situated in a large orbit experiences it in a long time. || 76 ||

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Twelve]

> **The Moon, traveling in a small orbit, completes many revolutions.**
> **Saturn, moving in a very large orbit, therefore completes very few. || 77 ||**

Moving in an orbit of small dimensions—the word "but" <note>implied in the Sanskrit grammar</note> indicates the contrast—the Moon traverses many <term>revolutions</term> <note>Sanskrit: *bhagana*; a full circuit of the twelve signs of the zodiac</note> many times. Saturn, moving in an orbit of great dimensions, completes fewer revolutions than the Moon. The singular form is used here to represent the class of motion. He completes the twelve signs fewer times; for this reason, he is called "the slow-goer" <note>Sanskrit: *shanaishchara*, the etymological name for Saturn</note>. || 77 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In a given period of time, the Moon, situated in a small orbit, experiences many revolutions; however, due to the greatness of Saturn's orbit, its revolutions are few. || 77 ||

Now, the author provides the answer to the question "Why are the lords of the days, years, months, and hours not the same?" in two verses:

> **Starting from Saturn and descending in order, every fourth planet is the Lord of the Day.**
> **In the same way, every third planet is declared the Lord of the Year. || 78 ||**

> **Starting from the Moon and ascending in order, the Lords of the Months are recorded.**
> **The Lords of the Hours likewise follow a descending order starting from Saturn. || 79 ||**

Starting from Saturn and following the descending order of their orbits, the planets at the fourth position become the Lords of the Days (the rulers of the weekdays). That sequence is: Saturn, Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus <note>This explains the sequence of the days of the week: Saturday, Sunday, Monday, etc.</note>. For the year consisting of three hundred and sixty days, the lords are said to be every third planet from Saturn in descending order. The word "and" implies a collection. That sequence is: Saturn, Mars, Venus, Moon, Jupiter, Sun, Mercury. Starting from the Moon and following the ascending order of the orbits, the planets are called the lords of the months consisting of thirty days. That sequence is: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn.

Starting from Saturn in descending order: the Lords of the Hours <note>Sanskrit: *hora*; the word refers to both the rising sign and half a zodiac sign</note> are determined. This refers to the twenty-four hours of a day and night—twelve in the day and twelve in the night—consisting of fifteen-degree segments. Others say an "hour" is two and a half <term>ghatikas</term> <note>A traditional Indian unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 2.5 ghatikas equals 60 minutes</note>, making twenty-four hours in a sixty-ghatika day and night. These lords are described as being separated by two from the Lord of the Month. That sequence is: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon.

Here, because Saturn is the highest of all and the Moon is the lowest of all, the descending and ascending orders are stated starting from them respectively. If any other planet were taken as the starting point, it would lead to logical inconsistency. However, Saturn being the first limit does not mean it was the lord of the day, year, or hour at the very beginning of creation, nor does the Moon being the first limit mean it was the lord of the month at creation; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the lords calculated in the previous section.

The reasoning here is: since the <term>ascendants</term> <note>Sanskrit: *lagna*</note> in the form of hours occur in the ecliptic in a descending order (Aries, etc.), it is appropriate that the Lord of the Hour follows a descending order from the highest orbit. Thus, there are twenty-four hours in a day and night. Three cycles of seven hour-lords pass <note>totaling 21</note>. The fourth hour-lord at the start of the second day becomes the Lord of that Day because he is the first hour-lord of that day. This continues subsequently. In this way, following the sequence of days, there are three days <note>remaining</note> in a <term>civil year</term> <note>Sanskrit: *savana varsha*; a year of 360 days</note>; therefore, the lord of the next year is the third in descending order from the previous year...

...answer. Thus, in a solar month <note>original: *sāvana-māsa*</note>, two days are added to the sequence of the Lord of the Month. Because the Lords of the Month follow every other planet in the ascending order of the orbits, it is established that the Lord of the Month follows the ascending order of the orbits. Thus, the two verses beginning with "From Saturn..." are explained. || 78 || 79 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The fourth planet in descending order from Saturn is the Lord of the Day, and the third planet is the Lord of the Year. || 78 || The Lords of the Month are those in ascending order from the Moon. The planets in descending order from Saturn are the Lords of the *Hora* <note>original: *horādhipati*; a *hora* equals 2 *dandas* or one hour</note>. || 79 ||

Now, wishing to answer the question "What are the sizes of the planetary orbits?", he first describes the measurement of the orbit of the asterisms <note>the fixed stars or *nakshatras*</note>—

## The orbit of the asterisms is sixty times the daily travel of the Sun.
## Above all else, the circle of the stars revolves by those many leagues. || 80 ||

The daily travel of the Sun, which is the measure of its orbital circumference in leagues <note>original: *yojanas*</note>—to be stated later as 4,331,500—when multiplied by sixty, becomes the orbit of the asterisms, which is the middle circle of the sphere where the stars reside. By those leagues measuring the stellar orbit, the circle of the stars revolves at the greatest distance above the seven planets (Moon, etc.), encircling the terrestrial globe. The logic here: since the stars have no motion of their own, the stellar sphere is placed high above. There, based on the Sun's motion, the Sun's orbit is determined. Even though the stars do not move, a motion of one minute <note>arc-minute</note> is assumed for calculation. By the rule of three, to achieve an increase in the result when the divisor decreases, an inverse proportion is used for simplicity. The Sun's motion is fixed at sixty minutes by the Lord. Because the stars lack motion, the multiplier of sixty is appropriate. || 80 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Multiplying the Sun's orbit by 60 gives the orbit of the stars <note>original: *bhakakshā*</note>. It revolves above everything else. || 80 ||

Now, to provide the knowledge of the measurements of the planetary orbits, he gives the measurement of the orbit of the sky <note>the edge of the universe</note>, answering the question "How far does that extend?"—

## The Moon's revolutions in a Kalpa, multiplied by the Moon's orbit,
## is known as the orbit of the sky; it is the limit reached by the Sun's rays. || 81 ||

"The Moon's revolutions in a *Kalpa*" <note>a *Kalpa* is a vast cosmic cycle of 4.32 billion years</note>. By the statement "These multiplied by a thousand are the revolutions in a *Kalpa*," the revolutions of the Moon in a *Yuga* multiplied by a thousand are the *Kalpa* revolutions. When these are multiplied by the Moon's orbit—to be stated later as 324,000—that product is to be known by the wise as the circumference of the "Orbit of the Sky" <note>original: *ākāśakakshā*</note>. If one asks how the infinite sky can have a circumference, he says: "reached by the rays." This means the extent of the diffusion of the Sun's light is the measure of the orbit of the sky. Thus, the circumference of the celestial sphere, bounded by the shell of the cosmic egg <note>original: *brahmāṇḍa-kaṭāha*</note>, is indeed possible. The logic is: since it will be said that "the orbit of the sky divided by the revolutions of a planet gives that planet's orbit," it follows that the product of a planet's revolutions and its orbit equals the orbit of the sky. || 81 ||

<summary>This page explains the mathematical derivation of the stellar and universal orbits, defining the "Orbit of the Sky" as the limit of the Sun's light and the boundary of the cosmic egg.</summary>

# Surya Siddhanta —
## [Chapter Twelve]

**Commentary:** If the total revolutions <note>Bhagana: a complete orbit of 360 degrees</note> of the Moon in one Kalpa <note>A vast cosmic cycle of 4.32 billion years</note> are multiplied by the Moon's orbit, the result is the orbit of the sky <note>Akashakaksha: the limit of the universe</note>; the sun's rays extend exactly to that distance. || 81 ||

->Now, the calculation of the orbits of the planets and the calculation of their speed in Yojanas is explained:<-

### That same [orbit of the sky] divided by the revolutions in a Kalpa gives the orbit [of a specific planet].
### Dividing that by the number of terrestrial days gives the daily eastward motion of all [planets]. || 82 ||

The orbit of the sky, which represents the extent of the sun's rays, when divided by the revolutions of a specific planet in a Kalpa, the resulting quotient is the orbit <note>Kaksha</note> of that planet. The word "same" is used for emphasis. When divided by the number of civil days <note>Visavana: terrestrial days from sunrise to sunrise</note> in a Kalpa, the result is the daily eastward motion <term>Praggati: the intrinsic motion of planets from West to East against the fixed stars</term> in Yojanas <note>An ancient Indian unit of distance, roughly 5-9 miles</note> for all planets. The logic here is: the orbit of the sky is the product of the revolutions and the orbit; thus, dividing the sky-orbit by the revolutions must yield the orbit. Since a planet travels a distance equal to the orbit of the sky in one Kalpa, the distance it travels in one civil day is found by proportion. || 82 ||

**Commentary:** If that [sky] orbit is divided by the revolutions of the planets in a Kalpa, it results in their own orbit. If the orbit is divided by the terrestrial days, it results in the daily eastward motion of all. || 82 ||

->Now, the conversion of the speed in Yojanas into the speed in minutes of arc is explained:<-

### The number of Yojanas of daily motion, multiplied by the Moon's orbit
### And divided by its own orbit, then divided by fifteen, gives the motion in minutes of arc. || 83 ||

The number produced from the daily motion in Yojanas is multiplied by the Moon's orbit and divided by the orbit of the desired planet. The resulting figure is then divided by fifteen. The result of this calculation is the motion in minutes of arc <term>Gatikala: the angular velocity</term> for that specific planet. The logic is: if the Yojanas of the full orbit equal the minutes in a circle <note>21,600 minutes</note>, then what do the Yojanas of daily motion equal? Furthermore, the "minutes in a circle" are defined here as "the Moon's orbit divided by fifteen." || 83 ||

**Commentary:** Multiplying the daily motion by the Moon's orbit and dividing by its own orbit [and then by 15] results in the motion in minutes. || 83 ||

->Now, the answer to the question "What are the altitudes?" is given:<-

### The orbit multiplied by the Earth's diameter and divided by the Earth's circumference
### Gives the diameter [of that orbit]; subtracting the Earth's diameter and halving the remainder gives the planet's own altitude. || 84 ||

The orbit of the planets in Yojanas is multiplied by the Earth's diameter <note>Bhukarna: literally 'Earth-ear', used here for diameter</note>—which was previously stated as 1,600 Yojanas—and divided by the Earth's circumference <note>Mahimandala</note>. The result is the diameter of that planet's orbit. When the Earth's diameter is subtracted from this and the result is halved, it gives the altitude <term>Utssedha: the height or distance</term> of the planet from the surface of the Earth. The logic is: as the Earth's circumference is to its diameter, so is the planet's orbit to its diameter...

<header>Chapter 12. Including Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.</header>

By the proportion "If the circumference of the orbit is so many <term>yojanas</term> <note>a traditional unit of distance, roughly 5-9 miles</note>, what is the diameter?", the diameters of the orbits are found. These are halved to find the radius of the orbit—which represents the interval between the center of the Earth and the circumference of the orbit. To find the distance from the Earth's surface, the radius of the Earth is subtracted from this; the result is the height of the orbit from the Earth's surface. This is done by halving the difference between the diameter of the orbit and the diameter of the Earth. Both methods yield the same result. The height of the orbit is indeed the height of the planet, as the planet is stationed there. By this, the knowledge of the mutual distances between the established planetary heights is easily understood. The answer to the question "What are the intervals?" is self-evident. || 84 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** By multiplying the planet's own orbit by the Earth's diameter and dividing by the Earth's circumference, the hypotenuse (distance) of the orbit is found. By subtracting the Earth's diameter from that and dividing by two, the distance from the Earth is determined. || 84 ||

Now, wishing to state the established orbits in ascending order, he first states the orbit of the Moon and the orbit of Mercury’s <term>shighrochcha</term> <note>the "fast apogee" or the center of the epicycle representing the planet's orbital motion relative to the Sun</note>—

->### The orbit of the Moon (the cold-rayed one) is 324,000. <-
->### Then, for Mercury's fast apogee, it is 1,043,209. || 85 ||<-

The orbit of the Moon is 324,000 <note>original: "three-four-three-zeros"</note>. The word "but" (tu) implies this should be accepted based on the authority of tradition. Otherwise, it would lead to the fallacy of circular reasoning. Above the Moon is the orbit of Mercury’s fast apogee: 1,043,209. Although Mercury’s fast apogee is not visible in the sky and thus stating its orbit might seem improper, Mercury moves above the Moon in accordance with the motion derived from the revolutions of its fast apogee, following the stated order: "First the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon." Otherwise, if the Sun, Mercury, and Venus were placed in an <term>orbit of identical revolutions</term> <note>referring to the fact that their mean daily motion is the same</note>, their spheres would collide; this is stated to indicate their distinction. || 85 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Moon: 324,000; Mercury's fast apogee: 1,043,209 from the Moon. || 85 ||

Now he states the orbit of Venus’s fast apogee and the identical orbit of the Sun, Mercury, and Venus—

->### For Venus's fast apogee: 2,664,637. <-
->### Then for the Sun, Mercury, and Venus: 4,331,500. || 86 ||<-

Above that, the orbit of Venus’s fast apogee is 2,664,637, stated to indicate the position of Venus. Above that, the orbit of the Sun, Mercury, and Venus—which is identical due to the equality of their revolutions—is 4,331,500. Although Mercury and Venus are below the Sun and only the <term>Sun's orbit</term> should be mentioned, it is stated for Mercury and Venus as well to establish that they are not different in terms of the proportion: "If in the total days of a Kalpa they travel the yojanas of their own orbit, how much do they travel in the elapsed days?" Otherwise, the consistency of the calculation would not be achieved. || 86 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Venus's fast apogee: 2,664,637 from Mercury's fast apogee. Sun, Mercury, Venus (mean): 4,331,500. || 86 ||

Now he states the orbit of Mars and the orbit of the Moon’s <term>mandoccha</term> <note>the slow apogee or apsis, used to calculate the equation of center</note>—

->### For Mars: 8,146,909. <-
->### For the Moon’s apogee: 38,328,484. || 87 ||<-

**Commentary:** Saturn = 127,668,255; Stellar orbit = 259,890,012.

# Chapter Thirteen

Now, the teacher addresses the sages who are the listeners in two verses:

->Now, in a secluded and pure place, having bathed, being purified and adorned,<-
->Having worshiped the Sun with devotion, as well as the planets, the stars, and the Guhyakas <note>Nature spirits or hidden celestial beings</note>, || 1 ||<-
->Following the traditional instruction as received from the mouth of the teacher,<-
->The Preceptor, for the enlightenment of the disciple, shall make everything visible to the eyes. || 2 ||<-

The word "Now" <note>original: "Atha"</note> is used for auspiciousness. The second "now" indicates the sequence following what was previously said. In a "secluded" (private) and "pure" (holy) place, the Preceptor—who is the incarnation of a portion of the Sun teaching Mayasura—having "bathed" and being "purified" (of pure mind), and "adorned" (decorated with ornaments on the hands, ears, and neck). This decoration is a sign of being free from anxiety; otherwise, due to the distractions of planetary calculations and worldly affairs, mental stability would be impossible. Having "worshiped the Sun," his own source of livelihood and knowledge, with devotion through praise and salutation, and then the "planets" like the Moon and others. The Sun is mentioned separately to show its primacy. He also worships the "stars" (the lunar mansions and zodiac signs) and the "Guhyakas" (minor deities like the Yakshas). The word "and" is implied here to connect them. "From the mouth of the teacher" means from the lotus-like face of the Sun. "Following traditional instruction" refers to how the Sun spoke to the sages, and the sages spoke to the incarnation of the Sun's portion, who then spoke to Mayasura—this is the oral tradition. In reality, this is said to emphasize the secrecy of the knowledge to inspire the disciple's eagerness. How else could the Sun-ordered incarnation speak to Mayasura while the sages were at a distance...
