# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Thirteen]

The Sun, being ready to speak, addressed the man who was a portion of himself <note>The text refers to the *Suryansha-purusha*, a divine avatar of the Sun's knowledge</note>. Why was he ready? Because there was no reason not to be. Just as he had understood the knowledge previously mentioned through his own power, he now showed it all—as if seeing it directly—to the disciple <note>Maya</note> to remove his confusion and ensure his understanding. This refers to everything explained in the preceding chapters. || 1 || 2 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The teacher, who sees the truth directly, sat adorned in a secret, pure place. After worshipping the Sun, the planets, the stars, and the *Guhyakas* <note>Nature spirits or guardians of hidden treasures</note>, he prepared to explain to the disciple everything he had heard through the lineage of teachers. || 1 || 2 ||

In response to how he demonstrated this, the words of the Sun’s portion to Maya regarding the purpose and commencement of the construction of the "Sphere" <note>The armillary sphere or celestial globe</note> are stated in two verses:

> One should construct a wondrous model of the beautiful celestial sphere.
> First, having caused a desired globe of the Earth to be made of wood, || 3 ||
> A staff should be passed through its center, emerging on both sides of Meru.
> Then, two supporting circles and the equatorial circle should be fixed. || 4 ||

A wise calculator or an expert in sphere-craft <term>Gola-shilpajña: a craftsman skilled in building astronomical models</term> should create a model of the celestial sphere <term>Bhagola: the sphere of the stars</term> which surrounds the terrestrial sphere <term>Bhūgola: the Earth-globe</term>, as described in the previous chapter, for the purpose of understanding its positions. 

Now, one might ask: "If all knowledge is gained through your words, isn't building a physical model useless?" To this, he says: *It is wondrous.* It generates an extraordinary understanding that arises from the realization of what was taught. Because the mind does not easily accept the idea of people living on the sides or bottom of the Earth, or the positions of the celestial sphere in those regions, or the fact that the Earth is unsupported in space, a physical model is necessary to achieve certainty.

Regarding how to build it: *Desired* means of a circumference chosen by one's own wish. Having had a wooden globe of the Earth made with a hole through it by a woodworker, a staff representing the axis of Meru <note>The celestial axis passing through the poles</note> should be placed through its center—that is, through the hole in the wooden celestial sphere—fitting loosely. *Emerging on both sides* means it should protrude from the two ends of the hole (which equals the diameter of the Earth-globe). The staff should be made to extend equally from both ends.

To fix the celestial sphere, he mentions two supporting circles: *Two supporting circles.* First, for the sake of support, two circles are placed—one vertical and one horizontal. One circle should be threaded onto the ends of the staff at an equal distance from the Earth-globe. Another circle of the same size should be fixed, bisecting the first and also threaded onto the staff. Without these two circles, the celestial sphere cannot be constructed around the Earth-globe. He then describes the beginning of the celestial sphere's construction: *The equatorial circle.* This refers to the circle of the equator <term>Vishuvan-mandala: the celestial equator</term>. It should be fixed by the calculator at the middle of the celestial sphere, bisecting the two supporting circles. || 3 || 4 ||

Since these are "diurnal circles," the reasoning for constructing the circles using the day-radius is sound, because the radius of the diurnal circle is the square root of the radius squared minus the <term>sine of declination</term> <note>krantijya</note> squared.

This refers to the degrees from the equatorial region to the ecliptic region, and by the word "and," the markings on the supporting rings are divided into equal halves. These are characterized by the north-south distance between the equatorial circle and the ecliptic circle, according to their own respective zodiacal...

# Surya Siddhanta - Chapter 13

<page-num>222</page-num>
<header>Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter 13]</header>

By means of the declination <note>original: "apakarama"</note> degrees brought forth in the **Chapter on True Motion** <term>Spashta-adhikara; the second chapter of the Surya Siddhanta dealing with true planetary positions</term>, one should form three circles for the signs starting with Aries—meaning those ending at the finish of Aries, Taurus, and Gemini. These three circles, previously described as being of a circular form, should be projected according to their declination. The word "apakarama" uses "apa" as a prefix, meaning "in order." The astronomer-craftsman should fix these to the two supporting circles toward the north, in accordance with the **equatorial circle** <term>Vishuvad-vritta; the celestial equator</term>. Regarding the signs starting with Cancer, he says: "those." The circles fixed for Aries and the others are used for Cancer, Leo, and Virgo by "reversal" or inversion. The word "and" implies a combination. The result is that the circle for the end of Gemini serves for the start of Cancer; the circle for the end of Taurus serves for Leo; and the circle for the end of Aries serves for Virgo. Regarding Libra and the others, he says: "likewise." For Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius, there are three other circles. Just like the others, these are based on the declination degrees of one, two, and three signs, but they belong to the southern hemisphere. These should be fixed by the astronomer to the two supporting circles in the southern part of the equatorial circle. Regarding Capricorn and the others, he says: "starting with the Sea-Monster (Capricorn)." The circles for Capricorn and the following signs are connected in reverse order. The result is that the circle for the end of Sagittarius serves for Capricorn; the circle for the end of Scorpio serves for Aquarius; and the circle for the end of Libra serves for Pisces.

Regarding the fixing of the circles for the stars, he says: "from the support of the circles." For the twenty-seven lunar mansions <note>Nakshatras</note> starting with Ashvini, which are situated in the southern and northern hemispheres—meaning those positioned appropriately north or south of the equatorial circle—the circles should be projected. For those stars whose true declination is north, they are in the northern portion; for those whose true declination is south, they are in the southern portion. The word "also" indicates the arrangement according to the sequence of northern and southern stars. "From the support of the circles" means from the two supporting circles of the spheres. <note>The grammar here uses the fifth case (ablative) in the sense of the seventh case (locative).</note> One should project the circles with a radius equal to the radius of the diurnal circle <note>day-circle</note> produced by their own true declination. The craftsman should fix them thus. He also mentions others: "of Abhijit." For the orb of the **star Abhijit** <term>Vega</term>, the orbs of the **Seven Sages** <term>Saptarshi; the Big Dipper/Ursa Major</term>, the orb of the **star Agastya** <term>Canopus</term>, and the orbs of the stars known as Brahma, Lubdhaka <note>Sirius</note>, Apamvatsa, and others. The word "and" should be understood to include these. Thus, their circles should be projected as appropriate. He concludes the method of fixing them: "in the middle." In the middle of all the aforementioned circles, in the central space of the non-supporting circles, the equatorial circle—related to the equinox and circular in form—is situated. The word "only" excludes any other arrangement. The craftsman should fix the circle in this way. The refined meaning is: one should fix the diurnal circles to the two supporting circles at a distance from the equatorial circle equal to their own true declination, using the measurement of the radius of their own diurnal circle. || 5 || 6 || 7 || 8 || 9 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Having created three circles with a diameter measured by the hypotenuse of the radius of one's own diurnal circle, one should mark 360 degrees on each. On the north-south line marked with degrees of declination and latitude, one should join the three circles according to the declination of Aries and the others. These same circles, in reverse, are the circles for Cancer and the others. Likewise, in the southern direction, one should join the three circles for Libra and the others. These same, in reverse order, will be the circles for Capricorn and the others. In the north and south, the circles for the stars including **Abhijit** should be joined above the supporting circles. In this same manner, one should make the circles for the **Seven Sages**, **Agastya**, Brahma-hridaya, and others. The equatorial circle will remain situated in the middle of all of them. || 5 || 6 || 7 || 8 || 9 ||

Now, he describes the arrangement of the signs of the zodiac, starting with Aries, on the celestial sphere in one and a half verses:

## Above the intersection of that support, there are two equinoxes at the solstices. ##
## From the equinoctial position, by the distinct degrees of the revolution of the circle, ##
## one should imagine the fields of Aries and the others by means of transverse chords. ## 10.

<note>The "support" refers to the prime vertical or the celestial horizon used as a reference frame.</note> Above the intersection of that celestial equator <note>Vishuvat-vritta</note> and the supporting circle—at their point of contact—are the solstices <note>Ayana</note>, the junctions of the northern and southern paths. Because the word "above" is used here, the supporting circle should be understood as vertical <note>upright</note>, not horizontal like the celestial horizon <note>Unmandala</note>. The result is this: on the vertical supporting circle of the celestial equator, there are intersections above and below. From the upper intersection, the diurnal circle of Capricorn is twenty-four degrees to the south; where it meets that supporting circle is the winter solstice point <note>Uttarayana-sandhi</note>. Similarly, from the lower intersection, the diurnal circle of Cancer is twenty-four degrees to the north; where it meets that supporting circle is the summer solstice point <note>Dakshinayana-sandhi</note>. Because the equinoxes are situated opposite to the solstices, and due to the relationship with the word "below" implied by the word "above," there are two equinoxes. The essential meaning is that the two intersections of the horizontal celestial horizon and the celestial equator are the east and west points, representing the start of Aries and Libra respectively, located at the equinoctial positions.

Now he describes the arrangement of the complete signs: "From the equinoctial position..." From the region of the equinox, by the distinct thirty degrees belonging to each sign through the movement of the Great Circle <note>the ecliptic</note>, and by "transverse chords"—meaning the regions of the circular cords that follow the likeness of the aforementioned circles—one should imagine the signs. "Of Aries and the others" means starting with Aries. In this way, following the method of imagining the solstices and equinoxes, a wise calculator should project the "fields" or positions in the intervals between them. 

For example: from the equinoctial point in the east, at a distance of one-twelfth of the celestial circle, is the position of the end of Aries on the diurnal circle. From there, at the same interval, is the end of Taurus on its diurnal circle. From there is the solstice point. At that same interval is the end of Gemini. From there, in the western portion on the diurnal circle of Cancer, is the end of Cancer. From there, on the diurnal circle of Leo, is the end of Leo. From there, at the same interval, is the western equinox point, which is the end of Virgo. From there, in the eastern portion on the diurnal circle of Libra, is the end of Libra. From there, on the diurnal circle of Scorpio, is the end of Scorpio. From there, at the same interval, is the solstice point, the end of Sagittarius. From there, on the diurnal circle of Capricorn and others, is the end of Capricorn. From there, on the diurnal circle of Aquarius and others, is the end of Aquarius and the beginning of Pisces. From there, at the eastern equinox, is the end of Pisces and the beginning of Aries. This is clearly explained. || 10 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Mark two equinoxes upward from the junction of the celestial equator and the supporting orbit. After that, determine the twelve fields of Aries and the others transversely at the intervals of the signs from the equinox. || 10 ||

Because the intervening space is composed of ether <note>Akasha</note>. # Surya Siddhanta
## [Chapter Thirteen]

> From solstice to solstice, there is another slanted orbit.
> Known as the Ecliptic, the Sun always travels along it, illuminating the world. || 11 ||

Starting from the point of one solstice until the return to that same solstice point. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> is used to signify the continuous cycle from start to finish without skipping any intermediate solstice points. There is another orbit in the sphere, circular in form and equal to the base circle, following the path of the zodiac signs. The word "only" <note>original: "eva"</note> is used to exclude any other path. This slanted path, which differs from the orientation of the celestial equator, is called the <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>literally "the path of declination" or "Kranti-samjna"</note>. This circle is conceived for the purpose of knowing the motion and longitudinal position of the planets. The essential meaning is that one should fix the <term>Ecliptic Circle</term> <note>Kranti-vritta</note>—marked with the twelve signs of the zodiac and connected to the two solstices and two equinoxes—onto the armillary sphere. It is the Sun that travels there, illuminating the worlds. By specifying the Sun, other bodies like the Moon are excluded from this specific rule. The Sun always, without interruption, travels along this orbit known as the Ecliptic by its own power, completing its <term>Revolution</term> <note>Bhagana-paripurti: the completion of a full 360-degree circuit</note>. The idea is that the Ecliptic is a fixed circle imagined in accordance with the Sun's motion. || 11 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** The slanted orbit that goes from one solstice to another is called the <term>Ecliptic Orbit</term>. The Sun travels upon it, providing light. || 11 ||

Now, one might ask why the Moon and other planets do not travel exactly on the Ecliptic. To answer this, he says:

> The Moon and the others, by their own Nodes situated on the Ecliptic,
> are seen pulled away from it at the ends of their latitudes, away from the Ecliptic path. || 12 ||

The Moon and the other planets (excluding the Sun) are pulled by their own "Nodes" <note>Pata: the points where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic, personified here as deities</note> which are situated on the Ecliptic. They are pulled away from their calculated positions on the Ecliptic. Because of the word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note>, they are drawn either to the South or the North by the distance of their latitude. For this reason, they are seen by people on Earth at the "ends of their latitudes"—that is, at the points of the calculated minutes of latitude—away from their own longitudinal positions on the Ecliptic. Just as the Ecliptic is situated relative to the <term>Celestial Equator</term> <note>Vishuvat-mandala</note>, so too is there a <term>Latitude Circle</term> <note>Vikshepa-vritta</note>. This circle is attached to the Ecliptic at the Node and at a point six signs away from it; it reaches its maximum North or South deviation at a point three signs away from the Node. The idea is that each planet travels on its own distinct latitude circle, imagined according to its specific motion. || 12 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** The Moon and others are pulled from their Nodes and rely on their own circles. Being thus drawn, they are seen at the limit of their latitude, away from the Ecliptic. || 12 ||

Now he describes the nature of the "Rising Sign" and the "Meridian Sign" mentioned in the <term>Chapter on the Three Problems</term> <note>Tri-prashna-adhikara: a section of astronomy dealing with time, place, and direction</note>:

> The point on the Ecliptic at the eastern horizon is the Rising Sign (Lagna); the Setting Sign is determined by that.
> The Meridian Sign (Madhya-lagna) is that which is above, at the middle of the sky, as calculated by the Ascensions at Lanka. || 13 ||

"At the eastern horizon" means the eastern direction of the horizon circle. The <term>Rising Sign</term> <note>Lagna</note> is that point of the Ecliptic which is connected to the horizon by the force of the celestial wind; it is the point of longitude (starting from Aries) that is rising at that moment. By implication, the Setting Sign is the point currently setting. <unclear>...not driven by the wind...</unclear>

<header>Chapter 13. ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. ( 225 )</header>

He describes the form of the setting point: **The Setting.** By the influence of the rising sign, the setting horizon—meaning the western region of the horizon circle—is understood. The point where the ecliptic <note>original: "krāntivṛtta"</note>, moved by the pro-vaha wind, meets that region is called the "Setting Sign" <note>original: "astalagna"</note>, measured from the beginning of Aries. Thus, because the ecliptic is always above the horizon, it is established that there is a difference of six signs between the rising and setting signs. This is calculated using the "Lanka Risings" <note>the rising times of signs at the equator</note> as described in the chapter on the Three Problems <note>Tri-praśna</note>. 

**The Meridian Sign** <note>original: "madhyalagnam"</note> is that which is above the center of the sky. Here, "center of the sky" refers to the region following the north-south meridian line of the visible celestial sphere, not the absolute zenith <note>the point directly overhead</note> favored by Bhaskaracharya, because the absolute zenith does not always coincide with the ecliptic. The essential meaning is that the point where the ecliptic meets the meridian circle is called the Meridian Sign, measured from the beginning of Aries. || 13 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The degree on the rising horizon is the "Lagna" (Ascendant); at the setting horizon, it is the seventh sign. That which is established as the "Middle" through the risings at Lanka is situated above one's own meridian line. || 13 ||

Now, he describes the nature of the *Antya* mentioned in the chapter on the Three Problems, and the nature of the *Carajya* (Sine of terrestrial latitude) mentioned in the chapter on True Motions:

### The sine situated between the meridian and the horizon is called the *Antya*.
### The *Caradalajya* (Sine of half-equinoctial shadow) is known as the interval between the Equator and the Horizon. || 14 ||

In the northern hemisphere, the *Antya* is the sum of the radius and the *Carajya*; in the southern hemisphere, it is the radius minus the *Carajya*, as stated in the chapter on the Three Problems. This *Antya* is the sine in the interval between the "Middle" (the meridian circle) and the "Horizon" (the horizon circle of the desired location) along a portion of the diurnal circle <note>the path a star takes over 24 hours</note>. It is a chord-like line extending from the intersection of the rising-setting line and the meridian line to the intersection of the diurnal and meridian circles. It is called a "sine" by experts of the sphere, though it acts as a linear measure. 

If one asks: "What is the nature of the *Carajya* upon which the *Antya* depends?" he says: **It is to be known...** Since the "Unmandala" <note>the equatorial horizon</note> and the "Vishuvat-mandala" <note>the celestial equator</note> are often used synonymously in the Three Problems, here it refers to the interval between the fixed equatorial horizon and the local horizon. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> implies a specific distinction: it is the straight line representing the half-sine of that portion of the diurnal circle situated between them. Effectively, it is the vertical/horizontal distance between the rising-setting lines of the equator and one's local station. It is the *Caradalajya* <note>Sine of the variation of the day</note> of that segment, not literally "half of a half." || 14 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The sine between the meridian and the horizon is the *Antya*. The difference between the Equator and the local horizon is called the *Caradala-jya*. || 14 ||

Lest the previous two verses be difficult to understand due to ignorance of the "Horizon," he defines the horizon in half a verse:

### Having placed one's own location at the top, the Horizon Circle is in the middle. || 15 ||

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Thirteen]

On the terrestrial globe, one should establish one's own location—representing a specific portion of the earth's surface—at the very top, above all other regions. In the center of such a globe, at the junction of the upper and lower halves, the circle that exists is the **horizon circle** <term>Kshitija-vritta: the circle where the sky meets the earth</term>. Following this principle, the horizon circle should be firmly attached to the model globe. || 15 ||

**Commentary:** Having placed one's own location at the highest point, one should fix the horizon circle in the middle. || 15 ||

Now, having completed this model globe, the author describes the method by which it may rotate westward of its own accord:

->**Covered with a cloth, and surrounded on the outside by the Lokāloka...**<-
->**...by means of the flow of nectar, the instrument for the passage of time is achieved.**<- || 16 ||

"On the outside" means upon the globe. The model globe is to be covered with a cloth shaped to the sphere. Upon this shining cloth, the various celestial circles should be drawn. It is "surrounded by the Lokāloka," meaning it is attached to the horizon circle, which sits at the boundary of the visible and invisible worlds. The word "and" implies a combination: the horizon itself should not be covered by the cloth; rather, the horizon should be fixed over the cloth-covered globe in such a way that it remains stable. 

"By means of the flow of nectar" <note>original: "amrita-srava"; here referring to water</note> means that after constructing such a globe, one should use the downward force of a water stream to create a "self-carrying" <term>svayam-vaha: automatic or perpetual motion</term> globe instrument. This causes the model globe to rotate in synchronization with the sidereal hours <term>ghatikas: units of time equal to 24 minutes</term>. 

The meaning is as follows: Having covered the model globe with cloth, the ends of its central axis should be placed into two tubes fixed on north and south walls, ensuring the axis points toward the Pole Star. Then, a stream of water directed eastward should strike the back part of the axis from below. The mention of the cloth covering is for visual effect; otherwise, seeing the water strike through the gaps between the rings of the globe would ruin the "wonder" <note>chamatkara: the sense of aesthetic or scientific marvel</note> of the mechanism. The cloth also helps simulate the appearance of the sky. This cloth should be kept moist and coated with a smooth substance like wax. A wall in the form of a trench should be made so that the lower half of the globe remains visible. However, the southern part of the axis must be loose enough to allow rotation. The water flow from the eastern trench should be hidden from view—this must be managed through clever engineering. || 16 ||

**Commentary:** Covering the area outside the horizon with cloth, one should achieve the motion of time through the impact of water. || 16 ||

Now, if a water stream is not possible there, how can the model globe be made self-rotating? To answer this, the author mentions a secret auxiliary method:

->**One should prepare the globe instrument equipped with the "Seed of the High One."**<-
->**This secret, though explained openly, remains accessible to all here.**<- || 17 ||

The astronomer or craftsman should prepare the instrument—the model globe—equipped with the "Seed of the High One" <note>Tunga-bija: literally the seed of Mahadeva/Shiva</note>, which means **mercury** <term>parada: quicksilver</term>. He should perfect it so that the globe rotates exactly according to the sidereal hours through the application of mercury. This involves... <note>The text breaks off here, continuing the explanation of the mercury mechanism on the next page.</note>

On the two ends of the axis extending outside the sphere, one should carve a rim or circumference at two or three desired points. Cover this with a smooth coating, such as palm-leaf paste, and create an opening. Through this path, mercury should be filled into half of the circumference, and water should be placed in the other half. Then, after sealing the opening, the ends of the axis should be placed into two tubes fixed in a wall so that the sphere remains suspended in the air. Then, the axis, pulled by the weight of the mercury and water, rotates on its own, and the sphere supported by it rotates as well. In this context, the covering with cloth is done only to achieve the appearance of the sky. Now, one might ask why this self-rotating action was not described explicitly; to this, the author says: **It is to be kept secret.** This method of creating a self-rotating device is a secret and should not be publicized. Why? He says: **Because of public disclosure.** If the method of creating a self-rotating device were described too clearly, it would become accessible to everyone in this world. And since no sense of wonder arises from a thing known to all, the intention is that it should not be disclosed everywhere for the sake of preserving that wonder; this is why the method was not explicitly stated. || 17 ||

**Hindi Translation:** One should perfect the spherical instrument using mercury; this is extremely confidential, for if it is told publicly, it will become common knowledge. || 17 ||

Now, one might ask: "If you say it is a secret, how am I to understand it, and how are others like me to understand it?" To answer this, he speaks in a verse and a half:

### Therefore, one should construct the excellent sphere through the instruction of a teacher. ||
### In age after age, this construction of the Sun <note>original: "Vivasvat"</note> is lost. ||
### By the grace of someone, it appears again according to their desire. || 18 ||

Therefore, because the method of self-rotation is a secret, a mathematician should construct the excellent sphere—the self-rotating model sphere—through the **instruction of a teacher**, meaning through the sincere explanation of a teacher received through tradition. The implication is: "I have told it to you, but it has not been stated too explicitly in the book because it is a secret." As for how others should know this, he says: **In age after age**, etc. This construction or mechanism of self-rotation belonging to the Sun <note>The deity presiding over the solar orb</note> is lost or disappears from the world over long periods of time. By the **grace** or favor of someone like me, it **appears again** or becomes manifest repeatedly according to one's desire. Thus, just as you have learned it from me, others must learn it from someone else like me, because time is infinite and the lineage of seekers is beginningless. || 18 ||

**Hindi Translation:** For that reason, one should make the excellent sphere by the instruction of the Guru. This is destroyed in every Age <term>Yuga: a vast cycle of cosmic time</term>, but by the grace of the Sun, it is revealed again to someone. || 18 ||

Now, he states that other self-rotating instruments, besides the self-rotating sphere, should be prepared for the knowledge of time using the aforementioned self-rotation method, and that their preparation should be done in private:

### For the purpose of determining time, one should likewise prepare instruments. ||
### One should secretly apply the "seed" <note>The "seed" refers to the driving force, likely mercury</note> to the wonder-causing instrument. || 19 ||

**Likewise** means in the same way the self-rotating spherical instrument was prepared. **For the purpose of determining time**, meaning for the precise knowledge of the elapsed part of the day and so on, one should prepare instruments—self-rotating mechanisms other than the self-rotating sphere.

# Surya Siddhanta - [Chapter Thirteen]

The astronomer <note>original: "ganaka"</note> should have these instruments constructed through their own manual skill and craftsmanship. In an instrument meant for calculating time, which is a cause of wonder, the "seed" <note>the secret internal mechanism or driving force</note> that makes it self-rotating should be applied by the astronomer alone, in solitude, without a second person. This means he should complete it himself through his knowledge of mechanics. Otherwise, if a second person gains that knowledge, the secret of the instrument's construction might reach the ears of the public, and the sense of wonder would be lost. || 19 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** For the purpose of calculating time, one should construct instruments; the wondrous "seed" (mechanism) should be added to the instrument by the astronomer alone. || 19 ||

Now, because these self-rotating instruments are difficult to construct, the author explains that the knowledge of time should be acquired through instruments like the gnomon:

-> Through the gnomon, the staff, the bow, and the circle, and various shadow instruments, <-
-> the knowledge of time should be understood by those who are diligent, following the instructions of a teacher. <- || 20 ||

Through the well-known <term>Gnomon</term> <note>Shanku: a vertical pillar used to cast a shadow</note>, <term>Staff</term> <note>Yashti: a measuring rod</note>, <term>Bow</term> <note>Dhanu: a semi-circular instrument</note>, and <term>Circle</term> <note>Chakra: a circular instrument</note>, which are instruments for measuring shadows, and through various mathematical methods and the sincere instructions of one's teacher, diligent men—free from confusion—should understand the knowledge of time, such as the elapsed portion of the day. This has all been clarified by the teacher Bhaskara in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*. Regarding the nature of the gnomon: "A <term>Gnomon</term> made of ivory, its top and circumference turned smooth on a lathe; from its shadow, the knowledge of direction, place, and time is declared." Regarding the Staff instrument: "Having drawn a circle with a radius equal to half the diameter, marked with directions... [technical details of the staff's placement and the sine of the altitude]... the remaining nadis <note>units of time equal to 24 minutes</note> of the day, past or remaining, are found." Regarding the Circle instrument: "A circle marked with degrees, suspended by a loose chain... having placed a thin axis in the center and facing the sun... the degrees of altitude from the earth are observed." Regarding the Bow instrument: "They say a circle cut in half is a Bow." Further detailed descriptions and mathematical inquiries into these have been omitted here for fear of making the text too long. || 20 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** A man free from confusion, following the teacher's instruction, should know the time through the gnomon, staff, bow, circle, and various shadow instruments. || 20 ||

Now, the author concludes the section on time-keeping by stating that one should accurately calculate the time, which is the support of all life, using water clocks and other ingenious devices:

-> By means of water-clocks, the bowl-instrument, and others; by peacocks, men, and monkeys; <-
-> and by instruments containing strings and sand, one should accurately calculate the time. <- || 21 ||

The <term>Water-clock</term> <note>Jala-yantra</note> and the bowl-shaped vessel <note>Kapala</note>—the water instrument known as the *Kapala* which will be described—are primary. By <unclear>these instruments</uncall>, such as sand-clocks and relative clepsydras, and by "peacocks, men, and monkeys" <note>referring to automated figures or automata that move to indicate time</note>. The self-rotating instrument named the Peacock...

# Chapter 13. | With Sanskrit and Language Commentaries. ( 229 )

The independent "Man-Machine," the "Conch-Machine" (a type of sundial), and the previously mentioned "Monkey-Machine" are self-moving and independent. These function by using "thread-filled dust" <note>original: *sasūtra-reṇu-garbhaiḥ*</note>, meaning threads combined with dust or sand contained within them. According to popular knowledge, these machines consist of sixty earthen pots strung on a thread; as the sand or dust exits from the mouth of a figure like a peacock, it moves from one pot to another on its own. Alternatively, it refers to the well-known "Sand-Clock" <term>Valuka-yantra: a device using the flow of fine sand to measure time</term> which contains sand particles shaped like a thread within its belly. Thus, the meaning is established: time is measured using these peacock-shaped machines along with the sand-clock. The word "and" <note>the Sanskrit particle *ca*</note> is used to include other devices such as water-clocks <note>original: *toya-yantra-kapāla*</note>. One should accurately determine the time, such as the elapsed portion of the day, with great precision. This means one should know it through these subtle methods. || 21 ||

<gloss>Language Commentary (Hindi): One should accurately calculate time using water-clocks, peacock-shaped devices, man-shaped devices, and monkey-shaped devices equipped with threads and sand-filled interiors. || 21 ||</gloss>

Now, one might ask: how are these self-moving peacock machines and others constructed? To this, he explains that the methods for their construction are many and difficult to master:

### Mercury, water, threads, mechanical skill, oil, and liquids; ||
### Seeds and dust—the applications of these in those machines are difficult to attain. || 22 ||

In those peacock-shaped machines, these "applications" <note>methods or experiments</note> should be applied intensely to achieve self-motion. "Intensely" means until the desired result is achieved. What are these? He says: "Mercury, water, threads, etc." This refers to spokes filled with mercury. As stated in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>A major 12th-century astronomical treatise by Bhaskara II</note>:
> "On a wheel made of light wood, equal holes are made at equal intervals on the rim. Curved hollow tubes should be attached, each half-filled with mercury. When placed on a supporting axis, that wheel rotates by itself."

"Water" refers to the application of water power. "Threads" refers to the use of cordage. "Mechanical skill" <note>original: *shulba* interpreted as *shilpa*</note> refers to craftsmanship and ingenuity. "Oil and liquids" refers to the use of water mixed with oil, or the separate use of both. As also stated in the *Siddhanta Shiromani*:
> "Having carved the rim or attaching it with wax, and placing a palm leaf over it, pour mercury into the hollow until the water poured on one side of the mercury does not pass to the other. When the hole is sealed, the wheel rotates by itself, pulled by the water. Using a hook-shaped tube made of copper or similar material filled with water, with one end in a reservoir and the other facing downward outside—if released simultaneously, the water falls out of the reservoir through the tube. Small pots tied to the rim of a wheel are maintained by the action of the water-machine. As the water falling from the tube enters the pots, the wheel is constantly pulled and rotated by the filled pots. The water falling from the wheel returns to the reservoir through a channel."

"Seeds" refers to the use of only *Tunga* seeds. "Dust" refers to the application of fine sand. The word "also" implies that while these methods exist, they are "difficult to attain"—meaning they are impossible for ordinary men to construct. Otherwise, self-moving machines would be found in every house. This science of self-motion <term>Svayamvaha: perpetual motion or automated mechanics</term> has been thoroughly mastered by the people living across the sea called the <term>Phirangis: a term used historically in India to refer to Europeans, particularly the Portuguese or British</term>. Because this involves "trick-knowledge" <note>mechanics that seem like magic</note>, it is only briefly mentioned here rather than expanded upon. || 22 ||

<summary>This page describes various mechanical "self-moving" devices (automata) used for timekeeping, including sand-clocks and mercury-weighted wheels. It acknowledges the complexity of these machines, noting that such advanced mechanical engineering was a specialty of Europeans (Phirangis) at the time.</summary>

**Hindi Commentary:** And all these—mercury, water, threads, skillful craftsmanship, oiled water, mercury, and sand—the application of all these instruments is extremely difficult to master. || 22 ||

### Now he describes the water instrument called the Kapala (Bowl):

> A copper vessel with a hole at the bottom, placed in a basin of pure water,
> sinks sixty times in a day and night; this is the clear Kapala instrument. || 23 ||

That vessel made of copper which has a hole at the bottom (the lower part). When placed in a basin—a large container—filled with pure water, it sinks exactly sixty times in a day and night (a sidereal day), neither more nor less. By the water entering through the hole at the bottom, it becomes full and submerged. This is the *Kapalaka* <note>literally "a bowl" or "skull-cup"</note>; because fragments of a jar are called *Kapala*, this instrument is shaped like the lower half of a water jar and is clearly a *Ghati-yantra* <note>a clepsydra or water clock</note>. Its construction is explained more explicitly elsewhere: "A vessel made of ten *palas* <note>a unit of weight</note> of copper, eight fingers high and twice as wide at the mouth. That vessel, which holds sixty *palas* of water and resembles half a jar, is a *Ghati*. A needle made of three and one-third *mashas* of gold, four fingers long, should be used to pierce it. That vessel is then filled by the water in one *nadika* <note>24 minutes</note>." The Lord <note>the author of the text</note> has described this subtly here. || 23 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In a jar filled with pure water, place a copper vessel (a bowl) that has a hole in the bottom. This *Kapalaka* instrument will sink in the water sixty times in a day and night. || 23 ||

### Now he states that the Gnomon instrument is for knowing the time only during the day and not otherwise:

> Likewise, the Gnomon instrument is excellent during the day when the sun is clear;
> through the calculation of shadows, the best means of determining time is proclaimed. || 24 ||

When the sun is "clear"—meaning free from the "impurity" of clouds and such—on such a day. The word "and" here implies "only," thereby excluding cloudy days. The *Nara-yantra* <note>literally "Man-instrument," referring to the Gnomon</note>, which is a gnomon of twelve digits, is an accurate determiner of time just like the water clock; the implication is that it does not work at night. Now, one might ask: the gnomon determines the shadow, not the time, so how can it be called a "time-measuring instrument" (*Yantra*)? To this he says: "through the calculation of shadows." This gnomon instrument, by means of the accurate determination and understanding of the shadow, is the "best" cause for determining the time, such as the part of the day already elapsed. It is superior to other instruments because of its constancy. Thus, by being a means to find the shadow, the gnomon becomes a means to find the time; therefore, its status as an instrument is not contradicted. For this reason, it is useless on cloudy days and at night. Since "Man" (*Nara*) is a general term for shadow instruments, the staff, the bow, and the circle instruments should also be understood in this category. || 24 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** During the day, when the sun is clear, the excellent *Nara-yantra* (12 digits) is prescribed for determining the time through the correction of shadows. || 24 ||

### Now, by stating a single result for the knowledge of the text from the beginning to this point, he unites the two divided sections:

The "movements of the planets and stars" refers to the mathematical knowledge contained in the first section of this book. "In its true essence" means according to the actual state of reality. This means the chapter of that name, which is a specific portion of this book, is now complete.

## Chapter Fourteen

Now, the Chapter on Measurements is begun to answer the remaining questions: "How many measurements are there, and what are they used for?" First, the author answers the question of how many measurements there are:

> The Solar, the Terrestrial, the Lunar, and the Sidereal—these are indeed the nine measurements. || 1 ||

"Indeed" is used for emphasis. There are nine distinct measurements of time. Among them, the first is the "Brahma measurement." The second is the "Divine measurement" (the measurement of the Gods), starting with "That is called a divine day..."

### Now, wishing to answer the second question regarding "what is the use of them," he first shows the measurements useful for worldly affairs:

**The sixty-year cycle should be known by the Jupiterian measurement; the others are not for constant use. ॥ 2 ॥**

In this world of mortals, "worldly affairs"—the arrangement of rituals and activities—are conducted by the four measurements: Solar, Lunar, Sidereal, and Civil. The "sixty-year cycle" refers to the sixty years beginning with *Prabhava* <note>the first year of the 60-year Jovian cycle</note>; the singular form is used here to denote the class of years. "Between those" refers to the intervals between the equinoxes and solstices. # Chapter 14. With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries.

Now, he describes the seasons, months, and years—

> **The seasons are governed by two zodiac signs each, beginning with the cool season (Shishira).**
> **The twelve signs starting with Aries are the months; by these alone, a year is formed. || 10 ||**

From that point, meaning from the sun's entry into Capricorn <note>the winter solstice</note>. The word "also" is used to include the duration of the northern transit of the sun <term>Uttarayana: the period when the sun moves northwards</term>. "Governed by two signs" means that each season consists of the sun's passage through two zodiac signs. The seasons—the cool season (*Shishira*), spring (*Vasanta*), summer (*Grishma*), the rains (*Varsha*), autumn (*Sharad*), and winter (*Hemanta*)—are specific divisions of time. These twelve signs, starting with Aries, which relate to the sun's movement, are the twelve months. The word "alone" is used to exclude any more or less. A year is thus a solar year. || 10 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** From that time (the Capricorn transit), all seasons like the cool season are experienced through two signs each. Twelve months starting from Aries make one year. || 10 ||

Now, in this context, he describes the calculation of the auspicious time (*Punya-kala*) during a solar transit—

> **The minutes of the Sun’s diameter, multiplied by sixty and divided by its daily motion;**
> **half of those minutes of time before the transit, and the same after, are auspicious. || 11 ||**

The minutes of the measure of the Sun's disk <note>the angular diameter</note> are multiplied by sixty and divided by the Sun's daily motion <term>Bhukti: the distance a planet travels in a day</term>. Half of that resulting number represents the amount of *ghatikas* <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>. From the transit—meaning the moment the Sun enters a new zodiac sign—that amount of time "before" is auspicious for religious acts like ritual bathing. "After" the transit, the same amount of time is likewise a giver of merit for religious acts.

The logic here is as follows: The moment of transit is when the center of the Sun's disk moves into the beginning of a sign. Because that moment is so subtle and difficult to perceive, a "gross" or measurable period must be accepted. This is taken as the period during which the disk itself is in contact with the start of the sign. Therefore, the proportion is: if the Sun's daily motion takes 60 terrestrial *ghatikas*, how much time do the minutes of the Sun's disk take? The resulting "disk-time" is the total duration of the transit from the moment the front edge touches the sign to the moment the back edge enters. Half of those *ghatikas* (representing the radius) before and after the central moment are considered auspicious because the Sun is transitioning during that entire span. || 11 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** Multiply the Sun's diameter minutes by 60 and divide by its daily motion. Half of the result, when subtracted from and added to the moment of transit, creates an interval that is extremely auspicious. || 11 ||

Having spoken of solar measurement, he now describes lunar measurement in its proper order—

> **The distance the Moon travels eastward every day after departing from the Sun**
> **is the lunar measure; a lunar day (Tithi) is known by twelve degrees of that distance. || 12 ||**

After leaving its conjunction with the Sun and becoming separate, the amount the Moon travels toward the east every day is the daily lunar measure; this is equal to the difference between the motions of the Sun and Moon. Now—

Just as a solar day is determined by the sun's degree, the author now explains how many of these degrees constitute a full lunar day. **By degrees:** This refers to the degrees arising from the distance between the Sun and the Moon, as that is its nature. **By twelve:** By the number twelve, a **tithi** <note>A lunar day, defined as the time it takes for the longitudinal angle between the Moon and the Sun to increase by 12 degrees.</note> should be known. This means one lunar day is to be understood. The implication is this: since the lunar day begins from the conjunction of the Sun and Moon and the month ends at their next conjunction, a lunar month consists of thirty lunar days based on the difference in their revolutions. Therefore, if thirty days equal the full circle of degrees, what does one day equal? One lunar day equals twelve degrees. Because of the definition "the New Moon is the union of Sun and Moon," and because the month ending with the New Moon consists of thirty lunar days, a *tithi* is the form of a lunar day. || 12 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Moving from the Sun, the Moon travels eastward day by day; the time it takes to move 12 degrees away from the Sun is called a *tithi*. || 12 ||

### Now he describes the practical use of lunar time—

### The lunar day (tithi), the half-day (karana), marriage, tonsure, and all such rites;
### The performance of vows, fasting, and pilgrimages are undertaken according to lunar time. || 13 ||

The *tithi* refers to the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipada*) and so on. A <term>karana</term> <note>A half-tithi; there are 11 types of karanas used in Vedic astrology.</note> refers to *bava* and the others. **Marriage** refers to the wedding ceremony. **Tonsure** refers to the first hair-cutting ceremony (*chaula-karma*). These and all other actions, such as the thread ceremony and festivals, as well as the performance of **vows, fasting, and pilgrimages**—meaning religious observances, abstaining from food, and travel—are all undertaken or accepted according to lunar measurement. || 13 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** <term>Tithi</term>, <term>karana</term>, marriage, tonsure, and all such rituals, along with vows, fasting, and travel, are all accepted in lunar time. || 13 ||

### Now, in this context, he describes the lunar month and the measurement of time for the Ancestors (Pitris)—

### Thirty lunar days make a lunar month, which is declared a day and night for the Ancestors.
### Their division is at the end of the month and the end of the fortnight. || 14 ||

By **thirty**—meaning thirty measured lunar days—a lunar month is formed. This is **for the Ancestors** (*paitrya*), relating to the Pitris. **Day** means the daylight portion, and **night** means the night relating to the Ancestors. The word "and" indicates the arrangement. Thus, the two are not separate but are remembered as a combined unit, as the grammar suggests. Therefore, a lunar month is a full day and night (nychthemeron) of the Ancestors. This is the result. **The end of the month and the end of the fortnight:** the end of the month is the New Moon (*darsha*), and the end of the fortnight is the Full Moon (*purnima*). These two points, **by division**—meaning in sequence—occur in the middle of the day and night of the Ancestors. This means the end of the New Moon is midday for the Ancestors, and the end of the Full Moon is midnight for the Ancestors. Consequently, it is established that their day begins at the middle of the dark half's eighth day (*krishna-ashtami*) and ends at the middle of the bright half's eighth day (*shukla-ashtami*). || 14 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** A lunar month of 30 *tithis* is one day for the Ancestors, and the end of the fortnight is the night; in this division, one month constitutes their full day and night. || 14 ||

<vocab>Surya Siddhanta, lunar measurement (chandramana), ancestral measurement (pitryamana), tithi, karana, New Moon (darsha), Full Moon (purnimanta)</vocab>

# Chapter 14. ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. ( 237 )

Now, the author describes the sidereal measurement in its proper order, and incidentally, the naming of the months—

**The constant revolution of the sidereal sphere is called a sidereal day.**
**The months are to be known by the names of the constellations, determined by their conjunction at the end of the full moon period. || 15 ||**

"Constant," meaning every day, the "revolution of the sidereal sphere" refers to the rotation of the entire collection of stars caused by the *Pravaha* wind <note>In ancient Indian cosmology, the *Pravaha* wind is the celestial force believed to drive the rotation of the planets and stars around the Earth</note>. This is called a "sidereal day" by those knowledgeable in measurements. By using the word "constant," the idea that a sidereal day is defined by the Moon's passage through a single constellation is rejected, as that would not account for the entire sphere's revolution.

Regarding the naming of the months: "by the names of the constellations" at the "end of the full moon period." This refers to the conjunction of the Moon with a specific star at the moment the full moon ends. Through this connection, the months receive their names. The word "but" (*tu*) implies that these are to be understood as lunar months. The essential meaning is that the month is named after the constellation in which the Moon is situated at the end of the full moon.

For instance, within the lunar month ending at the new moon, the name is derived from the constellation at the full moon:
*   From the connection with *Chitra*, it is **Chaitra**.
*   From *Vishakha*, **Vaishakha**.
*   From *Jyeshtha*, **Jyeshtha**.
*   From *Ashadha*, **Ashadha**.
*   From *Shravana*, **Shravana**.
*   From *Bhadrapada*, **Bhadrapada**.
*   From *Ashwini*, **Ashwin**.
*   From *Krittika*, **Kartika**.
*   From *Mrigashirsha*, **Margashirsha**.
*   From *Pushya*, **Pausha**.
*   From *Magha*, **Magha**.
*   From *Phalguni*, **Phalguna**. || 15 ||

<margin>Hindi Commentary</margin>—The daily revolution of the sidereal sphere is the sidereal day. The name of the month should be known from the constellation occupied at the end of the full moon. || 15 ||

Now, one might ask: if a specific constellation is not present at the end of the full moon, how can the naming be appropriate? To this, the author says—

**In the months starting with Kartika, the conjunction occurs with pairs of constellations starting with Krittika.**
**The last, the penultimate, and the fifth months are known to be associated with three constellations each. || 16 ||**

The use of the locative case here implies "for the sake of the conjunction of constellations." In the full moons of the months starting with Kartika: two constellations are assigned to each month.
*   **Kartika** is from *Krittika* and *Rohini*.
*   **Margashirsha** from *Mrigashira* and *Ardra*.
*   **Pausha** from *Punarvasu* and *Pushya*.
*   **Magha** from *Ashlesha* and *Magha*.
*   **Chaitra** from *Chitra* and *Svati*.
*   **Vaishakha** from *Vishakha* and *Anuradha*.
*   **Jyeshtha** from *Jyeshtha* and *Mula*.
*   **Ashadha** from *Purvashadha* and *Uttarashadha*.
*   **Shravana** from *Shravana* and *Dhanishtha*.

The author then mentions the remaining months: "the last, the penultimate, and the fifth." Since Kartika is the first here, the "last" is **Ashwin**, the "penultimate" is **Bhadrapada**, and the "fifth" (counting from Kartika) is **Phalguna**. These three months are "threefold," meaning they are linked to three constellations each:
*   **Ashwin** is established by the three constellations *Revati*, *Ashwini*, and *Bharani*.
*   **Bhadrapada** by *Shatataraka*, *Purvabhadrapada*, and *Uttarabhadrapada*.
*   **Phalguna** by *Purvaphalguni*, *Uttaraphalguni*, and *Hasta*. || 16 ||

<margin>Hindi Commentary</margin>—In the full moon of the month of Kartika and others, the name of each month is derived from two constellations. The names of the fifth, the last, and the penultimate months—Phalguna, Ashwin, and Bhadrapada—are established through three constellations. || 16 ||

<note>original terms: bhachakra-bhramanam (revolution of the star-sphere), nakshatra (constellation/star), purnimanta (end of the full moon)</note>

<summary>This page defines a sidereal day as the full rotation of the celestial sphere and explains the etymological system for naming the twelve Hindu lunar months based on the specific constellations (Nakshatras) where the full moon occurs.</summary>

### Now, in this context, the years of Jupiter starting from Kartika are described:

-> When the conjunction occurs on the fifteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight in months such as Vaishakha, <-
-> the years of Jupiter, starting from Kartika, are determined by his setting and rising. || 17 || <-

Just as a month is named after the constellation (Nakshatra) in conjunction with the full moon, so too—the word "and" here implies a similar logic—is the year named. Based on Jupiter’s proximity to or distance from the Sun (his setting or rising), if a conjunction with a constellation occurs on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight (the New Moon or *Amavasya*) in the twelve months starting with Vaishakha, the twelve Jovian years beginning with Kartika are formed. 

Specifically, if Jupiter rises or sets on the New Moon of the dark fortnight of Vaishakha, that Jovian year is named Kartika due to the connection with the constellation Krittika <note>The Pleiades</note>. Similarly, for the New Moons of Jyeshtha, Ashadha, Shravana, Bhadrapada, Ashvina, Kartika, Margashirsha, Pausha, Magha, Phalguna, and Chaitra, the years (Margashirsha, etc.) are determined by the constellations: Mrigashira, Pushya, Magha, Purva-Phalguni, Chitra, Vishakha, Jyeshtha, Purva-Ashadha, Shravana, Purva-Bhadrapada, and Ashvini. 

The previous rule regarding the grouping of two or three constellations per month should be understood here as well. This description is an illustration; the core meaning is that the Jovian year is named after whatever constellation the Moon occupies on the day Jupiter rises or sets. While the *Samhita* <note>astrological compendiums</note> texts mention both setting and rising, current calculators typically use the rising of Jupiter to define the start of the year. || 17 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** Just as months are named by the constellation of the Full Moon in Vaishakha etc., the Jovian year is named according to the constellation present on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight (New Moon) at the time of Jupiter’s setting or rising. || 17 ||

### Now, the Civil (Savana) measure is described in its proper order:

-> From one sunrise of the Sun to the next sunrise is declared to be a Civil day. <-
-> Civil days are determined by this; the rules for the timing of sacrifices are based on them. || 18 || <-

The duration starting from one sunrise of the Sun until the very next sunrise is defined by the authorities as a "Civil" (*Savana*) day. By counting the intervals between two such sunrises, the total Civil days (such as the 1,577,917,828 days in a Kalpa mentioned in the chapter on Mean Motion) are calculated. Regarding its practical use: the "rules for the timing of sacrifices" refers to the calculation of the time required for Vedic rituals, which is done using these Civil days. The word "but" (*tu*) in the verse is used for emphasis, to exclude other measures of time for this specific purpose. || 18 ||

**Vernacular Commentary:** The name for the time from one sunrise to the next sunrise is *Savana*. The procedures for the timing of sacrifices are decided by this measure alone. || 18 ||

### Now, other practical uses are described:

-> The determination of impurity periods, days, months, and years, <-
-> as well as the mean motion of the planets, is grasped only through the Civil measure. || 19 || <-

<note>The text concludes here mid-explanation of the Civil day's uses, including *Sutaka* (ritual impurity after birth or death).</note>

# Chapter 14: With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries

<page-num>( 239 )</page-num>

The term *Sutaka* <note>Impurity period</note> refers to matters concerning birth and death. The word "etc." <insert>in the original verse</insert> includes medical treatments and the *Chandrayana* <note>a lunar fast/penance</note>; the determination of these is based on this measurement. The lords of the day, month, and year are also determined here. Furthermore, the mean motion of the planets is used; the word "but" <note>Sanskrit: *tu*</note> is used to exclude true motion, because true motion varies every moment and lacks a fixed relationship to a single day. By this, the calculation of true planets using true motion is rejected here because it would be too imprecise <note>literally "gross" or "thick"</note> for these specific purposes. This is accepted by the learned using the Civil measurement <term>Savana-mana: time measured by successive sunrises</term> and no other. In this context, the plural usage should be understood as an expression of respect. || 19 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The days of impurity such as *Sutaka*, and the lords of the month and year, are taken according to the mean motion of the planets following the Civil (Savana) measurement. || 19 ||

Now, he describes the Divine measurement:

->**The day and night of the Gods and Demons are mutually reversed.**<-
->**That which is declared as the completion of the Sun’s revolution is a Divine Day. || 20 ||**<-

The first half of the verse was explained previously. That "day and night" mentioned in the first half, which is completed by the Sun finishing its entire circle of the zodiac <note>one solar year</note>, as determined in various ways by the ancients, is known as the Divine measurement. || 20 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Due to their mutually opposite locations, the day and night of the Gods and Demons are reversed. The time taken for the Sun to complete one full revolution is a Divine Day. || 20 ||

Now, he describes the remaining Prajapatya and Brahma measurements:

->**The arrangement of the Manvantaras is declared as the Prajapatya measurement.**<-
->**There is no distinction between day and night there; a Kalpa is proclaimed as the Brahma measurement. || 21 ||**<-

The "arrangement of the Manvantaras" refers to the duration of a Manvantara <note>a vast period of time ruled by a Manu</note>. As stated in the chapter on mean motions, "seventy-one [Great Ages]..." etc. This is called the *Prajapatya* measurement by those who know time, because the Manus are the sons of Prajapati <note>the Creator</note>. Now, one might ask: "Just as the distinction between day and night was explained for the Divine and Ancestral measurements, why is there no such distinction mentioned for this measurement?" To this, he says "There is no..." In the Prajapatya measurement, there is no distinction between day and night as there is in the Jovian, Solar, or Lunar measurements. He then defines the Brahma measurement: A *Kalpa*, which consists of a thousand Great Ages as previously mentioned, is called the Brahma measurement by the experts. 

<margin>Note on repetition: Although these were mentioned before, they are repeated here to define them specifically as "measurements" (Manas) for mathematical application, rather than just general definitions.</margin>

Even though the Ancestral and Jovian measurements were not mentioned immediately prior, and the description of others might seem repetitive, this is done to establish the technical definitions necessary for mathematical operations. Previously they were described as non-measurements <note>in certain contexts</note>, but here they are described as formal measurements to answer specific questions; otherwise, the student's inquiry would remain unsatisfied. || 21 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** The arrangement of the Manvantaras like Prajapati has been stated before. In this, there is no distinction between day and night. The *Kalpa* itself is the Brahma measurement. || 21 ||

### Now, he concludes his own teaching:

> This supreme secret, most wonderful, has been told to you.
> This is the supreme Brahman, holy, and the destroyer of all sins. || 22 ||

O supreme among the Daityas <note>referring to Maya, the recipient of the revelation</note>, because of your devotion to the Sun, this "supreme" second discourse has now been told to you in its entirety, leaving no desire for more. Previously, the teaching was left incomplete, which led you to ask further questions; this second discourse, given as an answer to those questions, is beyond doubt, meaning no further uncertainties should arise in you. 

Now, one might ask: "Why was this not told earlier without me having to ask?" To this, he says it is a **secret**. Why? Because it is **wonderful**. It is marvelous because it provides the knowledge of the positions of the planets and stars in the sky. Furthermore, only one who had listened to my previous words with great care could have asked the questions you did. Therefore, this second part was spoken as an answer after testing you; this is the sense of it being a "secret." 

One might then argue: "The bliss of Brahman <note>ultimate reality/liberation</note> is not attained through the knowledge of worldly sciences, so why study this?" To this, he says **Brahman**. This teaching of mine is like Brahman itself. While other sciences may not be equal to Brahman, there is no wonder that the bliss of Brahman is attained through this, as it is of the very nature of Brahman. Why is it equal to Brahman? Because it is **supreme**—meaning excellent. He provides two reasons for this: it is **holy** and the **destroyer of all sins**. It generates merit and wipes away all transgressions. || 22 ||

**Translation of the Commentary:** O Great One! This most wonderful secret has been told. This is extremely holy, the destroyer of all sins, and indeed, is the very form of Brahman. || 22 ||

Now, it was previously stated that one attains the bliss of Brahman from this, and also that one attains the worlds of the planets. What is the result of these two? To this, he says:

> The divine knowledge of the stars and of the planets has been shown to you as the highest.
> Having understood this, one attains an eternal place in the worlds of the Sun and others. || 23 ||

**Of the stars** means knowledge related to the lunar mansions; **knowledge of the planets** refers to their movements. The word "and" serves to connect them. This is **highest**, meaning superior to all other sciences. The reason for this is the adjective **divine**, meaning it originated in the heavenly world. Having been taught by me and having **understood** it—that is, having realized it—one attains a **place**, a residence, in the **worlds of the Sun and others** (the planetary spheres). This place is **eternal**, meaning a permanent station in the form of union with Brahman. 

The second "and" in the first half of the verse connects the results. Thus, the sense is that both fruits (heavenly residence and liberation) are attained in succession. 

<note>Textual variant note:</note> In some manuscripts, the verse "This supreme secret..." (22) does not appear before this verse. Instead, after the verse "The divine knowledge of the stars..." which concludes the description of time-measurements, the Chapter on Measurements is ended, and the following is added: "As the crest is to the peacocks, as the jewels are to the serpents, so is Mathematics <term>Ganita: the science of calculation</term> situated at the head of all the sciences of the limbs of the Veda. || 1 || It should not be given to the ungrateful, to the subverters of the Veda, to the greedy, the foolish, the arrogant, or the sinful. || 2 || It should not be given even to a son or a brother of such a nature."

<summary>This page concludes the Surya Siddhanta's core revelation, framing the study of astronomy as a sacred path to spiritual liberation (Brahman) and heavenly rewards. It emphasizes that mathematical astronomy is the "crown" of the Vedic sciences and must be guarded as a secret from the unworthy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the concluding remarks of the astronomical treatise, specifically addressing the "Correction of Parameters" (Beeja) and the proper transmission of this secret knowledge.</meta>

<sig>16</sig>

> ...the path would be utterly destroyed. || 3 || Both the teacher and the disciple would fall into the most terrible, blinding darkness <note>original: "andhatamisram"; a reference to a specific hell for those who misuse sacred knowledge</note>. Therefore, one should bestow this knowledge only upon a peaceful and pure Brahmin. || 4 || The mean position arising from the revolution of the circles and the true position arising from the degrees of the epicycle <note>term: epicycle (vritta); a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used to calculate planetary anomalies</note> will not remain equal to observation over time; therefore, the *Beeja* <note>term: Beeja (seed/correction); a periodic correction applied to astronomical parameters to bring calculated positions into agreement with observation</note> process is described. || 5 || Multiply the Moon's position (beginning with Aries) by half and divide by the number of lunar mansions <note>original: "nakshatra-kaksha"; the orbital path of the stars</note>. Take the remainder of those two remainders... || 6 || Subtract the smaller one from the orbital path of the stars multiplied by the lunar days. That result, in degrees etc., is the *Beeja*; it should be added to the Sun. || 7 || Subtract three times the amount from the Moon; add twenty-four times the amount to Mars. For Mercury's high apex <note>term: high apex (ucca); the apogee or point furthest from Earth</note>, the correction is additive or subtractive to match observation; for Jupiter, subtract thirty times the amount. || 8 || For the conjunction of Venus, the correction is subtractive, multiplied by ninety. For Saturn, the correction is additive, multiplied by seven. Now the circumferences <note>original: "paridhi"; the dimensions of the epicycles</note> are described. || 9 || The circumferences stated for the end of even quadrants are always considered "corrected." Those stated for the end of odd quadrants are to be known as refined by the "Great Correction" (*Para-Beeja*). || 10 || At the end of the odd quadrants, the degrees of the circles for the Sun and Moon are without correction. For the Sun and Moon, the values are 14 and 32, reduced by 18, 24, and 25 minutes... || 11 || For Mars, they are 5 and 6; for Mercury, 7 and 2; for Jupiter, 8 and 2; for Venus, 0 and 1; for Saturn... || 12 || ...12 and 6. One should calculate the correction with these. The correction, divided by 30, should be subtracted from the Sun's epicycle degrees. || 13 || Multiply by 12 and add to the Moon; for Mars, multiply by 2 and add. For Mercury, multiply by 1 and add; for Jupiter, add the amount multiplied by 14. || 14 || For Venus, add the amount multiplied by 31; for Saturn, subtract the amount multiplied by 12. Thus, the degrees of the *Manda* <note>term: Manda; the slow or "apsidal" epicycle used to calculate the equation of center</note> epicycles become corrected. Now for the *Shighra* <note>term: Shighra; the fast or "conjunction" epicycle used to calculate the equation of conjunction</note> epicycles: || 15 || For Mars, 230; for Mercury, 134; for Jupiter, 55; for Venus, 261. || 16 || For Saturn, 41. At the end of odd quadrants, these are without correction. Add twice the amount to Mars' degrees; for Mercury, subtract twice the amount. || 17 || For Jupiter, add the amount multiplied by 18; for Venus, subtract the amount multiplied by 1. For Saturn, subtract the amount multiplied by 1. By these, the planets become equal to observation. || 18 || This *Beeja* has been explained by me to you out of great affection. It must always be kept secret and not taught here and there. || 19 || It should be given to a tested disciple who is devoted to the teacher and virtuous—to a Brahmin, and to no one else who acts as a "cloak-wearer" <note>original: "pratikanchukakarine"; likely referring to a pretender or someone who hides their true motives</note>. || 20 || This *Beeja* is the supreme, clear secret of the entire *Siddhanta* <note>term: Siddhanta; a comprehensive treatise on astronomy</note>. It grants the successful accomplishment of journeys, marriages, and other works. || 21 ||

The "Chapter on the Application of Correction" (*Beejopanayanadhyaya*) found written at the end of some books is seen here, but it is not appropriate. Because the *Uttara-Khanda* (Latter Section) lacks the description of planetary mathematics, it is improper to write a chapter there that belongs to that context. It would have been more fitting to write it at the end of the *Spashtadhikara* (Chapter on True Positions). Furthermore, since there are no further questions after the question "What are the measurements and what is their use?", placing this in the *Uttara-Khanda*—which serves as the answer to those questions—is inconsistent. Moreover, since the *Beeja* (discrepancy) did not exist at the time of the original teaching and the future divergence is unpredictable, how could it have been taught as part of the original internal text? Considering this, it should be understood that someone, seeing the *Beeja* elsewhere, inserted this "Chapter on the Application of Correction" at the end here to give it the authority of the sages; therefore, it has not been commented upon. || 23 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** By attaining this divine and excellent knowledge regarding the planets and stars which I have spoken, one gains an eternal place in the worlds of the Sun and others. || 23 ||

# Surya Siddhanta — [Chapter Fourteen]

Now, the author describes the conclusion of the dialogue spoken to the sages:

> Having spoken thus and taking leave of Maya, being duly honored by him, ||
> the part of the Sun ascended to heaven and entered his own orb. || 24 ||

The person who was a portion of the Sun <note>original: "Suryansha-purusha"</note>, having taken leave of Maya the Asura <note>a class of powerful beings in Vedic cosmology</note> after duly teaching the movements of the planets and so forth—having spoken these two verses—ascended to heaven. He made the sky the object of his approach. Now, one might ask: what purpose was served by the Sun's portion giving this instruction? To this, he says: "by him." He was honored by Maya the Asura with offerings of scents, incense, food, garments, and ornaments. The implication is that through Maya, he attained success in the mortal world as an equal to the Sun. Where in heaven did he go? He "entered his own orb," meaning he took his seat within the disc of the Sun. || 24 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** In this manner, after giving the full instruction to Maya and being honored by him, the person who was a portion of the Sun ascended to heaven and entered the solar orb. || 24 ||

---

Now he describes the state of Maya the Asura at that time:

> Maya then, having learned that divine knowledge directly from the Sun, ||
> considered himself as one who had accomplished his purpose, with his sins washed away. || 25 ||

Now, after the disappearance of the Sun's portion, Maya the Asura—having learned that divine, heavenly knowledge of the positions of the planets and stars directly from the Sun (meaning through no other intermediary)—considered himself "one who had accomplished his purpose" <term>Kritakritya: the feeling of having fulfilled one's life mission</term> and "cleansed of sin." Since the Sun's portion was non-different from the Sun itself, having been produced from him, it is appropriate to say he learned it "directly" even if there was a perceived difference. || 25 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Maya also, having obtained divine knowledge directly from the Sun-Narayana, became fulfilled and free from impurity, and began to think of himself in this way. || 25 ||

---

Now, in response to the listening sages asking, "How did you obtain this knowledge?", the Sage tells them that "We, the Rishis, asked Maya for this knowledge":

> Then the Rishis, knowing that Maya had received a boon from the Sun, ||
> approached and surrounded him, and then asked for that knowledge with respect. || 26 ||

After Maya the Asura obtained the knowledge, the Rishis—including ourselves, who were in the lands adjacent to where the dialogue between the Sun's portion and Maya took place—knowing that Maya had "received a boon from the Sun" (the grace of knowledge), approached him. They surrounded him and then, with great respect and desire to learn, asked him for that knowledge regarding the movements of the planets. || 26 ||

**Hindi Commentary:** Knowing that Maya had received a boon from the Lord Sun, the sages came to him and asked with reverence. || 26 ||

# Chapter 14. ] With Sanskrit and Hindi Commentaries. ( 243 )

Now, it is described how Mayasura <note>A legendary figure in Hindu mythology, often depicted as a great architect and astronomer-scientist of the Asuras</note> imparted his knowledge to the sages, including ourselves, who had questioned him:

> **He, being pleased, granted to them the great motion of the planets,**
> **the most wonderful secret in the world, equal to the Vedas.** || 27 ||

The meaning is: Mayasura, being pleased and satisfied, gave—that is, explained clearly and without deception—to those sages (starting with ourselves) the knowledge of the positions and motions of the planets. This knowledge is immeasurable, and for that reason, it is "equal to the Vedas" <note>original: "Brahmasammitam"</note>. In the world of mortals, it is the most wonderful and excellent secret. || 27 ||

<note>Hindi commentary</note>
Hindi Translation: I have joyfully given to the sages the secret of the planets' character, which is extremely wonderful and equal to the Divine Truth. || 27 ||

Now, with the conclusion of the Chapter on Measurement <note>Mana-adhyaya</note>, the conclusion of the Surya Siddhanta is stated, along with verses to prevent any unauthorized additions to the chapter:

### The Chapter on Measurement in the Surya Siddhanta || 14 ||

In the commentary on the Surya Siddhanta composed by Ranganatha, titled *Gudha-prakashaka* (The Illuminator of Hidden Meanings), the latter portion of the Chapter on Measurement is now complete. || 1 ||
In the city of Varanasi, the city of Lord Shiva situated on the banks of the Ganges, there lived a wise astronomer named Ballala, who was a devotee of Lord Rudra. || 1 ||
His eldest son was Rama, endowed with five virtues and a knower of all scriptures. By his own intellect, he fully illuminated the proofs of the *Ananta-sudhakara*. || 2 ||
After him came Krishna, who attained great fame and prestige in the court of the Emperor Jahangir <note>The Mughal Emperor, reigned 1605–1627; this provides a historical anchor for the commentator</note>. He explained the "seed" <note>Bija, or astronomical corrections</note> of Bhaskara’s work and the system of Shripati. || 3 ||
The third was Govinda, an expert in that field. I am his younger brother, who obtained knowledge from my teacher. My mind is fixed on the lotus feet of the Lord of the Universe (Vishveshvara), I am a resident of Kashi (Varanasi), and I am respected by all. || 4 ||
I, Ranganatha, having composed this commentary called *Gudha-prakashaka* on the science originating from the mouth of the Sun, and being the younger brother of the scholar Mahadeva, have offered it to the Lord of the Universe for the sake of great prosperity. || 5 ||
In the Shaka year measured by the elements (5), the senses (5), and the world (1) <note>Shaka 1555, or 1633 CE</note>, in the month of Chaitra, during the bright fortnight on the day of Shiva (the 14th), on a Wednesday at sunrise, this commentary on the Surya Siddhanta was completed. || 6 ||
By seeing this *Gudha-prakashaka* born of Ranganatha on this earth, may astronomers easily attain the same knowledge as the Great Sage. || 7 ||

Thus ends the *Gudha-prakashaka*, the illumination of the hidden meanings of the Surya Siddhanta, composed by Ranganatha, the son of Ballala, the emperor of all astronomers.

->The Surya Siddhanta is finished.<-

->The Final Section is complete.<-
