# Example.

**Calculation of the Ahargana <note>The "Ahargana" is the total number of days elapsed from a fixed epoch to a specific date, used as the basis for all planetary calculations.</note> (Chapter 1, Verse 51).** On the first day of the Shaka year 1817 <note>Approximately 1895 CE.</note>, the total elapsed years of the Kalpa <note>A vast cosmic cycle.</note> are calculated as follows: the remainder of the Krita Yuga 1,953,720,000, plus the durations of the Treta and Dvapara Yugas 2,160,000, and the elapsed years of the Kali Yuga 4,996, totaling 1,955,884,996 years. Multiplying this by 12 gives 23,470,619,952 months. Multiplying this number by the number of intercalary months <term>Adhi-masa: extra lunar months added to synchronize the lunar and solar calendars</term> 1,593,336 results in 37,396,583,711,839,872. Dividing this by the total solar months 518,400,000 gives 721,384,716 (remainders are discarded). Adding this to the month count results in 24,192,004,668. Multiplying this month count by 30 and adding 18 for the lunar days <term>Tithi: a lunar day, roughly 1/30th of a lunar month</term> from the start of Chaitra <note>The first month of the Hindu year.</note> results in 725,760,140,058 days. Multiplying this day count by the omitted lunar days <term>Tithi Kshaya: "lost" days resulting from the difference between solar and lunar day lengths</term> 25,082,252 results in 18,203,698,744,900,506,16. Dividing this by the total lunar days 1,603,000,080 gives a quotient of 11,356,018,600. Subtracting this from the day count leaves a remainder of 714,404,121,458. Since it was a Saturday, the final Ahargana is 714,404,121,459.

**Calculation of the Mean Position (Chapter 1, Verse 53).** Multiplying the Ahargana by the Sun's revolutions 4,320,000 results in 3,086,225,804,702,880,000. Dividing this by the total solar days 1,557,917,828 gives a quotient of 1,955,884,995 revolutions. Multiplying the remainder 1,574,689,140 by 12 and dividing by the solar days gives 11 signs <term>Rashi: a zodiac sign, equal to 30 degrees</term>. Multiplying the remainder by 30 and dividing by the solar days gives 29 degrees <term>Ansha: degrees</term>. Further calculating the remainder into minutes and seconds gives 15 minutes <term>Kala</term>, 48 seconds <term>Vikala</term>, and 9 thirds <term>Anukala</term>. Discarding the final remainder and the full revolutions, the Mean Sun <note>The average position of the sun as if it moved in a perfect circle at a constant speed.</note> is 11s 29° 15' 48" 9'''.

**Calculation of Longitude <term>Deshantara: the correction for the difference in longitude between the observer's location and the prime meridian</term> (Chapter 1, Verse 60).** Multiplying the square of the Earth's diameter 1,600 Yojanas <note>An ancient unit of distance, roughly 8-13 km.</note> by 10 gives 25,600,000 (the square root of which is 5,060 Yojanas). Squaring a 5-digit shadow gives 25, and adding the square of the gnomon <term>Shanku: a vertical pillar used to measure shadows</term> 144, the square root is 13. This is the hypotenuse of the shadow. Multiplying the radius (3,438) by the gnomon of the equinox 12 gives 41,256. Dividing this by the shadow hypotenuse 13 gives a result of 3,173, which is the sine of the latitude. Multiplying this by the Yojana count 5,060 gives 16,055,380. Dividing this by the radius 3,438 gives the corrected circumference of the Earth as 4,669 Yojanas. If the distance of a certain place is 120 Yojanas, multiplying by the Sun's daily motion in minutes gives 8,890. Dividing this by the corrected circumference of the Earth results in 1 minute and 53 seconds.

Because this occurred in the eastern direction of the local country relative to the Mean Sun, by subtracting [the longitudinal difference], the value became 11s 29° 13' 55" 9'''. <note>The notation represents Signs, Degrees, Minutes, Seconds, and Thirds.</note>

**Calculation of the Slowest Point (Apogee).** (Chapter 1, Verse 54) Determining the <term>Mandocca</term> <note>The apogee, or the point in a planet's orbit farthest from the Earth</note> of Saturn at the end of the Golden Age (<term>Krita Yuga</term>). By multiplying the year count 1,953,720,000 by Saturn's <term>Kalpa Bhagana</term> <note>The number of revolutions in a Kalpa, a vast cosmic cycle</note> of 39, the result is 76,195,080,000. Dividing this by the <term>Kalpaman</term> <note>The total duration of a Kalpa</note> of 4,320,000,000, the result is 17 revolutions and the signs etc. are 7s 19° 35' 24". Due to the slowness of motion, the longitudinal correction is useless without the calculation of the mean motion and the Moon's apogee.

**Calculation of the Mean Node.** This is the calculation of Saturn's <term>Pata</term> <note>The ascending node, where the planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> at the beginning of the Shaka year 1817. Multiplying 1,955,884,996 years by 662 revolutions and dividing by 4,320,000,000, the mean node of Saturn is 29 revolutions and 12s 38° 16'.

**Calculation of the True Sun.** (Chapter 2, Verse 46) By subtracting the Mean Sun 11s 29° 19' 48" from the Sun's apogee 2s 17° 17' 28", the <term>Manda Kendra</term> <note>Anomaly of the orbit</note> became 2s 18° 1' 40". This is situated in an odd quadrant (Chapter 2, Verse 34). Therefore, the elapsed anomaly is the <term>Bhuja</term> <note>The sine of the arc</note>. Converting the anomaly into minutes and dividing by 225, and determining the sine according to the quotient of 20, the result is 3321. Multiplying the remainder by the sine difference 51 and dividing by 225, the result obtained is 41 minutes. Adding this to the sine 3321, the <term>Manda Bhuja Jya</term> <note>Sine of the mean anomaly</note> became 3362. The difference between the Sun's two <term>Manda</term> circumferences is 20 minutes. Multiplying this by the sine 3362 and dividing by the radius 3438, the result is 19 minutes 34 seconds. Subtracting 19' 34" from the even-end circumference 14° 0', the <term>Sphuta</term> <note>True or corrected</note> circumference became 13° 40' 26". Multiplying this by the sine and dividing by 360, the result is 2° 7' 36". This is the <term>Manda Bhuja Jya Phala</term> <note>Equation of the center</note>. Converting this to an arc, the degrees are the same: 2° 7' 36". Because the anomaly starts from Aries, by adding this to the Mean Sun, the True Sun became 0s 1° 23' 24". Multiplying the Sun's equation of 128 minutes by the Sun's true daily motion and dividing by 21,600, the result is 2 seconds. By adding this correction to the True Sun, the corrected True Sun at midnight became 0s 1° 23' 26".

**Calculation of True Saturn.** Subtracting the Mean Saturn 5s 29° 7' 8" from Saturn's <term>Shighra</term> <note>The "fast" anomaly or conjunction</note> 11s 29° 15' 42", the remaining <term>Shighra Kendra</term> is 6s 0° 8' 34". It is situated in an odd quadrant. The elapsed minutes are 8' 34", which is the <term>Bhuja</term> sine; the remaining minutes are 8' 34", which is the <term>Koti</term> <note>Cosine</note> minutes. Dividing those by 225 and determining the sine according to the quotient, then multiplying by the remaining sine difference and dividing by 225, the corrected <term>Kotijya</term> <note>Cosine</note> became 3437' 49". Dividing the <term>Bhujajya</term> <note>Sine</note> by the radius, the result was 9 seconds. True Saturn...

By applying the <term>correction</term><note>Samskara: a mathematical adjustment or refinement process</note> to the <term>circumference</term><note>Paridhi: the epicycle circumference used in planetary models</note>, the value became 39 | 0 | 9 <term>degrees, etc</term>. By multiplying the <term>sine of the anomaly</term><note>Bhujajya: the sine of the arc representing the planet's distance from its apex</note> by the corrected <term>true</term> circumference and dividing by 360, the <term>equation of the fast apex</term><note>Shighrabhujaphala: the result of the first impulsive correction, related to the planet's orbital motion relative to the Sun</note> became 56 <term>seconds</term><note>Vikala: 1/60th of a minute of arc</note>. By multiplying the <term>cosine of the anomaly</term><note>Kotijya</note> by the <term>true circumference</term> and dividing by 360, the <term>minutes</term> and <term>seconds</term> became 372 | 22. Since the <term>fast center</term><note>Shighrakendra: the anomaly of the fast apex</note> was in the signs beginning with Cancer, subtracting the result 372 | 22 from the <term>radius</term><note>Trijya: standard radius of 3438 minutes used in Indian trigonometry</note> of 3438 resulted in a <term>fast cosine result</term><note>Shighrakotiphala</note> of 3065 | 38. Converting the <term>fast cosine result</term> into <term>seconds</term> and <term>squaring</term> it gave 33833187844. <term>Squaring</term> the <term>sine seconds</term> gave 2136. Adding the <term>square of the sine</term> to the <term>square of the fast cosine result</term> and taking the <term>square root</term><note>Mula</note> resulted in 183938 <term>seconds</term> as the <term>fast hypotenuse</term><note>Shighrakarna: the distance from the earth to the planet on its epicycle</note>. Multiplying the <term>sine result</term> of 56 <term>seconds</term> by the <term>radius</term> of 3438 and dividing by the <term>fast hypotenuse</term> gave 63 <term>seconds</term>. This resulted in 1 | 3 <term>minutes</term> as the first <term>fast equation</term><note>Shighraphala</note> of Saturn (this is the first correction). Because the <term>fast center</term> was in the signs beginning with Libra, subtracting half of this from the mean Saturn resulted in 5 | 29 | 6 | 37, which is the <term>mean Saturn corrected by half the fast equation</term>. Subtracting this <term>mean corrected by half the fast equation</term> from Saturn’s <term>slow apex</term><note>Mandochcha: the apogee or point of slowest motion</note> at 7 | 26 | 37 | 24 resulted in 127 | 30 | 47 as the first <term>slow center</term><note>Mandakendra: the anomaly of the slow apex</note>. Converting this to minutes and dividing by 225, and taking the <term>sine value</term><note>Jyagrahana</note> corresponding to the quotient of 15, then multiplying the remainder of 72 by the <term>sine difference</term><note>Jyantara</note> of 119 and dividing by 225, the result was 40 | 4 <term>minutes</term>. Adding this to the <term>sine</term> 2859 gave 2899 | 4 as the first slow <term>sine of the anomaly</term>. Multiplying this <term>sine of the anomaly</term> by the 1-degree difference between the even and odd <term>slow circumferences</term> and dividing by the <term>radius</term> of 3438 gave 50 | 36 <term>minutes</term>. Subtracting this from the <term>even circumference</term> resulted in 48 | 9 | 24 as the corrected <term>true circumference</term>. Multiplying the <term>sine of the anomaly</term> by the corrected true <term>slow circumference</term> and dividing by 360 gave 387 | 49 <term>minutes</term>. Converting this to an <term>arc</term><note>Dhanu: the inverse sine or arc corresponding to the value</note> resulted in 388 | 28 as the <term>slow equation</term><note>Mandaphala</note> (this is the second <term>correction</term>). Adding half of this first <term>slow equation</term> to the mean Saturn already corrected by the <term>half-fast equation</term> (in the signs beginning with Aries) resulted in 6 | 2 | 20 | 51, the <term>mean Saturn corrected by half-fast and half-slow equations</term>.

# Example

By applying the <term>Mēṣādi Kendra</term><note>The anomaly starting from Aries</note> correction to the values 5 | 27 | 7 | 8, the second <term>Mandaspaṣṭa</term><note>Slow-corrected or mean-true</note> position of Saturn becomes 6 | 5 | 21 | 13. By subtracting this <term>Mandaspaṣṭa</term> Saturn from the <term>Śīghra</term><note>Fast anomaly or conjunction</note> position of 11 | 29 | 15 | 42, the remaining <term>Śīghrakendra</term><note>Anomaly of conjunction</note> is 5 | 23 | 54 | 29. Subtracting 3 signs from this, converting to minutes, and dividing by 225, we find the <term>Jyā</term><note>Sine</note> to be 3409 according to the quotient of 22. Using the difference in sines of 22 and the remainder of 84 | 29, the proportional result of 8 | 15 is added to the sine of 3409, resulting in 3417 | 15. Since it is an even quadrant, the elapsed sine becomes the <term>Koṭijyā</term><note>Cosine</note>. The remaining part is 3 | 6 | 5 | 25. Calculating the sine of the <term>Bhuja</term><note>Base or side</note> gives a <term>Bhujajyā</term><note>Sine of the arc</note> of 260 | 23. Dividing this by the <term>Trijyā</term><note>Radius of 3438 minutes</note> gives 6 | 21 minutes. Applying this to the <term>Śīghra</term> circumference results in a corrected circumference of 39 | 6 | 21. Multiplying the fourth <term>Śīghra-bhujajyā</term> by the corrected circumference and dividing by 360 yields 39 | 35 minutes and seconds as the fourth <term>Śīghra-bhujaphala</term><note>Equation of the conjunction</note>. Multiplying the <term>Koṭijyā</term> by the corrected circumference and dividing by 360 gives 37 | 13. Since the center begins with Cancer (<term>Karkādi</term>), subtracting this from the radius of 3438 results in 3066 | 47 as the fourth <term>Śīghra-koṭiphala</term>. By taking the square root of the sum of the squares of the <term>Śīghra-bhujaphala</term> and the <term>Śīghra-koṭiphala</term>, the <term>Śīghrakarṇa</term><note>Hypotenuse of the conjunction</note> is found to be 3068 minutes. Multiplying the <term>Śīghra-bhujaphala</term> by the radius and dividing by this <term>Śīghrakarṇa</term> gives 44 | 22; the arc of this is the <term>Śīghraphala</term> of 44 | 22 (this is the fourth correction). Adding this to the <term>Mandaspaṣṭa</term> Saturn (due to the <term>Mēṣādi</term> anomaly) results in the <term>Śanisphuṭa</term><note>True longitude of Saturn</note> of 6 | 6 | 5 | 35.

**Planetary Motion.** (Chapter 2, Verses 47-53) In the Sun's <term>Manda</term> correction, the difference in the sine of the anomaly is 51 minutes. Multiplying that by the Sun's mean daily motion (<term>Ravibhukti</term>) of 59 | 8 and dividing by 225 gives 13 minutes and 24 seconds. Multiplying this by the corrected true circumference of 13 | 40 | 36 and dividing by 360 results in 30 seconds. Subtracting this from the mean motion of 59 | 8 (due to the <term>Makarādi</term><note>Capricorn-based</note> anomaly) gives the Sun's true motion (<term>Spaṣṭa Gati</term>) as 58 | 38.

**Lunar Eclipse.** (Chapter 4, Verse 17 onwards) The Sun's diameter in <term>Yojanas</term><note>A unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note> is 6500. Multiplying the Sun's true motion by 60 minutes and dividing by the Sun's mean motion of 59 | 8 gives the Sun's true diameter (<term>Ravispaṣṭa Vyāsa</term>) as 6599 <term>Yojanas</term>. Multiplying the Moon's diameter of 480 <term>Yojanas</term> by the Moon's true motion of 860 minutes and dividing by the Moon's mean motion of 790 | 38 gives the Moon's diameter as 522 <term>Yojanas</term>; dividing this by 15 gives the Moon's true angular diameter as 35 minutes. Multiplying the Earth's diameter (<term>Mahīvyāsa</term>) of 1600 by the Moon's true motion of 860 and dividing by the Moon's mean motion gives a result of 1740 for the <term>Sūcī</term><note>The cone of the Earth's shadow</note>. Subtracting the Earth's diameter of 1600 from the Sun's true diameter of 6599, multiplying by the Moon's mean diameter of 480, and dividing by the Sun's mean diameter of 6500 gives 369. Subtracting this from the <term>Sūcī</term> results in a shadow diameter (<term>Chāyāvyāsa</term>) of 1371, and dividing by 15 gives the shadow's angular diameter as 91 minutes. Subtracting the Rahu node position of 0 | 15 | 6 from the true Moon position of 0 | 20 | 9 leaves 0 | 5 | 3.

<header>The Surya Siddhanta</header>

### The Surya Siddhanta

Multiplying its <term>sine of the arc</term> <note>original: bhujajya; the sine of the distance from the nearest cardinal point</note> 304 by the <term>maximum inclination</term> <note>original: paramavikshepa; the maximum latitude of a planet from the ecliptic</note> 270 and dividing by the <term>radius</term> <note>original: trijya</note> 3438, the result is 24, which is the true latitude of the Moon. By adding the shadow's <term>diameter in minutes</term> <note>original: vyasakala</note> 91 and the Moon's diameter in minutes 35 and halving them, we get 63. Subtracting the square of the Moon's latitude 576 from its square 3969 and taking the square root, we get 58. Multiplying this by 60 and dividing by the difference in motion between the Sun and Moon 800, the result is 4 <term>ghatis</term> <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> and 22 <term>palas</term>. This is the mean half-duration of the eclipse. Subtracting the Rahu <note>the ascending node of the Moon</note> position from the Moon's true position at this time (0s 19° 8'), we get 0s 4° 2', the sine of which is 242. Multiplying this by the maximum inclination 270 and dividing by the radius 3438, we get 19; subtracting this from the square of the sum of the radii gives 3606. Multiplying its square root 60 by 60 and dividing by the difference in motion, the true half-duration is 4 ghatis and 30 palas. By subtracting and adding this to the end of the full moon, the moments of first contact and final separation are determined.

<term>Calculation of Ascensional Difference</term> <note>original: charanayana; the difference between the celestial and terrestrial equator</note>. Determining the ascensional difference for Taurus. (Chapter 2, Verse 61) The sine of the sign, i.e., 3600 minutes, is 2978. Multiplying this by the maximum declination 1397 and dividing by the radius 3438, the <term>sine of declination</term> <note>original: krantijya</note> is 1215. Taking the <term>versed sine</term> <note>original: utkramajya</note> according to the 1215 sine of declination, we get 221. Subtracting the versed sine 221 from the radius 3438, the day-diameter is 3217. Multiplying the sine of declination 1215 by the equinoctial shadow 5, dividing the product by 12, multiplying the quotient by the radius 3438, and dividing by the day-diameter 3217, the ascensional difference is fixed at 537 <term>pranas</term> <note>a unit of time equivalent to 4 seconds</note>. By subtracting the ascensional difference of Aries from this, the segment for Taurus is found.

<term>Parallax</term> <note>original: lamban; specifically horizontal parallax</note> (Chapter 5, Verse 8). 5s 12° is the tenth house <note>meridian</note>. 3s 8° is the true Sun. The sine of declination of the tenth house is 430 and the arc is 430 minutes. Subtracting this from the latitude (22° 30'), the zenith distance is 920 minutes. Its sine is 910 and its cosine is 3312. Dividing the square of the sine of one sign 2924961 by the cosine, the divisor is 892. Dividing the sine of the difference between the tenth house and the true Sun (3090) by this divisor, the parallax is 3 ghatis and 28 palas. Dividing the sine 910 by 70, the latitude-parallax <note>original: nati</note> is 13.

# List of Queries

1. The author of the *Siddhanta Rahasya* <note>A "Secret of the Established Tradition," likely referring to a specific astronomical treatise</note> has written that at the beginning of the *Kali Yuga* <note>The current cosmic age in Hindu chronology</note>, there were 714,402,296,627 *Ahargana* <note>term: Ahargana; the number of elapsed days since the start of a specific epoch</note>. At the beginning of the Shaka year 1513 <note>1591 CE</note>, at Sunday midnight, they established the following positions: Sun 11s 17° 56' 41"; Moon 5s 11° 6' 52" 15"'; Moon's Node 11s 19° 9' 40" 26"'; Mars 7s 10° 13' 9"; Mercury's Apex 7s 11° 56' 33"; Jupiter 6s 29° 50' 48"; Venus's Apex 1s 2° 54' 0" 29"'; Saturn 2s 8° 1' 6"; and the Precession of the Equinoxes at 8s 26° 30' 41".

2. Mathuranatha the Astrologer has written that at the beginning of the *Kali Yuga*, the Moon's Apogee was 2s 17° 7' 38"; Mars 4s 9° 58'; Mercury 7s 10° 19'; Jupiter 5s 21°; Venus 2s 19° 39'; and Saturn 7s 26° 37'.

3. By multiplying the Moon's motion by 17 and dividing by 420, the lunar measure is obtained. By multiplying this measure by 10 and dividing by 3, and then subtracting 873 from 60 times the Sun's motion and dividing by 111, the resulting figure subtracted from the former gives the measure of *Rahu* <note>The North Node of the Moon</note>.

4. At 10 degrees of the *Shighra-kendra* <note>term: Shighra-kendra; the anomaly of parallax or the "fast center" used in planetary equations</note> for Venus, the resulting correction was 2 degrees and 12 minutes.

5. According to the opinion of the *Dinachandrika*, in the Shaka year 1521 <note>1599 CE</note>, the Sun's entry into a new sign <note>Sankranti</note> occurred at the Equator at the time 4 days 44 ghatis 8 palas 13 vipalas <note>Traditional units of time where 60 ghatis equal 24 hours</note> on the Prime Meridian.

6. Varahamihira <note>A famous 6th-century Indian astronomer and polymath</note>, in the *Jatakarnava*, has given 24 solar segments starting with 9, 7, 26, 34, etc. He has instructed to determine the results by taking these segments according to the ratio of the anomaly.
